"Oh that" said 12BZ2 casually, "Well, you have me gardening, and cleaning the kitchen and vacuuming and driving you everywhere, there's no time for things like cooking a healthy meal or decorating..." a pause "So I thought I'd hire additional" another pause, "assistance." Mark sighed and thought about it for a moment. A new robot would be useful after all and make sure things got done. He sighed again and turned and went back into the living room. 12BZ2 turned slowly, the grin fading, and whispered to himself "and if you think I didn't notice you buying that robo-vagina addon last week, you're very much mistaken......." 12BZ2 patted 12BZ3 on the head and went outside to clean the patio.

The tension in the air was so thick it was palpable. The scent of gunpowder and blood mixed together, causing the room to reek of death. Wolf stood by the wall of the tavern. He was cornered and he knew it as did the boy who he held with his arm around his neck. It's come to this, Wolf thought. It's been his most desperate moment since Fort Maynoor. Across the room from him were two young adults with their weapons drawn. only kids in his eyes. But despite their age, they stood before him on the opposite side of the remains of his entire gang. Some of the best outlaws and gunslingers he'd ever known all downed within minutes by these..... kids. One of which was only a girl. But it was mostly by her ability that the men he once rode, pillaged and murdered with we now lying in a pool of their own blood. And the only thing saving him from sharing their fate is the young Indian boy being held with one arm and a pistol to his head in the next. " Put him down! " The boy across the room yelled. Why a white boy would care som much about the Indian kid, he wasn't sure, but he understood. Despite the relation, it was too late now. " That's not gon na happen, boy. " said Wolf with a hopeless yet devilish grin emerging from his lips. There was silence for what seemed like an eternity until Wolf spoke up again. " It seems we have ourselves a bit of a..... predicament. " he chuckled. " I may not have much to live for, but I sure as hell ain't gon na die. " " Tough luck. " said Litonya, he revolver still aimed at Wolf. " Oh, there's only one person I'm referring to in this room and it sure as hell ain't you, bitch ." Litonya scowled in return. " No, no. It's you, Blondie. " he said, nodding to Sam. " What? " " The girl..... Bill's little love child..... she can't kill me. She knows it. She may only be half-blooded, but she knows her own customs. In fact, it's me who has the right to kill her! " " Molimo is not a part of this. It's just between you and me. " Litonya added. " Maybe not before but he is now! " Sam began to slowly position himself between Wolf and the door, not only to prevent his escape but to also find a chance take a shot on Wolf himself. The outlaw shifted himself to place his hostage between him and Sam. In that time, Litonya had an opportunity. The chance to take him out. The chink in his armor. It was the kind of vulnerability that she took advantage of in a hunt. Split the attention of the prey long enough to fire the killing arrow. It should have been simple, but this time was different. Litonya needed Wolf alive. As a fellow Miwok, she was her duty to protect her people and their customs. It was her responsibility to sacrifice herself to him and cleanse the sins of her father. But how could she? Why should she be forced to give up her life to this monster? All her life, her purpose had been clear. The needs of her people come first and above all else. She swore to defend the tribe traditions, no matter what the cost. To fail her duties is to no longer be Miwok. But the trail given to her was not clearly blazed. Now she faces her dilemma. Should she face her destiny and do what she'd been waiting so long to finish? Or should she take a new path, one away from Miwok tradition and stray from her intended purpose to save her new friends? Time to choose a side...

I remember it starting like any other commute, the air was cold and the fog hung heavily in Soho as I plunged from the station to the streets. It was a dense fog that felt dirty, heavier than the sea fog I had known as a child and the usual masses seemed more uniform because of it. I'm tired.... And I've made this trip now too many times to count. Seven days a week since I arrived here, in this city a million miles from what I used to dream of. Amongst an ocean of people, the pull of the tide slow and steady I sailed forward sleepily and further from the warmth I craved. I remember seeing my breathe that morning as I walked and thinking any promise of an early spring seemed out of the question. Suddenly I saw a light, a beacon so unmistakable amongst the crowd that I dropped my tea and stopped dead in my tracks causing a small pile up. On the other side of the road, walking in the opposite direction was a face I hadn't seen in 20 years. I was in a humid classroom, head propped between my hands, somewhere between sleep and a daze. A bead of sweet ran down my neck. Two desks in front of me and in the row to the left sat Saanvi, with long hair finer than silk down to her waste. I smelt her clean perfume, subtle and like a gentle breeze as I dreamed once more of her wrapped in my arms and slowly falling into slumber. Too long I have dreamt and desired with no action, I wanted to extend my arm and reach out, no throw my desk aside and kiss her like a man free of fear or anxiety, a free man with nothing to lose and the gods'entire world to gain! But I sat. I sat still with heavy limbs and a long sigh, starring, waiting and over the year's course of english lessons the only words we shared were lines of written dialogue from a sheet as we practiced for class. My heart sank as I realised it wasn't her, she was of similar complexion, but the girl walking across the street was not the same not Saanvi, just another face amongst the crowds and gone as suddenly as she had appeared. I was left hollow and small. Theres more than 6 million people in Greater London and there were around a thousand on that street alone but the busy, bustling world felt for that moment still. felt stranded on an island with Saanvi stretched far over the horizon. I moved on, a new sense of purpose filled me and was soon out breathe as I rushed through the streets, hungry for one thing. It's funny memory, but after years of slow erosion and dampening I'd lost all sense of myself, who I had been before the move, and who I'd left behind. Saanvi was my match and my kindling and now I saw those faces I'd shelved out of cold necessity once again clear as day. The cry of a child as a pram passed by was all it took, and again I found I was huddled in a circle as my grandmother held my sister who was born earlier that day. A slight smile in my direction, with her warm brown eyes that told a truth of simple love, reminded me that I was but a part of a larger family. And My nose! Reborn from depression and stagnation sipped at the sweet burst of tobacco as I passed a fat and hunched young man, cigarette in one hand and coffee in the other. My father, the complete opposite in size and stature was a true man who stood proud and strong. And yet I was once more in his smokey garage as he taught me fix a motorcycle from spare parts and scrap and listening to his stories of business men in Mumbai. I was caught off guard as an elderly woman's scarf in front me of was blown in a sudden gust of wind right into my hands. I wasn't ready for the lull the smooth fabric brought as I felt like a child for the third time in as many minutes. The woman asked for her scarf back but stunned I said nothing, lingering for a few seconds too long with the cashmere between my fingers. I passed it back without a word and continued, I remember holding back this particular memory at this point as my eyes began to water in the wind. I worked like a machine throughout the day and like a dam, held back the great flow of memories that scarf had brought. Without realising it, I was cleaning faster and more thoroughly than I had in weeks attracting a tip as well as my pay package that afternoon. It was only that evening, as I placed paper notes within an envelope ready for international postage, that the dam finally burst and I thought of the elderly woman, wrapped in cashmere to whom these notes would provide ten times the value in India that they could in London. As the floodgates opened I heaved and sobbed like a child as I thought of my mother, a distant light like a star above the sea.

Ever since I was a little girl, my dad always warned me to be alert at all times. " There are crazy people out there, Sarah, " he always says, and with good reason. To make him happy, I carry pepper spray with me, but I know I will never need it. You see, I can tell how dangerous someone is from a mile away. If I can see their eyes, I can tell. I just get this overwhelming feeling, this tingling in my fingertips and toes, my pulse starts racing. The more dangerous someone is, the closer they are to doing something awful, the stronger the feeling. Making eye contact with someone who is dangerous kind of feels like an adrenaline rush. I would never call myself an adrenaline junkie. Over time, I've developed a sort of scale to categorize the feeling I get. It's kind of silly, but if I don't keep track, something bad might happen. When I was really little, maybe five, my younger sister and I used to go to a friends house to play with Barbies. I remember that the first time we went over, I got this vague sense of uneasiness when I met our friends'brother. The brother was maybe six years older than us, and always seemed pretty friendly. Over the course of a week, the vague uneasiness developed to a feeling of downright dread every time I saw him. I could never figure out why. Then, one day, my sister and I weren't allowed to go to my friends house anymore. My parents wouldn't tell us why. My friend disappeared from school altogether. Being only 5, none of the kids really understood or cared- I mean, five year olds don't have a great mental capacity. But I was curious, and my mom would just tell me not to worry, we'd discuss it when I got older. A few years later, when I was in middle school health class, we learned about sexual assault and abuse, and that the most common perpetrators are people that we trust. Something clicked. I remembered Jamie and her brother, and I asked my mom about it when I got home that night. My parents explained to me that Jamie's brother had sexually abused her and then stabbed her, and it had happened two days after the last time I was there. Jamie's brother, they told me, was a psychopath. Jamie had died from blood loss. And so I keep track. I rate dangerous people on a scale from one to ten, and I write it in a notebook. If someone goes from say, a " 6 " to an " 8 ," they could be planning a robbery, or abusing a spouse. I can predict murders and leave anonymous tips on police lines. I can warn unsuspecting parents. I have a great amount of power, and I do what I can to protect others. But tonight, now, I'm not really sure what to do. Last Tuesday, I was sitting on the train, heading back from the mall with friends, when I began to feel a vague uneasiness. Just sort of stressed, like how I would feel the hour before an important exam. But looking around, I couldn't tell where it was coming from. There were too many people, and I couldn't make eye contact with everyone without looking like a crazy person. So I let it go. I went home and, feeling ill, I went to sleep. The feeling wasn't too strong, I knew there was no immediate danger, but I still felt it all night long. Wednesday at school it went away for awhile, but then during lunch, I felt it again, slightly stronger. The week went on, the feeling never left, I waited, resting at home, too sick to even eat. It grew stronger. If Tuesday night was a six, Thursday was a seven. Friday at lunch, I was eating green beans, chewing the salty green mush methodically and talking with my friends, trying to ignore the blood rushing in my ears. Suddenly, my pulse quickened, faster and faster, and I began to sweat. I wasn't even looking at anyone, but I could sense that whoever it was, they were really dangerous. Jamie's psychopathic and murderous brother was a ten, the highest I've ever met, and this was higher. I felt nauseous and faint, grabbed my milk carton to try to regain some composure, and looked at my sister. She turned to me, a look of concern on her face, and I felt it, stronger than I have ever felt before. " Are you okay? " I saw her say. I couldn't hear her over the buzzing in my ears. Then I passed out. I'm home now. My door is locked. I love Hazel. She is my baby sister; she is kind and quiet and shy. She is wonderful. She has never even registered on my radar, and now this..... this can't be happening. She gets home in two hours, and I have no idea what to do.

The faint smell of oxidizing blood lingered in the night air. Crouched low to ground as to avoid detection from the patrolling machines, I pin pointed the direction of the human body. My movement had to be timed just right to avoid the UV lamps equipped on the Sunbots hands. I ducked beneath a parked bus and crawled my way across the street. As I raced further into the town, I heard the mechanical grind of a patrol somewhere near me. "Shit," I whispered to myself. The stone wall I pressed my back against was cold and rough. Ever so slowly I leaned my head out to plan my next move. Three Sunbots were heading in the opposite direction down the street, shining their lights down every alley they passed. Once again I quietly yet nimbly crossed the wide open street. Not much longer I stumbled across the body I had been smelling. A pale human body lie in the street before me. Large claw marks and bites could be seen all over the corpse. The wolves had gotten to him. Judging by the large pool of dried blood on the street, there probably wasn't much left in the body. But I had to try anyway. My teeth sank into the cold neck and I pulled a tiny drop of blood. Still fresh, but just barely. I drank deeply all the while keeping my ears open for the sound of any approaching patrols. Getting caught while feeding wasn't my favorite way to spend my nights. As I had suspected the body didn't have much blood left in it to take, but it was enough to sustain me at least. Thinking back to how things used to be always made me miss the abundance of blood we once had. Humans had designed the damned Sunbots nearly 20 years ago. Vampires had become far too brazen, and had been feeding on humans at will pretty much. As an act of defense, the robots were created strictly to combat the vampires. It worked to an extent. Our ranks were decimated not only by the machines, but by the werewolves who attacked us while we were weak. At one point we were the ultimate hunters, and now we are no better than the humans once were. Shortly after the robots were created, their programming became flawed. They failed to see the difference between humans and vampires and as a result began killing humans. The ones they couldn't kill were either captured by the werewolves to breed and eat, or are living in seclusion hiding through out the city and such. Who would has suspected humankind would someday be an endangered species? The piercing sound of a siren startled me as I was feeding. Out of the corner of my eye I saw a Sunbot shining it's light down an alley. It had found something. I waited for the screaming of a burning vampire to fill the air, but it didn't come. Instead a large werewolf leaped from the alley way and ripped the machine apart. "Even better!" I said aloud. Wasting no time, I scurried into the nearest alley I could find. Werewolves were ungodly fast, and I wanted to get as much of a head start as I possibly could. This was of course made more difficult by the numerous patrols of the damned robots. Regardless, I had to escape. I hadn't made it even two blocks before I heard the roar of the werewolf. The beast was behind me walking upright. It was toying with me. "I have a surprise for you poochy." I reached into my backpack. Near the bottom of my backpack there were a few electronic sound emitters. I scooped one up and threw it behind me before I started to run. I could hear the werewolf panting as it began to run after me. "3..... 2...... 1." I whispered. A howl of pain filled the air as the device emitted an impossibly high sound. The poor bastard couldn't help but run in circles as the sound disoriented him. I climbed the nearest building to me and took off towards my hideout before the device shut down. Nearly and hour later I arrived at my sanctuary. Well, it was more like a hole in the ground that I had turned into a hideout from the sun and other dangers. But it served it's purpose quite well. Strangely enough, the pile of debris I usually had covering the entrance seemed to be moved already. Someone had found my home. I withdrew a silver dagger from my backpack before I cautiously descended the ladder. All was silent and from what I could see there was no one here. I closed my eyes and began to inhale, concentrating on the smells. One smell stood out from the rest. Human. My eyes darted to the right and I could hear muffled breathing coming from inside of my makeshift closet. I yanked open the door and saw a young woman clasping her mouth with both hands, staring at me wide eyed. "No, please don't kill me." She plead. I pulled her out by her wrists and stared at her. "Do you know how long it's been since I had fresh blood?" She was visibly terrified and began to speak frantically. "No please, you don't understand.... I'm pregnant." I released her wrist and glanced down at her stomach. Sure enough the humans stomach was accented with a baby bump. This changed things. Just because I must feed doesn't mean I'm a monster. The woman saw that I wasn't going to bite her and before I could think she snatched my dagger from my hand. My first reaction was to snatch it back and kill her. But I noticed she didn't seem to be threatening me with it. Instead she took it and cut herself open on her shoulder and began pouring the blood into a jar she had. She was offering me her blood. "If you can just protect me, I can provide you with as much of my blood as I safely can. Please, just get me back to my home." She handed me the jar which was about half full of fresh blood. I gladly accepted it and began to drink deeply. Fresh warm blood, what a treat. The woman began to wrap her shoulder in a gauze. "A vampire helping a human," I said to her. "How unheard of." "Look, I wouldn't ask if I wasn't desperate. It's a miracle I managed to escape the wolves. Are you going to help me or what?" Her arm was fully bandaged now. I thought about for a moment. This woman was clearly desperate and she would certainly die if I didn't help her. Not to mention the fresh blood would be great to have even if just for a short time. "I suppose I have no choice, I can't just let you die out there." "Great, can we leave now?" She asked. I laughed, "It is nearly morning out there, and me and the sun don't quite get along." She looked embarrassed. "Oh, that's right. We can leave tomorrow night then as soon as the sun goes down." "Sounds good to me." I said. That was all that was said for now. As I took off my backpack and began to lie down to sleep, I couldn't help but think how strange of a predicament I had gotten myself in to.

One eye open. Two eyes. How long have I been asleep? I remember the hospital room. The bright white lights that made time into perpetual day. The doctors muttering and the nurses with fresh bedpans. That was a lifetime ago. Or was it minutes? Sleep can do that to a person, though. "Jerry?" The sound of someone's voice. Only an echo, maybe a thought. "Jerry?" No, definitely a voice. It's to my left..... I think it's my left. "Yes, hello?" The words don't come out. I try again, but my throat feels weak. Incredibly weak. I move my hand to massage the muscles. But I don't. The arm hasn't lifted. My hand hasn't budged. My mouth flops like a dying fish. My tongue rolls across my lips. Was I anesthetized? "Jerry, blink if you hear me." The voice again. It sounds urgent. I squeeze my eyelids together with tremendous force and fight to reopen them. I'm in a panic. What is going on? What is wrong? With an exhausting effort I finish my blink. I hear uproarious applause. The voice again. It's behind me now. "He's returned!" The cheering is louder. In a rush, I suddenly remember. The beeping of the heart monitor. The shouting that faded to gray with the faces that surrounded my operating table. It was a heart attack, I think. Or a stroke? I turn my head to the side, but the only thing that really moves are my eyes. More applause. I must have been dead for minutes. Maybe an hour- Did the doctors beat some kind of record? "The first successful resurrection of a cadaver by the medical community." Papers are shuffling by my right ear. I can't see who is holding them. "And he was a corpse for 67 days! Incredible." My stomach drops. 67 days? Two months? I was dead for two months? "67 days, 11 hours." Another voice concurs. "Incredible." My throat releases a weak groan and the applause rebounds. I can feel the tears welling in my eyes as I understand. But how do I tell them? How do I explain to the world? I am only back from darkness.

She was back again. I could feel her before seeing her, which is what I'd come to expect. Sometimes she brought a chill, or a silence that seemed too loud, but each time it was the air that gave it away. It felt heavier; older, like it knew something I didn't. She had long since run out of family members and close friends to visit in order to get close to me. They were all gone now. She spent them all like a bad gambler at the casino. Now she grasped at straws. When I felt the chill, I glanced around the room, failing to see who she had taken to justify a visit. It took me a few a minutes to find the spider lying still in the corner. "A spider is enough?" I muttered weakly. "Not all spiders," came the playful reply. I turned and saw her there, on the other side of the room. She was beautiful in a way that no human could ever be. It was an awful, and yet magnetic kind of beauty. She wore a flowing black dress, and her eyes looked like midnight. "But this one is special. He was the king of spiders once, and so I thought he deserved a visit. It was a happy accident that it was in your company that he finally relinquished his grasp." She giggled. Her laugh sounded like time. "One day you'll have no choice but to take me. There won't be any excuses left." I said quietly. She smiled in a way that might have fooled some men into mistaking her for a human. "I'm quite adept at getting my way." Her smile turned serious for a moment. "I won't take you, Anthony. I'll take the world before I take you where I can't follow." I remained silent for several moments before replying. "Don't you have some kind time limit here?" She frowned at me with anger that slowly faded into sorrow. "You'll love me one day, you know. You'll stop seeing me as all of what you've been told before, and you'll love me so much." I thought of my mother and father, and of Jake and John and Matt, and Rachel. Oh god, I thought of Rachel. A tear rolled down my cheek. For one moment, she stared at my tear, and just as a faint hint of empathy began to cross her face, she was gone, back into nothing and everything.

You are an idiot. And you can't stop being an idiot. One would think there'd be a limit to how much stupid can be present in a person at any given time, but you have proved me wrong. And you prove me wrong everyday. You are a fool. You bandy out your limitless idiocy in soaring heaps to everyone you see, gifting it to innocent strangers like blankets infested with smallpox. The countless little games and schemes you play end up driving me, your one and only friend, to insanity. And the worst part, the very worst part of this all, is that you don't know this. You aren't being malicious. You aren't being cruel. You aren't clever enough to really hurt people on purpose. You genuinely believe your idiocy helps me and others. You think I appreciate your tendency to drag me into your misadventures, the way you make me stumble through life as your damned wet nurse, and your awful, Godawful, puns. I'm trying to get angry at you. I truly am. But I can't. You're pitiful. You're some brain delayed pet that's pissed on the floor, and every time I get mad at you, you give me that look, that sad expression of shame in your eyes that answers why I'm still your friend. Idiot.

The man slid the paintbrush slowly down the canvas. His left hand held the palette. "You know who I idolised the most?" he asks me. It's a surreal experience, hearing his voice. His true voice, his speaking voice. My exposure to this man has been solely recordings of speeches, where he ranted and raved and worked the crowd. Impressive, but offering no insight into his true nature. He was tired. His strokes were slow and focused, but a product of practice and experience. His face was gaunt, his shoulders slightly slumped, as if painting, the thing he loved, was all that kept him standing, kept him afloat. "No," I replied. I had come to hear his story. The CIA's declassified documents told us the truth of Hitler, but they didn't tell us why. Why he did what he did. The CIA had told him only to stop the nuclear war. Nothing more. So why the holocaust? Others dismissed his niceness as a facade. But I'd seen his reports to the future. I'd seen his paintings and writings from before he had went back in time. Either the past, and the atrocities he'd committed had warped him into a monster, or he had found a reason so compelling that the Holocaust was necessary. Whatever the case, I would hear him out. He deserved that, at least. We all do. "Bob Ross. I was raised on those videos," he smiled wistfully, putting down his painting materials, and sitting down on the couch opposite me. "I often wished they had let me bring at least one holo-vid back here. Just one, to pass the time, in this place," he looks around the room, with its stone and concrete walls. I had come to visit him in the FuhrerBunker. Just before the end. He would kill himself tomorrow. There were few, if any, time travelers around. The rest of this man's life is a constant battle in the shadows, of time travelers dueling to change, or retain history. "So, I assume you wish to know why?" the man asked. "Astute," I nodded. "I know about the rest. Without Germany as a major player in the war, Italy and Japan's decimation by the atom bombs of the US spurs the USSR into the'Blue Scare' that would destroy the world. But..... why the holocaust?" I ask. "I asked myself many times if what I did was right. Every second. Every day. I never had a good night's sleep. But I must believe it was. I don't think I could believe anything else. Tell me..... if the documents are declassified..... am I a hero there? I never expected credit for my work, but..." I shake my head. "That depends on what you tell me. I work for a very large news organistation. We'll get your story out. What happens next is up to them," I click my pen. "More than I could ever hope for. Thank you," he shakes my hand. It's a firm handshake, from a pale hand. No doubt he'd used it many times in his political career. "Write about the rest of my work, somewhere in there, would you? Write about how I railed against smoking, and animal abuse. About the jobs I created, and the economic travesty Germany was in," he bites his lip. I'm a journalist, I know what's going on. Those telltale signs spoke volumes about his situation. "Listen, Adolf. I know you're worried. Worried about whether they'll accept it, whether you did the right thing. I..... can't say. But you need to tell us what it is, so it may at least get out there. So the truth can be known." I put a hand over his, grasping it firmly. Hitler exhales, shakily, and nods. "Do you know what Israel is?" he asks. I nod, slowly, encouragingly. "It's a country in the middle east, no? A state created especially for the Jews," he continues. "Jewish persecution was nothing new. The pogroms in Russia..... you've seen the pictures. And the people did not blindly follow me. They hated them too. Before they sent me here, to Germany, I studied history intensively. Every facet of it, every little detail. In my world, the original world, the world you've never seen..... civil rights never exist. The blacks, the chinese, the japanese and the jews, they never leave the thumb of the Western world. The US continues to keep slaves. The Japanese, incensed by the lack of equal treatment, fight furiously against the Western world. China joins them, and the Russians and the West fight to the death," he declares. The fire is back in his eyes, the look that had enraptured a country. "Wars are fought on ideals, friend. The Russians had a point: the US would not look at their own shortcomings until a while after the cold war ended, until King and Mandela. In my world, they looked at civil rights, and decided against it. The lack of equality of man is what destroyed humanity!" Hitler is angry. The kindest man the world has seen, filled with righteous fury at what the world did. What it forced him to do. I keep writing. "The holocaust created Israel, a dam against political problems in the middle east. It forced the Americans to consider what they were, what they were doing, and what they wanted to be, and become the bastion of equality and peace, for a time. The United States was isolationist, back then. They refused to join the League of Nations, their own brainchild! It was a disgrace." "Tell them that, friend. Tell them Adolf Hitler committed atrocities so mankind knew to never consider them again. To be wary of the darkness in their own hearts," his voice drops to a whisper. I nod. What more is there for me to say. "Those who fight against darkness must spend the most time in the shadow. And they who fight monsters must take care not to become monsters themselves," he looks up at me, determination burning there. "That time has passed for me. My soul is stained now. Go. My work is done, and I must take a long, deep, reflection as to my life. Take the painting," he stands up to leave. "Eva!" he calls out, looking for his wife. I step over to the painting, which he had staunchly refused to show me. It's a self-portrait of the man, of Hitler himself, looking at the viewer. In his eyes are burning bodies and wire fences, images of regret and despair. It is magnificent. Scrawled at the bottom, is simply: "Forgive me." The sky is particularly blue today, like the colour of the ocean down at the tropics. Blue, with a bit of green. The sun hangs high and proud, beaming brightly with brilliant orange-yellow light. There isn't a cloud to be seen, except for the little one over there- I cock my head to the side, examining it. It's shaped vaguely like a dog...... Maybe a whale? I was never good at cloud-shapes more complicated than "triangle" or "popcorn." Yeah, I think with a contented sigh and slip my hand under my tank top to rub my stomach. I could eat some popcorn. But I'm much too lazy to get up right now, the sky is much too blue, and this grass is much too comfortable. So, instead of satiating my craving for buttery snack foods, I stretch my legs out and fold my left arm under my head, and continue my gaze upon the vast blue above. ..... And a person zooms by. Just..... right across the sky. "What the fuck?" I say, perhaps a little louder than I would have if I'd been policing my words. But, just. What the fuck?

It's on the news. On the radio. Everywhere. But I refuse to believe it. After all it has to be some spiritual bullshit. Right? I mean, I can not be the only guy in the world who is lacking a soul. An empty shell of a human being. A husk. A facade. A masquerade. So I turned my pockets out. Nothing. Checked under the couch, between the cushions. I found a few dollar coins that nobody uses and a couple of old business cards. I checked in the pantry. And under my bed. I searched in the closet. Things were starting to get hopeless. So I walked down to the corner bodega, bought a couple of bags of Lays chips. The extremely boring kind. I slammed them down on the counter. It crunched beneath my finger tips. After a few hours of searching and calling everyone I could think of I was starting to get really depressed. So I went to The Kiev. And ate breakfast. And as I was walking down 2nd Avenue, towards St. Mark's Place where all those people sell used books and other junk on the streets. I saw my soul lying there on a blanket, some guy was selling it. I had to buy it off him. He wanted twenty two bucks but I talked him down to seventeen. I took it home. Washed it off. And put it back on. I was happy again. Complete. People sometimes tell me I should get my soul permanently attached but I don't know. Even though sometimes it's a pain in the ass. I like having a detachable soul.

People could never learn to understand each other; here we are, stuck on this god forsaken rock, committing the same sins that trapped us here. As the boiling sun hangs above, a blur slowly moves away from the horizon. Either I'm going crazy, or God just might exist. THIS IS A ROUTINE CHECK FOR STOLEN ITEMS. PLEASE REMOVE ANY WEAPONS AND LAY FLAT ON THE GROUND." The commanding voice only helped me to shamble along faster. I take out my rusty rifle and fire off warning shots. At this point I can almost feel the tires on my heels, the heat of the engine on my back. The engine stops, and I can feel a blow to the back of my head. "YOU HAVE BROKEN LAW. I AM REQUIRED TO DETAIN YOU." Another one of these dumbshit enforchines. I almost wish my throat was being slit right now. As I'm slipping the pin off my grenade, I realize it's accompanied by someone else. "Sir I understand this is very inconvenient, but please bear with us. TMA-1 authority code bravo delta." Whoever it is, they obviously are well dressed for the occasion. Standing above me is 6 feet of fully shielded blast armor, and it's handing me a ticket. After my legs decide to cooperate with me and I orient myself, I find the cop standing there dumbfounded. "What, have you never seen a drifter before?" To be fair, I hardly looked like one. I looked closer to a maniac, and the dusty suit and tie didn't help much. Brushing off the forsaken dirt, the walking armor speaks to me "More surprised you didn't try to shoot at me." "Yea well I wouldn't wan na get my jacket dirty. It's hard enough to keep the color in this thing." "Well, good luck with that. Have a nice day sir." As the tin men walk back to their buggy and blaze off back into that dry horizon, I can feel a rumbling in my stomach. Walking on, I look back at the piece of paper in my hand. I quickly stuff it into my mouth, and divert the horrible taste by focusing on my headache. Shit. How am I supposed to survive out here on tickets? And where the fuck are they getting the paper for these?

China- gone, just like that. They said you can see the great wall from space, but suddenly I wasn't so sure. I had never really known much about China to be honest. I'd heard there were exciting festivals packed with people there, embracing a culture that had seemingly lasted forever. A culture that had just ground to a halt. Man, I wish I had a drink at that moment. There wasn't much left of the human race anymore- they had been thorough in their desires to rid the world of each other..... a strange thought when we had been so peaceful until recently. I had thought it would take a while for all the nukes to be sent out but I was barely sent reeling from a country's destruction before another the next followed its course. The first one with personal significance to me was New Zealand. I had taken a trip there and met the most caring woman in the world, the one that I took to be my wife. I thought about the time we had spent there staring at the night sky laughing at each-others jokes, no matter how silly. I slammed my fist on the nearest wall knowing that just like New Zealand my wife and friends would similarly be living only in my mind before long. With a sigh I then thought about humanity's first contact. We had recently managed to communicate with extraterrestrial life, and soon forged a bond with a number of races. We were aglow to show them all what a peace loving race we had become. Before long we were alerted that the Al'Dreth had started a galactic conquest. They brought a group of ships to home planet of the most powerful race known in nearby space, the Ghula, seemingly in peace. Before the Ghula realized the true intention of the visit, their planet had been dusted over with with a thin substance. The Ghula, previously known as a race dedicated to science then became the Al'Dreth's greatest ally as the mind control substance took over. With a gleeful shriek even a kindhearted grandfather would, and did, do unspeakable things to further the Ghula Dominion. When the Al'Dreth came for Earth a few weeks later we had no means to stop their ships from doing their work- we barely even had a foothold in space after all and so we lacked the defenses to stop them. Before the devastation spread too far mankind launched the plan they had developed in those few weeks, and engaged in its most noble moment. Without means to reverse the affliction all we could do was prevent ourselves from aiding the Al'Dreth in destroying the friends we had made in the other races. We united like never before to destroy ourselves before we could destroy others. Just now I got the final call my wife would ever have with me, and talked as much as I could until the connection suddenly cut out. I fell back in my chair and smiled a bittersweet smile through my tears. She had been working her hardest in these last few weeks, doing whatever she could to help others find comfort in what would be their final moments. I could only hope I was at least a slight comfort for when she met her own demise. The Al'Dreth, having seen their failure to secure another race in their "alliance," went on their way, not bothering to deal with the International Space Station since in their arrogance they only cared about turning others to their side. All the information that we collected on the mind control substance in the time that it coated our planet was sent to the International Space Station, and I relish the time in which I will be sending it to the races humankind had made its friends. Though we can not help them fight directly, mankind's final moments were devoted to saving countless lives. I have never before been so proud to be a human as I am at this moment.

My eyes stung. A trickle of blood had found its path down my cheek, gathering at one eye then falling to the pavement in a steady drip. I... was alive, at the very most. But I wasn't sure how long that would last. The shrapnel had pinned me to the ground through my shoulder, and the reminders of what used to be a car rested on top. The pain sharpened my senses, made every sensation unbearable. I needed to escape, but moving would only make it worse. I peered outside, view half-obscured by panes of shattered glass. " Anyone out there? " I called, voice rasping with the exertion. From my position upside down, I could see the remnants of a black car, in a state much worse than mine. It had gone up in flames. " Hello? " I yelled. " Help me! Please, anyone! " The small pool of blood had collected under my head, and I could see my face reflected in it. Contorted with terror. " Is anyone there? Please, God, I'm afraid to die! " Agonizing minutes passed, and my voice was gone. I was going to die, in the middle of fucking nowhere. I was alone. Something in me snapped. A burble of laughter sprung up in me, hysteric and crazed. I wanted to cry, to scream, to do anything. It dissolved into a coughing fit. My bloodied fingers curled around the piece of shrapnel, and without thinking, I yanked it out with an agonizing scream. I grit my teeth, pushing upwards with my hands and feet to pull the pieces of the car off me. Broken glass bit into my palms. I pushed it to one side, and the warped frame of the car skidded several metres away. I was... alive. I lay on the cool pavement, closed my eyes, and slept deeply. The wail of police sirens woke me with a jolt. The day had drawn dark, and the strobing lights of the police cars hurt my eyes. I sat up. A burly man in a police uniform stepped out of the car and approached me, pointing to the car wreck. He spoke, but I couldn't care less. I wasn't listening. My body was white-hot. Every move I made was effortless and measured. I ran straight at the man, knocking him onto the ground. His eyes widened with surprise. My hands were already at his neck. His face bulged. His struggles didn't hurt me, and my grip stayed firm. His pulse fluttered under my fingers like a dying bird. My back stung. I turned, and saw his partner- a tall brunette, gun levelled at my head. The bullet laid on the ground, smoking. With a free hand, I touched my back. It was unblemished. The man had stopped struggling. The officer screamed, firing a few shots into my chest. I staggered back with the impact, and felt my ribs. Nothing broken- only the bullets lying in the dust. I turned to her. nbsp; nbsp; It was over quickly. nbsp; nbsp; I left the mangled bodies and cars at the road, and started walking. My footprints left red imprints on the road. I..... was alive. nbsp; Unedited, just trying to get into the habit of writing. [ ] (s "Powers make you homicidal. Permanently.

Mobile formatting, please forgive. "Laura, bring me another beer," Chris called from the couch. He shifted in his seat and his flab dripped even closer to the floor. His stubby thumb tapped the buttons on the TV remote, trying to find a midday program that wasn't terrible. Nothing fit the bill, and he sighed. Time to start browsing Reddit on his laptop - except it was across the room. He stretched a little, thinking about making an effort to get up, but he gave up that idea quickly. His fat was so enmeshed in the armchair that clambering out of it would require an effort akin to conquering Mount Everest. He bellowed this time. "LAURA! WHERE ARE YOU?" This time, a blonde head peeked around the doorframe. "Yes?" Chris ogled her. He still couldn't believe she was so lifelike. He'd needed a helper, someone to take care of him, and robots were the new "in thing." She - it? - went to work every day, brought him food, and cleaned up the house around him. His friends had recommended getting a robot, and promised that his life would change completely. He'd actually have time to do things for himself again. It was true, and he loved it. His work had taken up most of his days before that, and then there was the bother of working out, cooking, and cleaning. When Laura had arrived, he'd sent her to work, and he'd been able to spend so much more time with his friends. He loved the freedom of being able to do what he liked whenever he liked. Over time, his life had settled into a routine. He often couldn't be bothered doing anything, and he found himself watching TV or playing video games all day. He didn't ever feel like exercising any more, but since it was only Laura around to see him, who cared? He socialized enough with his friends online, and didn't feel the need to deal with the outside world. His couch became his bed, and he sat there through daylight and witching hours, through changing seasons, through speeding years. Chris still considered Laura the best investment he could have made. She was absolutely stunning, and he had no idea how the engineers managed to make her so lifelike. He vaguely remembered her arrival, and how she'd said something about her name being Christine. He didn't like that name, though, and insisted on renaming her Laura. At first she'd protested, but the instructions said to persist and she'd reprogram herself. She did, eventually. He suddenly remembered she was still waiting for his request. "Laura, bring me another beer and pass me my laptop, too." She didn't move. Was there a glitch in her programming? He'd been meaning to upgrade her for a while. "Laura...?" She stared at him. "Can't you do it?" Her voice was almost bitter. That was a seriously bad glitch. He made a mental note to send her to the engineer's upgrade office tomorrow to install the newest operating system. He didn't want a disobedient robot. "Bring. Me. A. Beer." he repeated. She disappeared and returned several minutes later with the requested beverage. "Chris, when you took me on, you promised me you'd look after me in return for me helping you. I feel you're not keeping up your end of the bargain." He marvelled at how human her conversation was. "Laura, I have looked after you. You're clothed, you gave a roof over your head, and you have a great master. There are other robots out there much worse off." She drew in a sharp breath and turned around. When she didn't move, he asked for his laptop once again. "Brad," called Laura. A man wandered in from the kitchen, where, judging by his apron, he had been cooking. "Who are you?" asked Chris, more curious than concerned. "Chris, this is Brad," said Laura, with tears in her eyes. "When we met, you promised to take care of me, and to help me out. I didn't mind being the sole wage-earner, and I didn't mind being the only one to clean and cook, but I do mind that you haven't kept your promise to put in some effort to take care of me. You're not looking after me in any way. I hired Brad to help me keep on top of the housework, because I couldn't do that and work full time. He's been really good to have around." "But why would a robot need extra help?" Chris was thoroughly confused. "And there you go with that robot stuff again! Chris, there's something wrong with you mentally. I'm not a robot. I'm your wife. And I'm sorry, but I'm leaving you for Brad."

Have you ever wondered what it'd be like to truly enjoy the night sky? It's a nice breezy night in an open field on top a hill, up in the sky, all the stars shining down on you. Soaring with all your cares away..... I've wondered that every night of my life since I was a boy. Every night before I'd go to bed my mom would walk me to the top of the hill behind my house and then lay there with me as she told me stories of witches that soared the skies above and traveled all across the world. I used to take it as a fantasy. Until one night. I was about 12, a few years after my mother had passed, I saw a silhouette of a woman in the sky high above me. She was propelled by something beneath her that closely resembled your traditional broomstick. The silhouette whizzed beneath the stars so elegantly, it was like watching art being created and erased simultaneously as she flew through the night sky. She had the prettiest hair I'd ever seen on a woman. I could actually make out the color of it. It was a pure golden blonde hue, magnificently streaking across her midnight blue canvas. Her curls flowed behind her as she traced across my vision into the empty space of the night, far above me and out of reach... I cried that night. Her hair was just like my mothers. I've been there every night since then extending my arm out to the universe. Palm open. Waiting for the girl. Wondering; if she'd come and take my hand and take me away with her.

It's not first person but oh well. The blessing took the longest. If Gareth was allowed to operate on his own schedule, the executions would be done in less than an hour. Rope, drop, done. But no. No, the priests just had to be included. Just had to gyrate their way across the platform, chanting Our Fathers and Hail Mary's and making the sign of the cross with pale, flimsy hands until the crowd started shifting and murmuring, " get it over with, already. " Then the priests would step to the side and fold their hands and tip their heads to heaven, silently granting Gareth permission, as if he needed their say-so to do his job. One time he'd pulled the lever early, before the priests even got a chance to get started, and they'd threatened to excommunicate him if he did it again. (The man being executed was a Protestant, and he said he'd consider it a personal favor if Gareth would save him the embarrassment of being absolved of his sins by a Roman Catholic. Gareth was not one to deny last requests.) The trick to a speeding everything along, he'd explained once and only once, because people didn't like to hear about executions unless they were well drunk was the length of the rope. The further someone fell, the better chance you had that their neck would snap and that would be that. No twitching and suffocating and getting blue in the face. Thieves got the long drop, because no one cared enough to tell Gareth to " make it last. " The big men, though..... the officials and the bankers..... they got the short rope, because most people enjoyed waiting around for a fat banker to die. " It's funny, " they said. " Don't you think, Gareth? Isn't it funny to watch the big strong men wet themselves when the rope goes over their heads? " The priest on the platform stopped crossing himself and Gareth tightened his grip on the lever. An angry hum started in the crowd. It had been a long day, and they'd learned to conserve the shouting for the drop. Seven people had been executed so far, and each time the explosion of noise that accompanied the trap door's opening made the hairs on the back of Gareth's neck stand on end. I was a poisonous energy, different from any other execution Gareth had presided over. The priest nodded and Gareth pulled the lever. The trapdoor opened and hundreds of eyes followed the administrator's descent. They cheered and clapped and Gareth watched the thick rope bouncing as the man died. " What will you do after this, Gareth? " Gareth started. He glanced over his shoulder. There was a man standing near the stairs, watching Gareth casually. His hands were behind his back, the picture of patience as he waited for Gareth's answer. Gareth looked back at the rope. Still twitching. " Dunno. " " You don't know, or you'd rather not tell me? " " Haven't thought about it. " " You do realize you'll be out of a job after today? " " I figured. " " And no plans for the future. " The man smiled and shook his head. " That's not how successful people do things, Gareth. " Gareth shrugged. Thomas, the young boy who was something of an executioner's apprentice, popped up through the trapdoor, the noose slung over his shoulder. He tossed the rope to the platform and Gareth began winding the rope. Thomas pulled the trapdoor shut. A guard shouldered his way through the group near the stairs, dragging a wailing woman behind him. " Oh. " The man took a step back. " Pardon me, Lady Isabelle. " He turned back to Gareth as Gareth locked the lever in place again. " You could always be a farmer. " " Don't know how. " " I've heard it's really quite easy. " Gareth grunted. He pointed toward Lady Isabelle, who was looking faint next to the hanging noose. " I got ta..... " " By all means. " Gareth's appearance on the platform hushed the jeering crowd. Lady Isabelle's eyes were closed and her cheeks were drenched with tears as Gareth slipped the noose over her head. " Will you miss it? " the man asked when Gareth returned. Gareth shrugged. " Be a morbid thing to miss. " " Maybe, " the man conceded. " If you give them time, I'm sure they'll find someone for you to kill. " " Execute, " Gareth corrected. There was a difference. " And they said no. They said after this, executions are done. We're a democracy now, and we don't execute. " " Execute arbitrarily, " the man corrected. " There is a difference. " Gareth didn't answer. The priest nodded. Gareth pulled the lever and Lady Isabelle dropped. " I'd buy into this whole democracy idea if they hadn't decided the whole Cormac line had to go for it to work. " " You did have your chance, " Gareth said, and the man laughed. " So you do know who I am, " he said. Gareth tipped his head to the side. " Majesty. " " Just Edward now, I'm afraid. " Edward grinned maniacally. " It's a democracy now, Gareth, remember? " Thomas had crawled from the trapdoor again. Gareth began winding the rope. " You know, this is the first time I've been to one of these to watch you work, " Edward said. " You are efficient, Gareth. " Another soldier pushed past, leading a short fat man with a red face and bushy orange eyebrows. " Try to draw it out, Arthur, eh? " Edward called after him. He flashed his teeth at Gareth. " That fat windbag. I thought for sure he'd weasel his way out of this. " Gareth excused himself to squeeze the noose over Arthur's thick neck. " Savages, " Arthur spat. His small eyes were rolling in their sockets. " You're all savages. " " Told you, " Edward said sagely. " That bastard always has something to say. " Gareth didn't answer. " King's Executioner, " Edward said after a moment. " Is that irony, Gareth? For your title to be your job description? " " Dunno. What's irony? " " Not important. " Edward nodded. " I think they're ready for you. " Gareth pulled the lever, and Edward bellowed with the rest of the crowd when Arthur dropped. " By God, if I would have known how good that felt, I would have had him executed years ago. Who's next? " " Your wife, " Gareth said, and Edward's smile evaporated. " I thought she went yesterday, " he said. There was an edge of anger to his voice, and for a moment Gareth could see the proud king he'd been before the revolution. " They changed their minds. " Edward's eyes went hard. He turned to stare out at the gathered crowd. He did not say anything else, and when Gareth began winding the noose again Edward ducked his head and closed his eyes. Gareth saw his jaw tighten when the queen was dragged past, but he did not open his eyes; not when the priest started his chanting and not when the trapdoor slammed open. " I'd like " Edward's voice cracked. He cleared his throat. " I'd like to thank you, Gareth. For doing my dirty work. And..... " Edward jerked his chin at the crowd. " For doing theirs. " Gareth paused. " Well..... you never sent me any kids. So thanks for that, I guess. " Edward nodded jerkily. " You're next, " Gareth said, and Edward set his shoulders. Gareth followed him across the platform and the crowd fell deathly silent. This was what they'd been waiting for. The main event, Gareth thought. King Edward Cormac, the man who'd fought the Danes lived high on the spoils of war and wore silk to bed. King Edward Cormac, dying like a common man. " It's been enlightening, Gareth, " Edward said. Gareth placed the noose around his neck. Gareth paused. In his fifteen years as executioner, he'd never felt compelled to talk with the sentenced. But this was different. The end of an era. The last person he'd ever pull the lever for, and it was the person who'd sent so many people his way. " As kings go, you weren't all that bad. " Edward laughed. Gareth moved out of the way of the priest, back to his position on the edge of the platform. He waited patiently, watching Edward glare back at the people shouting and throwing rotten vegetables on the platform. Gareth felt a flash of annoyance until he remembered he wouldn't have to clean it up. After he pulled the lever, he wouldn't be the King's Executioner anymore. Wouldn't have to clean up anybody's messes. Not the King's Executioner anymore, Gareth thought, but always the King's executioner. He felt like maybe he was on the verge of understanding irony, but then the priest nodded and Gareth's arm pulled the lever for the last time and the crowd erupted. The trick, he remembered telling someone in a bar once, is to make sure you realize they're not cheering for you. Someone clapped a hand on Gareth's shoulder. Gareth turned. One of the men who'd sentenced the king's court and presided over the executions was watching him solemnly, his face painted white, his collar starched. " Executioner. " The man held out his hand. Gareth took it. " Thank you for your service. Gareth shrugged. " My pleasure. "

The great fires rained down upon the city near me, and in between my screaming like a frightened child (Which I was, mostly) and running for cover, I formulated a plan. Before I lost my sanity, I would take a boat out to the giant tentacly mass about a mile offshore. Funny. I bought a beachside condo so it would keep it's value, but here I am in the middle of the actual apocalypse. Best not to focus on property values right now, I guess. More important things were at hand. In the midst of screeching and smaller, less tentacly things roaming about the streets, I took a moment to remember all the weird garbage my dad had insisted would happen should I mess with the "other side of the great veil," which I had always assumed as him telling me not to get drunk and mess with Ouija boards, which I had followed. But lo and behold, someone had. And the things on the other side of the veil were angry, and also probably very slimy. By the time I had already sorted out all the shenanigans running about my mind, I had almost reached my home. I ran in, made sure the cat had food and that my nephew had taken out the kitty litter after he left. (He and my brother visited from time to time. They usually stayed in the guest bedroom and mine, while I slept on the couch. It's a very comfortable couch.) Upon seeing that all was in order, and that my precious fluffer buddy was safe, I grabbed the boat keys and ran down the dock I shared with my neighbor. Boats, however, are not usable when the majority is missing. I make a mental note that if I survived this, I should see if meteor insurance was a thing, because if this ever happened again, God knows I would need it. Possibly Gods, considering what's going on. In a strange stroke of luck, though, I remembered the dinghy I had borrowed once from my neighbor, years ago, and never returned. I was going to, I swear. Didn't matter now, though. He was dead, probably. After having dragged the craft to the shore, I promptly began scurrying away. I didn't fall, surprisingly, considering how turbulent the surf was. After reaching a safe distance from the great eternal terror (Fifteen yards), I cupped my hands and let out the most loud and strained scream I had ever made. "HEY, YOU BIG OLD CALAMARI ASSHOLE. WHAT GIVES?" The mass of angry water appendages turned to face me and, in a booming voice, screeched something about the great cleansing of the Hkardkahi. "WHAT DOES THAT EVEN MEAN?" In a slightly less booming and much more understandable voice, it replied that they were the sacred ones who were to sate the blood-appetite of the infinite ones so that humanity did not have to, and that my forebears had signed a great pact with the endless ones so that we did not have to suffer much. It also asked me to stop yelling. I realize now that everything my father had told me was stupid and that something dumb was probably about to happen. Just as I put two and two together, I heard the great voice once again, asking me if I was familiar with what was called, in my tongue, mosquitoes. I just about shat my drawers. "THAT'S WHAT THIS IS ABOUT?" Yes, of course, it replied, and then asked me what I thought it was about. "IF WE BRING YOU THE GATES WILL YOU STOP THIS?" No, probably not, it said. "PLEASE?" Silence, fool mortal, it replied. "WOW. JERK." And I dingy'd away, now furious about the stupid octopus jerk that was ending the world over mosquitos. At least my cat was ok.

For a 9 year old American girl, especially, her German was impeccable. As was her Latin, Russian, French, Japanese, etc. It was always her body, her voice, but the words, however, the words were never hers. All that changed was the crude, cut-from-paper masks that they tried on her. The guards stationed outside her room were not there to stop her from escaping, but to stop anyone from even approaching her, under threat of death. Chen studied the documents thoroughly, and a strange chill ran down his spine as he reviewed the testimonials. Unlimited answers. The moment the mask touched her face, she could embody any person, known, unknown, alive or dead, in complete manner and tone. The implications were astronomical. He peered into the window through her dorm door, watching as she lazily colored in her books, legs kicking back and forth in the air. Down the hallway he came, loud, hard-shoed steps echoed to Chen's ears. Maybe he was an'agent', or an'interrogator', but in another time they might have just called him'inquisitor'. With a flash of a badge and a signed document, he marched past the guard detail and came to the door with a briefcase clutched tightly in his hand. Chen didn't have to guess what was in the briefcase. Faces. Many, many faces. Bad people. Powerful people. Chen could see her life already, laid out in 8 hour blocks of constant discussion with people she knew nothing about. He was very scared for her. The man didn't even acknowledge Chen as he too came to the window to watch her. A moment of silence, before what would be a long storm. "Believe me. I never imagined one day that I'd be doing this." He said. Chen leaned his back to the door and fished out a pack of M Ms from his pocket. "Just take your suitcase of monsters and be done with it." The agent opened the door, but Chen's hand slapped it shut. "Whatever you do, whatever you ask her, whatever it is you're here to learn, just remember..... one day she'll probably be wearing your face." Chen released the door, and the agent stepped inside. Chen pushed it closed, hearing her chime warmly. "Oh, hi! Are we going to play pretend again?"
