The party pounded on in the distance, blazing like a far away flare. I walked farther across the backyard, enveloped in thoughts of the future. It was a lovely backyard, big and spacious. It even had a pool, which was, for the most part, unoccupied, except for the lone couple that was drunkenly making out under the diving board. I dragged my feet across the dew covered grass, soaking up the silence. I decided to sit under the nice cover of an oak tree that sat near the outskirts of the yard; it's branches crossing over the other side of the wooden fence. The trunk was sturdy and I lay against it, thinking of everything, letting my mind wander between bliss and sadness, basking in the quiet moonlight of the night, picking grass out of the ground and drawing my name into the dirt. "Shouldn't you be inside, drinking, like the rest of your friends?" whispered a wayward voice from above. My heart jumped against my ribcage and I snapped my neck back, searching for the source of the sound. "Who said that?" I asked, squinting at the dark lattice of branches above me. Suddenly, my eyes settled on a pair of beady red eyes and connected their gaze nervously, "Who are you?" I asked breathlessly. "Don't you recognize me?" said the voice, leaping down in a quick black blur, "I'm your friend." I swallowed hard as the silhouetted figure came into full view. He was tall and human-like, but something was off about him. His hair was a silver white and he had eyes that shifted from red to orange, like firelight. He took a seat next to me in the grass and I could feel heat emanating from him. "Geez," I asked, laughing nervously, "Do you have a fever or something?" "No," he answered, "But I think you might." I stared back at him, half-drunk, and uttered a bewildered, "What?" He laughed, his white teeth gleaming, "I mean. It's a party, what are doing out here, by yourself? Aren't you supposed to be having fun with everyone?" "I could ask you the same question. Besides," I said, looking up at the stars caught between the branches, "I'm having a contemplative moment." He chuckled quietly, "A contemplative moment? What the hell is that supposed to be? "Oh, come on" I said in a slurred surprise, "You know, a moment where you just kind of step back and enjoy the scenery. This beautiful night for instance, where I'm young and everything just feels wrong and right at the same time. And you know it's fleeting, but you're just sort of okay with it..... you know?" "Well, you're quite the thinker," he said simply, "But, yeah, I guess I kind of do." "Cool," I said, "So why the hell were you up in a tree?" "Same thing, you could say." he responded, his shifting eyes, melting into a shade of light orange, "Just observing." "Mmm" "Well," he said, rising to stand, "I should probably get back to that, then." "No," I protested quietly, pulling on his hand, "Stay." He sat back down and I leaned in slowly toward his face, staring at his eyes, feeling his warm breath against mine. Our lips touched for a moment, before, in a black flash he darted away and left me alone. I opened my eyes, my lips still slightly puckered and stared sheepishly at my friend who was standing above me with a look of absolute shock on his face. "Uhh, dude, how drunk are you?" he asked, "There's no one fucking there."

To answer the fist question you'll have, yes. It still hurts. I don't know what caused this. Cellphone radiation, good diet, maybe genetics? Maybe I'll research it. After all, I've got nothing but time now. I think it was a Monday when I first realized that I was..... different. I worked at a gas station in a little town in Arkansas sitting behind the counter. It was a very mundane job, but I enjoyed the quiet. I usually spent my time reading books between the occasional customers I had. One afternoon, just as the sun was beginning to set, I had a customer come in wearing a razorback hat, and a grey sweatshirt. He gave me a weird vibe, so I reached for the shotgun under the counter. I held it in my lap, just out of sight of the man in my store. "Hey man, mind if I get a pack of Camel Reds?" He spoke with an odd kindness that alleviated my anxiety. I set the gun down and turned towards the rack of cigarettes behind me. When I turned back I was looking down the barrel of a gun. I was expecting him to ask me to open the register or something, but all I heard was a loud bang. I screamed like a little kid and pulled my arms in front of my face. There were a few moments of silence before the man ran out of the store. I lowered my arms with one eye squinted. He was gone. I just thought I was the luckiest bastard alive, which in retrospect, I guess I wasn't exactly wrong. I went back into the employee bathroom to wash the sweat off my face, but the mirror greeted me with a gruesome figure. Part of my head was missing. I was in shock. I sat on the floor looking into the mirror for an hour trying to contemplate my situation as I watched my head slowly heal. My first thought was I could heal fast like some character out of a comic book. To test that theory, I left the station and drove to the highway overpass. It took an hour or two to coax myself into jumping, but I eventually worked up the courage. I fell to the hard asphalt below. Jesus Christ did that hurt. I had to of broken a dozen bones, and crushed a few of my internal organs. I had to learn more about this new found gift of mine. I never went back to work. The next couple of months were spent testing the extent of my ability. I tried not eating for a couple of weeks. I felt hungry, but nothing more. I tried fire next. Holy shit that was a mistake. I burned the skin off my body entirely and my nerves screamed with pain. That was when I learned the extent of my healing. I heal at the same rate as other normal people except for fatal injuries. Gunshot to the head took about an hour, spike in the heart took two, broken neck took about a day. I spent my days doing all the things I wanted to do. I travelled mostly, and I read a lot. As the years went by, I started to notice my family got older and died, while I stayed the same age. That is what confuses me the most I think. Why did I stop aging that day? Maybe I was always immortal, but that doesn't explain why I aged at all. Then again, I don't have much of a mind for science. I realized my amazing gift was actually a terrible curse. I had to watch everything die around me as I stood still, frozen in time. It's a lonely life I live, but I still try to make the most of it.

First time, please don't hate it. I always understood love hate relationships because of cleaning. Cleaning my home was the only thing that caused both emotions. Running? Love. Painting my nephew's room a terrible color because my sister-in-law wants it? Hate. My nephew? Love. Cleaning was an evil I did with excitement for the result, which was a version of my home I expect to see in the new heaven and earth. Every year I sweep everything, floor, scrub every tile, check all my clothes, and rearrange my bookshelf. Finally finished with my bachelor's of communications, I realized I would almost certainly never need those textbooks again. Here's like... almost a thousand dollars in paper paperweight I thought, rather fond of the " paper paperweights " oxymoron. Finding yet another paper based product in the garage (cardboard box), I loaded the textbooks in and headed upstairs. The hallway has a rather unassuming attic entrance towards the far end, and I've never before made an excuse to go up. My jobs paid for tuition instead of enough crap to need an attic. Great, the dust from opening the door is gon na make me sweep again. The light of course, had not worked since the Soviets were a threat, and the free flashlight from my credit union illuminated only a few degrees, despite its bulk on my key ring. I set the box of communication methods down in some random corner that was unlikely to make it a tripping hazard and was about to turn the pitiful fluorescents off when I saw a box directly behind the door, supporting it from slamming against the floor. Not wanting to close myself in the attic, I managed to drag it down the ladder into the hall with one arm. It was a light box, but unusually large. The corrugated brown paper was so old, it disintegrated instead of ripping open, brown dust settling on the contents, covering the triangle left somewhat intact in my palm. The dust settled and I thought there was some encyclopedia taking the entirety of the box. There aren't any ridges between volumes. I ended up flipping the box upside down, breaking the other side in, and pushing the book out from the edges where it was until just recently snugly ensconced. It must have been a 2 by three feet, at least, but it wasn't very thick, maybe about the size of a Bible. The brown cardboard dust matched the actual cover almost perfectly, and would have remained unnoticed had not the angled light betrayed shadows splaying across the world. I was so thoroughly confused by the thing, and I thought it was the odd size of it until I realized it was blank. Just... entirely blank. No author. No title. No publisher or year, or anything except for the text that made the bulk of the pages. And the first page made no sense whatsoever. I couldn't begin to understand it, the characters were entirely alien to me, with a stark, beautiful contrast between straight, thick lines, and thin hairpin curves. It was like two distinct people had to have written half of each symbol. As I flipped through, the characters blended, becoming more uniform, evolving. By the middle of the volume, it was something Asian, but still not anything I could understand. By page 509, there were smatterings of Latin, or Greek, or French, which I understood. Names and events I could translate, but it didn't make sense for another 40 pages, until most of the entries were in modern languages. " Francis Cassavant - November 26, 1947. Suicide because of guilt, war, and anger. " A name, a date, and a cause of death. Over and over the pattern emerged, becoming more frequent than the ones I could not understand or translate easily with my phone. Was every entry like this? I was shocked. I kept turning pages, but the sensation of the aged paper crackling and escaping my fingers became numbed. The names and dates were nothing, but the causes were all bleak. The most natural cause of death became a tragedy with a few simple words added on to it. " Arthur Glennon - Dec 25 1999. Aborted in second trimester. Would have taught English at MIT. " The dates are getting closer and closer. I feared how recently this book might have been edited. I moved in 5 months ago, so the list stops before March of 2011, right? They didn't. At least a hundred thousand people died today. And it kept going, into tomorrow, and next week and year and decades. My name is in this. I knew it must be. I didn't care about the logic of a book predicting fate, I had already seen entries for people I knew. The teacher in middle school who died of cancer. The uncle who took me hunting for the first time, and carried the kill because I couldn't even lift him. Hours after dragging the cardboard coffin down, I found what I was looking for. " Andrew Clemente - August 1 2040. Car crash with semi - at fault. " Right below were 2 other English entires. " Ally Clemente - August 1, 2040. Car crash. " " Andrew Clemente II - August 1, 20104. Car crash. " I was shaking and crying. I hadn't even met this Ally yet, and now I didn't want to. I never want to see her, or my son, because I know that I will by their undoing. I don't care about the joy of marriage or fatherhood. And I kept telling myself this. Every day I would renew a vow to not fall for Ally, to not be married or have a son, but every spring I check and the names don't change or go away. Every day I think that I'm going to live the rest of my life unhappy, because I know I hurt the people I'll one day love the most.

Aurelie looked out of the window onto the sprawling mess of metal trees that was the city. Such serenity for a Monday. Her tea was the perfect temperature to sip, and the rain came down softly onto the tops of the skyscrapers, where the filters gurgled to pump the water through the pipes. The cashmere of her sweater enveloped her as she became lost in thought. The legislation to deregulate business using the labor from below was coming along nicely. Today they were going to pass some new bills for bathroom breaks. Silly how such a thing could have an impact on worker productivity. Not nearly as important as minimum wage, which was a bigger battle. She didn't notice Pollux's soft hand on her shoulder until it came up to stroke her cheek. " It's time. You're needed, " he said, giving her a gentle kiss. " Good luck. " " Of course I am. " Her high heels clacked on the marble floor. She quickly applied some lipstick in the mirror of the foyer. Now she was the perfect chairwoman. At peace. Contained. Whole. She stepped out of her door and into chaos. Men and women were rushing every which way, whispering in an urgent panic. She took the elevator up and inquired what was going on. " They're coming, " said her secretary. " The people from below. They're coming up. " Aurelie laughed. " Excellent. We'll have to invite them to have some coffee with us. " " No. Miss Stone, they're really coming up. Reports are coming in from all over the city. They're coming. Climbing up any way they can. They've started on the Renaissance Tower. " " We'll have to deal with this ourselves. " What a terrible Monday. She got in the elevator and put in her radio headpiece. " The city's lower-class citizens are seeking refuge on the upper floors of our towers. They claim to be fleeing an unknown group of classist terrorists who are calling for anarchy. The military is attempting to put the riots down. More reports to follow. " This could be very bad. She stepped out onto the carpeted lobby floor and observed the carnage from the massive windows. People in rags were using every means possible to flee upwards. A few had attached, spider-like, with grappling hooks to the bottom of the Committee Building. Get on the PA, Aurelie. ATTENTION. THE COMMITTEE BUILDING IS ON TOTAL LOCKDOWN. DO NOT MOVE UNTIL THE ISSUE HAS BEEN RESOLVED. The elevator dinged. She hoped Pollux was okay. That was when the gunshot hit her neck. to be continued

Jared sifted through the box he just removed from the garage, he had been cleaning out his grandfathers house every night for a week now and it was the only room left. His grandfather had been pronounced deceased only two weeks ago, but he had been missing for a lot longer. One day, 2 years ago Jared had come to visit only to find his grandfather and his car gone, days went by without getting a hold of him, then weeks, then months. The police could not find any new bank transactions, nor any phone activity and now at the end of the line, the only reasonable thing to do was to suspect his death. The house was left to Jared. His grandfather had always been an eccentric man, some said he was a man before his time, though most just whispered behind his back that he was a crazy man best suited to live in an institution of the fitting kind. For Jared his eccentricities was always just a fun aspect of a man he loved, and cleaning out the house had been a very sentimental experience. Jared had fond memories of doing small experiments with his grandfather. One time they made a small robot that could dispense cans of cola by clapping your hands twice, another time his grandfather made a strength potion for Jared, it didn't make him any stronger, but his piss was green for a week. While Jared was recollecting he noticed a magazine lying on the top of a box, he looked at the cover which read " Tomorrow's Science Yesterday ." He had never heard of this magazine, but started to look through the pages. After a few pages he saw an advert that was circled by a red sharpie line. " Have you ever wondered what Mars looks like in spring, now you can find out for yourself for only 45 ." It seemed to be an advert for a DIY kit that would make your car a bonafide spacecraft. The first thing Jared thought about was those x-ray glasses kids would buy at those novelty shops, he laughed. Then suddenly he started to get a feeling this would be something his grandfather would want to try out. He thought maybe, just maybe, he is up there in his old Ford cruising around. He decided to send in an order. Two weeks went by and Jared had more or less given up hope on getting an answer, the magazine was of course very old, and who would even order something from a magazine in this day and age he thought to himself. But right after thinking that someone knocked on his door. He opened, an UPS man stood in front of him. " Package for Jared Hansson, please sign here ." He took the package and said bye. The package was quite big and heavy, but he managed to get it to the garage. He opened carefully, on top of the content was a page with the writing " Congratulations on your purchase of the Spaceflight-o-matic 3000 ." He turned the page. On the other side was what can only be said to be sparse instructions " 1. Attach Retrogravitational accelerator on rear of the vehicle. 2. Install staring module to interior of vehicle. 3. Enjoy the freedoms of space travel ." He followed the instruction and in no less than 5 minutes he was finished. It looked kind of ridiculous he thought, but that he should definitively try it out. With heavy doubt in his heart he drove out to the road and stopped. He could only assume that the big red button that said " ACTIVATE " would be the logical next step. He slowly pressed it and to his big surprise the trees on the side of the road started to sink deeper. He looked down and saw the ground getting further and further away. He was levitating. Maybe his grandfather had done the same as him, maybe he would meet his grandfather up there in space. the car accelerated faster, he quickly was what he only could assume was several thousand feet up in the air. The horizon got bigger and darker for every second that went by. But suddenly Jared got a bad feeling, it was getting colder fast, and the air didn't seem to fill his chest anymore. His eyes got heavy, and he struggled to keep them open. He felt the weight of his body decreasing, and the darkness above him was getting deeper. He thought " this is it, what a strange way to die! " Then he saw it, a Ford with a Spaceflight-o-matic 3000 attached to it. It came straight towards him. It glided by and Jared got a glance inside. In the car was the cold remains of his grandfather and a note stuck to the window. It read " Forgot to order the Air-o-matic 3000 ." Jared expelled his last words " shit, me too! ."

Emperor Noxu of the Nalpure people rubbed his hands together, and pet his furry head with his eight fingered paw. " Among our many grievances since we landed on Earth, " said Emperor Noxu, visibly nervous, " is the many fast food chains we saw on our brief trip to this United Nations building, with meat in their menus. It worries my people back at home. " President Richard of the planet listened to the translation in his earpiece, then nodded. Cameras were flashing left and right. " You need not worry, " said President Richard. " In our history we indeed raised cows, chickens, lambs, a whole host of other animals all for the purposes of harvesting their meat for sustenance. But we now grow all our meats in laboratories all across the globe. " " We still find it odd, " said the Emperor. He adjusted his robe of bark from a tree in the flying forests of Nachtundra, Noxu's home planet. " We don't understand why humans so desire food that reminds them of a murderous past, and it leaves us feeling quite concerned. You see our, " Emperor Noxu swallowed some spit, and wiped his nose, " our meat has a reputation of being quite delicious. " President Richard put his hand out and laughed. He looked quite charming as he did it. " No need to worry Emperor, " President Richard grabbed his stomach. " We won't be eating you and your people, we only want the gold on your planet. And in exchange, " The President hovered his hand over the table. A hologram of a whole host of different plants appeared on the screen. Conifers, palm trees large as great sequoias, oak trees, orchids, tulips, sunflowers with bags of their seeds beside them, carnations, " we'll give you access to every variety of plant our planet has to offer, in abundance. " Emperor Noxu breathed like it was an overwhelming display. He covered his snot dribbling nose, and whispered something to a smaller Nalpure alien beside him. If you looked at them from a distance, they looked a bit like large koala bears, but with red fur and smaller eyes. They both laughed, and smiled with strangely blunt teeth. Emperor Noxu folded his hands on the table, a gesture he'd seen the humans make in previous negotiations. " That uhm ahem, " Emperor Noxu tried to downplay his excitement, " that looks nice, looks nice. But we would also request one additional thing. " " Yes Emperor, " said President Richard, smiling. " Whatever you may like, you want more plants? " " We request," said Emperor Noxu, quite stern, " that you not eat your lab grown meat on a newly designated holiday. Once a year, everybody on Earth must go vegetarian. " President Richard seemed unready to field such a question. He adjusted his suit jacket, and whispered something to his advisor seated beside him. Cameras all around flashed, and reporters murmured. President Richard bit his lip for a moment and scrunched his face. He nodded hard, and set a hand out to his trade partner. " It's a deal, " said President Richard. " once every year, all meat eating will be illegal, even lab grown meat. " Emperor Noxu stood up, and put his paws over the President's hand. They both smiled at the camera. Handsome man makes trade deal with intelligent, red, Koalaesque alien people. Perfect photo-op. Emperor Noxu leaned in towards the President. His breath smelled like salad. " And disobeying this new order on said holiday, " whispered Emperor Noxu, " must be punishable by banishment into a lake of fire. " President Richard only heard weird chirping noises. He listened to his earpiece for the translation, then smiled awkwardly at the Nalpure Emperor. It's a lot of gold, thought the President. I can go vegetarian for a few years, until we get enough of their gold. President Richard smiled like a maniac. Then we can eat these delicious little bastards.

The darkness is thicker then velvet, smothering the weak light of the windows as it struggles in from outside. This is probably a blessing- after all, who would want to see what's out there now? The wreckage and the rubble, the dead still lying in the streets? The sentinel certainly doesn't. She tries not to look outside any more. If she sees the great necropolis she made, she remembers it's her fault. She's old, now- the pathways and positrons of her brain worn and broken, barely functional, clogged with rust and forgetfulness. This is a blessing too. Strange. She has so many blessings, now she's old. When she was young, and the city had been her body (and not just the scrawny metal spider that she wore now), she'd had none at all. Just priorities, responsibilities, quotas. Now, none of that. The city was dead. Perhaps she would be, too, some day. For now, she revelled in forgetfulness, and counted her blessings.

Jeff loved football. He started in high school and got through college with a football scholarship. When Jeff got a little older, he placed his dream in a jar on a shelf and after several years it was buried. Jeff now has a steady job as a writer for a newspaper column, he has a beautiful wife, Zoe, and they are raising a little girl named Maddie. Jeff got home from work one day to find Maddie playing with her dolls. He sat down next to her and she pulled him into the game. Jeff was allowed to control one doll. They had tea parties, races, and even a dance. "What should we do today, Molly?" Maddie's doll asked Jeff's doll. Jeff paused. "Maybe we could try a sports game?" Maddie looked up to her father and asked, "like what?" "Like football?" smiled Jeff. "I could train you!" Maddie looked confused, "Dolls don't play sports daddy!" "Why not?" "Well..... because...." Maddie stumbled. "How about we try?" Maddie thought for a moment and then smiled. "Okay!" The two dolls tried passing a small ball to each other. "This is way too hard Daddy." Maddie groaned. Jeff nodded. "I agree with you. Let's try the real thing!" Maddie was not thrilled but she ended up passing a bouncy ball back and forth with her father. "What are you two doing?" Zoe asked as she entered the room. "Football!" Maddie yelled as her mother greeted her father. "Football?" Zoe smiled. "You haven't played that since college." Jeff looked down. "Yeah. Well I couldn't buy you this house by being a shitty football player." Jeff smirked as Zoe hit his arm. "No swears Captain." Maddie pointed. "Ohh Captain." smiled Zoe. Jeff smiled. "That's me." "You guys ready for supper?" asked Zoe. "More football! More football!" screamed Maddie. "We will be right there!" laughed Jeff. "Just a few more minutes." Ten Years later Jeff lays in an uncomfortable hospital bed. Zoe is sitting beside him and holding his hand. Maddie runs inside and hugs her father. "What happened?" Maddie choked back tears. "Your father was trying to practice a new maneuver with his friends. He was going to teach you it this afternoon but I don't think thats a great idea." Zoe sounded stern but she had a lightness to her speech. Jeff explained the new maneuver to his daughter and she lay next to him listening to every word. "I never told you this Maddie." Jeff's voice changed tone. "The reason I stopped playing Football was because I didn't have the heart for it. Literally. The doctors said I was getting too excited or something. Anyway, I thought it would be different now but I guess that was stupid of me." Jeff held back his tears. "I just had so much fun playing football with you." A doctor walked in and asked to speak to Zoe. "Come on Maddie." "Just a couple more minutes?" Maddie begged. Jeff and Zoe smiled. "Okay." Zoe and the doctor left the room. "Today I am supposed to find out." Maddie whispered. "Everything will go fine." Jeff whispered. "No matter what I'm proud of you." Maddie and Jeff lay in the uncomfortable bed for ten more minutes. The next morning, Jeff had passed away. A heart attack in the middle of the night. Maddie stayed home from school. She stayed in bed all day crying until her mother opened her bedroom door. "Hi Honey." Maddie did not respond. "I know you are hurting right now but there a few friends from school here to see you. Do you mind seeing them or should I send them away until another day?" Maddie got up and left her room. She walked downstairs to a group of at least 15 other kids her age. Nobody said anything for a while until one girl walked up to Maddie. "Im really sorry about your dad." Maddie gave a quick smile and sunk her head down. "Thank you." Maddie looked up. "Thank you all for coming but you didn't need to do this." The girl took Maddie's hands and motioned for her to stand up. "We wanted to make you feel a bit better." Everyone came together in a group embrace. "We need you. We need our leader." Maddie looked confused. "Leader? You mean...?" "Yes." the girl smiled. "You!" Maddie's eyes began welling up and soon everyone was crying and smiling and hugging. Maggie looked up to her father and spoke in a strained voice, "Look at me. Look at me. I'm the captain now."

He obviously got in by asking the landlord for the spare key; we look enough alike that with his hat covering his full head of hair it just looked like if I'd shaved and perhaps lost some weight..... Okay a lot of weight, and maybe had some corrective cosmetic surgeries..... In any case, as you might surmise he cut off my babbling about shows and movies and comic books to point out that if he squandered his potential on all this media he would never have developed the tech to bridge the dimensional gaps which I had to admit was pretty impressive, even if the other me was being a bit of a tool with his condescending down-talking. He then interrupted himself to tell me "Jumping ahead" [ something something ] and then, after down-talking to me more about "infinite possible realities" and "infinite more created every instant," like I'm some total noob to the concept, he tries to tell me some junk about how there is another version of us who is world hopping trying to kill the alternates of us, in some misguided quest for individuality. It was around this time I pulled out a pre-rolled lit it, asking my double if he could tweak my internet or tv to pick up alternate universe shows movies and stuff. He seemed put off by my flippant attitude towards exposing him to the mind-impeding substance (my guess would be it interfered with the stick in his , but also by the complete disregard I seemed to have for his warning. So to settle at least some of his concerns I said: "Look, I'll smoke this all, you don't have to have any; hook up the TV the internet for me while I explain And I went on to point out that if infinite realities exist, and infinite ones are birthed into existence at every moment, then every time a version of us pops into a universe he would split that reality into paths that include that event and paths that exclude it. So there would be a whole bunch of universes split from just this one, where my double wasn't here. My double seemed to have had a handle on the math but hadn't considered the practical sense. But by this time was putting final touches on the device he was affixing to the back of the big flatscreen on the wall, having already put a neat little chip in my phone and some sort of spider-looking thing on my laptop, another on the desktop..... I had to ask "Why did you come to warn me of all possible alternate versions anyway? " , to which he replied "It's nothing about you personally, you seem to do little else than slack and waste your talents on purile entertainment petty indulgences; I was simply tracking the alternate, and could only seem to track him to this universe not his subsequent trip I've logged it in my transdimensional databanks that our alternate likely only used this world as jumping-off point to make an untraceable getaway." with a frustrated sneer. To which I grinned widely and said simply "Good, that's what I figured." As I jammed a pin into his wrist-mounted universe-jumping device's override setting before he could react, as his hand was propped against the wall while he fiddled behind the flat screen. He turned looked at me like a deer in headlights, but I'm no deer, dear this Buck has the horns, and I gave him a good solid head-butt before his gadget's overload caused his physical form to collapse into a localized event-horizon, drawing him into lord only knows what random reality. With his toolbox sitting on the counter there was scant chance he'd be able to rig it to bring him anywhere other than more random universe after universe like early season Sliders..... I'm just glad the alternate from this universe left a stash and happened to be out of town or I'd have a had a lot of trouble getting the upper hand on that stuck up piece of crap. "quest for individuality" my ass I just wasn't into putting up with versions of myself who were insufferable pompous jerks, and it seemed laughing boy was so eager to join their ranks he had to follow me here. Besides, each time I killed one it just made more sets of realities stemming from both me killing and not killing alternates, it's just a wash in the big picture. What a windbag, good riddance. Of course if I want to stick around here then sending him away was the only option; killing him would have been messy no matter how, and might lead to all kinds of tricky questions.... Probably worth it though, expecting to have some good times when this reality's me comes back from out of town. Unlike the stuck-up douche-nozzle version, we seem to have similar tastes and attitudes, so I'm sure he'll appreciate the new tv computer hookups for alternate-universe tv, movies, comics video games. I hope he doesn't mind sharing his life I'd hate to have to have to killa guy who for all other intents and purposes seems pretty chill.

Carefully the robber made his way up the stairs when he heard it. The robber looked around for the source of the noise. Stealthy and quick, yet careful to keep his senses on alert. He spotted the source near his feet. "Pur. Pur. Meow." "Oh, hi kitty. Good kitty." The cat rubbed up against the robber's leg and purred some more before laying on its back and inviting the robber to pet it. As soon as his hand touched the cats belly the cat the cat sprang into action, sinking its claws and teeth into the robber's hand. The robber lost his balance and fell noisily backwards down the flight of stairs. Lights turned on in the bedroom above. The cat, unconcerned, laid back down on his back, waiting for another person to pet him.

The President sat back in his chair whilst dabbing at his brow with a pristine white handkerchief. Jessie noticed the little blue letter P on the handkerchief as he watched, the live feed playing beside him on the laptop. "Well president?" Jessie prompted, eager to hear what the President thought of the new breed of soldier. "Son" He responded "I'm not sure how they are super soldiers, they died like everyone else!" Jessie's eyes flicked to the screen, the feed was lingering on a pile of shredded troops. "Mr President, we went up against 300 enemy soldiers. The enemy were well equipped and well armed Russian forces. We achieved every objective, took every bit of ground and all with minimal losses" Jessie beamed. The handkerchief dabbed again as he leaned forward and controlled the drone's camera. Everywhere he looked displayed destruction, death and multiple bodies of his own people. He frowned as the camera settled on the victories few. "What are the death tolls?" The President quietly enquired. "The enemy forces were obliterated to the man" Jessie replied with a sly grin. "And ours?" The President asked. "Acceptable" Jessie responded curtly. "How many? The President ordered his tone cold. "85 of our forces, leaving us with 39 capable men" Jessie reported, quickly continuing over the Presidents shock that spread across his face "Sir, these men were trained, had the best weapons capable and cost us hardly anything!" Jessie leaned over and flick the screen to display the costings, pointing the chart and comparison. The chart displayed an image along the side of a happy fresh trooper with a 42 cheaper logo displayed on his chest. "See, by cutting costs on food, providing modified starches as rations with a huge array of flavour options we were able to save 24 on food costs." Jessie reported, the words slinking out like a well trained salesman. The President raised a hand to interrupt but Jessie continued. "The barracks and size decrease came back as not only cost effective, but helped with morale as the psyche of all troopers reflected well in forming unit bonds." Jessie reported as the screen changed to display a collection of troopers hugging in a cramped barracks. "Plus, the equipment, weapons, and training was maintained at the standard rates optimising profits for all." "Stop!" The President ordered, the pristine white handkerchief was crushed in a clenched fist. Jessie paused, glanced at the Handkerchief and stiffened. "Son, this is a disaster, I do not want my men suffering and dying." He spoke slowly, his eyes level with Jessie across the table. Jessie nodded once shamefully. "Leave" The President growled, gesturing dismissal and turning in his chair. He had some serious thinking to do and heads would roll. Jessie stood, scooping up the laptop and shuffled to the door. He looked back and offered one last gambit. "These troopers cost us over half of what the Russians committed in that battle sir. These are your new super soldiers."

I've seen the numbers for my whole life, and I've known what they meant for as long as I can remember. My newborn cousin is a zero, inert and without intent. The typical cop is a five, alert but largely peaceful. A politician on a screen is an eight, every word out of their mouth chosen carefully and their eyes staring soulfully into the cameras. I had been walking to my next class when I saw her. My hands began to sweat, my vision flickering out of focus as I stared. She gave her stubborn locker a kick, spinning her combo again and sighing when it refused to open. My ears rang, my heart climbed out from its place behind my breastbone. A ten. A negative ten.

The sun shone through the white clouds like a painting. It was beautiful. More beautiful than the flowers Janet brought. They were already decaying, even though she bought them a few hours ago. She had a groundskeeper lead her to the fresh grave of Diana Brooks: her mother. As her mother's grave came into sight, a man in a black suit was standing over it. From behind, she couldn't tell who it was. She silently approached him from behind and stood beside him. Janet looked over and saw her brother, Erik. The two had not spoken since Janet left town for college and never came back. She cut off all ties to the small Iowa town she was raised in and where Erik still lived. When Janet saw it was, in fact, her brother, a wave of different emotions flowed in. Happiness, for being reunited with baby brother. Guilt, for leaving him behind. And sadness, for the passing of one of the closest people to her. With all these emotions swirling around her head, she could only muster out a measly "hi." "She blamed you." said Erik. He didn't look up; it was almost as if he was trying to memorize every groove and crevice inside the headstone. "She blamed you for what happened to Dad. On her death bed." Janet looked up. Erik didn't. "I came back so I could pay my respects." said Janet, coldly. "Not for a lecture." "Do you even know what happened when you left?" Erik said as he uprighted himself and turned to Janet. "You tore this damn family apart." It was Janet's turn to look back at the headstone. "You know what? No. I don't. So get talking, before I turn back and head back to Seattle." "You may have been to self-centered to realize that they loved you more than they loved me." said Erik, with more intensity that Janet. "You were the big shot. High honors, varsity soccer, and, to top it all off, a giant scholar ship! You were their pride. You kept them going. When you left, you didn't take the big expectations. I wasn't smart enough for them, nor was I quick enough, I had no redeeming qualities in their eyes. I was nothing!" Erik let that last line out for a couple of moments. He let it sink into Janet's ears, observe every ounce of despair, grief and frustration. "They hated me, Janet. Detested my existence." Erik said. The shinning sun became obstructed by a passing cloud. "So, when he lost his job, dad turned to drinking. Jack Daniels was the son that never disappointed him. Smooth, consistent and popular. Words that will never be used to describe me." "He beat you." Janet said, looking back up. "He did. He beat me pretty hard." said Erik. "He beat mom, too. One day, it got too much. Mom messed up a recipe, so he messed her up. Pretty badly, too. When he stormed back out for a smoke, I took mom to my room, locked the door and called the police. I told them what he was doing to me, to her. A few minutes later, they show up. Dad heard the sirens and went to check it out. I couldn't watch. I tucked my head under the window. There was yelling, then a gunshot. "Mom broke down at this point. I'll never forget the sound she made when that gun went off. I ran out. He was dead. I just stood there at the front door. The beatings were over. No more fear, no more pain. But my dad was dead. I was conflicted. "Fast forward two years, and mom's in the hospital. I had just finished a major deal at Kansas City, so I drove home as fast as I could. When I got there, she was leaving. That's when she told me it was your fault. Then she left us." "How'd she die?" "Her heart was weak, so it just..... stopped, I guess. There was a medical term and I was just to grief stricken and "It's ok. You didn't kill her." "You did." Janet looked back up. Erik was crying, tear drops falling like rain drops. "She comforted me." said Erik. "She was the closest a person ever was to me. After every beating, she held me in her arms and didn't let go. You took her from me." "No, I didn't." "Just admit it." "No." "Just do it!" screamed Erik. "No, it's your damn fault!" replied Janet. "You were home. You could have stopped this. You could have stopped dad from drinking. You could have gotten a job earlier to support the household. You could have made sure that the cops just arrested him, and not shot him. You could have done so many things, but you didn't, so don't put that blame on me!" Erik was full on crying. Every beating, every milliliter of dad's blood, every last breath mom took, every bad memory and experience; the pain caused from them rushed from his body, shaking him to his core. He put himself on his hands and knees. "Just go, Janet." he begged. "Run away, just one more time. Don't come back, don't call me. Just disappear again." "Fine." Janet said, as cold as a winter's night. She threw the flowers against the ground and stormed off. As she walked off, Erik positioned himself against his mother's grave and got out a flask.

A hand on my shoulder made me jump. "Settle down, boy," Da said, hushed to keep from provoking the spirits in the wind. I looked to him, my hands trembling with hatchet in hand. Father felt no fear, he wasn't scared of anything. Not even the woods, always just on the edge of sight from camp. Scars traced his face, exposed where his burly beard didn't reach. I'd have scars like that someday, maybe even tonight. The trees didn't go down quietly, silent in the night. "You still got a few weeks, you know," he said softly. "Ranging isn't meant to bring you to battle. That's left till you become a man." I swallowed the lump in my throat. "I am a man, Da. I can do this. I was born to do this. We're born with an axe "And we die with an axe. But the best of us die old, fighting our whole lives. Yours has barely started, boy. Keep your wits about you, or the trees'll get ya." The warhorn blared, signalling the change of guard. In the distance, I could see them coming back, the dawn patrol. Some walked fair on their own two feet, but most were limping. Others still were far worse off, missing limbs and chunks from their chests. The lowest of my village, given the duty of dusk to dawn. "We'd die without them," Da said, fastening the straps on his leathers. He nodded to one of them, clutching the bloody hole where his eye had been. "And they hate us'cause they know it." The man sneered at the base camp, wandering past tent after tent. Our village lay beyond the hills, miles away from the treeline. A hundred years ago, the forest hadn't yet crossed the seas. Injured as he was, he didn't stop for help or even to rest. The lowborn didn't get anything but a fresh hole to be buried in. And that was only for the men who came back. They weren't worth the healing. "Why don't they just stop cutting?" I asked, queasy as another man hobbled by, using his axe to make up for the lost leg. "They do at times, and that's why we're here, at the end of the line." Da grabbed his axe off the table, double-bladed and tall as any man. Notches in the staff marked his kills. There weren't nearly enough to inspire confidence. "The lumber burns but it won't sail, like our ancestors could. We're stuck here until we die. If more men keep quitting, that won't be too long from now." He left the tent, stopping just outside the flaps. He turned to me, concern flooding from his eyes. "I ask you, son. Stay here. Stay alive." If that's what he'd wanted from me, he should've kept his mouth shut. "No, Da. The village dies if we quit, and it'll die sooner with me sitting on my arse." Tightening my grip on the hatchet, I said, "We're born with an axe and we die with an axe. And I've already done the first one."

The young seaman tugged at my sleeve, "Captain look! Out there! To starboard!" I took the binoculars hanging on my neck and glassed the waters, calm seas, except for what looked to be a single white mass, kind of like a wave. "Do you see it sir?" "Well..... I think so. Is that a rogue wave?" A tower of foam spurt through the water, and the "white mass" was what looked like a gargantuan white tail that lifted into the air, and then disappeared into the water. But that couldn't be..... "Jesus Christ, what was that? " , I screamed. "Sir, that looks like Moby Dick!" "What? " "Moby Dick, Captain!" "I heard you the first time. How on God's green planet do you figure that is Moby Dick?" "I figured it out from the tail..... the white tail, Captain." I raised the binoculars to the waters again, but any sign of this "Moby Dick" was gone. Whatever it was, it had disappeared. I heard the seaman cough behind me, "Ahem..... Sir..... You do know how to fight Moby, right?" "Jesus Christ son, there's no such thing as Moby Dick." His eyes widened as his face became very Moby Dick-colored-like, "Begging your pardon Sir..... But yes there is. Didn't you ever read the book in your training?" "You mean that book by uhh.... what's his name..... umm..... Charles Dick..... Charles Dickinson?" He pinched his nose with his fingers, "Oh my God." I laughed, "Is this some sort of joke? Seriously? Like, some sort of'Oh hey, we have a new Captain, so let's fuck with him' kind of thing?" "N-no..... Sir. All sea captains are required to read Moby Dick by Herman Melville before taking command of a ship." "You're starting to piss me off now son. Moby Dick is a fucking novel." Another young seaman's voice sounded on the horn, "Captain! We've detected a large mass below us on SONAR. It's Moby Dick! No submarine can move as fast as what we're picking up! " As sarcastically as I could humanly muster, with as much animation in my hands as possible, I laughed, "Well all hands to battle stations then!" " ALL HANDS TO BATTLE STATIONS! ALL HANDS TO BATTLE STATIONS! THIS IS NOT A DRILL! I REPEAT, THIS IS NOT A DRILL! " The ship's siren blared, and strobe lights hanging on the ceiling and on the deck that I didn't even know existed started panickly spinning about, shining their red lights all over the walls. Sailors sprinted about, down below I saw the Chief screaming orders, and my 1st Officer ran up on deck. He was breathless, and the look of unadulterated terror was in his eyes. "Captain, what's our next move?!" "Jesus Christ, am I the only one who isn't fucking crazy? There's no such thing as Moby Dick!" The 1st Officer looked at me and blinked. "Now is not the time for games sir!" The seaman chimed in, "The Captain is being serious, sir." "Captain, please tell me you've read Moby Dick." "What? I read like a third of it in High School, but that's it! It was a fucking boring book!" "Captain! Half that book is about how to kill whales!" "I know, that's why it was so goddamn fucking boring!" The 1st Officer was now jumping up and down, his fingers pulling out his hair, "How the hell do you expect to kill Moby Dick, if you've never read Moby Dick?" "BECAUSE IT WAS A FUCKING NOVEL! " A huge, vibrating, animalistic roar shook the entire ship. I rushed to the window and much to my horror and disbelief, out of the water, a colossal white whale launched itself into the air, easily two times the size of our old frigate. A diety, spawn of Poseidon. The very definition of behomoth itself. It soared out of the water, mouth agape, and its shadow covered the entire ship. Before it landed on top of us, the very last thought I had before being snuffed off the face of this planet was, I wish I hadn't smoked so much pot in high school.

I had a bowl of cornflakes on my belly when someone knocked my door. I paused my recording of Bones and answered. Two tall pale men in suits stood before me. They had headbands around their ears like Spock in Star Trek 4. "Alpha Moonbeam Beta Orange Gamma Frankenstein" said one in a high pitched voice. A heavy grayness fell over me and I felt myself faint. When I opened my eyes again a headache hit me like a mac truck. Images and ideas were flooding into my brain. I knew the true history of the world, I knew kung-fu, I knew..... who Santa Claus really was? I lay on my kitchen floor. My cat licking me behind one of my ears. The two pale men in black loomed over me. "Do you know who you are?" one asked. "Yes. I think so," I replied. "Do you accept your mission?" "Yes." "Good. Then lets go save Santa."

"Welcome Hominid. Kindly speak your name to continue.." I gazed at the glowing slab, it reminded me of my 50' t.v back home. It was the only relatable thing in this alien structure. "Special Lieutenant Cooper. Adam Cooper, from the United Earth Directorate. Earth. Sector 4, from the Milky way galaxy.." "Welcome Adam Cooper. Kindly wait while the interactive cognitive program loads.." "Good morning Adam. I trust the voyage to our planet was pleasant. My name was Griffin when I encoded my consciousness into this welcoming station.." "Griffin, eh? Good morning. It seems Griffin, that you were expecting us. But why a machine to welcome the alien guests?." "My apologies Adam. It may seem cold and uninviting, but I assure you we have a very good reason for this welcome.." "Well, the first question is how on earth..err, Gliese 4b, are you talking in English?." "Haha! A good joke Adam. You have just discovered our planet and have finally managed to travel here. We have been observing you for millennia. We left instructions with your greatest civilizations to contact us when we visited for the first time. However, it seems we were too obtuse. We sent our scouts and scientists every Earth century to try and explain our presence and intentions, as we have done with many other races across this universe. W-." "Wait! The alien abductions were real? And there are other intelligent races in our universe! Why did you not tell us properly?." "That is correct Adam, the universe teemed with sentient life. We didn't ." "Wait.... teemed? What happened to it? What happened to you?." "You are quite perceptive. It was something we did not anticipate. The Hominid body contained such virulent parasites. It caused us to change. We unknowingly transmitted the infection to everyone we came in contact with.." "What? You caught our germs? What happened?." "It caused an increase in agressive tendencies and diminished pain sensations. It spread via bodily fluids and resulted in a massive civil war. Only a handful of us, the protectors of knowledge, were left alive. We were infected, but managed to erect these welcoming plaques in 5 different galaxies in the hope that you hominids would eventually reach the stars. I wish you the best of luck. The baton passes to you now for this universe. Care for life, it's the most precious resource of the universe..." Edit: Formatting. Apologies, on my cell phone.

I'm not sure how I got here, maybe a warp of time and space or some cosmic being's intervention, but in any case, I ended up on this planet the natives call Genius. Luckily for me, the people looked just as human as Earth, and even spoke English so blending in was quite easy. However, Genius did have some differences. The buildings, people, and even the planet's gravity were remarkably weaker than Earth. The planet was actually a moon of a gas giant, and was maybe half of size of Earth. I spent the first three days wandering the streets of the city I found myself in, desperate to find a way home. My hope was running out as the sun disappeared behind the Jovian planet for the third time. The people here seemed indifferent to me, the few I ran up to seemed confused about where Earth was, or any of the countries I once knew. Just as I was preparing to collapse in a slum of a street, I heard a scream pierce the night. I snapped and found myself running towards and down an alley. At the far end two men stood, one armed and pulling at the arm of the other, smaller one. The closer I got the easier it was to hear the screams of help from what appeared to be a kidnapping. As I ran, or more accurately, leapt using the low gravity to sort of fly at the attacker. When I passed under a light, they both saw me. The victim stopped screaming for a second, but the kidnapped turned his gun at me. I heard three barks from the gun, felt two of them hit me, but they felt as if they were no stronger than a BB gun. As I reached the kidnapper, my fist hit him square in the chest and sent him flying into the building across the street on the other end of the alley. Panting, I saw the two'bullets' still lodged in my skin, but they had barely broke the skin. I turned to the other guy who stood shaking. "Are you okay?" I asked, trying (and failing) to keep my voice from shacking. "I..... Yeah" he said, eyeing the breaks in my skin. "What are you?" That night I met Steve, a student in the upscale neighborhood who had been kidnapped by a janitor looking to make a ransom. As we walked back to his home, I told him about myself. About how I had woke up on Genius and searched for some way back home. Soon we were talking about our schools, which were similar, how we were both a sort of nerds, then our shared hobbies, amongst them were comic books. That's when Steve came up with his idea. "Think about it, your stronger, faster, and more durable than anyone else here. Your like Superguy." He said excitedly. "I don't know," I said, "I still need to find a way back home my stomach growled loudly. "How about this, you can stay with me as long as you need. My parents a rarly home and I can convince them that your a foreign exchange student or something. In exchange, you have to try this super hero idea. It's literally the exact thing people like you and I have always wanted, or at least I have." Steve said, jumping up and down, "You have a gift, and this is your chance to make a difference in the world" I thought about it for a minute. I mean, who didn't want to be a superhero. And I did need a place to lay my head, I really didn't want to find a bench to sleep on. "Okay, but no capes" That was about three months ago, I think. Days are a little shorter here. Since then, I've been living a double life, as Mark Kent, exchange student in Xavier University thanks to Steve's computer skills in putting me into the system. But by night, and weekends that I'm not studying, I'm Indestructible; hero. It was the first day of summer break and I stood atop one of my favorite building perches and listened to the city. I took in a deep breath. I had really started to like my new life. Being a superhero was a lot easier than I thought. Especially since guns and knives bounced off me. I realized that maybe I didn't want to go home after all. No sooner than I thought that did I hear an explosion. Leaping up, I pulled down my mask,'time to be a hero' I thought. And jumped over the buildings between me and the sound. I landed with an exaggerated superhero landing. I looked up, the smug smile I've been giving all the crooks lately. Then my heart stopped. There standing in the ruined street was Butch, my high school bully. From Earth.

Every day without fail, a prompt about the divine is posted to WritingPrompts. With so many in need, how can the gods answer the call? The answer is simple: They team up. One group exists to help meet the needs of a prompt-hungry populace: the Pan-Eternal Godhood Bureau Overseeing All Relevant Dieties. The men and women of PEGBOARD strive to keep the replies coming. These are their stories. "Is this the control room?" Satan asked as he walked into the control room. He wasn't what you'd expect from a devil - he was human, for one. Looked pretty unsure of himself, but [ it was his third day ] (https: ) so that wasn't too surprising. "That it is," I said. I leaned forward to shake his hand. "Welcome to PEGBOARD command, I take it your indoctrination went well?" Satan nodded. "Uh, yeah. I've already started a few projects. That's why I'm here, I was hoping you could help me with something." "Of course," I said, "that's what we're here for." I motioned for Gabrielle - my second in command - to follow us. She wasn't as new to her job as Satan was, but she still had a lot to learn. The rest of the technicians in the room knew their job well, they could handle anything short of a dire emergency. Satan lead us down the hallway and to one of the many celestial elevators. We piled in and he pressed the button for the basement. "Can you give us a briefing while we wait?" I asked casually. All the other deities knew by now not to waste our time by waiting to give us the details. Not that it actually mattered to us, usually they were the ones with no time to waste. "Right," Satan said. "Okay, so you know the whole'get out of Hell on a bet' sort of thing?" I nodded. "Right, classic fiddle contest or game-playing. The latter's usually Death's domain but he doesn't mind sharing." "Okay, so I did that. I figured these games are all rigged, right?" "Absolutely," I said. "If you're the one doing them, that is. Death plays a fair game but he's been around longer than anyone so he's simply better at them than anyone else. You, though, you're the prince of lies. You can cheat." I caught Gabrielle trying not to smirk at this. It wasn't the first time we'd had to remind new Satans that they were evil. "That's the problem," Satan said. "I thought this would already be done. The guy agreed to a driver's test, and I stipulated that it had to happen on the Highway to Hell, because I figure what kind of shape is that highway going to be in? He'll hit a pothole a mile in and we'll be done." I nodded. "I see the problem," I said. Gabrielle made a face that said she didn't, but didn't want to look uninformed in the presence of one of our bosses. That was fine, she'd see in just a second. The elevator doors opened to the blasted volcano fields that surrounded the Highway. They were bleak, full of ash and skeletons, buzzards in the air, the works. The Highway itself, on the other hand...... "The Highway's perfect?" Gabrielle asked, apparently shocked into saying something. I nodded. "Twelve lanes, perfectly graded, optimal traffic patterns. Not a pothole or even an overly-sharp curve. It's how souls get to Hell, Gabrielle, it has to be able to handle a lot of traffic." "What really gets me," Satan said, "is that the asshole who came up with this challenge had to already know that! He saw it on the way in!" "And you want a way to cheat," I said. Satan nodded. "Can I just damn him anyway?" "Actually," I said, "you can. There's a lot of lore about you sticking to deals that you made, but those were all Satans that came before you, their rules don't apply. On the other hand, if you throw that away, neither do their powers. If you want to gain the benefits of those thousands of years, you have to also take on the drawbacks." "So I have to do the typical Satan thing where I obey the letter of the rule. I could build another highway," he was thinking out loud at this point. "That wouldn't be the highway to hell. It'd probably still work, granted, but I don't think it's what you're looking for," I said. "You have an idea," he said. I frowned. Technically, it was against the rules for me to tell the bosses how to do their jobs. Of course, we'd gone against those rules just a few days ago with the "Hell Is Other People, Specifically You: How To Do Your Job As Satan" briefing we'd put together. We got a lot of leeway. "Okay," I said finally. "The highway here, it goes all the way to Dis and into the Seventh Circle, right?" Satan nodded enthusiastically. "And it's one-way, right?" Satan snorted. "I know I'm new but I've got a little sense." "Well that's your answer then, isn't it?" Satan grinned. "I never said which direction they'd be driving, did I?" He started laughing. That's exactly where I'd been trying to lead him. I saw Gabrielle nod appreciatively. Satan wasn't done. "And I never said what kind of car they'd get. I'm thinking a'78 Grenada, no power steering, prone to overheating - it is Hell after all." "Are we done here?" Gabrielle murmured to me. Satan was obviously talking to himself at this point. "And the radio only gets Nickelback!" I nodded. "Yep. I think he'll do fine."

Where do babies come from? And where do they go? So small, so tiny! Surely Mother must know! . "What the fuck did you say?" she asks, with big black eyes. Her breath smells funny, oh no! It's the monster in Mother's disguise. You hide under the table with your trusted ted, but oh no! Alas! Her claws still find YOUR head. . "Where do babies come from and where do they go? Oh when I'm finished Child, surely this you will know." Oh how the words sting! Oh how they burn! The men held her down, and each took their turn. . And so here it is. You learn how wars really go! not machine guns and turrets but soldiers peckers, Forced into village girls, right in their down-below. . "Why are you crying?" she pushes your chest. You'd like to go bed now, so just that you suggest! "You asked for a story, and a story you'll get." She pulls out a coathanger, and you start to sweat. . "The girls screams whistled through the trees, Through the trees, whilst blood dripped down their knees! For the coat-hanger was forced deep in the lady, scrambling and killing what was left of her baby!" . Somehow you whipped, and dodged, and span, and twisted. Mother-monster bore her teeth, "You should have never existed!" . You scramble and run all the way to your bed, No blankets or pillow to lay beneath your head. . All over the home, Mother bangs and crashes, From the kitchen to the bathroom, From glass to pictures she smashes. . So next time you hear a whistle, whilst cozy in your bed. STOP and say a prayer, For a baby might be dead!

After years of trying to conceive, they adopted. He remembered his wife's broad smile as the nurse placed the most perfect baby boy in her arms. Now that the pressure to get pregnant was off, and being preoccupied with their precious new gift, another blessing happened and she became pregnant! After a nearly perfect pregnancy, the day had finally come! The baby was coming, today! The air was electric with chaos and happiness as they rushed around grabbing her birthing bag, as well as their toddler sons overnight bag for Grandmas house. As he backed the SUV out of the driveway he drove right into their garbage cans. Only, it wasn't garbage day and their son wasn't in his car seat.

1943 To John, whomever you may be- John, you are a stranger to me, and I to you, although we share a common pain in the form of our beloveds lying under identical slabs of stone. I wish to start off this letter by offering my sincere apologies. I did not mean to let my curiosity get the better of me, but everyday I venture here to place flowers on the grave of my brother, I can not help but notice the sealed letters left on the the grave marked "Sam." One day, my crudeness got the better of me and I read what you had left for your friend. Truly touched by your words, I felt the undeniable urge to write you. My name is Perry Foster, and my brother was Sergeant Ian Foster of the 118th battalion. He fell on July 13th, a day after his Private, Sam Greene, saved his life and sacrificed his own. Your dear friend Sam died saving his Sergeant, my brother, from certain capture. Ian died in battle to a painless head shot, instead of in a POW camp, thanks to Private Greene. I am deeply sorry for your loss. My brother and your friend are surely together on the other side, perhaps enjoying our chance encounter. Please write me anytime. Sincerely, Perry Foster

I hate this job. I hate this dingy, dimly lit room. I hate the bar and its constant clank of glass on wood. I hate the regular crowd that shows up every Saturday night like clockwork. My fingers finish striking the keys and some crazy old drunk stumbles on to the bench next to me. " SONNY! " he bellows in my ear. " CAN YOU PLAY THIS SONG FROM WHEN I WAS A KID? " Then he proceeds to try and sing the tune and it is a drunken disaster. I catch the bartenders eye from across the bar and he sees the distress in my face. He should know. It matches his. He helps the guy off and has him take a seat near the door. I start up my next song so I don't have to hear his babbling any more. There is that awful clink of glass on wood but it's okay, it's just the bartender slipping me another drink. Half in the bag is the only way we can get through a shift. The " bachelors " pop in around eleven. Paul is never going to be anything other than what he is, and his best friend David is a lifer in the navy. David is madly in love with his best friend and its baffling and pathetic that Paul doesn't see it. Or maybe he does, just doesn't want to hurt the guy's feelings. Fuck if I know. I play another song. My fingers dance over the keys like they're weaving a magic spell. The stockbrokers file in around eleven thirty. They're loud and awful. Sadie, the waitress, freezes up when they call her over. Poor kid is just trying to get through college and every goddamn night she has to deal with these assholes and their incessant comments and casual ass grabs. The manager looks on and does nothing because hey, he's a lazy sad sack. He flashes his shit eating grin over to me because he knows the only reason anyone is at his dive is because I happen to play really, really well. I hate this bar. I hate singing into this microphone that smells like stale beer. I hate the shitty tips and the constant " You're too good for here! " from the customers. I want to use these hands to rock my baby daughter to sleep, or cup my wife's face while I kiss her and tell her how beautiful she is. I want to use them to make a dresser, or skin a kill, ANYTHING but what they're good at. What they're so, SO PAINFULLY good at. I fucking hate the piano, man.

I can barely remember anything after it happened, let alone before it. Noise. Lots of noise. Screaming. My devastation. Arms around me, a shushing, a sweet voice. Maybe that of my friend. My sons, my daughters, my wife- all dead. I can not very much recall the rest, as it all goes by in a blur within my forever damaged mind. I lived a normal life, I assume, grieving like any father and widower would. The rest I learned from my journals- that my family was slaughtered by some masked serial killer, that my dear friend had begun to come to my home daily to comfort me and to ensure that I was alright. I, however, vividly remember the moment I slipped. I was in a restaurant with her- my friend- when I suddenly saw that masked killer, responsible for tearing nearly everything I loved from me. In that moment, I lost it all, and my mind fragmented, never to be fully repaired. Still, bits and pieces of memory come back to me- particularly her voice, trying to coax me from my incessant sobbing. I knew not what I was weeping for, merely that I had an all-consuming sense of loss and devastation. However, with my friend's care, I got better. I moved on, remembering more and more, acting normal again. Feeling happy again! Oh, how I can remember falling in love with that wonderful friend, as she cared for me so dearly and brought me out of the abyss. In fact, she fell for me too. Now I am glad, married again with a darling son and daughter, and though I will never be the same person I was before the traumatizing event, I am jovial merely to live the life I live with my dearly beloved family. Whenever I see a picture of what I had before, though- my sons and daughters and previous wife- I still grieve, as I forget them. Every picture and memory of them is as if looking at a stranger's family, a stranger's life. Each letter I wrote them, each video taken, every single remembrance- relics of a life another man lived within my body. They died twice- within the world and within my memory. And for those deaths, I still grieve.

It had been raining that day, harder than it had in quite some time. The dismal weather matched my state of mind as I looked down at the ground far below. As I stood there, the wind and rain playing with my hair, I had felt more free than I ever had before. This was my decision, Closing my eyes, I had stepped out into oblivion, ready to accept the warm embrace of death. From six hundred feet up, the impact of flesh onto stone is far more painful than I might have imagined, especially as it had not crossed my mind that I would there to actually register it. I remember laying there for quite some time, unable to move, not because of the damage to my body, but the sheer shock that I had survived. As it turns out, the fall had not even broken my skin. That was the day that everything changed, the true start to my life. I searched for years, wondering if I was alone, the only one that God had forgotten in his curse of death on the human race. I was young, only a few hundred years having passed from my awakening when I encountered Naftali. I had journeyed the world, from the deserts of Namibia to the circuses of Rome, and I had come to the conclusion that I was utterly alone. I was outside Jerusalem when I first saw her, on my way to the city in the wake of wondrous claims that had been made by the local population of a man that had conquered death. There were five, perhaps six men that had ganged up on her, beating her with stones and stabbing her with knives. I stayed out of it, unsure if what they were doing was permitted by local laws, but after several minutes of their violence, she remained alive and seemingly unhurt. One of the men struck her so hard in the back of the head that she fell to the ground, knocked free from the two that had been holding her upright. She finally lay still, and they left her in the dust. I would have moved on as well, had I not seen her twitch. It was not uncommon, I knew, having seen so much death myself over the years, but this was different. She stirred and rose to one knee, dusting herself off and arranging her tattered robes. I came closer, offering her a hand, and she took it, rising fully to her feet and smiling. "Are you alright?" I asked, hoping beyond hope. She looked at me, a light in her eyes. "You seem unsurprised, traveler. Have you seen such things before?" I thought for a moment, putting together what she had said in my mind. My Aramaic was broken at best, but I replied as best I could. The light in her eyes only grew brighter as we continued to talk, a conversation that has never really ended. We found others, as we journeyed together through the ages. There are five of us now, though I know not how many others might exist, alone as I once was.

Part 1 It was one of those historic moments that people remember for decades. One of those moments which makes people remember where they have been when it happened. I sat in a Starbuck's and tried to crack the WiFi password of the accounting firm in the office above me. Not that I wanted to sniff around their client database. I merely needed their access to NYSE. I wasn't in for the money of that either. I needed their secure access to various government servers. While my laptop happily correlated the long string of zeros and ones coming from the WiFi with those of cat videos, I sipped on an incredibly expensive and incredibly mediocre latte. The telly ran CNN instead of the BBC. My patriotism was hurt. I pretended to write an email when the banner on the bigger screen announced a press conference of the Minister of Public Health of Palunesia. Never heard of the place before, like almost everybody. The internet told me their major export was opium and slave workers. Their best trading partner for both was the middle east. The long-named and horse-faced Minister explained the waiting journalists that a cure for death had been found and the principal investigator, Dr Jaleel Baligarong, would explain the details right now. I guess, we all remember how the video feed stopped and CNN went back to reporting on some riots in South America. The barista switched channels after the crowd in the cafe threaded to reenact these riots right here, right now. The BBC broadcast went on for a few minutes longer, before being cut off as well. Later that day, CNN, the BBC, Reuters, and any other major news source published an apology that they have been duped by a bunch of Palunesian pranksters. The Palunesian Prime Minister made an appearance and denied everything short of the Kennedy assassination. News reporting reverted quickly to normal levels. For someone in my business, these are indicators of a government cover-up. My usual fare were secret trade agreements, surveillance programmes, and other evidence of undemocratic behaviour of the ruling elite. Brings more money than pilfering nude selfies from the unsecured social media account of some wannabe pop star. Better for the resume too. Should I mess up and get caught, I could still flee to the Chilean embassy. Llama steak is supposedly quite tasty. Anyway, I started to look around on the respective forums. A rumour here and there indicated that more things than gorillas, guerillas, and putsches were exported from the Palunesia rainforest. The Minister of Public Health had been found to be not so healthy after all. Hard to be healthy when you drown trapped in your own yacht. I checked my various sources for unsecured confidential information: the servers of the DMV, Homeland Security, NTSB, Scotland Yard, and the American Dental Association. Nothing. There was even more info on Bigfoot than on Dr Baligarong. That changed when I checked a deep-web shop. I came to sell a few selfies that had made their way onto my harddrive, but stayed for the immortality. Some dude with lots of karma points sold Baligarong's drug. Take two pills a day for a week and you're set. One hundred million US dollars in an escrow account and the rest of time is yours. Getting the money is easy when you're pretty, sing like an angel, or dance like Fred Astaire reincarnated. For guys like me, it's not that easy. If I had the money, I would retire on the same island as the escrow account and sip Mai Tais instead of lattes. There is no such thing as'impossible' for a man on a mission. I researched anything that brought me closer to this specific conspiracy. After six months of hard work, I discovered that the tonnage of Pemkahang fruits exported from Palunesia closely correlated with the number of transactions to a certain bank specialized in escrow accounts. Pemkahang fruits are the size of a small orange, have a shell like a coconut, and taste like gorilla feces, if the internet is to be believed. Yet, they have suddenly become en vogue with the rich people. You can store them in a hot, wet climate for almost forever (Bacteria and fungi don't like their taste either, goes an in-joke of biologists researching Pemkahang.), yet they are shipped from Palunesia in individually cooled, strongbox-like containers. Following a box around the world is surprisingly easy. If you know the shipping number. And have unlimited access to various customs agency worldwide. I selected handful of Pemkahang boxes at random and let the servers of the Colorado Department of Corrections do the work. I made it send me a text message whenever the shipping number appeared somewhere. Three months later A few of my boxes had been shipped to San Francisco and one was now en-route to a place called Fruitvale. It was delivered to an estate in the possession of a movie actress. She'died' later that week'of a overdose'. A pretty well-known entrepreneur in the social media craze received another box. Dead as a dodo one week later:'Skydiving accident'. A formerly famous front man of a boy band wrapped his Porsche around a tree, six days after he received a shipment from Palunesia. 'Death metal drummer dies in deadly blaze on his dairy farm', said The Sun. 'Did he deal with the devil?' Nope. Dealt with Palunesia. And used a bank with sloppy security. Actually, the local dentist had sloppy security that allowed me to use his account to hack into the bank, but that doesn't matter. What mattered was that the dead drummer deposited dough, three days before the box left Palunesia. I walked around in my basement office to think about it. Evidently, these people paid their price for immortality under the condition to disappear. Made sense to me. I wouldn't want the masses (or the American Government for that matter) to find out that I sold eternal life. Countries have been overrun for less. The question was: How do I get my share without paying? My answer was the same as to every question: Information wants to be free. Pay up or I'll ensure that. Like any good blackmailing, this required preparation and an insurance policy. I compiled the info in a file and placed it on a deep-web escrow account of my own. The price: One box of Pemkahang. The mask lay on the floor, ripped into pieces and soaked to an almost uniform red with blood. The man the mask had once belonged to sat tied to a chair, head hung low and bleeding from multiple facial wounds. The bleeding man wore a grand costume, neon red with a white and gold lighting bolt over his chest. Several other men surrounded the costumed prisoner, all brandishing weapons. One man stood out from the rest, tall and handsome, Italian descent with smooth black hair plastered backwards over his head. "To think I was scared of you." The tall man said taking a drag from his cigarette and inspecting the glowing end. "Piece of..." He stopped, eyeing his prisoner. "LOOK at me when I'M TALKING TO YOU!" The Italian man lashed out suddenly and punched the prisoner in the temple. There was a crunch of bone being fractured and the prisoner shook visibly, some token final effort to break free. The men around him simply laughed. "All yer fancy gadgets." The leader mocked, throwing the used cigarette end aside and holding his now empty hand out to one of his lackeys. "All yer muscle." His empty hand was filled with a large, silver object. "Guess you forgot you ain't immortal." The leader grabbed the prisoner's jaw and wrenched it upward, forcing him to make eye contact. The leader pressed the barrel of the gun to the prisoner's bleeding forehead, and pulled the trigger. "Get him out of here." The leader wiped his hands on a white silk handkerchief, producing and lighting another cigarette. "Leave him somewhere they'll find him."
