A machine came out from beyond the light. A well dressed men with a monocle stepped out of the machinery. I recognise that face. I recognise it anywhere. Its Alfonso. Whats he doing here crashing our little party? "Ah, Conway. I figured you'll be here, along with..... Conway..... wait you're talking to yourself from the past?" Asked Alfonso. "Yeah whats wrong with that, you son of a bitch?" I replied. "Arn't you scared of Time paradoxes? I uh..... I have to take my leave now." Alfonso said, with a tinge of genuine horror in his tone. "Time para-what? Can you ELI5 that for me please?" I confusely asked. "Bye bye Conway! Remember, you're not a scientist!" Alfonso exclaimed as he blasted back into the beam of light. Present and past me stared at him. Not knowing how to react. But we both agreed whatever he said was rubbish "Ok, in the future you wi END Author's note: thank you for reading:). If you enjoyed please do tell me. If you didnt please also leave some constructive feedback for me to improve on! Merry Christmas!

In the canine world, humans are celestial beings who live for more than 500years at a time. The caretaker of you and the past seven generations of your family will soon die. As usual, I woke up at 7am in the morning to wake up my master. I ran down the hallway energetically to his room, and call out to master. "Master! Master! Rise and shine!" However, that day was different..... Master did not wake up immediately as usual, I continue to call him, but to no avail, it seems that my calls were not heard. He laid there sleeping soundly. I went up to him and licked him in the face, and only then he opened his eyes slowly. Master spoke weakly instead of his usual tone, "Good morning, Junior.." His voice was so faint, even my super sensitive ears could only barely hear him. "Master what's wrong?" I asked him. He replied "I'm not feeling well today, let me rest a little more..." He went back to sleep while I went downstairs to meet my Julie, master's wife to have some breakfast. She was almost done with watering her plants when I got down. I called out to her good morning. She gave me a pat on the head and went on to prepare my breakfast. Her face wasn't filled with the usual bright smile which greeted me every morning, it was slightly gloomy. I went in the house ate my hearty breakfast. By that time only did master descended from his room. He was frail and weak today. He saw me, and gave me a good scratch under my chin. I always love it when he does that! He ate his breakfast with Julie, asking her about her plans for the "future." I stroll to the living room and wait for master to play with me, preparing my favourite ball toy and positioning myself in front of his favourite chair. Breakfast took a while, and master stumbled slowly to his favourite and laid in it comfortably. I pounced to signal to him to play with me. Instead of throwing my toy, master carried me. He whispered as he caressed my face "Junior, you look just like your father and his father and the rest of the seven generations, handsome and a fine looking hound.." He continued even softly" I've got a request, take care of Julie for me when I'm gone." I looked at him in puzzlement. He continue to stroke me gently, each stroke more gentle and faint than the previous. He smiled at me and soon closed his eyes. I licked master, but he didn't wake up. I barked loudly, yet his body never respond.I looked over at Julie for affirmation and she went over to carry me. As she was carrying me I saw tears rolling down her cheeks. She whimpered and spoke in a shaky manner "Let John (master) rest, we will go visit Jack and Jill to tell them about the news.."

Prince Horace raised an eyebrow at his aging father. "Your Highness, that's..... that's your servant. Timothy and I stand before you; why did you go to such great lengths to crown a mere commoner?" "Silence," King Jerry croaked. "I have crowned the rightful heir!" "But I'm the eldest," Prince Timothy protested. "If you're going by inheritance, I would be the king." "And," Horace added, "if you were to go by competence, it would be Sir Kendrick. He has, by far, proved himself to be a wonderfully skilled knight, with the might and intelligence to match even the greatest kings. If you do not wish to pass on the crown to your sons, I suppose I understand that, but..... why Ian?" "Silence!" the king roared. "Ian shall rule after me!" "Father, he can't walk two steps without tripping on his own feet," Timothy said. "And he does nothing but gossip all day," Horace exclaimed. "And he scares the chickens," one of the maids screeched. The king stamped his foot. "Are none of you listening?! Ian is the rightful heir! He's my son!" The court gasped in unison. Sir Beritan, a particularly effeminate nobleman, stuck his nose in the air and scoffed, "Even our dear king isn't above fathering bastards!" King Jerry waved his hand dismissively. "Not like that, you presumptuous pansy. You see, once upon a time, I was convinced that I was..... er..... impotent, if you catch my drift." "Catch your..... Father, why are you using anachronistic language?" "Silence! So, I became concerned that I wouldn't have any children. Thus, I grabbed Ian and told him that when I died, he would be my heir. I am going to keep that promise and make Ian king!" Twelve days later, the kingdom was burnt to the ground.

All my life I had been fascinated with the memories I can recall that weren't my own. Heterochromia iridum was always fascinating to me. I always felt like one of those unique dogs you see with mismatched eye colors. As a child, I would fondly recall hunting in the woods. I chased humans, but I was as quick as a wolf. My dreams of creeping through the night, undetected by others, always were so vivid. Finally as an adult, one night during one of my chasing dreams, I finally achieved my objective, I caught the human in the chase. Once I caught him, I tore him apart with my teeth. I could feel the blood drip down the sides of my mouth. It felt good, tasty, like BBQ sauce. I didn't want to wipe it off, it was delicious and a badge of honor. I was thrilled with the kill. Towards the end of the dream, right before I woke up, I saw something that chilled me to the bone. In this dream, I wiped away the blood from my mouth. It wasn't a paw that wiped the blood away. I never caught the person in my previous dreams over the years. I wiped away the blood with my human hand. It wasn't until I confronted my mother that she confessed. I wasn't a person with an excess of melanin in one eye, I was the recipient of a donor eye.

There was another blockage in section 13-E of the New Albion metropolitan sewers. That would be why I'm down here 100 feet below the ground, wearing a hard hat on my head and a handkerchief over my nose. I'm the chief sewage engineer for the city, and it's my job to take care of these things, mainly because there's nobody else who has the experience to do it. Besides, having sewage back up into the commercial district is never good for business and New Albion prides itself on maintaining certain standards. I had two assistants with me Joe and Adam. It took us 15 minutes just to walk to this section from the closest access point. It's dark and the sewer smelled heavy and foul, so nothing unusual there. The section was made up of a main tunnel that was 18 ft tall with a vaulted ceiling. We had carbide lamps on our hats and we could make out that the center of the tunnel was filled with a river of sewage several feet deep. On either side of the smelly river, there was a sidewalk about two feet wide, which were were standing on. Along the main section, there were also smaller side tunnels with sewer water periodically spilling into the main river. Each smaller tunnel was about shoulder high and just large enough to fit one man. "We're here, boys" I said to my two assistants. "Let's get to work!" We didn't know exactly where the blockage was, but I knew it was one of the smaller tunnel leading to the sewage river. The problem was finding out which one, and there were about a dozen of them in this section. It was a dirty task of sticking half you body into the tunnel and prodding around. My assistants each carried a pole with a hook on the end that we brought along just for this purpose. Joe and I started checking one side of the main section, and Adam was checking the other. He was able to cross the sewage river by walking over a small bridge at one end of the section. After we checked about 4 or five small tunnels, I heard Adam say "Boss, come here quickly!" Joe and I turned and saw Adam pointing to a small tunnel. I guessed correctly that he found the blockage, but I didn't know why he seemed so frantic. Adam began quickly moving towards the small bridge. He was about to cross over when he saw Joe and I approach. He backed away to let us cross and he was keeping an eye on the small sewer tunnel the whole time. "What did you see, Adam?" I asked. "Something large is moving in there!" He said. It's not uncommon to find living things in the sewers, especially for a city as large as New Albion. Rats and small jellies were common. However, for something to plug up a side tunnel, it must at least be the size of a man. I prayed it wasn't a large jelly, because that would take all day to pull it out. I walked up to the side tunnel and stuck my head in. The carbide lamp mounted on my hardhat show a bunch of garbage - offal, bones, bits of wood, etc. It was blocking the way and in the center of it, there was indeed something moving. I stuck my hook into the pile of garbage to pull some of it loose. When I did this, I saw a squirming mass emerge from the garbage and several large tentacles slither out. I backed away as several octopus tentacles emerged from the side tunnel and started to grip the edge, trying to pull itself out. "Bog octopus!" I yelled. My two assistants immediately got between me and the octopus. It was trying to pull its elastic body out of the tunnel and we used this time to cross the bridge to the other side of the sewage river. With a wet "plop!" The body of the bog octopus freed itself from the side tunnel and fell onto the sidewalk. It was a lot larger than I expected, easily the size of a cow. I had only heard of a bog octopus before but never seen one up close. From time to time, they swim up the sewer pipes and wreak havoc on whatever city they happen to pop out in. The three of us began retreating to the street access point. Thank god bog octopus are slow! Despite this, we still ran as fast as we could. As we stood at the bottom of the manhole, we heard no signs of the octopus. "What do we do now?" Joe asked. "We tell the mayor, and he hires a couple of adventurers, maybe battle-wizards to take care of it." I said. "This is way out of our league. They should just be happy we unclogged the tunnel."

Randall approached the Pearly Gates slowly, unsurely, with the unsteady gait and expression of a life-long agnostic facing down what he had always written off as metaphorical narrative fantasy. "Hello, Randall," spake (they always'spake' in these things) the bearded old Caucasian man standing behind a lectern. Or podium. Randall never did figure out the difference. "Uh, are you..... are you Saint Peter?" Randall asked, confused, somewhat fearful. Catholic school had painted a rather unflattering picture of what would happen to nonbelievers..... a picture that was suddenly dominating Randall's imagination. "I am. Welcome to the Pearly Gates." Before Saint Peter lay a gigantic book, millions of pages long, with Randall's name engraved in gold on the cover. His life. Every moment, every detail, every sin and every kindness written out in excruciating detail. He sweated a little bit. "Okay, let's get this started," said Saint Peter. "Now, if I could just get your appendix, I'll be able to work my way through this." "My..... appendix, sir?" asked Randall. "I'm sorry, but I had it out when I was a kid. It was inflamed, so the doctors removed it." "Ugh, for Christ's sake, not another one. How the hell am I supposed to find my way through this tome without a proper appendix?'Faith, page six hundred and three thousand, four hundred ninety five."Crisis of faith, page seven hundred and forty two thousand, sixty three.' And so on. You mortals and your modern medicine really do make my job a pain in the ass." Grumbling, Saint Peter began thumbing through the pages of the impossibly long book, mumbling things like "Catholic school..... married..... kids..." After a few minutes, Randall noticed a line had formed behind him. It was fast, but the line seemed to go on for tens of thousands of people. They looked to be all Asian, as far as Randall could tell. Looking up, Saint Peter noticed them and cursed. "Crapshackle, the typhoon was today, wasn't it? The hell with it. Just go in." The gates swing wide and Randall strolled into Heaven. As he passed the lecterndium, he could hear Saint Peter yelling into an intercom about outdated library technology.

"What do you mean no adventurers allowed?!" Maz growled at the guard, her hands already on the handles of her axes. Gregor held both of his arms in front of her, holding the disgruntled Orc back. "Maz, sweetie, if they say no adventurers, then we can just go somewhere else," Gregor shouted at her, trying to channel as much arcane strength into his arms as he could. He really wasn't in the mood for fighting the town guard. Maz was nigh uncontrollable when she was angry, and while he was no slouch, he wasn't really much of a match for an orc warrior. The guard watched the human mage struggle with the orc, utterly disinterested in pretty much everything. He'd never wanted to be a guard. He'd wanted to be a cobbler. But, he'd completely beefed his cobbler's exam, so he needed to raise money to retake it. And being a guard paid well enough for the time being, so here he was. He chewed some tobacco like a goat chewing cud, and spit periodically on the ground next to him. "Squatbird shit! This town is the closest one for kilometers with a Buffalo Wyvern Wings, and I don't want to miss watching the Rook Abbey Lancers again! " Maz shouted, pointing one of her axes over Gregor's shoulder at the guard, knocking Gregor's wide-brimmed wizard hat off in the process. "Maz! Chill! I'll handle this!" Gregor shouted at her, pushing her back. Maz growled loudly, and snorted in Gregor's face, pushing him back in retaliation as she finally relented. Gregor stumbled back at the forceful push and eyed her angrily. She hooked her axe back into its sheath, and leaned against the wall of one of the parapets, furiously digging around in her satchel. "Get this jizzwaddle to let us through, wizard. If I miss Ollie McDougal's first joust of the season, it's your ass," Maz grumbled, producing a small leather pouch stuffed with the hardest jerky Maz had been able to find at the last town. She bit down, tearing the dried beef apart and chewing rapidly in frustration. Gregor knew that most of the time her hard persona towards him was simply bluster; the two of them worked well together, and she knew it. But when she started calling him ' Wizard,'that was when she was serious. If he couldn't pull this off, he thought, then being unable to shave and running low on Ol Toby would be the least of his worries. He whipped his hat up off the ground as he walked to the guard, dusting it off and plopping it on his head. " Okay, what the fuck, dude? " Gregor asked, trying to put on his most official look, which happened to be about as official as goblin in a suit. " Carl, " the guard said. " What? " " My name is Carl. Not ' dude, the guard sneered, spitting onto the ground again. " Whatever. What's the deal here, Carl? Why no adventurers? " Gregor asked. " Lord's orders. Nobody gets in today. " " Penrith was totally fine with adventurers and travelers last week! What happened? " " New lord now, " Carl said, spitting again, " Came in... Ehh... Probably about five days ago. " Gregor groaned and slapped his palm to his face. Some lord coming in and taking over wasn't anything new for the Kingdom of Penrith, or whatever it was called now. It happened pretty regularly, as was common in adventuring towns. But a new lord coming in and ruling that adventurers were no longer allowed was definitely new. Gregor rubbed his eyes and exhaled loudly. " Match starts in twenty, Wizard, " Maz said nonchalantly from the wall. Gregor spun around on his heel, and leveled a finger at her, his eyes burning with arcane energy. " I'LL HANDLE THIS, MAZ, " Gregor spat in frustration. Maz rolled her eyes and bit off another chunk of jerky, chewing loudly. Gregor huffed and turned back to the guard, who seemed genuinely surprised the wizard was still trying to get in. " What happened to the old king? " Gregor asked, relatively certain he knew the answer. " Dead. Good riddance, too. All these laws about business owners have to have a license, no drinking in public, no pleasure houses. Bunch of goblin shit, " Carl said, punctuating his statement with a spectacular spit. " Uh-huh. Who's the new king? " " Some evil lord. Shug-rth Yurl Durf or something. I dunno. He pays guards more. People can pretty much do what they want now, you know? So, big celebration going on; the town's closed off for the next day. " " Is that why you're so butthurt about letting us in? Cause your worthless ass is stuck out here? " Maz quipped. " Yeah, pretty much, " Carl admitted. Gregor sighed. He was getting nowhere with this. It was all well and good if the villagers and townspeople were happy with a new lord, even if he was some loony dark lord who worshipped elder gods, but he really needed to bathe. And get some more wizard weed. And shave. And make Maz take a bath; she smelled terrible. Maybe I should try a pity approach, he thought. " Look dude, " " Carl. " " Look Carl, I'm wicked low on Ol Toby. I haven't shaved in three days. I'm hungry. My companion smells like a slaughterhouse. " " I noticed. " " Eat hot shit, " Maz said to both Gregor and Carl, still chewing with her mouth open. The guard gave Maz a rude hand gesture. " Can we please just get in? We won't do any adventuring. We just need to use an inn, and we'll be gone tomorrow, " Gregor pleaded. The guard seemed unmoved by his plight. " Nope. " " Oh come on! " Gregor lamented, leaning forward and shaking his hands. " Like I said, the town is closed off for the next day. Besides, who's to say you won't come in and try to overthrow the dark lord? " Carl grumbled. " We won't! " Gregor exclaimed, " We'll keep to ourselves! " " ...Seems strange, some weird wizard and a pissy orc coming up to the gate, on the day of a big celebration. Asking all kinds of questions about the dark lord. Things are great now. We don't need some lousy adventurers mucking that all up." " I don't want to take over! I lack any and all aspirations for leadership! All I want to do- " Gregor shouted, dropping to his knees on the dirt road and throwing his hat off, " is get some more Ol Toby, eat some Buffalo Wyvern Wings, have a shave, and sleep in a shitty bed in the shitty inn! IS THAT TOO MUCH TO ASK? " Carl stared down the wizard, a look of severe irritation on his face. All Gregor could hear were the sounds of merriment inside the town, and Maz's loud chewing. " My cousin owns the inn, " Carl grumbled, leveling his pole-arm at Gregor " And I don't appreciate you talking shit- " Maz, who had nonchalantly walked over, took the opportunity to grab the distracted guard, putting her palm against his helmet and smashing his head into the wall. With a loud clang and clanking of metal, he crumpled to the ground, unconscious. " I hope they didn't run out of extra spicy wings, " Maz said simply, walking through the gate, leaving Gregor kneeling on the ground next to the now passed-out guard. Gregor stared at the collapsed body, and then looked up at Maz, then back at the body. He grabbed his hat off the ground and walked quickly after her. " Why didn't you do that when we first showed up? " Gregor said, plainly irritated. " I like watching you humiliate yourself, " Maz said with a dull smile, " Now buy me some wyvern wings. "

The most tedious part of the new program was the reintegration of mimics. While legal provisions were made to ensure the success of society's newest and brightest, most of the practical details had to get worked out at ground level. At first glance, it sounded feasible. After all, with the retention of most memories the mimics carried a majority of their parent's educations, qualifications, and emotions. Where it got dicey, though, was the prevention of future incarceration. Inspector Lewis Hill, for the third time in as many years, shared an interrogation room with Robert. The system's problem child. Roberts had sprung up all over America and while the law had stipulations regarding the incarceration of convicts, it cared little of the actions of their mimics. "Am I being detained?" Hill snorted. "Asks the man cuffed to the table. Fuck you, you know the drill by now." Robert smiled, tapping his fingers on the desk. A monster like him had no right to three lives, let alone one. And yet he sat across the table from Hill, blissfully indifferent to his future. The system had created an entirely new issue when people like him started showing up all over the map. Robert, now a third-generation mimic, had murdered two of his families. If he'd had time to start a third, he would have done it again. Instead, he murdered his fiance's parents. He likely counted on the next mimic to take care of the woman herself. "I'm thirsty." "Try swallowing your spit. You'll be here awhile." Hill shrugged, struggling to maintain his demeanor. He felt ready to burst at the seams, sharing a room with a monster like Robert. "I assume you'll be asking me some questions before long." Robert continued tapping his fingers on the stainless steel table. Hill despised everything about the man, from his balding white head to his white collar business casual attire, complete with tan loafers. Something about the man just rubbed Hill the wrong way. It was as if Robert lacked something every other human had, and not just because he was a mimic. "Do you know what you are?" Hill asked. That smile again. "Are we playing this game once more? Very well, I'll bite. No, Hill. I don't know what I am." Inspector Hill cringed at the response. He felt like he was being played. Where was his partner? "You're a mimic. Created as a stand-in for someone who is no longer fit for society. Except you aren't fit for society either. Never were." Robert laughed. "And this should surprise me? I've read the news. I know what I'm capable of." "Do you? So what does the cleaning crew do next time to take that away? How do we keep Robert'the Fourth' from committing the same atrocities?" He was just burning time now. Reyes should arrive within the hour to get the testimony on paper. "Honestly, I have no clue. I can still tell you something you probably don't know, though." Hill rolled his eyes. He imagined gouging Robert's. "Yeah? And what's that?" "Do you think it's a little strange that I'll be getting a fourth iteration? And after that, a fifth? Possibly sixth? What of those who fail to commit felonies? They get only one chance at life, so where's the payoff?" Hill shrugged. He had no idea where Robert was going with this and didn't care. His time was better spent imagining how gratifying it would be to just end Robert's line entirely with a single shot. Felons get mimics. Murder victims, though...... "Has it never occurred to anyone how useful this technology could have been if implemented in almost any other fashion? How America might have actually changed for the better if Capitol Hill wasn't overrun with lobbyists for private, for-profit mass incarceration facilities?" He actually had a point. So did the rounds in Hill's chamber, though. "These prisons are cash cows being milked for every- " The door behind Hill opened and two men stepped in. "Reyes, took you long enough. Let's get this over with. He's another waste of time." Robert Stephenson was incarcerated within the week. They had gotten a full testimony without any trouble and the process to reinstate his new mimic was practically streamlined at that point. It would be just a few months before the next one was back on the street and the cycle would start all over again. Hill knew there was only one way to end it. The system made sure of that. Some felons were redeemable. A lot of the less violent ones were simply victims of circumstance, and a second chance for the mimic was as good as a new lease on life. But the few that were deeply bothered could not be corrected. Whatever caused them to run against the grain of society had to be genetic. Hill didn't know the science behind it, nor did he care. When he murdered that last Robert, all felt right with the world. Seeing the blood spill from his skull was the most beautiful thing he'd ever witnessed. Hill would never have children, and he would spend the rest of his life behind bars, but at least he'd sleep at night. Life behind bars with at least three men he was responsible for convicting. He'd expected that. Being welcomed by hundreds of Lewis Hills, though. That was what made the entire thing worth it.

The words on the page disappear as soon as I read them. Nothing holds, not time, not space, not names or faces or colors or things, not for more than twenty minutes at a time. I go somewhere and twenty minutes later I forget where I am, or how I got there. I never leave home much because when I do, I get lost. I have no family, for they left me long ago. It's hard to understand someone like me, and so rather than help, most pull away. I do not blame them. Every once in a while I reach back and realize another is gone. I'm locked in a constant race against time. If I don't stay busy enough, maybe it's my daughter's wedding. A nap, maybe the sound of my mother's voice. I never know when I will lose them or when. Or which ones. I don't remember the order of them anymore. And so I keep a frenzied pace. I read. I watch videos. Sometimes the same ones over and over. I rarely sleep because sleep is to lose, and no matter how hard I try I will not lose her face.

They all loved Christmas, the people of Groot, The tinsel and presents, twas such a hoot! They put up the trees and they put up the lights. Christmas was coming, in just seven nights! The shops were busy, they were all buying gifts. Some lazy parents left their kids by the lifts. People sung songs, and others were kissing. No one had noticed the children go missing. Three nights before Christmas the children returned, They sung new songs from someone they'd learned. These songs were not happy, not merry, or cheerful They were dark, long and solemn, and quite the earful. On the night before Christmas, all through Groot came a song It seemed quite alarming, like something was wrong. The sky cracked open, as did the ground. There was no more Christmas with Cthulhu around.

Today one of my underlings told me how hard it is to fall. I promtly answered that falling is easy, you simply don't stop at the edge of the cliff, just like the last 00-agent they sent. That got me the usual " please don't kill me " brand of nervous laughter, followed by an explanation on how he meant falling to villainy. I knew what he meant, of course, but he was one of the meatheads, so I allowed it. He was wrong, you know. Falling to villainy is even easier that falling from the top of the vulcano, you simply, lose your focus. The day you think that the big picture is what you see in the mirror is the day you've fallen. It's not about blowing up banks in London, firebombing offices on Wallstreet or kidnapping the children of world leaders, all of that is just frosting, making your cake look good. You know why I became a villain at first? The world was suffering. Pityful politicians, devilish dictators and evil economics, all running rampant. There was no focus, no clarity. Everyone was looking out for themselves, having nothing to unite them. That first assassination was out of anger, I must admit, but it felt wonderful. More important; it got everyone's attention, good people and bad. They looked at me. They were worried. Some was laughing after the first one, but only briefly. The next handfull of kills made everyone afraid, everyone was looking. And I was looking right back at them. It soon dawned on me that I had found the one uniting factor that no human could deny; anger. I had to ride it, use it to unite the world in a common goal. It took a while, building the organization, stealing the funding, hiring muscle, building a brand for myself. But was worth it. In a world with no super heroes to deal with him, the super villain is everyone's problem. As long as I am here, they will be more busy fighting me than each other. And life has improved for everyone, well almost everyone..... So what if it costs someone a president every now and then? Most of the hostages are usually saved, especially the children. Very few normal people actually suffer harm when I strike, I am very adamant about that, you know. I have never lost my focus! I do have one big regret though. I should have found a like-minded companion to share my crimes with, having the meatheads and amoral scientists as my only conversation partners is really a chore in the long run. And now I'm talking to my cat..... great..... I guess it's time to kidnap some more stimulating conversation, perhaps a nobel prize winner...

"We need to talk..." I stood there speechless, mouth agape. 5 long years it had been. And suddenly, there she stood on the doorstep. Her hair was matted. Her skin was a pale blue hue under the moonlight. Her face was worn and tired. She wore a strange necklace. The past half decade must have been rough on her. Silently, I let her into my home. Her clothes were soaking wet. I offered her a sweater and some sweat pants. She declines, preferring to just sit by the fire. The myriad of conflicting emotions overwhelm me. Anger, confusion, and happiness swirl messily in my head. She had seem troubled the days before disappearing, but could always muster a smile. "As long as you're here with me, I could ask for nothing more," she would always say to me. But, one day, she just left. No note. No explanation. How could she leave without telling me? The anger rose within me. I thought that we had always been close! I thought she could tell me everything! There were no secrets between us! Anger quickly gave way to the fonder memories. She always let me have the last cookie. "I'll just get fat. You can have it," she would say. When the neighborhood bully Tara the Terrible I would call her came after me, my sister gave her a good whooping. She was grounded for a month, but Tara never bothered me again. "Why did you leave? Why did you not tell us you were leaving?" I demanded. My sister tugged at her necklace. It appeared heavy and uncomfortable. "I didn't have the strength to tell you, Sis. I knew you would be disappointed in me. You would have called me weak. I couldn't resist giving in. There was nothing for me here. This promised me freedom and salvation." She lifted her necklace as she spoke. "What do you mean you had nothing? You had me! I was here for you!" I could feel the aching pain rising in my chest. "Yes, Sis. You were the only one I had. That's why I couldn't tell you I was leaving. You would have convinced me to stay. Anyways, I realize I had been wrong. The pain I caused you was much more than the pain I ever felt. I came to beg for your forgiveness. I promise to stay here with you. You can talk to me any time. I am here for you." Tears were streaming down my face. For the last 5 years, I was so angry. But, here she was once again. I knew she cared about me. She came back just for me! "Yes, I forgive you. Please don't ever leave me again." My sister continued playing with her necklace. "Would you like a cookie? You look like you haven't eaten for 5 years. You're all skin and bones." "Haha. No thanks, Sis. I'll just get fat. You can have it." "Will you stay the night?" "Sure Sis. I'll sleep right here by the fire. It's nice and warm here." The next morning, my sister was gone. On the floor was her necklace. I picked it up. It was simple and cheap. Only made of rope, with a running bowline knot in the back. I put it in my purse and got into my car. It was a 30-minute drive, but it was a drive I had made numerous times in the last 5 years. I parked on the gravel lot. Across the road was a flower-lined path. I saw my sister at the end of the path. "Here. You forgot your necklace. If you don't mind, I'd like to hold onto it for you. It was only making you uncomfortable. I brought you some cookies. I know what you're going to say, but I really want you to eat them this time." A tear rolled down my cheek. "Thanks for coming back to me. I really missed you." I set the tray down by her grave. I got up and began walking back to my car.

A., I feel unresolved. For the longest time, you were my best friend and favorite person. There is something you may not know, and it is not easily expressed. I'll give it a try: Things I feel in my relationship with you: respect, kinship, awe. There are more, but those are very alive. It's significant in that you were the first person with which I truly felt that way. I felt connected, in a very content, tribal sense. As though you were my long, lost sister and I had found you, and life was wonderful again. I tremendously enjoyed all of our adventures. I felt challenged, and I appreciated sharing that with you. I had a bit of a rough time at university. After I'd gotten out of it, I had wanted more than anything to spend some time around you again, if only for a short while, to help with my perspective on going forward. I was a bit lost, and you were my favorite person. I don't really know what happened with you around that time, and I'd love to talk about it. I had always imagined we'd grow old and be neighbors, or at the very least, live in the same region. The distance has been rough on me. Perhaps more than I'll ever admit. I've gotten better, though, I think. I imagine you'd be proud. I'd love to see you again.

The subway system had been built a long time ago, so long that there were not really any good records of its design, or even of the exact date when it had opened. It had been here as long as anyone could remember, as far back as paper records lasted. In all that time, if the records were to be believed, not a single train had malfunctioned, and the only maintenance that the cities had done on any of the trains was to reupholster the seats every once in a while. Molly supposed then, that she was actually quite fortunate to be present on the one train where something did go wrong. Fortunate in a certain specific way, at least. It had been two weeks now since she had wished silently that this train journey would never end so that she wouldn't have to go to work. So far it hadn't ended. And while she was grateful for not being at work, Molly now wished that they would actually reach their destination soon. She had known just like everyone else, that the subway system was weird in certain ways. The amount of time that a train took to get from one place to another had very little correspondence to the distance between those places over the surface, and it was usually much less than one would expect. The journey from New York to Paris, for example, took a mere ten minutes, despite the fact that the trains seemed to move no faster than 60 kilometres per hour. It was uncanny. There were other questions too. Strange things sometimes flashed past the windows in the dark of the tunnels. The tracks didn't appear to electrified, and the trains still ran even when the power was out. And perhaps most strangely of all, exploring the tracks on foot quickly led you back around into the very same station you started from. People walked through the tunnel on one side of the station, and five minutes later they came out the tunnel on the other side, with a confused look on their faces. Something wasn't quite right about the subways, but no one could quite put their finger on it, and it was the fastest method of travel that anyone knew of, so people used it despite the mystery. And if there was one thing that the subways were, it was reliable. Not a single train had ever been late. Until now, anyway. Molly was amusing herself by looking out the windows, to see if she could tell what the occasional bright objects that flashed by in the darkness were. She never could. There were vague hints of form, but nothing identifiable. They had been fortunate in that this train had been making a journey that on the surface would have crossed an ocean. Thus there was a plentiful cargo of food and water in several of the cars. They had enough for several months. There were also a few crates of rubber ducks. As for what happened to the food and water afterwards, well there was one car in the back that they always kept to door closed to. Sleeping arrangements were uncomfortable, but they could have been worse. Nevertheless, there were a few outbursts. Being cooped up in the same train for two weeks with a bunch of strangers was starting to get to some people. Heck, it was starting to get to Molly too. It seemed that the only people who were at all happy about this development were the Trainists, a religious group that worshipped the subway system. There were ten of them on this particular train, and they all believed that the occupants of this particular train had been selected by the Great Subway System to fathom its deepest secrets, and then enter into the paradise at the center of the earth. "Who knows," thought Molly, "maybe they're right." Molly had befriended two other passengers named Ernest and Lily. The three of them hadn't known each other at all before, but now they were sort of like a team. They played card games with each other to pass the time, and told long, elaborate, silly stories. Each of them had revealed some secrets to the group that they had never told anyone else. Even if they didn't die on this train, Molly knew that she would be friends with Ernest and Lily until she died. They were really good people. And Ernest was kind of cute. Molly got up from the window. The past few flashes had been vaguely human in form, and it was starting to creep her out. She sat down by Ernest and Lily. "Are we there yet?" she asked. It had become a classic joke in the first few days of the journey, and now it had evolved into a sort of universal greeting. "We'll be there in twenty minutes," Ernest and Lily echoed back. They fell to discussing their favourite topic: crazy plans for getting off the train. "We could shatter one of the windows," suggested Lily, "and jump out." "People tried that in the shit car," said Molly "to clear out the stench. It didn't work. The windows on this thing are super tough. Its like a rolling prison." "Plus, how would we even get back?" pointed out Ernest, "we don't know how to navigate the tunnels, and since no one can leave a station except in a train, probably no one can enter a station except in a train too." "Huh," said Molly, "okay, how about this? We all stand on one side of the train. Maybe it'll tip off the tracks or something." "And why would we want to do that?" asked Lily. "I dunno," said Molly, "just a thought." Some sort of commotion was going on in the car in front of them. The trio went to investigate. A man was standing in the middle of the car. He was holding some kind of clicker in his hand, there was a lot of space around him, and he was yelling at the top of his voice. "Okay everyone, if I press this button the bomb goes off. If anybody gets any closer, or tries anything, the bomb goes off. Nobody try anything." "A terrorist," Lily hissed to Molly, "after all this time." "Apparently," said Molly. "I was going to do this when we got to the station," said the terrorist, "but it looks like that ain't gon na be happening, so I'm just going to have to settle with killing you train people." Molly remembered that he had called himself Lucas, or something like that. "Why am I doing this, you ask," said Lucas, "simple. There is something deeply wrong about this subway system. It is the work of the devil, no doubt about it. Am I the only one who has seen twisted demons flashing past the windows on the way to work? This has to end. This demonic train ride proves it." "Sacrilege," cried out a Trainist, and he rushed Lucas. Lucas clicked the clicker, and nothing happened. Lucas was rapidly restrained while muttering something under his breath about the "dead bloody battery." Soon, it was over. "Well, that was dramatic," said Ernest, trying to hide how relieved he actually was. "Yeah, well we're safe now," said Molly, "I think that She was interrupted by a loud explosion coming from underneath the train. The entire train shook violently, but no one was seriously injured, and miraculously, it kept on moving. Apparently, these trains were more durable than Lucas had calculated. Then everyone heard a sound. It was the beautiful squeaking noise of the train's brakes being applied. They were slowing down. Cheering erupted across the train, and Molly, Lily, and Ernest got into a super excited jumping up and down three way hug. "Are we there yet?" asked Molly. "Heck yes, we are," Lily shouted back at her. They pulled into the station. It was completely empty. No one was around to greet them after their ordeal. Had they arrived in the wrong station in the middle of the night? It didn't matter: they were safe. The people rushed out of the train, like a tide. They ran up the station's steps to the surface, and looked out at the world. Ernest, Lily, and Molly looked out with them. She didn't know where they were, but it certainly wasn't Earth. "Aw crap," thought Molly, "I'm going to be soo late for work."

An estate sale's a hell of a thing, cleaning out someone else's garbage and wondering, the whole time, whether any of it's worth a damn to them or to you. All a matter of preference, I guess, but this place, far as I could tell, didn't have a single thing worth preferring. Down in this fella's basement, ran into a stubborn old sheet of plywood stuck against the wall. "Nothing left behind," the client's worksheet had said, but this goddamned board wouldn't budge. Last bit of junk always ended up a pain in the ass. Why couldn't it have been a Rolex. Or a rare painting. Who am I kidding, though? God knows a dope like me wouldn't know good art if I painted the damned thing myself. Art curator could send me a letter, proclaiming perfection, and I'd still probably junk it. Had to go out to my truck and grab a crowbar to pry that wood board from the wall. Damn near bent the thing on my first tug, though. "Determined son-of-a-bitch," I said, my lips pursed as I pried at it again. "For the love of Christ," I yelled out, "get off the fucking wall!" I guess that final pull was a real good one, because just then, as I wailed out curses that would've made my daddy proud, the wood flung free and the lucky guy I am hit me smack dab in the forehead. I laid there, half-conscious, whispering angry little things to myself. Fucking estate sales. A Rolex. Just once, a Rolex, please, you sadistic gods of estate sales, just once give me that watch. Even if it's one of the cheaper ones, a used one, silver even, I'll never ask for another thing again. I noticed the crowbar next to me, lying there, bent right down the middle. Never seen wood do a thing like that. Matter of fact, I don't even remember pulling the board free. I guess a blow to the head'll do that to you. As I got up, right where the board used to be, I saw what looked like an elevator: two chrome doors, cut right down the middle, with a set of buttons on the side. Went up and tired the buttons. Nothing. No lights, no click, no ching. Weird. Looked like it might be some visual art, something you'd see at one of those contemporary art museums. You know, the ones with the upside down toilets and stuff. Maybe, I thought, this was like that. Thing is, behind those doors, through that little crack right down their center, I could see the slightest bit of light. Real feint. You could easily miss it. For a second, I thought that maybe it was coming from the outside, but then I remembered that I was in the basement. What a dope I was. Blow to the head'll do that to you. If that stupid crowbar hadn't bent so far, I'd use it to pry those doors open. Who knows, though. Maybe it would. I walked over and examined the thing. It looked like a crooked spoon at this point. There was no way I could get enough leverage with it to open the doors especially not these ones, heavy as they looked. "Ding!" The fucking shit? Behind me, just like that, with a ding, the doors opened. It was fully functional had lights and everything. At this point, I was thinking, "you know what, keep the damned Rolex." Too weird for me. But the thing is, it's a lot easier to say'no' to another roll at the craps table when you're back home sitting on the couch; when you're in Vegas, though, temptation, more often than not, says, "c'mon, lucky number seven!" That's why, God help me, I stayed the hell away from Vegas. I found myself in a remarkably similar situation, though. And while my gut said, "walk away," the gambler in me rolled the dice and walked inside. It was pretty nice in there swanky, even. Had these little designs, looked Greek, running along the edges of the mirrors. Red carpet, too. There were only two buttons: "UP and DOWN." And I figured since I'd already seen upstairs, why not take a look down below. "Oh..... well..... fuck it!" I said as I pressed the down button. I started smiling nervously. Almost a laugh, really the kind a meth head gets as he waits his turn, watching as his buddy lights up and gets off. A "hand-it-over" smile. Wait a minute..... What the fuck was I doing? The doors closed and I felt the elevator jerk. "Ohhh!" I screamed out, looking around for someone to share the fear with, but finding only my reflection in the mirror, terrified and smiling like a meth head. EDIT: Making some coffee. I'll work on it some more in a few.

I had been dragged out with the girls last night on a tour of the clubs in town so felt like death when I was suddenly woken by the big old alarm clock by my bed. At least I hadn't been drinking, I don't think I could have gotten up at all if I had been, but as it was I had stayed sober, knowing I had to work today. I got ready as quickly as possible and tried to make myself look presentable but still felt uneasy on the drive into work: worrying about my slightly scruffy hair, my unfinished make-up and messed up nails. The school I was working at this day had a terrible reputation so that was making it even worse - knowing that if I made a single mistake, then the students here would undoubtedly jump on it and tear me apart. I was hoping that would only be figuratively but due to some of the wild rumours I had heard I was pretty scared that they may just literally tear me apart too. The minute I stepped in that classroom it all seemed to change though; the rest of the school was a mess but this small classroom was clearly looked after by the teacher and respected by the pupils. The guy I was substituting for had left a couple envelopes on the desk but I only noticed these after being nosy about everything else in the room, finding whole draws filled with sweets and motivational leaflets, this guy was serious about teaching. The envelopes had instructions on the envelopes: one said to open it before the day started, and the other after the day ended. The first started short and sweet: " It's going to be okay, just smile and above everything be encouraging! - J " Then going into basic instructions for the tasks he wanted me to complete today. It was looking like it may all be good after all - nothing to be nervous about! It wasn't long until the students started entering though and I was getting instant death stares. It seems that they don't like to miss out on lessons from this guy and I knew I would be terrible in comparison of course. I smiled though and I tried to be encouraging and so my morning went well. I spent the rest of the day doing marking until my last class. The marking was incredible, I was constantly catching myself laughing as I flicked back through the books to see jokes and pictures which ' J'had scribbled onto the ends of certain pieces of work. I tried my best to mark up to his standard but felt drained by the time they all started filing into the room once more. I did it though, I forced on that smile and I told them that they could do it when they were yelling out that they were stuck and that they hated the work. It was such a relief to finally sit back in that big leather desk chair and open the second letter, waiting to be cheered up by advice, or a drawing or something. I wanted this guy to tell me that I did well, that I should be proud, just like he had told all his students; I needed to hear that. The note was simple though: " Thanks for filling in for me, and remember to check your back - a couple of them like to stick ' kick me'notes onto substitute teachers - J " The sadness I felt at seeing that this was all I got from this guy whose world I had been living in for the day crushed me. It was then that I realised the power he had gained over me; this ' J'had completely won my heart in the way he had looked after his pupils and obvious love for his job. I realised I loved him - and I needed to find him.

I have appointed myself to die today; a bewildering amount of people are expected to watch. I pray that they are entertained. I'll stick around to observe their reactions. Do I fear death? Of course not. I'll elucidate. Most humans die nowadays. It's a spectacle, usually. Planned and pandered. Of course, by this time death has been bested. Did you think that humankind would let Death continue his funny little game? Of course not. So we play our games now. We live on the edge of forever, indulging in whatever strikes our fancy every odd century or so. Eventually, though, ennui sets in and we simply set ourselves free. It isn't with fear or regret or fight; we just grow bored. We see it all and once there's only one thing left to try we step through that door and don't look back. Very few people can conceive of living until the stars die. There would be no fun in that. My fun for the past millenia and a half has been jettisoning our undesirables into the void. It's seen as a public service; I'm quite the popular fellow for it. Such a fate is allotted only to those who deserve it, so fear not. Unless you've murdered, raped, disrupted a planetary ecosystem, or anything else on that scale, you have nothing to fear. I've clenched quite the monopoly on the business and, due to my services to humankind, I am being given an honorary death, visible to all. The thing is, I won't be setting forth into that unknown just yet; I've got one more thing to do. See, I've recently grown dissatisfied with what I've done. No human deserves to somersault through nothingness for hundreds of millions of years. I've done it myself - for 300,000 years I floated through Andromeda and it was terribly boring the last hundred years or so. The occasional comet would sail past, keeping me entertained. A few chance visits to solar systems were interesting. I even once saw a single, living fish swimming in a sea of interstellar space. Racing alongside him was quite strange. I grew fond of him before we floated apart. I digress. The moral of this story is that immortality spent doing nothing is a fate worse than death. Even the worst of us do not deserve such torture. So I will stage my death. I will venture into the cosmos following the launch paths that I sent my poor criminals on, and I will find them all and allow their lives to finally end. And then I, too, will rest.

A stolen starship flies just as fast, and I use mine to approach my last. I grew bored of the incessant expansion of humanity's ceaseless obsession to own the stars and all between. So I left to reach the unending. I approach the event horizon and time begins its dilation. The instruments slow to a crawl and my view of the universe sprawls. I can see ages pass as the ship tears and mankind makes good use of its years. In no time at all the Milky Way is ours, through conquest or flight from wars. The eons flow by and I feel the tide, pulling me from all sides. One last looks to the heavens splayed, and I feel my hope in humanity betrayed. The lights dim and die faster than they should, and I feel that we have done more harm than good.
