" Sir, you can't be serious. " Matt grabbed at his hair, trying to figure out if what I had just said was a momentary lapse in judgment or if months on the campaign trail had finally fried my brain, which was a possibility for sure. " I stand by what I just said. If I am elected, I will not rest until I am impeached, " I replied, seeming only to exasperate him further. Matthew Kaine was a good friend and an even better campaign manager: tough, fair, and optimistic only when absolutely necessary. Yet he never was able to grasp the grand design of things, to play the long ball, or even to understand what I had just said. Then again, I doubt many people would. " Look, sir, I get it. I really do. But you can't go around continuing to spew this nonsense. I understood when you wanted to ban all guns. That, at least, made sense to voters. Then, you decide to go all high and mighty on us, damn near preaching about how the president is supposed to act as instrument of justice for the people, and changing our primary message from helping out the average citizen to something you could find in the Old Testament, and not even the good part of the Old Testament, but the part that no one, not even the Evangelicals, reads. Now, with our polling at an all time low, you're popping off to interns about how your goal as president is impeachment. If you get any crazier, we're going to have to switch to the Republican ticket. " Ever since he was kid, Matt would do that, end a tirade with a joke just in case he went too far. But, now, I could tell he wasn't afraid of offending me, but was just tired. Tired of running a multi-billion dollar campaign, tired of spinning every comment, or tired of trying to set a grieving man back on track, I wasn't sure. " Sir, I know this has been extremely tough on you. I can only imagine how Meg's death... " " Murder, " I interrupted softly. " It was murder, Matt. She was shot in cold blood. And you know what, the next day all I saw on the news were pundits asking questions about how this would affect my positions or how many points I could expect to jump in the polls. No one cared, Matt. Everyone just moved on, maybe pausing for a moment to feel some fleeting glimpse of sympathy or posting a half-baked message on some stupid social media site before returning to their lives as if nothing had happened. As if there were no problems to solves. Nothing changed, Matt, and that's the world we live in. And if that's our world, where apathy and fear of change rule as kings, what can one good go? What about a hundred, or even a thousand? At best, a great man might be able to only slow down the rate at which our world crumbles. So, I have decided to try a different tact. If I win this presidency, which is pretty likely considering how apt my opponents are to shoot themselves in the foot, it will be my solemn duty to be the worst possible leader, corrupt in every fashion. I intend to surround myself with sycophants and criminals, to use every debased method the system allows to further my own goals, to pass legislation that benefits only the few, if it benefits anyone at all. Maybe then, with the country on a fast track for ruin, people will finally start to see the filth that surrounds them. " " Sir, you're insane. " " You're probably right. But, doesn't every story need a villain to bring out its hero? "

"If you asked most people about their general opinion on trees, they would probably answer, "Trees? Those things still exist?" The truth is, most people don't much of an opinion on trees. Most people born in the past few centuries haven't even seen a tree before, and have never been graced by the subtle wonders of the colorful shades of oak in the fall, or the retreat of a willow, or the brawn of the sequoia. These sorts of things only existed in photographs of old encyclopedias. "When synthetic wood was first created, most were quick to adopt. Synthetic wood possessed superior qualities, they claimed. It was not flammable, it was sturdy, it was cheap, and it looked just like wood. So we didn't need trees anymore! In fact, every reason for which a tree is useful - for shelter, for warmth, for oxygen, for wildlife habitats, for aesthetic pleasure on a nice evening walk - has been invalidated by synthetic wood and other equally absurd human inventions. "Anyone who has ever struck a match before can understand what I'm saying, because when you strike a match, it grants you a sort of control, a dominance, over something that is untamed. On the tip of the math dances a flame that disregards everything else, and only burns so long as you allow it. And seeing that wood burn away, being consumed by raw nature, is something that is lost on people these days. I read stories about great fires that could be seen from miles away, burning away hundreds of thousands of trees, leaving behind nothing but charred yet fertile ground, on which new trees would grow. A cycle that would've continued indefinitely, until humans said, "we don't need trees anymore. Trees are bothersome, ugly, and catch on fire. Let's do away with them." And so they did. "This is why it is important to plant trees. Trees give us life, they give us beauty, and they give us joy. We must not let people forget where our humanity is rooted. We must remind them of the trees!" Everyone was required to read this passage written by the founder when they were accepted into the Tree Planting Club, which was hardly a club, and more like a collection of distinct and autonomous cells operating in different cities around the country. I was introduced by a childhood friend to this club, David. David was obsessed with trees ever since childhood, and would show me pictures of all sorts of trees when we were kids. "My dad's a botanist," he would say, "but he hates trees." In all honesty, I often doubted the validity of the goal of the Tree Planting Club. Humanity has gone hundreds of years with most people not having even been influenced in some minute way by a tree. Not even food grew on trees anymore. Every food was replaced a synthetic version that (supposedly) tasted better, was cheaper to make, and didn't require constant watering and maintenance to produce. I joined the TPC soon after I found out Dad had been arrested for planting trees in public spaces. He was a writer, and one I looked up to, even though his novels never sold well. He had a spunk and determination that made him a great writer, but a terrible father. I wanted to follow in his footsteps, and if it wasn't my path to follow, so be it. I would quit TPC and get a normal job. But I'd like to think that I'm a writer too, and I wanted to write about something interesting, like trees, and how they affected people. That's how I found myself in the back of a cargo truck, sitting on the floor (if you can even call the sterile, metal base of a cargo box a floor), fiddling with the lamplight, which seemed to flicker and die every few seconds. David held a grim look on his face. After all, we were about to commit one of the greatest acts of vandalism: planting a tree. Because no one likes to admit when they are nervous, we sat in the humid box in silence, allowing the solid air to pull the hair on our necks up straight and pull the sweat from the pores on our palms. In between us lay a great maple tree. According to the books, the tree stood shorter than most, but it largest one I've seen and was apparently the largest one we could fit into the cargo box. "A minute from the plant site," Camille said from the front. We began to prepare our gear. We revved up our motorized shovel, our Chizzler, and suited up into our exoskeletons, and Camille flicked on her police signal interceptor. Planting a tree used to be easy. I read a pamphlet once that taught people how to plant trees, and it went like this: Find a soft area of dirt and dig a hole, and then drop the tree in the hole so the leaves are facing up. Then refill the gaps in the hole with dirt, pack it tight, and leave the tree. Tie ropes to support the tree of necessary. Obviously there was no dirt patches or soft soil in the middle of Times Square, where we were headed tonight to plant a tree. Luckily, we arrived when there were only a few people walking the streets, perhaps tourists who think it would be a neat experience to walk around Times Square at three in the morning. Even at this hour, you couldn't see the moon even if it were straight above. We built these buildings to look as if they were stretching out to reach for the stars, yet we blocked out the whole sky in the process. So people don't look up anymore, except to watch the endless panels of advertisements flash by faster than we can understand them. As the truck came to the stop, we slid open the backdoor of the cargo box and hopped out. We had a short window of operations, so we moved quickly. David grabbed the Chizzler and spun the motor up to a speed where it could destroy even fortified concrete. The plan was simple - drill a hold in the sidewalk, fill it with soil, roll the tree in, and cover the hole back up. Just as described in the pamphlet. As the Chizzler hit the concrete, the machinery made an awful, dull roar that probably awakened anyone within a three block radius of us. But it worked fast, and within 30 seconds, there was a tree-sized cavity in the sidewalk, filled with loose concrete and industrial dust. I used the shovel to remove all the excess rock fragments, while David lifted the tree out of the cargo box with the help of his exoskeleton. "Hurry up, people are watching, it's only time before someone calls the police!" Camille yelled from the truck. We didn't say anything, but it was clear to her that we acknowledged the urgency. We moved like clockwork, yet it still didn't feel like enough time. David was holding the tree upright as I ripped open bags of soil and began emptying them into the hole. It took nearly five or six large bags to complete fill the hole until the soil was packed tightly enough that the tree could stand upright by itself. "The police are on their way, we got ta go," Camille said. There wasn't enough time to clean up after ourselves. The Tree Planting Club had a policy of never leaving a mess when they planted, because it would reflect poorly on the organization. The TPC also had a policy of "not getting caught" because people who were truly enthusiastic enough about trees to commit great acts of vandalism were obnoxiously hard to come by. We dashed back into the cargo box, and as the truck pulled off we watched the tree become smaller and smaller through the open back door, until it was a stub in the urban landscape. "Let's hope that went well," David mumbled as he pulled the back door down, which hit the floor with a mighty bang. I fully expected the tree to be removed when I woke up. The city was usually pretty good about vandalism. However, I opted not to read the news that morning and decided to take the metro into the city and see for myself the result of our work. Would they tape off that section of the sidewalk? Would the lasting impact of our highly rehearsed tree planting just going to be a brand new section of concrete in Times Square? I sipped my coffee as I rounded the corner into the Times Square center. There was a huge congregation, with people clamoring and yelling and shoving, which was naturally the result of thousands of New Yorkers and unwitting tourists packed into one tiny block. But above all their heads, I could still see it. The brilliant radiance of burnt orange maple leaves, "the color of Autumn." The tree was taller, grander, and much more majestic than I remembered, and had apparently not been cut down. It stood gorgeously in the autumn sunlight. I later discovered that soon after we planted the tree, a group of locals, woken by the noise, took interest with the tree and surrounded it when the authorities came, to prevent the tree from being cut down. In a short period of time in the early morning, the news had spread and hundreds of people rushed to the tree's defense and created a human wall. And by noon that day, it had become national news, and everyone who enjoyed the bustle of pivotal events gathered at Times Square. They kept the tree, by the way. It was one of the only trees planted by TPC that didn't get almost immediately removed. This tree is almost twice the size, many times the awesomeness of the original tree we had planted years ago, and is maintained by the City of New York. Hopefully, now, when people visit Times Square, they'll have something to look up to that isn't those chrome edifices and their gloomy dispositions. No, I know they'll just be able to stand under the tree and look up, and they'll understand something inexplicable they hadn't before, like they'd solved a great mystery in their lives they hadn't known even existed. edit: slight edits to the story to make it more consistent

Dear Dad, I miss you more than words can say. Not a day goes by that I don't feel your absence. I wish that you'd been here when I needed a friend and a guide. I wish that I'd been there for you more, smiled more, hugged you every day, and told you how much you meant to me. I wish that I'd had the forethought and the courage to tell you what a great dad you were when you were still alive or aware enough to understand. I had plenty of opportunities and wasted them all. You were the best father I could have ever hoped for, I didn't deserve you. I'm sorry for being the ungrateful little snob I was when I was younger. Your patience and love helped me grow from that person into who I am today, I walk in your immeasurable shadow. I have a girlfriend, a career, and I'm your grandson's favorite uncle. You deserved more time with him than you had. I wish you knew how lucky I felt to have a you as my father. I feel ashamed of the times I didn't appreciate you. There are times like today, where shame and moments of intense sadness grip me and I can't stop the tears. Since your absence every unanswered e-mail, ignored link, or under-appreciated gift haunts me. I wonder if you thought your son was ashamed of you, I wasn't. With all your faults, I was proud of you, I wish I had told you so. I'm not half the man you were. I promise to keep trying. -J

She's the loveliest, most beautiful woman I've ever known. I'd never met a kinder person until my path crossed with hers. Anne is always smiling. She's the kind of girl who can get so excited about something she loves. She uses wild hand gestures as she speaks, bouncing on her toes, sharing with you whatever she is excited about. Like her newest favorite novel, or the science behind nature, something she loves so much. Doesn't that sound wonderful? Anne always has something interesting to say. I sometimes call her the Internet; I feel she knows everything. But she isn't obnoxious, oh no. She's just as interested in what you have to say. Her small, adorable chin fits perfectly on my shoulder whenever we hug. That would be often, too, as she's such a loving, encouraging person. She can be so supportive of whatever I'm going through. When we we embrace, I stroke her soft, light-blonde hair. She's a great hugger. But, I always loved Anne's eyes the most. They're like sapphires, the brightest blue of day. When she looks at you, she sees right into your soul, and loves every bit of it. No one had ever looked at me like that before. I always wonder how I got so lucky to have her. It was only a few months into our relationship before we both knew it was time to get our object. We were almost hopelessly in love. It was time to take it to the next step. "Are you ready for this?" she asked me. She grinned, playing off being confident and prepared for whatever the world could throw at her. I knew her too well. Her thin leg was jiggling as she sat in the uncomfortable waiting room chair. "You bet." I didn't have much to say. Back then, I'd usually just let Anne do the talking. She stopped moving her leg and sighed. "You know that it's possible fidgeting may be genetic. I probably got that from my mom. You look nice today. Your pants are a great color. Why isn't there a pile of magazines or something in here to keep people occupied? Or a book? Well, they probably have something better to do. I always thought being an Object Maker would be an interesting profession if I didn't get into writing. They have such a busy job, but they do it so well. It's fascinating. Do you have a book? I just finished re-reading Tunnel in the Sky this morning, or I would have brought one." "Anne. I bet our object is going to be perfect. And even if it's not, it'll only get better. We will only get better." I reached for her hand. A lady with a clipboard interrupted the motion by calling our names before I touched her. I just gave Anne a supportive look as we stood up to follow her into a back room. She had such beautiful eyes. "Just as a warning, your object can not be returned. It can be broken however, though I highly suggest that be avoided. It results in the death of the buyer." That would be Anne. It's tradition that the family of the girl pay for the Object, like with weddings before our time. I didn't think we would ever break ours. I would do anything for Anne. Anything. I never knew how much. Anne waited until we were home before unwrapping and opening the small white box. She was a bit anxious that the box was small, I think. She paused. "A phone?" She smiled and turned it on. "A smart phone?" Her eyes lit up. We could have never afforded one before. She sat down in an old armchair and was caught up in its amazing power. It was round and white, fitting perfectly in her trim fingers. "The internet, games..... it has everything!" She played until the wee hours of the night. I went to sleep. She never followed. "Anne?" I asked the next day. "Huh?" Her eyes never left the screen. I kissed her head and went to work. Always caught up in knowledge, I assumed that she couldn't resist knowing just a bit more. It didn't seem as if she'd moved when I returned. I brought her favorite dinner home from the local Italian joint. Calzones with extra ricotta. I just put it next to her and went on with my evening. Her fingers flew as she typed a reply to some article. I had to fill out a couple of reports at my desk. It was quiet that evening. Usually her voice permeated the small house, but it was silent. My few attempts at conversation were either answered with one monotone word or completely ignored. I again went to bed alone. This continued for days. The phone grew into a small tablet. For a while I thought her fascination cute. But I missed Anne. It was almost like she wasn't even there. I couldn't even get her to look me in the eyes. Days turned to weeks, and the tablet grew into a large computer. The newspaper had fired her, I learned later. I didn't know Anne had been neglecting to send in her weekly column. I was scared. A beautiful Anne became a thin zombie of a girl. I didn't think I would ever see her eyes blue again. A year went by, and I didn't know how she survived. I never saw her eat. My dreams were only nightmares, if I could ever sleep. Our object had taken her beautiful, beautiful soul. It wasn't her in that chair. I had no idea where my Anne had gone. The Object had to go. That's why I did it. That's why I'm here now. I'd do anything for Anne, anything for even the chance of freeing her. Even kill her.

"I don't want you to go to the store. I want you to WANT to go to the store!" Her eyes were like fire. We had been arguing for the past 30 minutes about who should go to the store for toothpaste. I felt like we were in a sitcom but there was no laugh track, witty comeback, and there sure as hell wasn't going to be any make up sex. There was just fire. Fire in her eyes and in her voice. We'd be fighting a lot like this, lately. Little things turned into big things and big things turned into a massive heap of shit. Just a 6 months ago we were newly weds. Just smiles and laughs and if you told those two happy people about this argument they'd roll their eyes and say "That'll never be us." "Well goddammit Jenny! I'm going to the fucking store now!" That did it. We're now at stage: big heaping pile shit. "You just don't get it!" she screamed back. She pulled her hair in frustration. "Just go. You know I didn't hear what she said after that, I was already out the door and ended our argument with a slammed door. Driving always relaxes me. I decided to drive a little further than usual just to clear my head. I passed our regular grocery store and just kept going. At the very least I was going to the store at the far end of town near the highway. It was one of the discount stores. Things were slightly cheaper because they were either damaged or nearing expiration. We shopped here sometimes when money was tight after I was laid off. I grabbed a shopping cart and decided that just a tube of toothpaste wasn't worth the drive down here. Plus, I've always been a sucker for a good deal. I grabbed a cart with a squeaky wheel and rolled it through the aisles. I started to fill the cart with various things that we needed. We're out of plastic trash bags. Jenny likes the get the heavy duty ones because it's worth the extra money to not have a bag rip on you. She's also been begging me to do the weeds in the yard since I'm home now. So I'll get a shovel and a hand saw for the weeds. Got ta get some anti freeze too for the winter. I've been driving the same car since high school and I know from past experience that it's always good to have anti freeze on hand. Is that passion fruit kool-aid?! I thought they discontinued that. It's probably worth a fortune on eBay. A couple bottles of cheap whiskey wouldn't hurt. Might down a couple of swigs before in the driveway before I head back into the house. I'll probably need some gloves for the yard work as well. Duct tape for the shower curtain rod. check. And there I saw it. from across the store was a bob dylan greatest hits album. I parked my cart next to another idle cart and walked over to the cd display rack. Bob dylans greatest hits on cd? Yep. In the cart. I stopped before it got too bad. I'll admit the bob dylan CD may have been a little over the top but it might be great to get high to later while Jenny is working late at her lawfirm. I grabbed my cart and rolled it up the nearest open register. Normally the employees at any discount store is not what society would consider attractive. I'll be blunt. They're typically trolls. But this cashier was the exception. She was gorgeous. "Hi. How are you doing?" she said smiling Oh if I wasn't married. Actually, at this point even if I am married. I attempted to flirt with her as I unloaded my cart onto the belt. Or I think I did. It's been awhile since I've flirted with anyone. I paid the bill and placed my bags into my cart and tried to think of something clever to leave the cashier girl with. I fumbled out a "bye" before I turned around to leave. Red faced I wheeled my cart to car and unloaded the bags into my trunk. I drove home replaying the glimpse of her ass I managed to sneak as I walked away. Everything felt a little better and I didn't think I would even need to pop open the bottle of whiskey before I faced Jenny. I pulled into the driveway and brought the grocery bags inside. She was waiting for me. She eyed the bags curiously. "What's all this? Did you get the toothpaste?" she asked "yeah. I got the fucking toothpaste." I replied. I guess I was still a little bit mad. Maybe I should have popped open the whiskey. I put the bags on the table and began emptying them. Something wasn't right. I don't remember buying a hose, or scouring pads, dryer sheets, a questionable steak. All the bags were filled with the wrong items. I let out a soft goddammit. No way in hell I was going to let on that I had grabbed the wrong shopping cart and didn't notice during check out because I was too busy trying to flirt with the checkout girl. "no toothpaste. the one thing we ACTUALLY needed." She rolled her eyes and left the room. About a month had passed when Jenny started working later nights at the law firm. She came home and expressed her frustration with the case. She normally isn't supposed to tell me any of the details of what she's working on but sometimes she does to get it off of her chest. "what happened?" I asked. "Well the defendant is a man that dismembered his wife with a hacksaw and buried her body parts in trash bags in the backyard." She explained. "That doesn't really seem out of the ordinary as far as murders go jen." I replied She continued, "and the autopsy revealed that he killed her by giving her passion fruit kool-aid laced with anti-freeze. When the police arrested him he had bloody gloves on and was listening to bob dylan while drinking whiskey. The weird part is that he claims he was just following a sign from the universe. Isn't that crazy? Are you okay? you don't look so well."

"It's enough! " , I screamed knowing that no one could ever hear me. "That's too much to bear!" I came here to get rid of the dullness, to get rid of my thoughts. But now that I'm all on my own it just gets worse. No moment of rest and my mind feels like it wants to burst out of my head. To crack it open and flee from the pictures I still see every day and night. I remember every detail of it. Even the bright green color of his shirt and how it went dark, when soaking with blood. The worst was his facial expression when I hit him. One split second from happy to terror. His head hammered on my front lid, while my bumper crashed his legs. I stopped immediately, but his body was strangely sliding over the ground. Just then I noticed his wife screaming at the foot-walk. It sounded so strangely far away, like it came out of an old radio. I freezed in fear and I could barely see through the smeared windshield, but I knew there was nothing to do anymore. I was too fast and I didn't even break before the impact. I instantly knew, that I just ended a man's life. My body refuses as I step closer to the abyss, but my mind desires to fly. Is there no other solution? How long will it take? It's a long way down. Maybe long enough so it'll let me grow wings. Maybe..... At least I don't have to crawl any more.

"How much is that armor there?" Askar, the not-so-great adventurer asked the pruned blacksmith. "Oh uh, that's not armor that was a bit of a mess up..... I can't really sell it, it's no good." "Two gold coins then?" "Uh, sure," The blacksmith nodded and looked at his new coins as the odd adventurer sauntered off. Askar's entire goal since he was kicked out of his home was to be a famous adventurer, to hear tales of glory sung in his name, to be recognized as a hero across the land. Yet thus far all he managed to do was recover an old lady's cat, which fortunately led to two gold coins, which he then turned into some new- albeit odd looking- armor. Now he would be able to get past the gatekeeper and begin his quests. The tall figure loomed overhead, far more oppressive than even the rough iron gate behind him, and boomed, "Who would pass the city gates?" "I'm Askar!" "The world outside is a very dangerous place, you must best me in a duel to prove yourself capable." "Oh uh, alright then," Askar held up the only weapon he had- his hiking stick- as the gatekeeper rose a massive piece of steel that could very easily have weighed twice as much as Askar. "Or um.... maybe I could reconsider." But the challenge was issued. The gatekeeper swung, paying no heed to Askar's words. The impact of his sword resounded throughout the busy streets with a tremendous clang. A clang that signafied the gatekeeper had struck the ground- not Askar. The mountainous figure of the man struggled to free his sword from the gravel, and Askar managed to simply slip right past through the gate that had fortunately been left unlocked. The gatekeeper cried after him but Askar continued on his merry way smiling at his upturn in luck. He followed the path with no real direction until he came upon a fork in the road with a man lying in the middle. He was bleeding and looked quite ready to die, which is why Askar was quite surprised when the man spoke, "The demon king..... laid the royal army to waste..... so much death..... the north is in ashes..... run while you can..." And with that the old man died. How increadibly convienent that the man should live just long enough to deliver that message to Askar. He had heard rumors of the Demon king, and defeating the fellow seemed like quite the way to make a name for one's self. So with that though in mind, Askar took the path that led north, towards the demon king. The path eventually led to a dark and ominous forest, where the very branches and trees seemed to be reaching out in anguish. It didn't deter or bother Askar in the slightest, he hiked right through whistling all the while. After a bit he felt as if he wasn't alone amongst the trees, and so he stopped to look around. In the instant that he stopped an arrow struck the ground in between his feet. As he leaned over to inspect it another one flashed over his head. Looking around revealed no clear source of the projectiles so he shrugged and continued in his way- leaving a trail of arrows in his path as his assailants continued to miss. Eventually the forest gave way to burnt fields of crops. Askar continued on his journey unfazed by the destruction. He pushed northward past an astounding array of adversaries: there was a hoard of goblins that mistook him as one of their own, a troll under a bridge that had forgotten its riddles, a witch that mistakenly cursed herself instead of Askar, and a massive talking serpent that was struck by lightning halfway through giving a speech about how it was the guardian of the demon king's castle. Askar stepped over the snakes corpse and approached the towering red doors of the demon king's castle, they opened on their own accord. The entirety of the castle seemed to be almost a maze, Askar randomly wandered through the dark stone passageways and often times activated traps that he just barely avoided. It didn't take him long at all to reach a grand door lined with gold and gems of all sorts that seemed to glow in the darkness of the passageway. He pushed his way through the doors and found himself in a large throne room with hundreds of torches lining the walls, and a horned, red-skinned, figure that would have made the gatekeeper look like an ant, that sat in a throne the size of a house. It's voice- no, it's roar- shook the entire chamber, "WHO ARE YOU TO ENTER MY KEEP?" "I'm Askar, I've come to defeat you so I can be famous." The creature rose what could have been an eyebrow, "I'm amazed a mere mortal could make it through my labyrinth, and completely unscathed as well. You must be a truely legendary warrior." "What? That was a labyrinth? It took like ten minutes to get here..." "WHAT? There have been mortals who have spent months in there, gave their blood and dying breaths trying to get to me. I have heard grown men cry and plead for the chance to see the sun one last time before they perish. And yet you say it took you ten minutes?" "Yeah, and all of those traps were kind of silly as well..." "ENOUGH! I will destroy you here and now- you are no more than an annoyance," The creature rose from its throne, trailing an embroidered cloak behind it that would be large enough to clothe an entire village. Each step bounced Askar off the ground, but still he smiled. If getting to the Demon King was so easy then defeating him couldn't be any harder. Askar held up a hand, "Hold on! All of these torches..... it's so hot in here! Let me just take off this armor really quick then I'll be ready to fight you." The demon king gave pause, respecting the request. Once Askar's armor was off he felt so much lighter, more nimble, and so he rose his trusty hiking stick over his head and charged at the demon king- only to have his head chopped off in a single stroke of the monster's claws.

My parents told me Winston was coming back today. For the past few months he'd been at grandma's house. I don't know why he was there, they said Winston wanted to be on grandma's farm but I know Winston. He doesn't like the outdoors. He just likes sleeping. "Hey sport," Dad tousled my hair, "We've got a big surprise for you!" Then my mom opened the front door and Winston bounded through. He licked my dad, he licked me, he even licked the couch. I grabbed him and I started petting him. Winston had this green collar on his neck though, with a name tag attached to it. I gave Winston a blue collar a long time ago so I checked it. The tag said Luke. "Dad I don't think this is Winston," and I looked at him. I wanted my dog. This wasn't my dog. Mom looked at dad too, "You said he wouldn't notice," and dad smiled, probably because he was stuck between the crossfire of his kid and wife. He said, "It's okay sport. You won't even notice Winston's gone." I ran outside. I'll go to grandma's farm and I'll find Winston myself.

The weapon's casing was warm in her hands. The gun was designed to keep cool, venting the excess heat from plasma discharge along its long barrel, away from her body. She'd fired the thing so many times in the last two hours however that it was taking its toll. She was sure that the overheat warning sounds would ring her dreams for weeks after this. She took a moment to slow her breathing and focus. With no sound than the slide of her boots on the metal floor she spun her body around the corner of the wall and through the opened door. She proceeded slowly, sweeping her gaze and her weapon from side to side. At her feet were at least a dozen Imperial soldiers, the plasma burns still causing smoke to waft from their wounds. They didn't move, they didn't bleed - the heat of the plasma melted and cauterized flesh and bone on impact. To her surprise no one got up, no one appeared from around a corner. She was able to walk right up to the command console in the back of the room, and the massive window overlooking the city beyond it. She allowed herself a small sigh of relief. There were ten of them when they stormed the facility. Some had been lost along the way, others pinned down and had to escape. She was the only one who made it this far. She would succeed. She would succeed to avenge him. She took her left hand off her rifle and pulled the necklace over her head. Dangling in place of a charm was a device given to her by the resistance. On the console in front of her, next to the hologram emitters that displayed information, was an data jack that fit the device perfectly. At her moment of triumph she hesitated briefly. She remembered her brother's corpse. She remembered how it looked having had its head severed. She remembered when Zaren, the resistance leader, sent her the photos and told her what the Imperial Security had done to her poor little brother. He was always an idealist, susceptible to these kind of fast talkers, manipulators. He didn't do anything to warrant a beheading, and she was off-world when it all happened. Today she would avenge the little brother she couldn't protect. This device would steal millions of credits from the Imperial offices, and make those in charge of his executioners lose their jobs and reputation. "For you Aiden" she said aloud. Her heart swelled with pride as she thrust the device into the port. She tapped her left ear once. The micro-transmitter implanted here gave her a short chime to indicate the channel was open. "The device is inserted," she reported. "Proceed with the upload." As she waited for the program to do its job, she looked at the hologram screens emitted by the console. That was when she noticed a picture of herself. It displayed her service record with the Imperial Military. Next to her image was her brothers'. The occupation, his marital status, address all seemed accurate. Her pulse quickened as she kept reading. He had a criminal record. An unbelievably large number of homicides. Millions in property damage. Arson. Kidnapping. Treason. A bounty exceeding a million on his head, cashed in by a bounty hunter. Her plasma rifle hit the ground with an audible crash. He was the New Fairfax Bomber. His organization, The Pure Front, were there terrorists behind the bombing of the Imperial embassy that killed 200. She never new. She had no idea. He'd always kept to himself after he left home and she'd gone into the service. She'd always thought him the naive one, and yet here she was. Her mind raced as she realized all she'd ruined for this organization taking advantage of her love for a brother she hardly knew. Then there was a loud explosion. She looked out the window and watched in horror as the planetary defense missiles stream into the air. Her eyes followed them as their assent ended prematurely and they turned their warheads downwards. With a bright flash, they reduced the Imperial government buildings downtown to utter rubble. She covered her mouth with her hands as she thought about all the people working and living in that area. It would be this moment, not the overheat warning of the stolen plasma rifle that would haunt her. She heard the sound of armored boots on the floor behind her. She turned around and faced the Imperial soldiers as they raised her rifles. She put her hands up. She cleared her throat and filled herself up with a new conviction. "I'm Corporal Sara Morrison," she told the soldiers. "I surrender. I can tell you how to get the bastards responsible for this."

The room was still, with only the rhythmic ticking of a clock to indicate any signs of movement. In this room, a man stealthy moved across from one piece of furniture to the next, careful not to add any more sounds to the steady ticking. Tick. Tock. In his hand, the man gripped a silver tool. To the average person's eye it would appear to look like a compass, but in the man's deft hands it served a much more sinister purpose. Sticking to the shadows, he waited for the right moment to strike. In the next room, a lady was sitting, unaware of what was about to happen. She was sitting in a brown leather chair, one hand gripping a glass filled with red wine, the other resting on the arm of the chair. Flames flickered across her face. Tick. Tock. One swift movement and by the man was by the woman's side, the silver compass in the woman's neck. The man pressed harder and waited until blood gushed from the newly created wound. The woman slumped over, and the glass of wine tipped over in her hand and onto the floor. Satisfied, the man straightened and walked over to the flames. There was no need for silence. He reached over and grabbed the glass to drink the last dregs of wine. He took a sip. Tick. Tock. And spat it out. And turned around. Behind him the woman rose, pulled the compass from her neck and licked the edge, her tongue caressing the sharp edges. Tick. Tock. " Allow me to explain. "

I knew this day would come. Honestly, I did. I could only avoid it for so long. I'd spent my childhood shying away from pool parties, water parks, and the like but now my day of reckoning had come. Now my best friend was drowning. "Foot?" Or at least I assumed he was. I mean, he wasn't flailing around or anything. He'd just gone down and hadn't come up yet. " ..... Foot, if you can hear me come back!" I got no response. He'd dove under there after dropping a can of beer. I didn't drink but he did. Like a fish. But I swear, if he's drowning over some shitty Natty Light when there were five more cans on board I'd choke him. "Foot!" I had a bit of anger in my voice. Now what was more infuriating; that he'd jumped into that nasty lake without a second thought or that he'd dragged me out here in the first place? I hated the water, he KNEW that! I spent most of my childhood dodging pool parties and water parks for a reason, dammit. And now, here I was, leaning over the edge of his old rowboat with a knot in my stomach and a choice to make. I could either let him drown which he very well deserved in my angered opinion or I could take my first and what could very well be my last step off this boat and into the water. "FOOT!" Still no answer. And as mad as I was, I couldn't just let him drown. I mean. I could call the cops and get someone down here, but already the seconds were turning into minutes and he was STILL down there. 'shit', I swore in my head and felt my legs start to get all weak. I was starting to realize there was only one thing I could, no, HAD to do and it was the one thing that terrified me. My eyes blurred with tears and I struggled to stand. I was crying now because I really didn't want to do this but I couldn't just let him die! 'oh God, oh my God please', I thought as I wiped my face and approached the side of the boat. Casting one last glance behind me, I saw nothing that would aid me. Yeah. Because that's the kind of idiots we were. 'Don't worry, Tia, it's just a ride across and back. It's not like we'll be getting out.' My ass. Again I felt that anger. As I climbed overboard, I vowed I'd throttle that ginger friend of mine once we both made it out aliv 'COLD!' The icy waters permeated both my thoughts and my clothes and within a few seconds I was soaked and was starting to sink. It must have looked hilarious, me kicking and whipping my arms around, but I was sure I was going to die: either by drowning or suffering cardiac arrest. I continued to grasp blindly and then gave up. I was tired and heavy and this was it. Water flooded my nose and I chokes and coughed. Wait. I blinked. I hadn't realized'til now that my eyes were shut tightly but I opened them wide and even wider when the tip of my shoes touched onto the earth. I looked up and saw what I thought was the bottom of the boat and looked around. Wait wait. I sniffed in a tiny breath, expecting to choke but the water just rushed in and right back out. It wasn't like breathing, it never even touched my esophagus. It was like it hit the back of my upper throat and got pushed back out through my nose. What the hell? Brighter than sunlight was the flash of orange and yellow as it darted past my face. It was a fish, like a flounder. It swam circles around my head, swam ahead a few feet, then stopped and faced me..... expectantly? It wanted me to follow. I felt like a clumsy novice as I pushed off forwards. The earth gave way under my shoes and I sliced the water with my arms, lifted my legs behind me, and started kicking my feet. From there it was like I was on autopilot. As if from muscle memory my body glided expertly across the lake until I was keeping the pace with the fat little fish. I was so caught up in this surreal experience that I forgot about my friend. Foot! I turned my head and didnt see him anywhere. In front of me, the fish swam on. I abandoned it and swam erratically in search of my redheaded companion. I couldn't find him anywhere but I did find a cliff. And when I went over it, I saw that fish. And some'people'. And a giant, half-buried sign that read,'Welcome to Atlantis' Ugh. Not really satisfied with my work but hopefully, as I spend more time on these prompts, I'll become a better writer

"Is this your card?" I produced the queen of hearts, and the woman clapped. "Yes!" It was cold out, and her cheeks were flushed. She was very pretty. I smiled, and gave it to her, tucking it into the strap of her purse where it crossed her shoulder. "It suits you." She smiled back, and shyly opened her purse, dropping a few dollars into the can at my feet. I tipped my ragged hat, and she went on her way. When she was a safe distance away, I flicked the queen of hearts out of my sleeve and shuffled it back into the deck of cards, glancing down at them. There were tiny markings in the fine details of the card backs. Anyone could spot them, if they know what to look for. But noticing them at a glance, and not making a fool of yourself shuffling through a deck looking for a matching mark, that took skill. And skill took practice. So I practiced. "King of spades," I muttered under my breath. Then I spread out the deck upside down in one hand, and plucked it from the fan of cards. I flipped it over, and saw that I'd had it right. "Jack of diamonds." I tried again, and found it easily, though my cold fingers stumbled and grabbed two cards instead of one. I sighed under my breath, and slid the deck of cards into my pocket. Sitting down against the brick wall of my alleyway, I reached into my shanty and took out a package of plastic-wrapped hand warmers. They didn't fill my belly or warm me at night, but without them, in the winter I would be a beggar, not a homeless street performer. Knowing all the sleight of hand tricks in the world is useless if your fingers are too cold to perform them. I took out one and opened it. Exposed to air, it heated up quickly, and I held it between my stiff fingers, enjoying the warmth as it spread through my hands. My eyes were closed as I leaned against the wall, and I dozed off slowly, even though I knew I should keep an eye out for people to perform for. I woke up to something hard tapping against my leg. I opened my eyes, sitting up quickly from the slump I had fallen into while asleep. The hand warmer was in my lap, and I tucked it quickly in my pocket, aware of how much it had cost. Looking up, I saw a tall man, around thirty. He had a thick and curly beard, and a wide-brimmed hat with dark eyes peering out from beneath it. "You were snoring," he said, not unkindly. "And it's too cold to sleep outside." I stood quickly. "That's the only place I have to sleep," I said. "But thank you all the same." Then my brain kicked in, and I asked him, "Sir, would you like to see a magic trick?" "A magic trick," he repeated, smiling. "Yes, I would very much like to see you do that." So I slid out the deck of cards from my pocket, and spread them. "Pick a card," I said. "Any card." He considered, his fingers hovering over the deck. Then, he plucked one from the very edge. Even without the markings, I could have told him it was the jack of diamonds, the card I had just drawn and put back. But the show was worth more than the knowing, and so I let him look at it. Then I held it out and let him place it back into the deck and then shuffling it expertly, letting them flick between my hands in a manner most impressive. He smiled pleasantly, watching. Then I spread out the deck upsidedown again, finding the marking for the jack of diamonds, and flicked it up. "Is this your card?" I said without looking, knowing it was. "No," he said, still smiling. I frowned, and looked at the card. It was the three of clubs. I flicked it back over, and saw that the markings on the back agreed. But the markings on the jack and the markings on the three looked nothing like each other, and I knew it had not been the fault of cold fingers. Confused, I put the card back, and said, "Sorry sir, cold fingers and a sleepy mind. Certainly this is your card!" With spectacular emphasis, I flicked over the card marked as the jack of diamonds. "No," he said again, laughing a little. I looked again, and was deeply embarrassed to see that I held the ten of diamonds, not the jack. The markings were more similar, but I still should have been able to tell them apart. I put the cards back together, starting to stammer out an apology as I slid them back into my pocket. The man held up a hand, and said, "No, no. Don't put them away. In fact, let me try." I hesitated. The cards were my livelihood. Buying another marked pack would cost more than I had, and this stranger was asking me to entrust him with them. Even if it was just for one trick, he might drop them in the snow, or bend the edges, or any number of things that would ruin them. Then he held out a fifty dollar note, and my eyes widened. He dropped it in the can, and my jaw dropped with it. I didn't know what to say, so I simply looked up at him, astounded, and amazingly grateful. He still had his hand held out. "Just for one trick. I promise to take good care of them." His eyes twinkled, and he looked so very kind. So I handed him the cards. He spread them out in front of me, not even bothering to shuffle. "Pick a card," he prompted gently. So I did, taking one in such a way that the markings were obscured. Flicking it over, I glanced at it. It was the five of clubs. I put it back in with the others, still attempting to obscure the markings. He shuffled them briskly, and pulled out a card at random. "Is this your card?" he asked, flicking over the five of hearts. So very close. I smiled, and said, "No." Then he flicked it with a finger, and it became the five of clubs. "How about now?" My eyes widened in surprise. This man must have been a master of sleight of hand, to have performed such a switch in front of my eyes, without me even noticing. If he could do that, maybe he had even swapped out the jack of spades. I started to feel much better. "Yes," I said, letting my amazement show. "How did you do that?" He laughed again, and handed me the deck. "Take a look." I did, spreading the cards out in front of me. To my shock, every single one of them was the five of clubs. Then I blinked, and they were back to normal. They spilled out of my hands, fluttering to the wet pavement below. The man frowned. "I didn't mean to scare you," he said. "Just a bit of fun." Then he waved his hand, and the cards fluttered up into it, like a reversed video of how they had fallen. Not a one of them was soaked. I rubbed my forehead, my eyes. I was certain I was going insane. When the man handed me back the deck of cards, I took it on mere instinct. He smiled, and said, "Thank you, for the magic trick." "T-Thank you," I said, stammering. "For the same. And the money," I added, almost forgetting. Then he walked away, whistling cheerfully, and I slunk into my shanty to close my eyes and get some proper sleep, hoping that everything would make sense when I woke. Instead, after I had laid down, I took the cards out of my pocket, wanting to look at them one last time to make sure he hadn't swapped them. As I did, I noticed that they felt strange. Very cold, and heavy. Even after I took them out and spread them, it took me a moment to figure it out. They were so well painted, I could hardly believe it. I could hardly believe any of it. The cards were solid gold.

"Hello there," said Kytros, of the Derhy tribe, greeting the unaware human receptionist, sitting behind the information desk at the United Nations Headquarters in New York City, "I should like to meet with your leader." His portable shape-adaptor device allowed him to look just like any of the thousands of workers and diplomats that entered that building daily. "You mean my supervisor?" asked the woman, not certain of what had been requested. "I mean the Secretary-General. I should like to speak to him," said Kytros. The game had started not half an hour previously, and Kytros wished to win the bet that took place every eight cycles between the players of The Lawful Game - to conquer a world using that planet's own rules. It had developed as a thought-experiment from the Theoretical Law department at one of the Galaxy's most prestigious education establishments, and soon it had gained a following throughout most sectors. So far, no planet had managed to resist the meticulous attention to detail and nuance that the players had, and the Earth looked to be just as easy to conquer as the rest had been. Intent on winning the game as quickly and swiftly as possible, Kytros landed and immediately headed to the UN, as that was the highest organization on the small planet, and it had proved easier in the past, when he had conquered Lherqwa, to make use of the laws of the most dominant form of organization. The receptionist, whose tag indicated was named "Diana," looked at her computer monitor and back at Kytros. "I don't see any meeting scheduled for the Secretary-General. Did you have an appointment?" Kytros' instant translator had some difficulty processing that last word. "Appointment? " , he said, "What's an appointment?" "Well, you can't expect to just walk in and have a meeting with whoever you want, much less the Secretary-General. You have to make an appointment in advance." "And how do I do that?" Diana reached behind her and took a sheet of paper from a pile. "You can begin by filling out this form. Hand it back to me when you're done, thank you," she said, smiling, before turning to face another waiting visitor. Kytros was taken aback. Never had he faced this situation. Perhaps things were run a little differently here on Earth. Never mind that; as the receptionist said, he only needed to fill in that piece of paper and he was set. After a few minutes of struggling to figure out how to use a pen and some seconds of writing, Kytros returned to the smiling Diana, who promptly took the form from his hands. "Oh, I'm sorry, Sir, but you need to fill this out in capital letters. It's written right here at the top, see?" she turned the paper, but Kytros failed to recognize the requirement from a half page of small, cramped letters. "But here, have another." Kytros returned to a seat by the revolving doors and again filled out the form, carefully writing in capital letters. Once he was done, the smiling receptionist again took the paper and expertly took a look at it. "Very well, Sir, now you have to fill in this other one," and she handed him a second form, nearly identical to the first. "But, I just handed you the other one..... Why do I have to do it again?" inquired a baffled Kytros. "The first one is for the appointment and will be sent to the General-Secretariat's administrative department. This one is to be sent to the office of the Secretary-General himself, who might approve or reject the meeting." Resigned, Kytros, again took his seat and filled in the necessary paperwork. Handing it back to Diana, he began to fear the welcoming smile with which he was received. "Fantastic, Sir. Now, you will need to contact the UN security department as soon as possible. You need to have a security approval before you can get that meeting," she said. "And how do I do that? " , asked Kytros. "You need to send a letter to their department," indicated Diana. "Isn't it in this building as well?" said a stunned Kytros. "It is, yes. Third floor, I believe," she said. "Then why can't I go there directly? And why a letter?" "Oh, they need you to make an appointment as well. And for security reasons, mail is their preferred method of communication, I'm afraid." Kytros grew irritated at the pointless paper-pushing. "And when will I be done with all this and see the Secretary-General?" "If all goes well, 6-7 months," answered Diana. Disconcerted, Kytos figured he could perhaps use his legal expertise to bypass these months of waiting time. "Look, surely you have a set of procedures. May I have a look at them?" Taking this for a request to see the original Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Diana was quick to answer. "That will also require an appointment, Sir." Kytros was just about to reveal himself as the alien he was, just to get a different response than that tyranical smile, when he thought of something else. "Then, where can I find the one responsible for your global armament?" he asked, thinking that if he could use the law to blow this ridiculously fastidious planet up with their own weapons, then he would win the game easily. When he saw the begining of a smile forming on the receptionist's lips, however, Kytros knew something worse was to come, perhaps a new appointment to be made. "Sir, the United Nations is not responsible for the world's armament. That lies with the countries themselves. If you wish to address that topic at our Disarmament Committee, you will have to make an appointment with each nation's delegate. "Oh," realised a suffering Kytros, "And how many countries and delegates are there?" The alien knew, when Diana showed the largest smile so far, two rows of white teeth in a flashing grin, that this would be the end of it. If he had to go through this procedure more than a couple of times, all was lost. "One hundred and ninety-three."

My mouth tastes metallic, like blood, and my eyes peel themselves open. I'm in a crowded room and everything is shaking. People are running over to my bedside gripping my arms. I look down and see my body writhing and convulsing uncontrollablly. My arms are twitching, my body shakes and twists. "This is normal everyone. Stand back! Stand back," one of the men gripping my arms is yelling to the crowd. They don't move an inch. The other man holding down my arms shoves a hard bit of plastic between my teeth and my jaw clamps down on it, hard. I'm panicking now, I can't breathe! I gasp in huge gulps of air and the yelling man tells the other to "sip in 7 cc's animorphine, aqueous, no saline." The IV drip next to me whirs and I start to feel calmer now. I get a better look at the men. They're both doctors, and the one on my right is considerably older. He looks about 60, with serious gray eyes and a stiff body type. His hands are sinewy and experienced. The other is much younger, probably in his late 20s. He has intelligence and energy in his movements. The older doctor pulls down his surgical mask and examines me carefully as I lie panting on the hospital bed. The crowd is eerily quiet. "My name is Dr. Fillow. How are you feeling?" My mouth still tastes metallic. Young doctor takes the bit out of my mouth. "What happened? " , I ask. Dr. Fillow glances at young doctor. Then back at me. "You just had a seizure. Your brain is refiring its neurons, doing a systems check, if you will. Can you hear me okay?" I nod. "Alright, good." Young doctor pulls out a small flashlight from his breast pocket and peers into my eyes and mouth as Dr. Fillow continues to speak. "This is going to come as a shock to you, but for the past 67 days, sir, you've been dead." I blink. "It's important that you do exactly what we tell you to do. We used a very dangerous experimental technique to get you back, but the ramifications of it are..... unknown. I need you "I died!" I panic, tears welling in my eyes. "Is this a joke. Is this a joke? Why are you doing this?!" "No, this is real. Everything here is real, and it's going to be alright. This is the first human revival of this kind of all mankind. You are the the first." I feel like I want to cry. Im happy and scared, and confused and my body begins to ache. The crowd in front of me is full of reporters and cameramen, watching closely. They split down the middle and a man in a dark blue suit and red tie hurries into the room. He looks like he's in his 50s and has the smile of a politician. He grips my hand firmly and smiles. "It's good to have you back Mr. President. But we have a situation at the White House, and you're needed as soon as possible."

Tobias didn't have time to see the guard's face, he had thrown him the gun from the cell door and ran up the spiral stairs. Tobias, not wasting anytime, followed as quickly as he could, six weeks of starvation and no exercise took the speed out of his step, but the adrenaline fueled him. He took the stairs two at a time, using the handrail to propel his body forward and up, forward and up. How far down was I? he thought, slowing his steps to one at a time now. The staircase went on and on. He was tired, his legs were positively shaking, sweat poured from his forehead. After a while he tripped and fell forward, hitting the stairs with the shoulder of the arm that he was carrying the pistol with. Gasping, he called out, "Where are you? " , but got no response. Tobias lay there for a moment, catching his breath, and wondered what would happen to him when he got to the top. He wondered which guard it was that had saved him, for all had been so cruel to him in captivity. If one was working for Frank as well, why hadn't he cut him any slack? A slice of bacon here or there, or an extra scoop of rice, a wink, a knowing glance, something. He racked his memory, searching for any overlooked sign of camaraderie, perhaps one had kicked his ribs with a little less force than the others? The thought made Tobias laugh- grunt was more accurate. He saw a speck of dirt move as the air escaped his mouth, and it filled him with desperate hope. He propped himself up on his elbows, then, grasping the hand rail once again, he rose to his feet. That was when he heard the second explosion. Tobias jumped in his skin. The sound came from under him, and shook his feet. He stood still for a moment, his tongue moving idly in his mouth. He looked down, then looked up, and started climbing again. He gritted his teeth as the weakness in his thighs begged him to rest. He knew he could not stop moving till he had reached the top. He tried gauging the air pressure to get a sense of how close to sea level he was, but no matter how much he climbed, it felt the same. There was no way of knowing. Eventually his calves joined his thighs in protest, but higher still he climbed. He heard a third explosion, louder. This time he felt hot air rush by him from behind. He stopped moving and leaned on the wall. How long had he been climbing now? It felt like hours, but he knew that was unlikely. He knew he was just tired, and thirsty and scared. Where the hell did the guard go? Tobias gathered up all the energy he could muster, and roared from his diaphragm: "HELLO!" Nothing. He sat down and began to cry. Another explosion went off, close enough to make his ears ring. He yelled again, tears streaming down his cheeks. "Hello hello someone please hello! Where are you, guy? Where did you go? Frank? Frank help me please Frank!" His voice became a wail, which crescendo'd into a deafening "BOOM" which shook Tobias to his gut. He whimpered, looking at the gun in his hand. He looked up, then back at the gun. He sighed. Tobias made an explosion for himself. At the bottom, Frank sat with a stopwatch. Five men dressed as guards sulked in the corner, pulling wads of cash from bags and counting them. The rest of the guards were sitting near Frank, watching the stair case, listening to the thud-thud-thuding. "Here goes my month's paycheck, goddamnit." said one of the men pulling out cash. "He was so close, so..... so close."

"The usual, Amir." I smile and provide the black clad man with a acknowledging grunt as I slap a steaming hot dog onto a perfectly grilled bun before drizzling it down with a heady mixture of potent sauces. He grins and stops me just am I'm about to add the final finishing squeeze of garlic sauce. "No, no, stop. No garlic for me today please." I stared at him dumbfounded. "But Mr.Blackwatch, you love my garlic sauce, always wanting extras!" I protest. "Yes, but the wife has been giving me hell about my breath." He smiles ruefully as he trades me a tenner for the dog, "So I have no choice." "Ah, what a shame!" I nod at him as I tuck the bill into my apron pocket, he waved me away as I tried to hand him his change, "But if you ever change your mind, you know I am open every day!" He grins as he takes a bite out of his dinner. A few moments later, the unmistakable red, blue and white musculature I have come to recognize and dread slams into the ground not far from my cart. I hesitantly pull away even as Blackwatch tries to stuff the rest of the hot dog into his mouth. "Blackwatch! Today, you will pay for your crimes!" The heroically built Captain Apex growled through his immaculately pearly white teeth, "And Amir, would you please get me a gluten free hot dog, only lightly baked with olive oil, with tofu bacon, kale, iceberg lettuce, extra onions, no garlic and just a smidge of sweet onion sauce. Today's my cheat day." "Oh come on Apex, its closing time! Just order something simple!" Blackwatch snarled as he clenched his fists. "Justice has no closing time!" I carefully prepared the meal while the two of them tore up the streets. Captain Apex returned to my cart just as I was closing up. With a slightly forced smile, I handed him his order. He takes a sniff of it, nods appreciatively and hands me a fiver. "Perfect as usual! Keep the change!" The brightly colored hero grins as he blasts off into the stratosphere, my best customer hoisted over his shoulder. I sigh as I pocket his money and begin packing my store. There was, and is, no change for a fiver.

I don't like it when he cries, but at least it doesn't last long. The woman comes and picks him up, and when she presses him to her chest, he immediately stops. She then sings to him about a star that twinkles in the sky, bright and shiny. I am covered in little stars and moons, and I always feel so special, like she is singing about me, trusting me with to keep his dreams free of nightmares. She has the softest voice, even I want to just curl up into a little ball and fall asleep in her arms. I will never let her down. He will always be safe with me. My only contact apart from the little guy is when she washes me every few days. Sometimes she wipes her own tears with me before she pushes me in the hot water that smells like lavender. I do appreciate her care very much. I am usually covered in snot or drool or tears, though not much sweat. He is a leaky little bugger, but I love him! And he loves me too! He hugs me sometimes when he sleeps, his cheek pressed tight against one of my stars. He sleeps a lot, not only at night, so I am always on guard to be at my fluffiest and softest. My delicate lace sometimes tickles his nose and he giggles, and that is just the happiest sound in the whole world! If it is one thing I am sad about though, is that I haven't seen his face yet: (I dream about it sometimes, his tiny nose, his rosy cheeks. How would he look like? I know all there is to know about the back of his head. I can tell you exactly how much hair he has, and how fast it grows. It was so strange when we first met - his hair was so dark, almost black. After just a few months, it is the same as the golden hair of the princes he learns about every day. I know from the bottom of my feathery heart that he will grow up to be one someday. I only get one side of his face at a time. I also know he has a teeny tiny little mole on his left cheek, and that he drools the most when on his right side. He has such soft lashes, and I wonder if he hears me when I wish him goodnight and sleep tight with his ear pressed right on me. He usually sleeps on his back though. I am so happy she fulfilled my dream tonight, his soft face left the cutest imprint on my cotton. And just like always when she comes around, he isn't crying any more. So peaceful. So calm. I love the little guy!

These small, close-knit groups encountered each other extremely infrequently over the course of hundreds of thousands of years, thus developing interpersonal traits ill-suited to vast, shifting confluences of an advanced civilized world. Grygxxxfyqzxxx found the whole thing baffling, and, frankly useless. These upside-down creatures could never contribute to the massive, smoothly-humming machinery of the galactic ultra-cartel. Undoubtedly, they would only get bogged down by some biased personal priorities like kin and local communities, or - at best - align themselves with whatever slightly larger (300 million? 900 million? Bah!) organization who sells their own tribal biases back to them. Better to turn the whole damn muddy ball into a tetra-magnophyraxian gamma-ball stadium, he decided, and launched the fleet's entire swarm of genocidrones to wipe the little backwards planet clean of organic matter.
