The sound of a small creature scavenging in the underbrush rouses me from slumber. My chest heaves as I will open my eyes to search in annoyance for the creature that disturbed me in the dark forest understory. The piles of small crystalline petals I used to keep myself warm enough to sleep shifted as I breathed, making a soft rustle. " I haven't eaten, " I thought to myself, but my motion must have scared my potential prey motionless. Before falling asleep I had managed to make a small clearing in this forest of bizarre alien trees. Their deep maroon or violet trunks were crowned with branches holding rigid crystalline orange petals. The forest was so dense that only small patches of orange light were visible through the canopy. Shuffling through the piles of accumulated delicate orange petal shards on the forest floor to the middle of the clearing makes a sound that alternates between swishing and crunching. I want to sit here under the Sun and feel what it must have been like to sit in a field on Earth and look up at the sky as just a normal human. I am probably the only normal human left. But as I am sitting, looking up into the sky at the Sun and seeing all the stars surrounding and beyond it beaming their more faint and distant brilliance, just like normal humans used to on Earth, I feel an overwhelming urge to walk into the forest. It feels like I'm being drawn in. I feel a growing urgency to find the source of this draw, or is it a feeling of being chased? I can't tell if it is fear or excitement, but I find myself bursting into a running stride. I can feel a force emanating from the largest of the trees I've seen in this forest. It is as wide as my outstretched arms, and no other tree grows inside the radius of its immense branches. The thinner canopy here lets enough light through to make the metallic dark purple trunk of tree seem to be surrounded with a golden halo. The golden aura of the tree flashes brightly as I hear the words in my head " Why are you doing this? " " Because I am human being. " I respond verbally to the tree. It seemed natural. " Do you mean: ' Because you are a human being,'or ' Because you are being human, the telepathic tree mentally responds, almost shouting in my head with impatience. " I don't know, what is this, a grammar exam? " I'm growing frustrated at the intrusion. " I know one of your functions is to keep my systems in optimal condition, but you're not my personal therapist. " " Actually, I very much am. Do you know how much damage you caused? Your little clearing over there has completely destroyed seven stage five development collection arrays, and reduced operational efficiency on twenty-three more. " " So, I need this. I need to feel what it was like to be a real person. A real human. " " Oh really? " the pitch of the voice in my head raises at the end to emphasize the sarcasm of this comment. " Do you think a real human could look directly at the Sun and see the UV wavelength radiation emitting from the stars in the surrounding sky? Real humans needed a ribcage to pull air into their lungs, not the pure vacuum of space. This is an immense waste of resources. I read your brain activity, you were thinking about hunting down that poor reclamation droid earlier, " " I needed a snack, " " You don't need a snack! Your artificial body is sustained by the energy field of The Ring. This experiment is just a dangerous waste of resources. " Maybe Guardian was right. Spending the time and credits to grow this body was worth it just to see if the simulations lived up to real life, but the truth was that the twenty ninth century was no place for a human anymore. We long ago disassembled the solar system to make The Ring around the Sun's equator. There was no more air to breathe and no more plants or animals to eat. It's a shame I won't get to find out what pooping was like. None of the old simulation writers felt it was important enough to record while humans still were using old fashioned meat-sacks, but I imagined it would be a lot like farting, only heavier. I did get to take a nap though, and that felt really authentically human.

Christopher Hitchens pulled up his golden chair and scooted right up to me, face to face. Which, to me, makes little sense, as I was just skiing. Literally just now. "I'd like to preface this little situation with an apology up front. I am sorry you're here." Said Christopher Hitchens. He took out a cigarette and lit it unceremoniously. "Uh..." "Notice the omnipresent white light, the kind of wispy glow to everything? Yeah, clearly this is how you imagined death." It took a moment to connect the memories, you don't really know death, even when it's just happened to you. The wire. Oh, shit, there was a wire fence, no wonder that slope said no entry. Fuck, I'm gon na kill Jeff. "What, um, are you doing here, then?" I manage to ask. "That's preposterous. I'm not, this isn't defineably real." He flicked his cigarette directly onto the glowing white floor. "Okay." I could start with that. "Am I in a coma or something?" "Mm. Could be." He had a glass of whiskey now, clearly he was enjoying this. "I haven't really made up my mind on it, was hoping to come to a more informed decision." "Well, if I'm dead, and you're dead, and we're dead together, and there IS an afterlife sorta makes sense you'd be here, but at the same time..." "Did you, at all, follow my exploits? Just because I'm dead and appearing to you now doesn't mean I was wrong, or that I'd abandon logic after crossing the big finish line. You exist, sure, at least as far as you can prove to yourself. You're the only one experiencing you, there is no outside perspective that you couldn't have crafted within your own mind, just as easily this could all be in your head right now. People do it all the time and chalk it up to God. But also just as much that could have always been the case, every facet of your perceptions could just be the workings of a mind not actually tethered to a physical reality, but the other way around. It could be that yours is the only valid perspective, the actual hub and meaning of the entire universe, and it is as far as you know. So I really could just be a figment of your imagination and always was. Sort of egocentric, really. My money's on just being a coping mechanism to deal with the inherent trauma and inevitability of death. I could just as easily be Jesus or Muhammed." "You got me there." I conceded. "Still, you're kind of a strange candidate in terms of first person I meet." "Well, most people have big questions, don't they? They think that they'll get the answers on this side of the equation, kind of rubbish logic, that. I'm sort of an authority on the subject." "Well, do you have any answers?" "No. I have fantastic questions." "Such as?" "Right. So, if we're alive, and then dead, how long does that actual transition take? It might seem like it takes an instant from the outside, but at the same time, when we're under duress, time itself has a way of flexing, somewhat, our thoughts speed up to compensate. A small moment can be stretched very, very thin and very long. And there's no duress like death. So perhaps'eternity' from a personal perspective is an infinite division of a measurable moment." "I'm not sure I like that concept." "Barely dents the surface. What if, after billions of years of development, the human race creates a computer designed to analyse and experience the entire multi-dimensional spectrum of reality, from the big bang to the'present' to quantify it's meaning and trajectory? And that you can not'die', because you are an extension of the computer itself, analyzing and interacting with the data in the 4th dimension." "I hadn't thought of that, either." "But maybe you did. Well, there'd be no way of telling, either way. If it can be asserted without evidence it can be dismissed without evidence. Exactly the sort of nonsense nobody needs. Could you imagine waking up remembering this? People'd think you lost your marbles." We both had a pretty good laugh at that. He got up from his seat and cashed the cigarette into the empty whiskey glass. "You know, here's one more and then I think I'll go. When you're born, there was a whole universe of events leading up to that, and it's like when the tape recorder of the mind first pressed'record'. You weren't alive during that time, there's no memory of it, to you it doesn't exist, the tape doesn't go back that far. But, when you die, when the tape stops, you're basically skipping the remaining events of the rest of the universe, even through the end, when the it collapses and all of that. So whatever properties of reality that brought us here to begin with may even occur again, perhaps even inevitably. So, as far as you know, it just flips to side B and keeps right on recording as if nothing in between occurred." He put his hand on my shoulder. "I wish I had an easy slice of'this is how it is' to sate your questions. Not today. Dying is a lonely thing, you're born alone, you live alone inside your own head, you die alone, like a rat drowning in a sinking cage. And that, that is the rough edge of it, isn't it? Don't worry, you may or may not have all eternity to come to terms with it, if you do, take your time, if you don't, waste none of it." He put on his coat and turned to leave. "Well, best of luck to you, maybe you'll wake up, maybe this is it forever. I'll leave you to it." And he left. Just like that. Well, I was no closer to understanding where I was or if this really was the big blank. But the more I thought about it, the more I liked where I was. And that was a good start.

To say they were shocked was an understatement. To say I was shocked would be hardly telling the truth. I had fallen asleep at the command of my starcraft, a small spaceship capable of going supersonic speeds. Luckily, the starcraft had recognized the impending atmosphere and had slowed down a great deal before activating and deploying the auto-land feature. The ship was basically idiot proof, and I was a great deal lucky. I woke up to a tapping sound. It was soft, but it was on my window. I pressed down on a touch screen to open the glass encasing me. My suit had ample oxygen, so I crawled out of the ship. I was greeted by a large crowd of curious creatures, There were murmurs around them, but it was all gibberish to me. Suddenly, a hornlike sound could be heard and the mysterious creatures parted in two, leading a path leading directly up to me. I decided to stay by my starcraft, which I didn't really feel like parting with. Creatures holding white banners began to make there way up towards me, and all of the other creatures were saluting the large creature making his way down the path behind the banners. I turned on my Universal Translator. The leader made his way towards me, and with him I noticed a group of decorated individuals. There was a silence as the leader approached me. He gazed at me as if uninformed of my appearance, and signaled a translator towards him. The leader spoke something to me, but my Universal Translator device couldn't register anything of it. "So much for Universal" I thought to myself with a smirk in my helmet." It was broke half of the time anyway. "I am from Planet Earth. I have accidentally landed on this planet. I can not understand you." The translator glanced at the leader and said something. The leader pointed his golden scepter. He muttered something, and suddenly the guards came forward towards me. They tried to seize me, yet they could not take hold of me. I simply pushed them forward and they fell with a great might. The ruler suddenly halted them. He commanded them to shoot at me, yet their ammunition simply bounced off of me. The leader's eyes opened wide. He moved toward me and commanded the trumpets to sound. He placed his crown on my head and turned towards to the translator, who did know the common language of which I had spoken. "You clearly are a god of some type. But come, be our leader." I nod in approval and hold the scepter out over the people. "Today, you have made me your ruler. Today, I have made you my people. Go back into your community. I will protect you." The creatures scurried off, except the guards, the leader, and the translator. The leader spoke to me, "Come, live in the castle prepared for our ruler. From there you can lead these people." Day 54 A messenger from the ruler came to me earlier this afternoon. Another ship such as mine had landed, and another god had made his impression onto the people, yet he had slain many if them. I was to go and fight this new god of evil. However, I left the castle with no attention. My spaceship was parked in the courtyard, I activated the glass door via a screen button on my suit, stepped in, and prepared the rockets for lift off. "Stabilizers, check. Orbit path, check. Safety systems, check. Commencing liftoff." I hit the big red "takeoff button." and hit "confirm" as the creatures made their way towards my ship. One, realizing the impending force, pulled the others back, while some tried to run towards me. "3..... 2..... 1..... Liftoff. Preparing to leave atmospheric conditions." The starcraft AI voice said. The rockets pushed me forward at such a great force, and pushed me forward through the air. All that was left of my legacy was a circular smoke trail plowing through the orange sky against the horizon. The rocket re-loaded the destination into its autopilot flight featured and carried me onward.

The unmistakable aroma of the air wafting off of the lake tingled his nostrils as they finally arrived to their destination. 10 hours in a 1970 Chevy Kingswood station wagon, that dad toted as "the tank" had taken it's toll on the entire Thurmont clan. 15 year old Zach tried drowning out the sound of his 8 year old sister's insistent nagging as to when they would arrive at the lake house, by delving into his favorite C.S Lewis book. As much as mom tried to quell Samantha's whining, the 8 year old proved her persistence and managed to carry on for what seemed like the entire drive, only quieting long enough to devour the brownies Mom had brought along for a snack, making it impossible for Zach to get any reading done. His mind was hardly in a place to read anyway. This summer was supposed to be one of glorious adventure with his friends. The morning of their departure his parents practically had to drag him out of his room and stuff him into to the back seat of the busted up wagon. Zach sat sad and helpless in the rear view seat as the tank pulled out of the drive. When they arrived, the night sky had consumed the dusk, and all that could be seen was the poorly lit walkway about 20 yards from the gravel driveway that led to the most rickety pair of steps Zach had ever dared climb. Each step giving more than the last, certain to give way with the slightest misstep. Samantha quickly took note of the dilapidated steps, and aptly refused to climb the treacherous structure. Zach, ignoring Samantha's tantrum, braved the steps, carefully planting his feet in the most strategic places to avoid a total collapse. He managed his way to the front door and quickly found the hide-a-key so ingeniously hidden under the damp front door mat. Pushing open the pale wooden door, Zach reached in to the right side of the wall, slid his hand half way up from the floor a flipped the light switch up., He patiently waited for the light to flicker to life, to no avail. "Guess the breakers blown" shouted Dad as he stumbled to the top step, Samantha holding onto his neck for dear life. "There's a lantern right inside, wait here." Dad faded into the darkness for a few seconds before returning with a kerosene fueled flame, dancing inside a blue hued glass lantern. The Thurmont family all piled into the small stale living room which was overcome with the smell of mildew and kerosene. Zach collapsed on the couch, exasperated by the long day. " I will call Randy in the morning." said Dad. Randy was a friend of the family who lived a few miles down the road from the Thurmont cabin. He was charged with keeping an eye out on the place during the winter. Mom, sensing Samantha had exhausted herself from the endless outbursts of the day, said her goodnights and headed for bed with Samantha closely trailing behind. Zach, fearing Dad would soon retell the story of how he and Mom had come to find this cabin 100 years ago or whatever the story was, hastily headed for the steps and up to his cramped back bedroom, leaving Dad to rustle up a fire all alone. As Zach hurried up the rickety staircase Dads voice rang out stopping midway between the living room and freedom. "Goodnight, see you in the morning " Dad's voice rang out. " Also, Remember the rules of the lake house, let your mother and I know if you go somewhere, and don't go into the shed." Zach breathed a sigh of relief elated that he had gotten away so easily. He never understood why his dad was so intent on keeping out of the shed. He assumed it had something to do with the fact that the thing was barely standing. but never had enough curiosity to care about exploring the forbidden structure. He would much rather head to Ron's house about a mile up the shore. Ron had a huge house with all of the amenities, A.C, XBOX, jet skis, and endless supply of root beer, and Zach's arrival was always a welcome event in Ron's otherwise lonely existence. The next morning arrived sooner than Zach had desired. Staggering to his feet, Zach threw on his favorite camo shorts, and a tee and headed for the kitchen. Hurriedly making his way toward the door, he grabbed an apple, barely managing to get out "I'll be at Ron's" before slamming the back door. A short 5 minute walk and Zach was making his way up the driveway toward the large white house. Ron's mom answered the door, excitement consuming her as she greeted Zach, only outdone by Ron's enthusiasm as he turned the corner and saw Zach at the front door. They spent the rest of the day lounging in Ron's room, chugging more root beers than one person should consume in a single day, and mindlessly playing RPG games. Around 9 Zach he hadn't checked in with his parents all day, He politely asked to use the house phone to call his mom. scarfing down 3 or 4 chocolate cookies, he sat on a kitchen stool listening to a redundant ring on the other end of the line. "You have reached the Thurmont's, leave a message." I'd rather not Zach thought, as he hung up the receiver. Feeling satisfied, he hopped off the stool and headed back toward Ron's room when Ron's mother interrupted. "Zach, you are welcome to stay as long as you'd like but you must let your parents know you're okay. Why don't you and Ron run to your cabin and see if your parents are there." Zach not willing to jeopardize his luxurious accommodations quickly obliged. He hollered for Ron as he slipped his worn out sketchers on, and the two headed out the door, grabbing a handful more of cookies on their way out. In less than 5 minutes Ron and Zach had reached the outskirts of his family cabin. Making their way through the thick untamed yard, they arrived at the death trap known as the front stairs. By the time Ron had hopscotched his way to the top step, Zach was already in the living room. "Mom" the call echoed through the empty house. Several long seconds passed, as the boys waited hushed, waiting to hear any response. Nothing, quiet. feeling that they had made a considerable enough effort to satisfy Ron's mom, the boys turned and headed for the door. Zach in a hurry to get back to the paradise of controlled air temperature and chocolate chip cookies, hurdled himself off of the porch, clearing all of the steps and landing on both feet in the front yard. Ron, knowing his height and athletic ability left something to be desired, opted for a step by creaky step descent. As Ron reached the bottom step, Zach, being impatient, turned and headed for the path that lead back to Ron's house, but before he could take his third step through the dense lawn, he heard Ron's voice calling for him in a low frightened tone. "Zach" Ron called, almost whispering "What is that?." Zach turned around, unable to hide the annoyance from his face "what is what Ron?" Ron pointed towards the side of the house, across the lawn where the hut of a shed stood clinging to the wood line. Zach followed Ron's finger to the soft amber glow shining through the cracks in the doorframe of the shed. "It looks like your shed is on fire" Ron cautioned. "Yea the shed is on fire, sure Ron!" Zach responded, sarcasm dripping from his words. "No one uses that shed, it's probably just a light or something." Zach assured Ron. The two shrugged it off, and turned to head back to the path, when the unmistakable scream of a girl burst out from the shed. Before they could react the door swung open, and the glare of a lantern flame illuminated the opening. Out from the small shed came a large man, dressed in all black, face shadowed by the light surrounding his large frame. He looked like a giant, his shadow spilling out of the doorway 15 feet across the yard and meeting the now trembling feet of the two boys. Whoever this was, they hadn't yet spotted two young figures that stood helplessly a few yards away. As the boys watched in horror the man walked out of the shed made a quick turn and headed for the woods, carrying a large object over his shoulder. In a few seconds the large figure had disappeared into the tree line, leaving the two teens standing frozen with fright, unable to muster the courage to turn and run. After a few moments, Zach snapped back into reality and quickly realized that whoever had come out the shed would probably soon return. He turned to Ron gave him a firm shake and whispered that they need to get out of there. Ron still in shock could barely muster a head nod in agreement. The two boys, as quiet as they possibly could, turned and headed away from the shed. They tip toed silently across the yard, and into the shadows, doing everything possible to not make a sound and alert the man of their presence. They were a few footsteps from the path back to Ron's when the echo of a stick snapping under one of the boy's feet rang out and everything went black. The next thing Zach remembered he was waking up to the familiar dancing flame of lantern light with a throbbing headache. As he regained consciousness, he slowly lifted his head to try to get his bearings. The first thing he noticed were the binding leather straps that were tightly bound to his wrists, feet, and chest. Panicked, he violently thrashed his body, feeling the weight of the leather bindings tightening with every attempt. As he thrashed something caught the corner of his eye. He body went limp as the gruesome sight across the room came into focus. Hanging like the prize antlers of an ten point buck on the opposite wall, were the severed heads of Ron, Samantha, Mom, and Randy. Blood stained the walls in thick red streams as it streaked down the warped walls. Overcome with emotion Zach let out a horrifying scream. never seeing the cold metal of a bearded ax hurling through the air towards his exposed neck. one swift swing was all it took. Moments later Zach's father stood over him, holding the blood stained ax, admiring the newest ornament to add to his growing collection. Ever satisfied with today's haul Zach's father threw his lifeless body over his shoulder and headed for the woods.

"Between the midst of the 17th century and the 23rd, humanity entered what is now known as the second Dark Age." The voice-over narrated the timeline which stretched from one end of the room to the other, displayed by the holo-teach. It went on. "At one end of the room, you can see 1492 and the'discovery' of the Americas by Columbus. At the other, on the right side of the room, 2246, the year in which Jalil Balakrishnan first reached Sirius by superluminary travel. The Alcubierre drives back then were horrifically inefficient and required gigatons of hydrogen fuel to be fused to even jump between stars, but for the time, they were a quantum leap in technology over what had existed for the 800 years before." I already knew a lot of this. The Second Dark Ages were one of my favourite periods of time, although the third age of war was also intensely interesting. "So why are these times known as a Dark Age? See for yourself." Immediately, the timeline faded and was replaced by several common items of the time. Primitive kinetic firearms were the first to appear, all the way from flintlock pistols used by the sea captains of old, to type-34 heavy bombardment cannons which were utilised in the great wars of 2134. But these were only a small section of the array of objects which were now distributed all over the room, and were labelled under a large sign reading "WAR." Carbon-driven automobiles, horse pulled wagons, Orion class spacecraft - they were all here. The deep, bassy voice of the narrator spoke again. "From the beginning of recorded history, humans have used fire as a tool. But from the 1600s onwards, the power of the flames was truly harnessed by man - for better, or for worse." Factories appeared, and spewed fumes into the room. Although I knew they weren't real, the compulsion to cough still tickled at the back of my throat. "But soon enough, man was to learn the error of his ways. His greed began to damage the world around him." A graph showed at the front of the room, with a curve which bent upwards exponentially. "Between 1850 and 2055, global temperatures rose by a total of 4 degrees celcius as a result of carbon dioxide and methane pollution in the atmosphere. The notion that such gases would be allowed into the environment is abhorrent to us today, but their effect was not fully understood until the decade of the 1980s, and ignored willfully for years after that." "Of course, this had dire effects on the biosphere. The holocene extinction event wiped out 94 of species on planet Earth, and human population began to fall from a peak of 9 billion in 2029 to a low of 2 billion by 2086. But even this was not the greatest danger. In fact, instead of banding together against the storm of their own making, mankind turned on each other. By 2046 two major geopolitical blocks had developed - one known as "the West" and the other "the East." As resources dwindled and famine spread, it was the East who struck first. Tensions rose to a breaking point and it was the invasion of a small rich nation known as "Korea" which caused war to break out." "This war, as you should all know, is now called the Third World War. The specifics of the war are both complex and incomplete, as much of the historical data and evidence was destroyed. But it is known that there were two major stages: the conventional war, lasting from 2047 to 2065, in which both sides fought using traditional kinetic weaponry and drone warfare. Over 300 million people died in this stage of the war, and the East took the brunt of the losses - nearly 200 million - leading to a near victory by the West." The narrator paused for a moment while maps and battle clips played across the room. It showed a long, arduous struggle; red and blue armies pushing against each other across the world while around them, the seas advanced unstoppably. "By 2065, the East had been pushed back and the situation was dire. Famine and revolution were commonplace. If the conventional phase had continued, estimates show that the East would have collapsed and lost by 2070. And so, cornered and in a state of desperation, the East unleashed its final weapon, and the war entered the second phase: thermonuclear bombardment." All around us, nuclear warheads detonated and rose in huge plumes of fire and smoke. "Over two weeks of continual nuclear warfare, more people died than in all the wars in history combined." The narration paused again to let the fact sink in. "Although the specifics are unknown, it is known that both the East and the West were annihilated almost completely. It is estimated that 2 billion people perished in nuclear fire over the course of a month. We will look at the war in far greater detail in coming lessons, but for now, this is all that is necessary." "However, despite the horror of this war, there was an upside. The resulting nuclear winter cooled global temperatures by almost 2 degrees." The temperature graph showed again, with a distinct dip after 2065 after which it did not rise. "This was a blessing for the nations which had survived the war. Most notably, India, one of the few nuclear states which had made it through the war, became the new superpower - the only superpower. The nation's population of 360 million, down from a 2019 peak of 1.37 billion, began to recover. With cooling global temperatures, climate change was suitably negated to support agriculture on a scale which could provide food for the entire world population again. Although still plagued by problems, human civilisation began to recover." - Thanks for reading! Every hiss of the nail gun and every rotation of the circular saw was one minute closer to the time. The rain had been pouring all day, but at 4:25 the sun had finally broke through the clouds. The sun streamed through the window and by 4:36 I had finally reached the most important part of my day. The Bane of Kings, the Harbinger of Death himself, has returned. Some thought him a myth, merely a legend to entertain children, but now the tales have proven to be much more than lore. Only the Chosen One, a man with the body of flesh but the soul of magic, can stop him. But alas, this man is no brave warrior. Alas, this man is no staunch mage. Alas, this man is no cunning knave. This man knows one trade, one way: the Way of the Drunkard. Talbjorn, a man of about thirty, has lived in my village for many years. Nobody knows where he came from, but he stumbled into town with an arrow in the calf some years ago and has since remained. He doesn't speak much, nor does he act much, only wastes his days traversing this sleepy village. Some days he looks to work the forge, others he hunts for pelts, but most days he simply drinks. His wound has left him a near cripple, a noticeable gimp in his walk, and his poor routine has not done wonders for his health. Since his arrival, he's gone from a dashing young man with the strength of ten men to an obese sycophant who can barely carry his own weight. While many, including he, seem to think him a wounded animal, an old horse than can no longer pull his cart, I know better. I have studied him on his hunts, seen his expert marksmanship and proficiency with an ax against all manner of nature's worst, and yet he has stayed in this sleep village among the common rabble rather than continuing his adventures. While it may not seem like it, this laziness and gluttony will lead to the world's demise. With the return of the Great Harbinger, the world as we know it will not be safe until the Chosen One can slay him. This is why I must get this man back on his feet and into action, out questing and gallivanting across the plains and tundras and in shape to face such a foe. I must convince him to leave this village and out on the path to his destiny, before it is too late. Why have I not told him this? I am a chicken. No, not afraid, for I am of the noblest, wisest and boldest of my kind; I am a literal chicken. I laid and nested for years, watching this once great warrior as he crumbled into but a husky shadow of his former self, until one day opportunity struck and I hatched an idea. Wolves. A whole pack of the dastards came bolting into town. There were no guards, for the village was too small and isolated for such luxuries, and so the townspeople are left to defend for themselves. The local men and women took up arms against the feral beasts, but alas, these villagers were no warriors. As the casualties grew, Talbjorn awoke from his slumber and let instinct take over. He drew his bow and put down a wolf with a single shot before emptying his quiver into several others. When he ran out of arrows, the newly able warrior grabbed an ax from a fallen villager, ironically the barkeep who'd served him ale for years, and went headfirst into the pack swinging away. I watched as the warrior cut them down with savage blows. While he was powerful, Talbjorn has not as much of a finesse player with his ax as he was with his bow. On multiple occasions, he nearly struck down an ally with his berserk blows. This was my chance. I had always been one of the noblest and fairest of chickens, my feathers never ruffled and my peak always clean. I could lay eggs on command, as if by magic, and had faithfully served my town no matter the hardships they had faced. I was loved and respected by all, despite my status as a mere bird, yet I always knew I was destined for something greater. Perhaps I was the Chosen One as well. I flew, not literally of course, into the heat of battle. As Talbjorn swung his ax downward in an attempt to behead one of the final wolves, I intercepted. Instead, his red wet blade met my tender breasts. As I felt his ax crush my frail body and my life fade out, I knew I had won. I had done my duty. I watched from the Heavens as the village went into shock. Their prized bird had just been slain in cold blood, indeed a crime most fowl. The villagers turned away from the wolves and united against their common enemy, the forsaken one. After attempting to fend off attacks from all sides, women and wolves alike seeking to rip his flesh, Talbjorn fled into the wilderness. He could no longer return to his cushy life as a drunkard, now an outcast from society. Years ago he thought his adventure had ended, but alas, it was just beginning.

As THEY came we all stopped what we were doing. We left our homes, our workplaces, religious temples and stared. We stared in disbelief. How long did it take? Mere weeks. It was a strange preposition. Councilman Avurr stood on the podium and spoke to us: "Fellow Dalurians. We have to make a difficult choice. Death is upon us, and we can not stop it." The council murmured, no one knew what we should do. What we could do. We never knew war. We have been living as a single entity all our life, and this strange race which we call "Devourers" had come to destroy us - They never gave a reason. But the Councilman didn't stop there. "But there is a race that can. The humans of earth have shown brutality that rivals that of the Devourers, and I have sent a request to them to aid us. They will receive our FTL technology, but we will survive." An uproar. The FTL technology passed on to a race so bloodthirsty? I have studied them for decades now. The Devourers, yes, they come and destroy without mind or reason - but humans? They are calculated. They are brutal. They are..... special. The humans are not like us. They are divided into many tribal regions that prey on each other for the most miniature gains. Our brightest scientists do not understand the differences between those human tribes. What makes the "American" tribe so different from the "French" tribe, the "Mexican" tribe. Or any of the hundreds and hundreds of tribes. Only a human can discern the different tribes from one another, and if asked would give reasons that none of us could understand; "He has a darker skin colour," "He greets people differently," "They wear different clothes," "Whorship another god - or none at all!." And yet, here they are. Destroying the ships of the invading Devourers with such precision and destructive force. Thousands of human ships swarming our home planet. Like the "Ant" creature that are native to the Earth. A hive mind bend on killing with cold calculation. They sent us this letter as an answer: "We the United Nations Alliance will send 400 Destroyers, 700 Falcon-Class Ships, 30 Carriers and 2000 Interceptors. Our risk-assessment suggests a minimal loss of life, and more importantly a insignificant economical cost for this war effort. We look forward to the payment and future business. Signed, Tonald Drump, CEO and Head of the UNA of Planet Earth" I hope it will not come to haunt us, inviting the monster to our doorstep. Trusting, that they will not turn on us once the Devourers are defeated, for what are we if not a planet ripe for sacking and exploitation in their eyes?

April 11th, 2011 Famous events throughout history have typically had observers that seemed out of place, and strangely enough, out of time. Reports occasionally surface in some of the less reputable tabloids of people in odd garb waiting outside major political buildings shortly before assassinations and important speeches. A report from a Roman soldier shortly before Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon details the most common of these "watchers." This watcher was a woman, very tall, with large eyes and dressed all in black. Dubbed the Lady of the Night by contemporary historians who knew of her existence (and not many did), she was believed in ancient times to be a grim omen, sent by the gods to signify the coming of a great tragedy. The Lady of the Night has been present for many of mankind's darkest hours, though as freedom of the press was explored it quickly. fell to various governments to expunge her existence from the public eye. I work as a historian of sorts for the US government, and it is my job to research things that aren't allowed to make it into the evening news. My studies take me all over the world, and I've looked into many topics that pertain to the abnormal, from Stonehenge to the possible crash at Roswell 40 years ago. I'm not a high-ranking man, and I don't have access to classified information. Honestly, the true purpose of my work is to ensure that a civilian could never find out why these things happen. Anytime I am successful in my investigation, all the leads I have taken end up dead or destroyed, and the results are typically classified immediately. My bosses say the secrecy is to preserve the illusion of stability and security in a world that, truthfully, is anything but those things. I'm writing all of this down because, right now, as I look outside my apartment window, the Lady of the Night is standing outside. Dark-skinned, with dark hair and large, black eyes, she seems to me very shadow-like, a grim omen indeed. Not many notice her as they walk by, too intent on whatever frivolous activity they happen to be in the amidst of or on their way to, but I have heard all the stories, and I am unable to take my eyes off her. Upon realizing that I am staring at her back, she seems confused and then angry, as if I shouldn't have noticed her. As I write this last sentence, she smiles up at me, and when I look up again she has disappeared, and the ground begins to shake. This report was written minutes before a large earthquake impacted Fukishima, Japan. Aaron Jacobs would perish in the disaster, though his notes were recovered once the devastating nuclear meltdown that followed had subsided. Mr. Jacobs' injuries are inconsistent with being crushed by debris, and his face is twisted in what appears to be horror.

"I'm not going. I wan na change schools." I harrumphed at my parents. "Kelsey, you'll be okay. It's just a uniform. It evens the playing field. Rich or poor, everyone will look the same. Those horrid starched khaki slacks. Not even skinny slacks. Straight legged. Like I was some sort of homely woman with no style. I didn't even have shoes to match. Come on! I was forced to wear my mom's plain slingbacks. What is this, the 90's? I walk up to my friends and see them in the same thing as me, but a different variety of black, or red shirts and blue slacks. Jessica was one of the one's wearing red. She so shouldn't have. It's sooo not her color. She's already a bit on the chunky side. The red wasn't doing her any favors. In the year 3021, wraps and burritos had become the lunch of choice for many Americans. Sandwiches were passe now; their crumbs made too much of a mess, and this posed a problem when the standard human body had more crevices to infiltrate than ever before. If the thought of injecting bread into your bloodstream sounds gruesome, imagine hundreds of tiny crumbs rubbing against your circuitry, burning out your processors, padding up against the inside of your neck, wracking whatever was left of your brain with headaches until you eventually went to a mechanic. We called these types of malfunctions "crumbs," an etymological nod to the story of the first computer bug. Everyone had heard horror stories of crumbs, and most people shied away from bread, cookies, and other messy foods for this reason. But today, Meg wanted a sandwich. She pointed at her plate, and the material transmitter embedded in her index finger summoned two slices of bread, an assortment of deli meats, and some toppings. Meg could've procured a pre-prepared sandwich, but the old-fashioned streak within her compelled her to assemble it from scratch. She set to work, arranging the contents in an aesthetically pleasing manner and topping it off with some finger-produced mustard. As she bit into her creation, a spray of crumbs fell and landed in the crack marking the juncture of her chest pad and neck framework. For a few moments, she felt nothing and continued to munch on her sandwich. Then, the pain began. Meg doubled down to the floor clutching her throat. Sparks crackled between her fingers. Heat began to swell within her. "Help!" she cried into her cerebral phone, "I'm burning up!" A robotic voice answered her. "Have you tried turning your body on and off again?" The system was not responding. "No! I can't - " Her thoughts choked in their processors, consumed by the heat. Acrid steam billowed from her nostrils. "Have you tried running a virus scan?" Fire erupted from the seams connecting Meg's shoulders to her neck. Her body tried to run the extinguishing program, but everything was shutting down. Meg screamed, trying to stuff the fire back into her body, only to brand her palms with angry weals. More flames erupted from the cracks between her joints. She ran around her kitchen, colliding off the walls, against the sink, into the refrigerator, anything to try and stop the burning. The flames leapt from her body, spreading up the walls and through the room. Meg finally slumped to the floor, exhausted, aflame, and mechanically all-but-dead. The metallic voice rang in her head. "Please hold while we connect you to one of our mechanics."

Dear Amira, It has been a long time since we've talked. Well atleast while I was sober. What has it been 6 years? That time went by so fast and I hardly remember most of it. Most of it was all bullshit anyway, just me making bad desicions over and over and refusing to get help. I'm 25 now, not much to show for it. You'd be 15 now. I see you sometimes, in my dreams, my nightmares, sometimes even when I'm awake out of the corner of my eye. I even hear you, you yell at me most of the time but you do talk once in awhile. I remember back then when our unit would come to your village to talk to your chief of police. I used to give you candy for keeping the other children away from our trucks, you were the toughest iraqi kid I know. The candy was never enough you always wanted something else, every time you asked me for my watch but I couldn't give it to you. I used to get in trouble for playing soccer with you and you're brother and not keeping guard. We were on our last mission to your village before I was going to come back to the states, I tried to explain it to you but you didn't understand. Right before we left I gave you my watch, I never saw a happier kid in my life. I was smiling as I watched you show off to the other kids. I was getting back into my truck when I heard yelling and I turned to look, everything was so slow it felt like it was frozen. I watched the iraqi policeman shot you and take the watch from you and put it on. I ran over to you but you were already dead. I wanted to kill that cop but we couldn't intervene in iraqi civil matters. I just had to sit there and watch your body lay on the street while we pulled away and went back to base. I have never forgave myself for that, if I had just kept the watch you would still be alive today. I'm sure I'll talk to tonight or tomorrow or whenever I can fall asleep next. Until then, I'm sorry. Joe

I was browsing for some shirts when I heard the cellos. I was born with a built-in radar for danger. Normally, my brain would play some lively tunes that one would hear on a children's show, but every time I go near harm, the deep basses coupled with the invisible string quartet would warn me to run away as fast as I could. It helped me know when to stay away from dark alleys, or to cancel some road trips.So far, it had been an effective way to keep me alive. I slowly turned around and went for the exit, my eyes darting left and right in search for the culprit, my ears trying to listen for real-time danger amidst the blaring orchestra in my head. My heart followed the beat of the song, thumping quickly as I start to walk faster. The ever-increasing crescendo was an indication that I was not going far from the disaster that is about to come. I veered left into the children's section, startling a group of kids gawking at the life-sized mannequin of their favorite superhero. I attracted eyes from all of the other shoppers as my half-hearted run turned into a full-blown sprint. I was positively running for all of the exits, yet the music would not stop. I decided that staying in the second floor would be stupid; I had to go back down and bolt for the exit of the department store. I ran down the stairs back to the ground floor, pushing unsuspecting bystanders out of the way. I flipped racks in my hurry, and I skidded across glass displays of jewellery. I heard the security guard call me but I can not stop. At last, I made it back into the atrium of the whole mall. But something was off. The music hadn't stopped. The danger wasn't over. I looked over my shoulder for signs of someone following me, because why else would the music not stop? As I scan the crowd of shoppers mindlessly strolling in and out of the department store, my mind formulated another conclusion on why the music would not stop. The correct answer dawned on me, and it was horrifying. I realized that it wasn't just me, but the whole mall was in danger. My flight instinct told me to get out of the building as quick as possible. I bolted for the exit quickly, but something caught my eye. A young girl, crying in search for her mother who lost her in the crowd. I felt a tingling sensation in my gut. I was the only one in the whole mall who knew what danger it was in. I had to save these people. I had to act. I knew it was suicide, but I ran back upstairs to the top floor, frantically searching for directions to the security room. I passed stalls in a blur, and I pushed through crowds of shoppers. "Sorry!" I shouted back to an old lady who fell down when I went past her. At last, I found the Office of Security. I opened the double doors and walked in straight to the long and white corridor to the room at the end. The orchestra's music has reached full fortississimo that I can barely hear myself think as I opened the door to the control room. I quickly scanned my surroundings, half-blind from the glare of the dozens of monitors. My eyes settled on a stout security guard at the far end of the room, staring at me with bewilderment. I saw him reach for his radio on his pocket, and I was scared that he would not listen, but I managed to exasperately tell him what I came here for with what little breath I have left. "Danger!" I managed to say through heavy breaths, clutching a stitch on my side. "W-we are in danger!" I gripped the nearest table, struggling to stand on my two feet. I felt the guard's intense stare, and I looked back. Why was he not acting? Why was he not calling the security? Why was he not announcing the evacuation? We stared at each other intently in a defeaning silence. And that was when I noticed it. A defeaning silence. The orchestra stopped playing. There was only a reverberating echo of the last violin doing the last note in a rich vibrato. I looked at the floor beside my adversary. It was a guard lying down haphazardly by his feet, with the blank eyes warning me of the unstoppable fate that I had caused upon myself. I stared back at the only other man alive in this room, and I was too stunned to move. "I don't know how you found out," he said in a voice that was surprisingly deep in relation to his stature. "I applaud your attempt to be a hero, but you were too late." Behind him, the televisions showed a collage of the entrances, with each camera capturing by detail the deaths of the guards who tried to stop the terrorists forcing their way into the mall. He pointed a pistol in my direction, and as I hear gunshots from outside, I also heard the echo of the violin's vibrato drift farther away. And then came the silence. ..... Thank you for reading! It was my first time, so please bear with my noob and cliche writing skills)

(So I worked out a concept based on the idea, taking it into a little more extreme direction. I found the concept really interesting, especially taking it to its logical conclusions of brain enhancement. I may have took the'Religion' part a little too literally, but if you're interested in more or more detail about the world I was thinking of, let me know.) Even for the trusted, it's a hassle getting down here. Three biometric scanners get me into the Ecclasiarchy's data center. Bodyscan, DNA, mental key. I stand in the final chamber, listening to the low-volume hymns in soft white light, and think of the well-worn pages of the bible on the lectern, the first day I gave a sermon. The light flicks on, a golden-white, and the door hisses and opens. It's pointless really, the thing could have verified who I was without me having to do anything, but we've always held ourselves to tradition. The hum of cooling systems is all I can hear; the man-sized blocks of alabaster computing substrate aren't hot enough to glow on their own, but they do radiate heat if you get close enough. I'm tech support now, well, I'm still a priest. But there's an ever-increasing personnel shortage and we all end up doing double duty somewhere. The facility's Seraphim dispatched little more than a shade of a angel saying some piece of equipment down here needed maintenance, so I'm here, in my robes, and a toolbox. I know if the Seraphim wasn't able to fix it remotely it's going to be a pain in the posterior. Walking past those alabaster pillars you can't help but think about what they represent. One hundred forty five million and counting. Looking directly at one, I could almost hear a choir of angels in my head. My metabrain said it was a synesthetic thing, that I was doing it to myself, but I wouldn't put it past the Seraphim to add a little trickery to it all. They're all devious bastards in some ways, God forgive me. My own modest neural circuitry pointed me in the right direction, down hundreds of rows of radiant white substrate like gigantic tombstones laid out in a perfect grid. Rounding the final corner, the ground was covered in hundreds of coppery, metal swirls, spread out like someone dropped a jar of them. Copper shavings. Looking at the scatter, they all seemed to have come from what looked like a dead camera. What could have happened here? The camera dome had a blackened hole where the ultrahard material had fractured outward. Some kind of overload? I unfolded a step ladder, and took the panel off the ceiling with a crowbar, reaching up to the conduit. These things are quadruply redundant, built to last out of nanospecced material, internal power supply, wireless, conduit backed up. I grabbed my headlamp and looked around in the ceiling space. The conduit was severed, pinched on two ends with something strong enough to bend the metal until the interior links were cut. More copper shavings everywhere. The area around the camera had been sawn open, cleanly. I shook my head. It looked like sabotage, but how? And what use was sabotaging one camera? Exiting the ceiling I looked from the hole in the camera's dome forward. On the substrate pillar around 4 meters away, there was a black dot. I rushed over to it, triggering a gentle haptic feedback from my brain as I approached the personnel restricted boundary and could go no closer. But from there I could see the black dot; A little spike embedded in the substrate. Invaders in heaven. I instantly called for help, and found my sensorium elevated through the choirs almost instantly to the Seraphim's level. Couldn't even look at the thing directly of course, but it didn't waste time asking any questions, just rifled through my brain for the appropriate information. I'm guessing. In the church you sign away your own private key for that stuff to the Administration. A matter of trust. An insane thing to do anywhere else in the world, but if I didn't buy into the whole righteous-servants-of-God-on-earth thing I wouldn't even be here. Of course men are fallible, even the most righteous man is, but the Angels are not. If they fail in anything, it was because it was impossible, not because it was an oversight. And it solved the problem of those lip-service priests with ulterior motives, no force on Earth could lie so thoroughly to itself that these things couldn't see their true colors. My sensorium returned to the real world as quickly as it was snatched away, my body steadfastly holding itself up until I resumed control. There were no lights on the attacked substrate in front of me, but I could tell something had been done. It just didn't seem to glow the same.

" Shit, " Arnold muttered under his breath as he swerved to miss the red Toyota Corolla that turned in front of him. He'd run a red light on Main Street while his mind was set to cruise control, and he was ninety-nine percent sure cameras had been mounted at the intersection. He mouthed a silent sorry at the other driver, who replied with a loud honk as she turned right in front of him. Several blocks later, the red Corolla turned into Walkerville Cemetery, and a mildly surprised Arnold followed until he reached the parking lot. A familiar black-haired girl stepped out of the car, gasped in recognition as she looked at him, then immediately marched right up to him. " What the hell was that, Arnold? You nearly got us both killed! " Arnold felt himself shrink backwards a little. " I-it was a mistake. Sorry, Wanda. I was just thinking about..... " Wanda's glare softened. She closed her eyes and sighed. " It's all right. I'm sorry. This isn't the time for this kind of outburst. " Arnold raised his eyebrows, stunned at how quickly she'd calmed down. A silence took hold; they hadn't talked in almost a decade, and he didn't quite know what to say. " You don't look good in black, " Wanda finally said. " O-oh? " " I mean, it doesn't suit you. Not like orange or white. " Arnold choked out a chuckle. " Yeah, maybe. Red suits you more, too. " " How's Phoebe? She couldn't make it? " " She couldn't get time off. The vet clinic she works at only has three full veterinarians, and one of them is on maternity leave, so they're kinda tied up. " " No kids for you guys yet? " " No, not yet. " Arnold scuffed one foot against the other. An awkward silence fell again; the pair stood as though they were waiting for other people to interject. Finally, another car pulled up. " Hey guys, what's up? " called a too-convivial voice. Carlos poked his head out the window and flashed a smile as Dorothy Ann stepped out from the driver's seat. " A funeral, " Wanda flatly replied, eyes narrowing in disapproval of the brightness of Carlos's voice. Carlos visibly deflated, and mumbled an apology. Dorothy Ann sighed, then walked up to Wanda and Arnold. " But really. How are you guys doing? I heard you landed a grant to do alpine field work, Arnold? " " Oh, that was a few years ago, " Arnold replied, then smiled sheepishly. " I guess that's still pretty recent these days. But yeah, I did. Collected a lot of valuable rock and ice cores. " Carlos finally joined them, having adjusted his tie to his satisfaction. " Never would've thought you'd be the type to apply to the government for field trips, Arn, " he said with a grin. " Yeah, well, I owe that to... " Arnold couldn't bring himself to finish the sentence. " Anyways, what about you guys? "

"Welcome to the shed, kid," Peter said as he threw open the door to the large warehouse and strode inside followed closely by Carter. Carter stared wide eyed at the rows and rows of tanks and stacked as high as the ceiling, each with a porthole showing a human face in side. From the outside the building looked as a football stadium. He tried figure out how many people that might be but math was never his strong suit. "Who are all these people?" Carter finally asked. "Geez they really didn't tell you anything," Peter said with a laugh. "You must have pissed off somebody important. This is the shed, where we store all the spares. As you're hopefully aware when a felony is committed any DNA belonging to the purp is used to create a clone. This serves two purposes. First it helps to locate and apprehend the criminal responsible, things like facial recognition and fingerprints become easier as well photos for visual identification. Second the void they leave in society can be filled by the clone so families aren't broken and industry can keep rolling along. The system is great when things roll smoothly like that. This is what happens when it doesn't." He gestured widely as he walked down the aisle. They were heading for a small booth at the far end of the building which was virtually the only space not dedicated to frozen clones. "These are the spares. Clones whose originators were never found. Kept on the off chance that they will be eventually located." Carter poked at the computer screen next to one of the tanks. It flicked on displaying details of the case that the ice man was connected to. A couple was murdered in their apartment on 32nd Avenue and their home ransacked. Some pictures showed the two bodies sprawled across the bed with blood covering the walls and blankets. Carter recoiled in horror and hurried after Peter. "How many are there?" he asked. "Here?" Peter considered the question. "I'm not sure what the total is anymore but I think it's north of 10,000 now. That's just for this area mind you. There's a lot of other places like this around." "Seems like a pretty poor system if so many end up here," Carter commented as he glanced at the unending mass of silver cyclinders before entering into the small office. "I once heard that something like 10 of all clones end up in the shed," Peter responded. "We solve a lot more crimes than we used to because of this program." Carter groaned. "That'd be great if I actually got to go out and solve crimes instead of being stuck in here with the popsicles." "So what did you do anyway? Bang the chief's wife or something? Somebody must really hate you to shuffle you off here on day one," Peter asked as he dropped himself into a chair. "I don't know," Carter admitted. "Honest," he added when he caught Peter staring at him. "Whatever," Peter said with a dismissive wave. He pointed at the bank of monitors on the back wall. "These are all the security cameras for the building. Most of them are on the outside, the delivery bay, and the main entrance." "You get a lot of people trying to break in to kidnap random nobodies?" Carter asked with a chuckle. "Don't get too comfortable with that joke, kid. It happened one time in Arizona, and it didn't end well for the guards there," Peter said in an unexpectedly serious tone. "Only time I've heard of it happening though. Mostly we're here to run the terminal." He pointed at a screen in the center bottom row directly about the keyboard. It was the only one that wasn't running a view of the building. Instead this screen showed a menu with a search box and a list of case numbers. "From here you can view each spare and their case, sorted by case number because they don't have names. You can also locate them, crack their tanks open, and if they're in an upper row you can have them brought down all from this console." Carter tapped a couple of buttons and opened up a file. Up popped an image of a red haired woman with pale skin and freckles. Next to her face were the details of her creation and dates. "You ever go looking through here to see if you know anyone?" "Yeah," Peter answered almost sheepishly. "You ever find anyone?" "No." "That'd sure be strange, wouldn't it?" "Indeed." Carter turned to face out the window. "This job is boring as hell, isn't it?" "That it is," Peter admitted with a sigh.

The view provided by the front screen seemed to betray what we had seen of this world coming in. Our expectations where of a world of green and blue. Yet, our plan is to land on a stark desert, with it's immense heat and excessive dryness. Much too dry for our comfort. But, we are guests. The felt the best place for us to finally meet is in an open field south of a Smaller city called Phoenix, nestled in the heart of a nation known as the United States of America. The ship continued to veer along the course provided to us by the race of Humans below. Their industrious cities still belching various pollutants into their atmosphere by our studies, but as a people, experiencing the longest stretch of relative peace in it's entire history, as far as we aware. After all, it was only recently, a few hundred of the planet's rotation around it's Star, which we have deemed Selaphim'Gal, named after our home Colony, that we have been able to observe this nascent race of sentient lifeforms. This system is ripe with resources. The discovery that the Asteroid belt containing immense quantities the rare Saanium metal. A very hard, brittle, silvery-white transition metal, used to create our most powerful armors for Flocks of war as it is generally credited with being the second densest element that we have ever found. To find a colonizable world, with people whom can provide much to our People. The discovery of a sentient race, even one as far along as the Humans are, is always a wonder that is celebrated among our people. And spirits are high among the crew. They are an industrious people, who can adapt to any change and any environment, provided enough preparation. They are well on their way, as many others have, to creating a singular purpose amongst themselves. Even without our intervention, they will have soon reached the stars on their own. That is to be sure. But, our intervention is necessary. For they are but babes, fumbling in playful ignorance of what they have done. For years they have been broadcasting, faint, unintelligible signals, but signals nonetheless. Signals are traceable, the signals have tracked more than just us, for we are the first. For, while they are not the ultimate goal, they are the gateway to it. The ship began to slow as we reach our destination. The screens pick up the massive crowd of onlookers. The people. By the gods, the people. Staring up at us in wonder, and fear, as we stare back the same. Although they see our ship, we see their faces. So different from ours. Where their faces flat, ours are beaked. Their eyes, affixed to the front, seem small, unable to see in the more dark periods of their planet's rotation. Whereas ours are wide, will barely be able to withstand the brightness of the day. Their scaly skin, not reptilian in nature, but a skin none the less. No feathers, like us, and our flying forefathers. But, they are bipedal, like us. Clothed, clothes are good. Albeit some designs didn't seem to show obvious purpose. These people understand civility. Their language is alien to us, as we are to them, however, communication will be simple. It was relayed that we will be bringing a device off board that will translate our languages. So that we may speak as one People. We land. On our descent, we did notice the conspicuously placed obvious military strength off to the side of the crowd of people. However we deemed ourselves safe enough as the crowd of people did appear to be civilian in nature. This military, through our studies, values civilian life as much as possible. This line of thinking gives me and my crew hope. Trepidation is felt throughout the crowd and throughout the crew. We leave our stations and gather our gear and materials. We reach the exit bay, closing the airlock behind us. I look to my crew members, six flying souls in all. Each one, eyes aglow with fear and wonder, nod at me. They are ready. We are ready. We hope they are ready. The latches begin to systematically release, with a loud clunking sound. The personnel ramp begins to release, sending in a wave of the atmosphere. We breathe deep. Drinking in the essence of the world of which we now stand. As a scientist, and an explorer, this is the moment we wait for. Breathing in the new air. This is why the Gods gave us the Star Ways. Each crew member breathes deeper, as I do. The feeling creates stars in my eyes as my body begins to adjust to the dry, warm air. We take our first steps down the ramp. As we descend, there is little sound. Every being is holding its breath. We first touch the dirt of the planet called Earth and spread out, drinking in the sight around us. All around, there are people, standing, sitting, staring. The young, crying in protest of the heat, the old with unmasked fear in their eyes. I look back at my crew who are all watching everyone, watching us, turn back to me. We nod. Slowly, as instructed, we raise our claws skyward. Extend our primary and secondary of our 6 talons, closing the others in a fist. Our indication of the number 2. We were instructed this would signal the crowd that we are here as friends. What happened next, we did not expect. The masses of people suddenly erupted in noise and crying. Causing my crew to jump in fright and even made my heart beat fast at the sudden change. But, I knew, and soon the crew realized as well, that this was a happy sound. The crowd understood the symbol we made and thus it seemed that we are not the threat we seemed. A male, flanked by several other members, both male and female stepped forward and made a sound we couldn't understand. I indicate that I do not understand, and signal for the Translation Matrix Device. My second hands me a small computer, which I speak into to calibrate it. I indicate that the man do the same. He does so, stops, and looks at me with a questioning face. I indicate more, thinking rolling my claw would get the point across. He seems to understand and continues to speak in the device. It ejects a tone. Which startles the male but then his face lights up. He seems to already understand the process is complete. He hands it back to me. I have the device begin processing. After a short time, it indicates it is done. I turn the device on. It beeps and flashes bright green. It is ready. My heart races. I look at the man, he looks at me. "Hello?" The male jumps. "Yes? I can understand you now?" Asks the male. "Our Translation Matrix seems to be working. This is a momentous occasion! I am called Sh'rriik of Gold Claw! I am a scientist and explorer for the Great Confluence of M'rraak. Our empire spans a great number of stars across our Galactic home. As a representative of the Council, I greet you all with peace and friendship and I hope that we can learn much from one another! Who am I communicating with?" The male, in a strange garment of Black cloth with a white undergarment and strangle hanging cloth made of a bright Red fabric, open his mouth in a strange way, showing his many teeth. We've learned, throughout our exploration that the eyes are what you watch for reaction of sentient species. The eyes will ultimately betray all intention. There was nothing but joy and curiosity in this males eyes. "My name is Ricardo Samuelson, President of the United States of America. On behalf our nation, and of the entire Human Race of Earth, I greet you and welcome you to our Planet. I do hope that we will live in peace so that both our peoples may prosper. What brings you to our humble home?" Ricardo, the male replied. So began the official dialogue between our 2 peoples. We told them of our journey, of the systems resource importance and the most dangerous information of all, they are no longer protected. We told them that their world was once in the domain of an Ancient Empire that has fallen low. It's worlds that it never claimed, or never had the chance to colonize are now ripe for picking. Many nations are hungry. This empire's reign over the Galaxy has waned and for the last 200 years, the Human race has been broadcasting their position. Ricardo was receptive of this news and brazenly told me that they would be able to handle any challenge. I admire them. The humans, they were like we were before we became enlightened. After several seasons of dialogue, we both had a firm understanding of one another and that cooperation is not only acceptable but will be encouraged. Mine and my crew's reports reached the council and our people celebrated their existence for several cycles. Simulations reported back that these people had the potential for greatness, greatness to even rival ours. It was decided that they should achieve that greatness on their own, but we shall give them a head start. For we shall plant the seed of an ally. Someone to watch over and claim this new territory that we can not and that we would rather not have claimed by other powers that are contrary to ours. Another transport of ours arrived not long after Ricardo was re-elected as President of this United States. We left on that transport, leaving our initial one behind. For, if they could deconstruct it and learn how to travel faster than light, than they are worthy. We will watch, we will wait, and we will help this seed grow into something more. Iridium. I had a thought that an alien race would probably not have our names for things.

"Liam..... Liam, honey, wake up," The bed was beginning to shake, "Honey, you really have to get up now, okay?" "Just, like, 20 more minutes Ma," The shaking slowly subsided. "Honey, we don't have 20 minutes, you have to get up now..." Liam's mother poured water on his head, causing him to spring up with enough violence to knock over his bedside lamp. "What the hell Mom, what is so goddamned important that you had to wake me up with," he glanced at his clock, now on the floor beside the broken lamp "3 hours of sleep?!!? Geez Ma..." After a few calming breaths Liam settled back onto the bed, the wetness of his wake up call seeping through his pajama shirt, and he looked over at his mother, who had retreated to the door, knowing full-well what reaction Liam would have to her chilly good morning. Liam's concern over his bed's wetness turned to dismay as he took in what his mother was wearing, an army green tank top with forest-camo cargo pants and a massive backpack, loaded down so completely he was surprised it didn't burst it's seams. "Liam, we have to go, now, your father is already preparing the truck and, knowing him, it'll be ready by the time you're changed," she said, in that scary calm way that mother's use to avoid panicking their children. "But, is it real this time, it is, isn't it, please, please tell me it's a drill, tell me I'm wrong," Liam wasn't quite panicked yet, he was still trying to work through the dread at what was about to happen, he knew what the camo meant, it meant they were leaving, and probably wouldn't be back for a while, if ever. He couldn't figure out why though, it didn't make any sense, before he went to sleep there hadn't been anything in the news, either mainstream or back-channel, that indicated anything apocalyptic was happening. The economy was generally stable, as stable as ever in fact since the crash a few years ago, and the only wars, cold or hot, were in Asia and Africa. "Honey, NOW!" his mother yelled, he hadn't realized he'd been sitting there stunned. Her yell snapped him back to reality where his training kicked in, he sprung from his bed, far more controlled now without the ice water spurring his movements, and was inside his closet almost instantly. With a pleased nod, his mother hopped the banister behind her to the first floor and was gone, likely to toss her pack in the "truck" and grab anything they may have extra room for. With a swift kick to the side, Liam popped open a false wall in his closet, revealing a bugout bag, his own camo gear, his AK-47, and a decently sized box of pre-loaded magazines. He tried to don his gear swiftly, the way he'd been taught, but nervousness had an icy grip on his chest in a way his training hadn't prepared him for. As such, he tripped while trying to pull his other pant-leg up, landing in a pile of dirty clothes, with his cap on, his green shirt around his neck like a scarf, and an 80lb duffel bag over one shoulder making him feel like a turtle that some petulant child had flipped. He quickly thanked God, Buddha, and The Flying Spaghetti Monster that his brothers weren't here and used his indignation to quiet his nerves, if only for the moment, so he could at least dress properly. Exiting his room, Liam glanced around to find quite a few of his parents knick-knacks out of place, this was disturbing considering his father's borderline OCD concerning his, so-called, "finds." "There must have been a tremor or something, was that what shook the bed?" Realizing he was standing like a doe in the headights, Liam mentally berated his internal monologue. He prepared to vault the banister as his mother had done when he stopped again, looking at himself in the floor-length mirror at the end of the hallway, and he liked what he saw. A vision of the action heroes from the old movies his parents had introduced him to as a child, decked out in his survival gear and AK, all now properly donned, despite his earlier mishaps, if it weren't for the circumstances, he could've stared at himself all day. Instead, the windows began to shake violently and the ear-splitting sound of a sonic boom cascaded through the house, snapping Liam out of his self-reverie. He hopped the banister, landing on the floor below in a crouch, feeling the impact shockwaves cascade through his lower extremities and wishing he had thrown his bag over first, the extra weight made the landing unexpectedly rough. Liam stood and looked around, taking in his childhood home for, most likely, the last time. The couch where he'd had his first kiss, the wall of old gaming consoles he had repaired with his dad, the bathroom where he crawled out the window the first time to sneak out, the liquor cabinet he'd repaired after some friends wrecked it during a party, but it was time to go, he'd always have those memories, even if he wasn't there, Liam turned and bolted for the open front door without looking back. Upon emerging from the house, he stopped, dropping to his knees, mouth agape, staring at the sky in horror. What appeared to be a huge tear had formed in the sky, like some god had unzipped the heavens, but what Liam saw didn't make him think of heaven, no, it was nothing of the sort. Huge tentacles were knurling and whipping around the edges of the tear, almost like they were trying to force it open farther. He couldn't make anything out inside the tear, however, it just seemed to be a mass of purple and black darkening the formerly clear, blue sky. It almost felt as if it were sucking him in, not physically, but mentally, dragging his mind away from his body. As he noticed what was happening to him, the tug on his mind intensified, the more he fought against it, the more agonizing it got and, before he knew it, he heard screaming. But, where was it coming from, he couldn't look away to find the source though. It was close, maybe one of the neighbors? Then muffled speech, but, why was it muffled, and why can't I look away from this damned rift. Rift? When did I start thinking of it as a rift, that implies it leads somewhere, doesn't it? The muffled speech came back again, louder this time, he could almost make out the words now, but they were so distant, and couldn't really be important could they? Damn I wish that screaming would stop, it's driving me..... insane?
