Many have asked me why we tell stories. Why we spin threads of hope, of lucky, of wit, ingenuity, and steadfast tenacity. I've wondered that myself. Why do we tell children stories of brave knights felling evil monsters, of clever mortals outsmarting petty gods, of men and women with all the odds stacked against them, and prevailing nevertheless. Why do we teach children that what is good and what is fair will always prevail, when in this world it is often better to be mean, and to be cruel? I could say because stories imagine the world as it should be, rather than what it is. I could say that it is to inspire hope, to perhaps give some of them the spark of heroes, though many will wish to extinguish it. Truth be told, I have no idea, but I do know there is weight in spinning epic threads, weaving tragic yarns, in creating a tapestry of battles fought, love earned and lost, of gallant kings and clever rogues, of wretched villains of glorious heroes. I know there is weight in telling stories. So listen here children, and men, for this is a tale of glory, of struggle, of the victory that we all hope to achieve. Listen well, youngsters and elders, for this is tale borne of reckless confidence, and too cautious wisdom, and between the two of you, it might be understood. Finally, listen well, those with broken hearts, mended hearts, and empty hearts, for this is a tale that might not exist, but you desperately hope for it to be so. Listen here, for this is a story of a beginning, of glory, of corruption, and of despair. A story of strength, of weakness, of cowardice and bravery. Listen here, for this is the story of a hero named Artur, a king named Ourelion, and an assassin named Catheryne, spelt with a y instead of an i, simply because she liked the way it looked. But most importantly, listen here, for this is a story of hope.

The Grim Reaper sighed, he had become increasingly irritated "If this didn't work the first time, it should have at least worked the second time. But an hour has passed and I still can't reap you!" I didn't care how long it took. You always heard stories of things like the Grim Reaper and the supernatural growing up, but how often do you have the chance to stare it right in the face? "Are you sure you're doing it right?" I asked gingerly. "OF COURSE I AM! I HAVE BEEN DOING THIS FOR THOUSANDS OF YEARS AND THIS," he barely faltered, "NEVER HAPPENS!" His response prompted me to keep quiet. Asking questions, even offering help, would do no good here. In fact, it would benefit me not to say anything. As far as I know eternal nothingness awaits me as soon as he gets that thing to work, might as well enjoy this. "Hang on buddy I got ta make a call." His tone had changed. He was still pissed, that was obvious, but had managed to collect himself enough for a phone call. From his billowing cloak he removed a flip phone, turned his back to me, and strolled forward. He carried his scythe as if it were the handle to a briefcase rather than a proud, ancient object. "Ye, I wan na know just what the fuck you idiots are doing down there?" Never mind professional chat whilst talking to customer service. I began to ignore the next several minutes of talk, as the Grim Reaper mimicked everything the woman on the other end said. It wasn't until he had been silent for several minutes, stiff as a board, that I began to pay close attention. " ..." A sudden, sharp inhalation and then- CRACK The Grim Reaper slam dunked his phone into floor, shattering upon impact with the dank stone. He errupted into a fit of rage, smashing his scythe against the wall. All the while cursing..... "FUCK COMCAST!" A million questions raced through my mind. But I had learned from my mistakes and decided to remain quiet. This was no easy task though, I was very curious to learn the connection between Death and Comcast. His fury went on for several minutes, with varying curses and attempts of wrecking his prized possession. The frenzy concluded with Death doubled over panting before he turned back to me. "I can't take it anymore. I don't know why I decided to work with them in the first place. This thing..." he held up the scythe, "Only works as long as they are doing their job..." He got back to standing position. With flames of determination bouncing in empty eye sockets he held his head high and stuck out the arm closest to where the scythe lay mangled on the floor. "Know this..." he was looking at me now, but it was if he was talking to all of existence. "Death seldom feels emotion..." He began to choke up, but continued, "But what those sons of bitches at Comcast..." The flames burned more fiercely now, illuminating the room. "I'LL BE DEAD BEFORE THEY GET MY SERVICE!" In an instant, the scythe flew into Death's grip and in one fluid motion the edge had been dragged along the Grim Reaper's neck, and the flames extinguished as he fell down face first.

I'd always maintained that a little bit of water didn't matter. "It's just the rain." I'd proclaim arrogantly, "A little water won't hurt you." I'd happily wandered through forests of umbrellas feeling confidently smug at my free hands and damp hair, if not slightly apprehensive at the occasional threat of a rogue eye-gouging from an errant brolly. Headphones were always left smugly sat atop my head in a downpour, never once betraying their deliverance of music despite the liquid barrage that would attempt to disrupt a playlist. I forever indulged in the painterly atmosphere that a shower at dusk would indulge me with, getting lost in the fresh smells of a glistening concrete jungle. I never cared if my jacket or pants got a little damp from sitting on a dew-covered bench. Rain always brought back memories of my childhood, spent adamantly attempting to empty all puddles of their contents using nothing more than the bottom of my Wellingtons and a lot of vigour. This, though..... this was different. I stared in disbelief at my hands, not fully comprehending what my complacency had let happen. How could I be this stupid? Carefully crafted handwritten words gave way to a vague blue smudge on the upper right of the paper. All the effort and care that had gone into the crafting of this personal, heartfelt creation meant only for me was slowly dissolving into the fibre. What possessed me to leave this in the pocket of my blazer? I didn't even need to come here for lunch. How could I forget something so dear to me in these conditions? The last picture my daughter ever drew for me.

Dammit Joe. Pull yourself together. I slowly raised myself from the floor between the couch and the footlocker that I was currently using as what some would call a coffee table, but what could more accurately be described as a whiskey table. As soon as I was in the sitting position, I knew I had made a grave mistake. Fumbling around the cushions of the couch, I eventually found a bottle that was not completely empty. Breakfast of champions, I thought, and downed its contents. The clock on the wall said it was two in the afternoon, but such details matter little when you have no plans other than to drink away pain. Hefting myself onto the stain-riddled couch, my gaze settled onto the framed picture of my brother. It was laying on the ground, having been knocked off of my pitiful table at some point during the night. I picked it up and held it close to my throbbing head. There he was, my brother Steve, smiling like an idiot in that ridiculous green striped shirt. He had always been odd, and his obsession with having a singular wardrobe of khaki pants and a green striped shirt was just one manifestation of that oddness. What the hell happened to you? My thoughts were disturbed by a wimper from the kitchen. Oh yeah, I thought. The dog. One of the hardest parts of coping with Steve's disappearance was watching that dog of his. If I was taking it hard, that poor animal was in hell. While Steve always personified it, I've never been one to identify human traits in animals - that is, until I saw the way my brother's dog responded to its master's sudden absence. There was an evident depression of that beast's soul that I couldn't help but notice. Making my way out to the kitchen, I cleared my throat and spoke for the first time that day "What is it, Blue?" The dog was clawing at the base of a cupboard. I looked closely at the base and noticed the edge of a piece of paper that had slide underneath. Pulling it out, the words "Joe, whatever you do, don't tell the police about this letter" greeted me at the top of the page. My God, Blue, I thought. You've found a clue.

It's cold down here. And dark. It's always dark anymore. And honestly, I can't remember when I was put down here. It's been so long that it's started to fade. But that's okay, because I think I am too. They use to come more often. My friends, my family, the people who love me. Or loved me, which I guess is more appropriate. But times change, people change. Sometimes it's just forgetfulness, pushing it into the back of one's mind until it's not so bad or painful anymore. And eventually, people move on. Everyone does, one way or another. But I'm still around. Whenever they want to talk, I'm here. My son use to come and read to me when my favorite author came out with a new book. That was nice. He told me when I became a granddad. How his son was doing in little league. When he was learning to drive a car. It gets lonely sometimes down here, alone in the dark. But as long as people remember me I'm still around. That's just how it works, I guess. Maybe I'll fade away in time, when everyone I knew and loved has moved on, when I'm just another name with no one to come and visit me..... but I hope I don't fade away too soon. Last week my wife joined me here. I felt her next to me when they laid her down here too. Right along side me forever. I've missed her so and we've got so much to catch up on. It'll be nice to have company again, to be able to talk to someone who can hear me. I'm so tired though. I know I won't be here much longer. But I want to stay as long as I can with her. I don't want her to be as scared and alone as I was when they first buried me..... nbsp; - Author's note: My greatest fear is that when we die there is no afterlife like many believe to be. Nor is there just the end where all thought and existence ceases. Instead when we are laid to rest, part of us remains on, trapped in our bodies, aware and unable to do anything but wait in that long dark, our only company our thoughts and those precious few times someone is kind enough to visit us, to sit and talk for a few minutes, to share a bit of their life with us. An endless time alone and aware, down there in that cold earth...

I can remember the day when it happened, when the numbers appeared. I'd just got home from school and let myself in and was looking forward to watching my favourite shows on the TV, but I couldn't. The TV was just news, rolling news, about the numbers. The newsreader had a number above her head, a 22 if I remember correctly. The reporters had them too, as did the scientists, bishops, imams, psychics and UFO hunters they interviewed. I checked in the mirror, I had one too, 77. My brother came in, his was 97, we looked at each other quizzically. "Have you seen it out there?" He asked. "Its madness, everyone running around looking at the numbers!" "Look at the news," I replied, "its everywhere, and no one knows why or what they mean." Its been 20 years now, I'm nearly 30 but my number still remains the same, 77. Its part of life, but no one has been able to work out what the numbers mean, or how they got there. Just that everyone has one and they don't change. There are theories of course, Scientists say its random and they probably mean nothing, though research is ongoing. The Vatican declared the start of the end of days, and a hundred cults were spawned. Quack therapies started to be pedalled to change the number. UFO hunters think its aliens, religious people, angels. Me, I'm not sure, its part of me now, I'll always be a 77.

No letter only meant one thing. The first year was hard, the second easier. We spent more time than I could tell you planning, plotting, trying to figure out how to stay one step ahead of the inevitable. We looked at cabins in the wilderness away from crime. We pored over brochures for the most comprehensive health insurance money could buy. We tried to decide what martial arts to learn, and which to teach our child. We contemplated changing careers. Then one day we realized that there were just too many ways for a person to die, and we could the next ten years preparing, and still lose. We decided, for better or for worse, not to raise a child in fear. For all we knew, there could be another explanation. We told no one, for all our sake. Nobody should live the that specter hanging over them. It never fully left us. We didn't use babysitters, we didn't drink. We held a weapons permit, but never went hunting..... and while we told ourselves we had other reasons, it's no coincidence we lived so close to the hospital. But we tried. We tried so desperately to live normally, promising ourselves that we deal with it when it happened, not before. Even so, every trip to the ER for a standard childhood malady was a nightmare. Being late home from school was terrifying. I can't begin to count how many times the words "Please don't let this be it" were whispered silently over something that would otherwise be normal. We got better as the years went on, and worse as the 18th neared. At 16, car shopping. We wanted something safe and reliable..... but a 16 year old has other priorities. We'd raised a good kid. There was no pushing, not even a request, but you could see something light up when we walked past it. It was more than we could afford, and certainly more than any sane parent should buy a teenager. Hell, it was more than any sane person ought to spend on four wheels and an engine. It was insanity. But in the back of our minds, something cruel whispered "Only two more years." Fuck it. We knew that car would be wrecked as soon as we signed the papers. What else could it be at that age? Small comfort though it was, at least it wouldn't happen in a used shitbox. One year later, the wreck. Go figure, you spend a years pay on a car, and you can get decent safety ratings. Nothing left of the car, but no fatalities, no injuries. We replaced the car with the newest model. A year later, our nightmare almost came true. A light on late at night. Leaving for school a little early. Telling us about an errand before school. I almost didn't see it. I ran out the door screaming, crying, waving my arms like a madman. I realized I'd forgotten my keys. I couldn't chase in my own car. "Please don't let this be it." But the car came back. "Don't send it"

Halloween was the night for the strange, the odd and the queer. It was for the cute, the gory, the brave and of course, the sexy. I have many wonderful memories of Halloween. I remembered dressing up and trick-or-treating with my older brother. I remembered being scared and reaching for my brother's hand. Of course, there was never any real danger, and looking back it was childish to be afraid, but my brother's hand - it was always there for me. So it occurred to me as I made my way to Three alone that my secret, really was my secret. If I can not tell the one person in the whole wide world, who would protect and defend me no matter what, who could I tell? About a month ago, I overheard the girls in class talking about Three. It was a gay bar. I have never been and not just because I was underage, though that was a pretty good reason. They had laughed and giggled and joked about checking it out. That was how I learned of the Halloween costume party and decided that no matter what, I would go. There was after all, something about being anonymous that made people braver. And me? I was no exception. I managed to get into Three without much trouble. It was packed. People were constantly coming and going through both their main entrance and their side door. And since it was no longer legal to smoke in clubs, a lot of people were smoking outside. I was surprised to see so many people like me. Never gave it much thought before, but I definitely never could have imagine so many if I tried. I found it oddly comforting navigating through the energetic crowd. Men smiled at me and I smiled back. There were women too. They smiled too in a warm and friendly way that was a little different from the men. Everyone was having a great time - drinking and dancing. A few brave or drunk ones were dancing on the bar tables along the side of the club that bordered off the sunken dance floor from the booths. On one of these tables, a drunk woman was trying to drag a man dressed as a pirate with a paper masquerade mask onto the table. He was clearly not interested and kept trying to pry her fingers from his costume. I made my way over, not sure exactly what I was going to do, but just as I was arm's reach away, the woman slipped and tumbled off the table and landed on me, dropping us both onto the floor. A sudden fear of being trampled filled my head and I tried to push the woman off of me so I could get up. She was all over the place herself and too drunk to be of any help. Just as I was starting to panic, she was off, and someone grabbed my arm and pulled me up to standing. I looked around, confused, and saw that her friends had found her. I think they apologized to me for her, but the music was too loud to be sure. I smiled weakly and shrugged as they left. Someone was still holding my arm, steadying me. It was the pirate. He leaned close and asked me if I was alright. I nodded, but he didn't seem to believe me. I let him lead me out the side door away from the loud music and into the cool night air. " Are you alright? " he asked me again. He was clearly about my age and was honestly pretty hot with his soft black curls and intense dark eyes. It felt as if he were staring straight through me. " Yeah. Just didn't expect to be picked up this way. " He laughed, said, " Glad you're alright, " and started back to the club. " Wait! " He stopped and turned around. " Nice pirate costume, " apparently this was the best I could come up with. He smiled and made an unsuccessful attempt to brush a stray curl of hair out of his eyes. " I was actually going for gypsy, but I guess that's close enough. " " Can I buy you a drink? You know, for helping me out back there? " " Is that the only reason? " he asked with a sly smile, his eyes still staring through me. " No, it isn't. " He smiled and walked right up to me, such that our faces were just inches away. I felt the back of his fingers brush my forearm, and then the cool touch of his rings as his hand closed around mine. I could smell the light scent of his last drink. " You're cute, " he told me, as he lightly brushed his lips against mine. When I didn't move away, he kissed me again. This time much more deliberate. As I kissed back, I felt his arms surround me, holding me close. Unsure what to do with my own hands, I awkwardly wrapped them around his surprisingly narrow waist. Someone drunkenly bumped into us and I lost my footing for the second time tonight. His arms tightened protectively around me, keeping me upright and pressed so close to him. I let out a nervous chuckle and he met it with a warm smile. " Let's get away from the drunks, " he suggested. " Your place? " " I'm afraid my place is filled with drunks too, " I lied. " Let's just go for a walk then, " he suggested. He let go of me and started walking, leaving me to follow. A strange uncertainty bubbled in my mind and made me trail him slowly. He noticed though and held out his hand to me. I accepted it with a familiar ease that I could not explain. Hand in hand, we walked away from the light and the noise, and away from the warmth and the chaos.

Even at that young age I knew that something about me was different. The world was one big game, and I was determined to play it better than anybody else could. So I watched, and I learned. Single handedly, I ushered in an era of peace in our community. Townsfolk talked, of course. They whispered to each other, and even to me occasionally, saying how fortunate we were to live in our happy little homes without any of the problems that plagued other cities. Life was ideal. I was not happy - I have never felt happiness - but I was content. Janice Harper ruined my perfect system. She became chief of police after Harold Manor retired, and she made it her personal goal to find out what happened to people when they disappeared from our town. She assigned detectives to follow vagabonds as they drifted into town like a foul breeze. I was careful, so very careful. Eventually though, even I could not maintain perfection. I made a mistake. A biker had stopped at the dime shop for gas and refreshments. It's not called the dime shop anymore, of course. It's a new and shiny gas station, but it still has a milkshake counter and I still watch the people as they travel in and out of town. This biker was enormously obese, heavily tattooed, and extremely foul-mouthed. I would have been happy to see him ride his filthy motorcycle right back onto the highway, but instead I heard him ask the cashier which places were hiring nearby. Ordinarily, I preferred to watch and wait. I would remove the offending person when the time was ideal. However with Chief Harper on the lookout, I knew that I had precious little time. I followed the biker to South Street, and flashed my lights to get his attention. I waved for him to pull over, and he obligingly did. I jumped out of my van and called to him as I advanced, "Your rear tire is nearly flat!" He clambered off the motorcycle and stepped around to the back, looking at the tire all the while. He never saw the syringe coming. I struck and injected in one fluid motion, forcing the thick liquid into his neck. He yelled and swung wildly at me, but the mirocane was swift and so was I. The biker stumbled, then toppled to the ground as his heart beat its last. I quickly got the emergency blanket from my van and used it as a litter to drag the man's massive body to the rear doors. Then I drove the motorcycle directly into my van, using his body as a ramp. Lifting him in behind the bike was no small effort, but I managed. I slammed the doors shut and took off. For years I had been disposing of bodies in the same place. An old quarry hit a spring in the early seventies, turning it into a local favorite for cliff-jumping. I used an out-of-the-way section that was only about 10 feet across and untold hundreds of feet deep. In summer the quarry was crowded with swimmers, but it was only March and the grounds were deserted. I backed the van up to the hole directly and shoved the biker's body in. The bike was a concern - it was not biodegradable. Eventually I decided to take it out to the train trestle off Mason Drive. I rolled it into the gorge and headed back home. It was there that they found me. I was scrubbing motorcycle grease out of my van's carpet with little success when Marilyn came to the garage and said some men wanted to see me. It all went downhill from there. With the evidence in my van and the eyewitness to the murder, I was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison. However as I had a clean record and was very convincingly apologetic in my trial, the judge agreed to allow me to try a new isolation program. They left me here on this island. I have shelf-stable food to last the first year, along with seeds and tools to grow my own food afterward. It is generally understood that I may not survive my 20 years, but I have no doubt that I will make it easily. For years I have been watching, and learning. Now it is time to put my lessons to the test. 15 May, 2005 They came for me today. Men in dark uniform said I could go home, my sentence was finished. I refused. My life is here, with my goats and my farm. My seeds are growing in perfect rows, and my goats will bear kids in a few days. In all my 61 years I have never before felt so..... happy.

Young shemp stood before the council awash in fear. He, at the tender young age of 150, had to come up with a routine so comical, so amusing that the esteemed council would see him fit to be granted the immortality they themselves had achieved. This would be no easy task. The esteemed council of three, the mighty Moe, the honorable Larry, Curly the wise, had practically invented the concept of slapstick humor, highest and most revered of all art forms. This had to be good. Shemp took a deep breath and launched into his routine, a series of prat falls and prop gags that ended with a grand finale of a piano being dropped on his head. Shemp gave out a sigh of relief, he had done all he could, it was in the councils hands now. They quickly deliberated and he anxiously awaited their answer. "Close enough!" proclaimed Moe. Shemp would live to see another day.

Death sighed, pulling his robes over his hands. He didn't like being so exposed in a place like this. The thin skin stretched over his fingers made a scraping sound as he clenched one hand into a fist. He could hear the laughter and strum of harps nearby. Bees buzzed around gardenias and chrysanthemums that rose up high around him, and each stretched out to reach for the sun's light. Death reached out and plucked a nearby carnation, holding it to his thin cold lips and twirling it around. He had dreaded coming here all day, dreading that he would be the cause of the quietness and reverence. The garden was always so much more enjoyable with the laughter, with the smiles, with the..... The life, he thought bitterly. It made no difference, it was what would have to be done. What if there was another way? But he knew there wasn't. Death sighed again and laid his scythe down on the cobblestone, feeling over its thin and warped staff as he continued on his way down the pathway. Over the hedge he could see the girls, all of them giggling and playing in the flowers, looking up to Giselle for guidance. It was certain her beauty would never fade, long trailing golden hair falling over her shoulders and back in locks, and soft wings laid aside, the corners fluttering every time she laughed. Death smiled to see it. At least she was laughing, even if they both knew it would be short lived. "Peter keeps putting himself in trouble," Elise complained, putting her harp aside and rolling onto her stomach. The small angel's wings spread out onto the grass. "Peter does that too?" Rosie exclaimed, looking over to Elise. "Lidia won't stop! She wandered off by herself the other day, and I was flying all over the place trying to pull away thorn bushes, shoo away the animals, I even had to push a badger back into his den. Look what he did!" Rosie sat up straight and held out the tip of her wing for the others to see. Feathers were missing, scratched away, or crumpled and ripped. Elise gasped. "Now, now," Giselle laughed, and lowered Rosie's hand, "no need to fuss. Yours are both very young, they will grow wise in time. But for now, you two must guide them and keep them from harm's way." Both of the little ones smiled bashfully, and went back to their playing. Giselle followed their smile, and pulled Josephine into her lap. The girl will have her mother's beauty one day, Death thought with a smile, Maybe even more, She had her mother's hair, with more of a reddish tint. Giselle would laugh and say it was because she would play in so many roses. Death laughed at the thought, but remembered what was to happen, and his smile faded. "You're so lucky you don't have to fly around and be a guardian to anyone else," Rosie continued, "You just have to watch after Josephine." "Yes, I am very lucky." Giselle smiled and pulled her daughter onto her lap. Death could see that her smile was forced. The flowers bent aside as he walked through to the small clearing of grass that was secluded in the garden. Elise and Rosie froze, and looked to Giselle for guidance. She gave a smile and turning to them, spoke, "You two go on, I'll join you later." Both girls reluctantly obeyed, giving Josephine and Giselle their last goodbyes. "Bye, Giselle." "Yes, goodbye Giselle. Will you teach us the next song tomorrow? "Yes, I can teach you two tomorrow." "Okay," and they went. Death was acutely aware of their eyes on him. "So it appears they're getting on well enough," he began. Death sat down next to Giselle, and offered her the carnation he had plucked. She didn't answer him, but smiled sadly and took the carnation. In her lap Josephine squirmed up to a sitting position and reached out for the flower, taking it from her mother and clutching onto the stem tightly. "Why does it always have to be this way?" Giselle whispered. This was what he had been fearing all day long. He felt his heart sink. "You know why. We both made that choice." She acknowledged his words with silence. "It won't be all bad. The other two are already on their way to getting their wings. You can see them again then," Death comforted. It was a vain attempt, and Giselle's wings folded up along her back with agitation. "And how long has it been since I've seen either of them? You said the same thing each time." Too long. It's been too long. Death sighed and wrapped an arm around Giselle, her hair soft under his arm as he looked down at the girl. She had his dark eyes, and full dark eyelashes to pair with them. Josephine reached up to take his hand and he forced himself to pull away before she could touch him. That had been the worst curse of it, not being able to touch them at all. For no tiny fists to clench his thumb, no slobbery kisses, not even being able to hold them. "Death is not the worst thing that people endure," he said, pointing the comment to Giselle, when really saying it to himself. Giselle saw Death's cautious movements and pulled the babe away, and laid her down on the grass. It did little to stop the girl from rolling around again and climbing onto her hands and knees. A butterfly landed on the daisy in front of her, making her eyes go wide. "Life is given to us for a reason," she insisted, "it's unfair to take it away so quickly. She's so small..." Her voice broke. Death felt a knot tighten in his throat. "It's how it is," he said plainly. Josephine was giggling now; the butterfly had landed on her nose. The sun shone through the monarch's wings and cast the girl's face the same color as her hair. Giselle watched and wiped the tears that had spilled out of the corners of her eyes. "I can't do it again," she whispered, "not anymore. I can't bear it." Death had known it would eventually come to this, so all he did was hang his head and nod slowly. They sat there in the sun for as long as they could afford, watching the babe sit and entertain herself with the flowers and small creatures around the garden. Even a thrush came to say hello at some point, and opened its beak to serenade the three of them. When it was done with its song, Death stood. "Come, let's do it now." Giselle followed suit and stood as well, tears cascading down her face, and she lifted her daughter up to her feet. Death walked away a few paces, then crouched down. He watched Josephine giggle as her mother held her hands tight and helped her to stand. "Go on, Josie. Go to Papa." Josephine smiled and took a step forward. Death outstretched his arms. A few more steps with her mother's guidance, and the girl laughed, her pace quickening. Giselle let go with a small cry, a smile only on the corner of her lips. Death's mind screamed at him to pull away, but he couldn't. He wanted to hold her, if only once. Josephine walked straight into his arms with a smile. And Death held her, pulling his suddenly limp daughter close to his chest. The summer sun had warmed her skin. She was warmer than his first two children; it had been winter for the both of them when they took their first steps. He knew she wouldn't stay this warm for much longer, so he savored the few moments in silence. He grew thankful for the large hood over his head, because it concealed the tears that rolled down his cheeks and blurred his vision. He saw Giselle move, but wasn't sure of what she was doing. She had probably turned away. After the silence had grown to be too much, and the tears subsided for both of them, Death shifted Josephine into one arm, and kissed Giselle's cheek. She didn't mind his cold and dead lips. "It won't be long," he whispered. "In an eternity, anyway," she replied. Death realized there wasn't any point in pushing further. He found Giselle's hand and squeezed it softly. "I'll make sure she's taken care of." He turned away, and pushed his way through the flowers again, holding his daughter close and kissing the top of her head. (I'm sorry for bad quality, I'm pushing my way through writer's block. And I am more than happy for critique.)

Lt. Surge sat down on the couch, slumping forward with his elbows on his knees. He was waiting. The psychiatrist said that he'd have a specialist come in today, someone else to talk to. The door opened, and a woman with an impassive face walked in. "Sabrina?" She nodded silently, and sat down. "Hello, Surge." "You're the specialist?" The man's eyes widened briefly before returning to their deadened look. "I guess that makes sense. You're a psychic, after all." "While true, I am actually here because of our common experiences as Gym Leaders," she replied, her voice betraying no emotion, just as Lt. Surge had remembered from their last service together. Her Kadabra had laid bleeding out from dozens of cuts inflicted by a Victreebel's Razor Leaf, and she had merely taken out another Pokeball. The memory sent chills down Lt. Surge's spine. "How can you be so..... detached?" he asked, shaking his head. Sabrina's eyes narrowed almost imperceptibly. "We do what needs to be done for the safety of the world." She had said something like that on the battlefield, Lt. Surge recalled. It was during the last war, one in a string of many. Red had just been drafted for combat after becoming Pokemon Champion. The boy was merely ten. He was too young. His Charizard, unchained by the Pokemon power limiting radio frequencies in Kanto, charged onto the battlefield, and scorched everything in its wake. Dozens and dozens of wild Pokemon fell, succumbing to the blistering burns of Fire Blast - Pidgeys and Pikachus, Jigglypuffs and Poliwags. They achieved their objective through brute force, planting more radiowave emitters and expanding Kanto's safe borders by a few dozen square miles littered with the dead bodies of Pokemon. After the battle, Red had asked Sabrina something - Lt. Surge couldn't quite remember the words - but Sabrina's answer had been the same. We do what needs to be done for the safety of the world. "So, we train child soldiers." "We need the best. If that means children, then yes." Red had been an energetic, talkative boy when Lt. Surge first met him at Vermilion Gym, but the war built a wall of silence around him. After the war, Red retreated to the mountains, refusing all outside contact. "Don't you feel any regret? Sadness? Anything?" Lt. Surge's bitter voice growled more than asked. When he got no response, he looked up from the ground. Tears rolled down Sabrina's expressionless face. "Yes," came the toneless reply. The pair of veterans sat in an awkward silence, each lost in the painful memories of the past. Finally, Lt. Surge reached out a hand. "Hey," he started, but couldn't think of anything to say. Sabrina wordlessly took his hand. On her face was the faintest of weary smiles.

" Attennnnn...shun! " The men all quickly snapped their feet together in proper, instinctual fashion. Major Cartwright waited for the silence to slowly lay itself upon the still scene, then stepped forward to address his troops. " Right, as you were, men. " The soldiers all relaxed in place ever so slightly, remaining on the edge of anticipation for some as-of-yet unforeseen order. The Major was not without his peculiarities, especially whilst on parade. " Sergeant Powell? " " SUH! " came the sharp reply, as the Sergeant snapped immediately to attention, stepping off in confident strides and carried forth a small grey box, which he placed in front of the Major. Sergeant Powell shot his hand quickly upwards to offer a courteous salute, which the Major heartily returned. His task complete, Sergeant Powell turned about swiftly yet properly, and marched back to his place off to the side of the formation. Major Cartwright allowed for a moment of pause, letting the continued silence to lend gravity to the seriousness of the situation. After what he felt to be an appropriate delay, he turned to address the gathered men. " Men, " he spoke, his voice forceful with the weight of his rank and position, " I have gathered you here on this dreary morning... " " Afternoon, sir " came a voice from the formation. " What's that now, Jackson? " " It's afternoon, sir. " " I was told that I would be addressing you men this morning. " The Major shot a quick glare towards Sergeant Powell. The Sergeant cautiously cleared his throat, and then respectfully explained. " Indeed, sir, " Sergeant Powell said, " But if you'll recall, your driver was late this morning, which held up your morning Orders with the Colonel, sir. " " Ah yes, " admitted Major Cartwright. " Well, I've already memorized what I wanted to say, and I'm bloody well not going to try and change it now. You men just understand that when I say morning, I of course mean this afternoon, understood? " " Yes sir " came the unanimous reply. " Right, good. As I was saying, I have gathered you here on this dreary morning... " " It's actually quite sunny out, sir. " " Yes, Roberts, I can see that, but as I've said, I have already memorized the speech. Just understand that even though it's not dreary out by the grace of God, I will still be saying it is dreary out, but just know in your own mind that it in fact is not. Is that clear?' " Yes sir " the soldier replied. " Is that clear with everyone? " " Yes sir " the soldiers answered. " Good. Okay then, I have gathered you all here... " " Some of the lads aren't here yet, sir. " " What? How's that now, Williams? " " Some of the lads are at the Kit, getting sorted out. " The Major shook his head in defiance. " That's no matter, " he hastily admonished, " Just all of you hear me out, and pass the information on to them. Everyone understand? " " Yes sir " the men responded. " Fine. All right, I've gathered you here on this dreary morning, to explain to you the purpose and function of this black box in front of me... " " Box is grey, sir. " " What? " Major Cartwright tilted his head ever so slightly, just enough to look at the box, while maintaining his place of authority in front of the assembled soldiers. " Ah yes, so it is, Baker. Good catch, that. But so you all understand, it was meant to be black, so if I describe it as such, just know that I am in fact speaking of the grey box in front of me here, and not some other black box, not presently here in front of me, where the grey box, in fact, is. Clear? " " Yes sir " the men answered. " Excellent. Now, I've gathered you here on this dreary morning, to explain to you the purpose and function of this black box in front of me. It will signal an alarm in the event of a nuclear, biological, or chemical attack. The various lamps on top will indicate the type and severity of the attack. Any questions thus far? " " Is it heavy, sir? " " What? I...it doesn't matter, Kingsmith, you won't be carrying it. Now listen up. In the event of any such attack, you must look to see which of the 5 lamps... " " 4, sir. " " Ah, yes, thank you Sergeant...which of the 4 lamps is illuminated. The Green indicates a nuclear attack, the blue indicates a biological attack, the red indicates a chemical attack... " " The red label says ' Comical ', sir " " Yes, Patterson, I am aware. It is merely a typographical error. Ignore the red label, and simply know that the red lamp indicates a chemical attack. Understood? " " Yes sir " the men replied. " Good. Now when I press the test button, it will show the illuminating of the lamps, so that you understand what you will be looking for in the event of a real attack. Watch as I demonstrate this now. " Major Cartwright pressed the solitary button. " Now men, as you can see, the lights illuminate, indicating that you are under the specified type of attack. " " Then what, sir " " I beg your pardon, Waters? " " What do we do when one of the lights goes off, sir? " The Major shifted uneasily, struggling to maintain his dignity. " Well, as we are not a forward line unit, we will not be provided with the required equipment for dealing with any of the aforementioned attacks. So, I suppose, you will simply die. " The men all looked at each other with uncertainty. " It really doesn't matter much. Look... " the Major once again pressed the lone button, activating the test sequence once more. " See. If it turns green you're dead - blue, dead. Red? Dead." "Sir..... it's turned purple." The Major let out a defeated sigh. He looked at his men, and made up his mind that far too much effort had already been expended on this particular subject. " Alright, men. That will be enough for now. Sergeant Powell, they're all yours. " Major Cartwright turned and headed off past the left of the formation. " I have more urgent things to attend to this morning... " " Afternoon, sir. " The Major spun quickly on his heel, never missing a step, and instead strode back past the men, off to the right. " Right you are. Carry on. "

The whole thing was one big happy self-fulfilling prophecy of death and crime. To think, that there once was an era where being a " tough on crime " politician meant supporting three strike laws. Oh, how I yearn for such merciful days. Overcrowded prison systems led eventually to cries for wholesale execution for anybody who committed a crime. It started with every felony, then slowly crept through all the various misdemeanors. People eventually started to inquire into the ethics, that naughty little thing that ruins every politician's day, of executing people who accidently stole from a vending machine when it dropped an additional bag of chocolate chip cookies. In a show of ' mercy'they decided to grant clemency to everybody in the top 10 of the FBI's most wanted list. After all, if those care-bear politicians demanded that every no-good criminal be granted such luxuries as " not being killed for accidently tripping and brushing the shoulder of a politician who was having a bad day, " why not start with the worst of the whole lot? I think their motives were a bit more sinister than a faux show of mercy. The new system incentivized anybody who committed the most minor of crimes to immediate try and extravagantly escalate their spree to reach the top of the list. Suddenly, all the politicians who had been crying that any criminal was evil enough to deserve execution were now justified. Clearly, all these people attempting to commit mass murders were just truly evil at heart, and definitely not incentivized by a system that would gladly execute all of their victims anyway to try and commit such acts. As you can tell, I'm not the biggest fan of these laws; though I think if they did anything right, it was to piss off for-profit prisons. I think that they're a kind of perverse American dream: with a little bit of ingenuity and lots of hard work, you too can rise to the top and receive the great pleasures of life such as not being on death row or not living a life of fear and death. And just like the American dream, the criminal justice system has a bit of a glass ceiling. The names on the top 10 list haven't changed in over a decade. All of them are organized crime bosses, the kind of people who probably wouldn't have to worry about law enforcement anyway. These people had built up massive empires that spanned the entire country. Most of the people who get involved in organized crime start out as someone who gets tricked by a higher-up into committing a ridiculously small offense, who then has to accept protection of the organization or risk execution. That's what happened to my brother. I'll spare you the gruesome details of my brother's horrific grand larceny of a box of watermelons he found unattended on a roadside, but suffice to say that he had already received competing offers from some of America's finest entrepreneurs by the time he was home. Unfortunately he was too young and naive to immediately sell his soul to a devil, so within three hours he had been shot by a cop. With all the unrepentant and unpunished police violence that goes on, I wouldn't be surprised if police officers weren't just criminals trying to make it to the top of the list, or at the very least robots piloted by teenagers who thought they were playing a video game. Of course, since all criminals are executed as soon as they are found guilty (every criminal trial usually has an executioner on standby who licks his lips in anticipation of a guilty verdict), nobody much cared about my brother's death. So much so that it wasn't ever referenced on the background check conducted when I joined the FBI. More important were my connections to underground human rights (two words you would never say in front of your grandmother) organizations that went unnoticed. I worked my way up through the ranks of the FBI, never so much as pissing on a sidewalk, until the day I would become in charge of the algorithm that determines who would be on the top 10 list. It's only been two weeks and I've already pocketed some sweet cash from the people on top of the list to make absolutely no changes. Unsurprisingly, some concerned politicians had removed bribery from the criminal code. I wasn't planning on actually upholding my end of the bargain. Of course, even so much as accidently adding an extra letter to a single line of code without congressional approval was enough for execution. My job was mainly to update the records that were being fed into the algorithm and make sure that nobody dead was still on the list. The record was a 6 month period where number 10 had been murdered by number 9 and my predecessor didn't noticed until the automated monthly bribes expired. Today however, the list was going to be changed. The president (who, as it turns out, would have been number 17 if it weren't for a world-record number of pardons) had signed a bill authorizing me to increase the number of people on the most wanted list from 10 to 20. For a 24 hour period, I have access to all of the code that made up the algorithm that decides the fate of the nation. I think it's about time for an upgrade. I think that crimes such as " loitering " and " being homeless " are about to allow people to hit the top of list instead of getting shot on sight by a cop. The bill had also authorized an adjustment in weight to violent crimes against politicians. Of course, I'm happy to oblige. I'm even going to do them a favor and add an unlawful amount of 0's to that number. That would put me on the list of corpses-to-be, but that doesn't bother me too much. I'm headed to the Senate with a rather heavy bag tomorrow. And after the changes come into effect and I'm done with my business on the Senate floor, I think I'll be safe from prosecution. EDIT: A couple of words changed to make some more sense.

A few weeks ago when my Uncle John passed, I was asked to clean out his estate. With no friends or other close family willing to do it, his estate would go up for sale this coming weekend. Getting to his house was easy, the largest one in the block since I was a child, many items of his estate were just odds and ends scattered about that I never paid attention to. I opened a large closet in his living room, and found a number of old newspapers were stacked neatly in the corner in a milk crate. "The Wall Street Journal" as I read the title. Why would he save copies of a newspaper dealing with finance, I thought Grandma said he was in the oil business? My Uncle was a wealthy man at one time, but he gave away most of his money before he died. Reading through some of the articles, it was mostly boring business things that never appealed to me, and I thought that these could easily be tossed as junk. We were never really close, and other then our family dinners, we never spoke much. I dumped the crate of newspapers into the trash bag, but the bottom paper stuck inside the crate. Going to fish it out with my hands, I saw it. And it didn't make sense..... "Market up 600 points, Biggest One Day Move in History!" It wasn't the headline that caught my eye, it was the date: October 29th, 1929. Maybe this was one of those funny newspapers you could get made up I thought to myself. After all, everyone knows that the day is Black Tuesday, the most devastating day in the history of the United States Stock Market. Uncle John spoke of that day with glee, but from what I remember, most people were poor and left with nothing? But it wasn't a spoof. It was the real print, with the same articles and authors, just different stories. I pulled out the other papers, and they were normal. Other things throughout history made sense, they lined up. I went back to the original paper to continue reading the article when I saw it a small note between the two pages. I almost fell out of my chair went I read it. Nephew, Reading this, I know the family has left you to tend to my affairs. This is the only paper we ever had printed. What really happened? Well, if you're reading this, then you know: The Great Crash was a lie. We had to do it for our family. The failures, Rigging the Markets, putting the country in economic ruin, it was all necessary. Without it, we wouldn't have been able to do everything we needed to for the world to be a better place. We wouldn't have solidified our place as one of the wealthiest families in America. Our family will be known forever because of our most heinous deeds. But I didn't expect our family to get greedy. That's why I made it clear that you would be the one to handle my estate. I I know that you may never forgive me, but I hope you one day you will understand. Your Uncle, John Rockefeller

Here we go, into the deep. They secure the mask, and seal up my capsule. I give the thumbs-up, and they press the button. I wait patiently as they begin to celebrate with champagne. I thought I'd feel something by now. They finish their little party and start packing up their things. I'm still here, guys, how long is this supposed to take? The last person shuts off the lights as they leave. What the fuck, they're not even going to wait until I'm out to see if it works? Nothing left but the low hum of the capsule and the glow from the monitor. 2,629,799,960 minutes remain. Okay, I mean, I can't feel anything, but I thought I'd be asleep by now at least. 2,629,799,940 minutes remain. God, this is fucking boring. Any time now. Count sheep? 2,629,799,900 minutes remain. There's no way this is how this is supposed to work. This really fucking sucks. 2,629,799,215 minutes remain. I want to come out now. Please let me out. The door opens. A light turns on. A man walks in. He grabs his pen off the table, clicks it a couple times, smiles, and puts it into his pocket. He walks over to my capsule. Yes, finally! He taps on the glass, lets out a bit of a chuckle, then leaves. No. Please God, no. What the fuck! 2,629,797,118 minutes remain. And that's how we can achieve world peace, the end. 2,629,792,845 minutes remain. I'm so lonely. 2,629,791,900 minutes remain. Crackalacka. Brack-brack-brackalack. Ching-chong-sing-along. B-b-b-baster. 2,629,774,401 minutes remain. Mmmmmmmmmmmm. Ssssssssssssss. Fffffffffffffff. 2,629,759,689 minutes remain. . .... ...

I am an old shop keeper who ran a shop for a big city where adventurers gathered for ale, purchases and everything of those sorts. Ah, yes, and I ran the cheapest shop! I would've taken almost anything to get that shop off my hands, anything above eight thousand gold pieces before selling price, of course. Then one evening, near the begging of autumn season, I got lucky because of one dumb schmuck! This man was as wide shouldered, tall, rough, and handsome as they came, but his brain was probably smaller than a peanut. "Hello sir, how may I help you this evening?" I greeted him as any other customer as though I should. He looked up and down to ceiling and floor, he looked at my shelves and items for sale, then he set his eyes on me and wandered back over to the front counter. The man spoke in a low tone and stated, "Your establishment here is quaint and quiet." "Indeed," I answered him, "This store is my baby, too bad I'll have to give it up sooner or later." The adventurer raised his brow, "For sale? Well, I say old shopkeeper, I've been searching for a shop to retire from quests and settle." What a marvellous opportunity I had been given in front of me, so, naturally I bargained with this soon to be fool. "What do you posses to offer me in an exchange? Gold or merchandise?" He started to ruffle and search his pockets, "I have squirrel hides and meat." He offered. I shook my head, "I have no need for that, boy!" I exclaimed. He searched again. "What about this?" He pulled used candles and a lizard's eye from his backpack. I shook my head again, "No, something more." I responded. Once more he looked and found a ring full of keys in dungeons he had explored. "I'm waiting for death, not searching for it!" I refused. "I have this." He placed a peculiar round crystal on the counter. I examined the object. Light blue and light to hold, but no sign of properties other than a haggling money value. "What does it do?" I furrowed my brow in question. The larger man thought a moment, "It does something, but I'm not so sure as to what." He admitted. As I was to retire soon I thought I'd take the chance and agreed to the trade. We shook hands and I handed over the deed. What a trade of a life time I had made. This stones properties weren't revealed immediately, no, but in time. Time was all I had, until one day I realised that time is now all I've got. In fact, with this stone I've lived to see that adventurer pass on that shop after fifty years and that gentleman pass it on, too. Although old and frail now, I hold onto one object, one I love more than that little shop. That adventurer thought it was junk, what a blinded fool! A schmuck! I hold onto the stone and will continue to until welcoming the end. This little stone and it's magic.

This feature was particularly annoying as it impedes my ability to ignore messages. I picked up the phone with the care you might expect from somebody handling roadkill. What could be so goddamn..... I had him right in front of me - the man who killed my big brother Ryan. I had a gun with a full barrel in my hands. I did not care if I would go to jail for this. The criminal justice system had failed me. They decided that the killer - John Ramsey, had done it as an act of self-defense. My brother would never try to kill someone - he was the nicest person ever. He had raised me on his own, paid for my education, and was more like a father to me. Ramsey was sleeping in his bed, unaware of my presence. Tremors flew in my hand as I was about to press the trigger. I did not realize that my aim was so bad that I would miss him, have the gun fly out of my hand, wake him up, have him tie me up and call the cops. I had never done tough-guy things before. Twenty-four years in prison, however, had changed me. I went inside an innocent man, and was coming out as a crook. I had learnt all the tricks of the trade. I once again found myself facing John Ramsey. The situation was strikingly similar to before - me with a gun in my hand, Ramsey sleeping in his bed, with his back to me. I wasn't going to miss it this time. I shot him 24 times. That motherf had no right to live after what he had done to my brother. I did not care what happened to me now. After shooting him with all the bullets I had, I just collapsed on the floor, waiting for someone to come and arrest me. Curiously, nothing of that sort happened. Instead, out of nowhere, the corpse of John Ramsey had come alive and started speaking to me, "Why did you this, Tom? I thought we had made it clear - no killing anyone and you get to go the park this week." I had no idea what was happening. I suddenly felt a jolt of electricity run through my body. John Ramsey's bedroom disappeared. In it's place, was an empty office, with John - neatly dressed and sitting in a chair. I was strapped to what seemed to be an electric chair. "Listen to me, Tom. You couldn't kill your brother's killer, so you started hallucinating with the only face visible to you. You've killed so many innocent people, don't you remember that, Tom?" Tears flowed through my eyes when I heard all of this. "I had him once, for real. I wish I only got a second chance. I want to KILL HIM! That monster John Ramsey! " , I screamed. "I am John Ramsey, Tom, your doctor. You shouldn't kill me. It was YOU who killed your brother, Tom. You thought he was the one who killed your girlfriend and you killed him. Don't you remember?" "Over the past week I'd almost succeeded in making you a different person. You were supposed to be a guy who wanted to killed, but was clumsy. We could have worked upwards from there, but I failed again." "No! You're LYING!" I screamed as I tried to free myself from that chair to run away from there. I immediately felt a jolt of current run through my body. The last thing I remember was the doctor carrying a big syringe towards me.

Admiral Asshole enters, staring slack jawed at the tattered sails and improper rigging. "My God, this must be the worst fucking boat in the entire navy." Captain Obvious and Sargent Sarcasm stand tall and salute. "Yes Admiral, when you assigned me this ship one week ago you told me it would require a fair amount of maintenance." The Admiral pauses for a second, unsure whether the Captain is mocking him or just an imbecile. He turns his attention to the seaman, Sargent Sarcasm. "Captain, your man looks terrible. "Sailor, get your disgusting face below deck before the full force of the entire navy rains down on your head." "It's been a pleasure sir." Sargent Sarcasm skips off below deck. "Just what kind of ship are you running here?" "It's a sloop, sir." "I can fucking see th The Admiral gives up mid-sentence. It's hopeless. It is clear he will need to find a new captain for the ship. He looks out over the railing at the waves and whitecaps. He's contemplative, but his face shows a capacity for anger far greater than any sea. A clanking noise overhead forces him out of his meditative brooding. He looks up and stares in a combination of horror and awe. (under his breath, rhetorically) "What the fuck is that?" "It's the ship's rigging sir. The man I assigned to it turned out to be a stowaway. Very interesting man, how he ended up here is quite a tale. He's in the brig now. Shall I have him brought up for you to meet him?" (suddenly returning to his old cantankerous self) "Of course not. Have him thrown overboard once we reach the Bay of Sharks. Sargent Sarcasm arrives, still out of uniform, but clean shaven and looking well. He may have had a drink or two. "You're out of uniform Sargent?" Sargent sarcasm considers a whole host of responses, before deciding to be serious for a change. "It's been stolen, Sir" "We have a thief on board?" "I would imagine it was the stowaway." "The rascal." He turns to the Admiral. "Admiral, I'm afraid I must inform you that we seem to have an impostor roaming our ship, wearing the uniform of an officer. Keep your eyes open, he might be on this very deck." "He might even be talking to the Admiral." The Admiral isn't interested. He's trying to figure out the rigging. The Captain glares at the Sargent. The Sargent looks a little nervous, realizing he may have gone - and sent himself- overboard with his last remark. But no, the Captain looks back at the Admiral, then glances around the deck to see who might be within speaking distance of the Admiral. He settles on a shifty looking sailor crouched down and fiddling with something. "You there! (Seeing the patches on his uniform) Sargent! Come over here" "Yes sir?" "Just now, what were you doing?" "I was over there." "Right. Well, have you seen anything suspicious on board?" "Suspicious in what way, exactly?" "Well, there is a stowaway on board, wearing a stolen uniform and masquerading as an officer. He might try to blend in by helping with the ship, but an experienced seaman would be able to tell him apart from the rest." "Well to be perfectly honest sir I'm kind of new here myself" "Yes, I know what you mean. I've only had a weeks time to familiarize myself with this particular ship." Amid the increasingly frequent clanking of the sails, the Admiral has had a breakthrough. (sort of shouting) "Captain, I think I've got it. See how that line is running in between the mast and the mainsail?" (shouting back) "It's not supposed to be that way." The Sargent, who has been sizing up the other officer the whole time, realizes that he is in fact the stowaway. "That's a nice uniform. I used to have one just like it." The Captain, half paying attention to the Admiral and half in the conversation, chides his Sargent, "Well the sooner you find the man who took your uniform, the sooner you'll have it back." The Admiral shouts again, "It looks like its all tied through that over there." He points to the, partial knot the Sargent was tying earlier. The Captain glares at the Sargent. "That knot. Your doing, isn't it?" "Yes?" "Will you buffoons fucking hurry up and untie that knot?" "It's clear you can't help me Sargent.
