The Yellow Man was a strong man. His hands were rough and leathery. He'd done this before, too many times. The Yellow Man moved his hand to my trigger, caressing the area around it lightly at first but then moving even closer until he was rubbing the tip. When we go closer to the Black Man, I was ready to burst. The Black Man sat in a chair, reading a book by the firelight. When he heard us approach and turned around, the Yellow Man put my barrel right to the Black Mans head. He finally gave my trigger a firm press, and it sent me over the edge. I shot my load all over The Black Mans face. "Colonel Mustard, in the Study, with the Revolver."

"And over here, we have the Iron Throne. The real one." To the amassed eighth-graders, it looked small, far smaller in its' roped-off Plexiglas case than in professional photographs and their imagination, and the seat was smoother as well. Nonetheless, camera phones came out and kids began jostling for pictures. As the tour guide explained, "From the founding of the Republic until 1973, anyone could sit on it long enough to have their picture taken, but it was wearing out, which is why we put it under conservation and built the replica in the next room..... follow me..." The tour group started crowding through the door, hoping to get a good spot in the line for a selfie on the replica. All except one tall, dark-haired boy in a brown zip hoodie and gray cargo shorts. Bran Stark, latest of the name, felt it unseemly for him as a member of the only surviving Great Family to sit on the Throne, real or replica. He held back a bit, took one last look at the real thing and left the room as quickly as he could. He had gotten a chill.

Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and tired, Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore - While I nodded, nearly falling asleep, suddenly there came a sharp repetitive sound, As of some one gently rapping, knocking at my chamber door - Tis some visitor," I muttered, " tapping at my chamber portal - Only this and nothing else. " nbsp; Ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak January; And each separate dying spark wrought its ghost upon the ground. Eagerly I wished the dawn; - vainly I had sought to borrow From my books surcease of sadness - sorrow for the lost Peggy - For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Margaret - Nameless here for evermore. nbsp; And the silken, sad, uncertain rustling of each purple drapery Thrilled me - filled me with fantastic terrors not felt before this; So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood saying again and again, Tis some visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door - Some late visitor asking to be let through my chamber threshold; - This it is and nothing else. " nbsp; Presently my soul grew less weak; hesitating then no longer, " Sir," said I, " or Madam, truly your forgiveness I implore; But the fact is I was sleeping, and so gently you came knocking, And so faintly you came repetitively hitting my chamber entryway, That I scarce was sure I heard you " - here I opened wide the door; - Darkness there and nothing else. nbsp; Deep into that darkness looking, long I stood there wondering, afraid, Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortal ever dared to dream before; But the silence continued, and the stillness gave no token, And the only word there said was the whispered word, " Peggy? " This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word, " Margaret! " - Merely this and nothing else. nbsp; Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me on fire, Soon again I heard a tapping somewhat louder than the last time. " Surely," said I, " surely that is something at my window lattice; Let me see, then, what it could be, and this mystery put an end to - Let my heart be still a moment and this mystery explore; - ' Tis the wind and nothing else! " nbsp; Open here I flung the window, when, with many a flirt and flutter, In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of long ago; Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute did he stop; But, with mien of lady or lord, perched above my chamber door - Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber entryway - Perched, and sat, and nothing else. nbsp; Then this ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into being a bit amused, By the grave and stern decorum of the countenance it had, " Though thy crest be shorn and shaven, thou," I said, " art sure not timid, Ghastly grim and ancient Raven wandering from the Nightly coast - Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night's Plutonian shore! " Quoth the Raven " No, never. "

Melanie shuddered, thinking about how close she had come. She needed to stop drinking so much, which wasn't going to happen. What really was the problem was that she kept calling him. It wasn't fair. Most people never met their soul mates, and with good reason. There's an old theory that says that when the Big Bang happened, particles that were close together that just happened to end up as part of humans alive at the same time would try to find each other. The universe would try to be solid again. What the theory didn't tell us was that we had evolved a mechanism to stop everyone from doing that, because there was a good chance that the universe would implode if the particles lined up the right way. This mechanism would make your heart and "soul" ache when you were near your soulmate. You would love them to the point of risking the entirety of mankind, and your body didn't really like that. Melanie had met Andre two weeks ago, at this bar she never went to. Her regular was shut down because of a shooting, so she adventured out. As soon as she had seen him, she knew. It was like a punch in her gut, only warmer. It was like being in pain, but being the happiest you've ever been. Her throat felt like she had just done a few shots of fireball. He could feel it too, he told her later. They had gone home together, against their better judgment. It was obviously the best sex either of them would ever have, and that's what made it so dangerous. Melanie shook her head and slowly undressed. She was going to take a cold shower, maybe that would sober her up and calm her soul down. She didn't need that so good it was bad feeling anymore. She was drunk and wanted to fuck but he would damage her and she should block his number. When she climbed out of the shower, she didn't bother getting dressed. She climbed into her unmade bed and pulled her dingy quilt around her. She sighed deeply, then reached for her phone and dialed his number.

The Sentarian war was a quick, brutal engagement that nevertheless filled history books with lessons on the ways things should have been done. The casualties from only two solar revolutions were immense, but in the end, integrity of the fleet was maintained. The search could continue for a new homeworld. Could things have gone better? Ethicists say yes, military analysts say they could have gone much worse. There is no right answer. One thing we all agree on: the loss of our humanity was too high a cost. The atrocities we committed during the war are countless, but sacrificing an entire slave species and their planet Earth for simple resource denial, is beyond any rational justification. Now with only two major races in the galaxy retaining control of planets with significant human stock, the demand will undoubtedly drive the cost up for those looking to purchase human slaves in the future.

This city's full of people with superpowers. Some use them to get what they want, consequences be damned. Some try to use them to keep the peace. Some just use them to get through their daily lives. Some don't want to use them at all. Superheroes? Supervillians? Pah. They're just people. Give a man a gun or a bomb, he could do the same. Me? I'm the only goddamn hero in this town. I don't kill people, in the name of justice or in the name of greed. No. It's two o'clock AM. One hour'til close. I'm at Jake's Lightning Burritos. I'm Jake. And I feed people. - A chill wind makes my little trailer shake. Can't tell whether Windsday sneezed again or if it's just the weather acting up. I don't mind; it gets hot in here, what with all the cooking and refrigerators. I always meant to pipe the fridge exhausts to outside the trailer, but it keeps me warm in the winter and nobody wants to start melting when they get near me in the summer. I'm a tough guy. You have to be, in this town. Hot in the summer, freezing in the winter, wet all year round. At least my trailer keeps me dry. "Hey!" It's The Ballerina! She always tips well. Love that gal. "Hey, Bally! The hell you doin' up so late?" "Went to go see some Balanchine, had to go stop a guy who tried to rob the place. I'm famished." Even so, she starts swinging her leg back and forth, kicking above her head and then back again above her hips. Think she said it was gran-bat-maw or something like that? I dunno. "Well, it's late, so I'm runnin' low on stuff. You know the drill, what I got on the menu's all I have." "Ooh, I don't think I've had the Vegan Tiger before." "Mmm, one Vegan Tiger I take another look at her. "Nah, you're gon na need four of these bad boys tonight." Bally blushes. "You know me too well, Jake." "I know everyone too well." Ah, the vegan burritos. One of my best ideas, to be honest. Veggies are cheap if you know where to get them, and they'll sing loud and proud for ya if you treat'em right. Everyone needs to eat more veggies, and it gets me the business of the high-and-mighty types too. I don't like a lot of'em, but it ain't my job to like nobody. I'm here to feed'em. Give'em an ear or two if they need it. An earful if they need that, too. "A'ight, Bally, eight bucks." She sticks a hand down her leo and puts a sweaty twenty on the counter. "Keep the change as apology for the boobsweat." I grimace and hand over the burritos. "Come on, Bally, don't do this to me. Get some damn pockets!" "Alright, alright already." She starts wolfing one of her burritos down and making noises that belong in a bed, not at a food cart. I make some damn good burritos. I also have to pick her sweaty twenty up with a spare set of tongs and hang it up to dry. She wanders over to a bench to go sit down, only to dart off and return dragging a guy with handcuffs on. "You've never had Jake's, right? This is your last chance before that stupid three strikes law puts you away forever. My treat." The man stops struggling and resigns himself to being dragged along. I don't help matters by laughing my ass off. "You the guy that tried to rob the ballet?" "I was trying to rob the audience. Thought only rich people went to the ballet." He looks down at his feet, face starting to burn. "Man, I don't want this. I don't wan na go back to prison." I lean over the counter. "You made your bed, man. Now you got ta lie in it. Last bit of food on the outside, what's it gon na be." He looks up at the menu with tears in his eyes. "I know. I know..." He sighs. "I think I'll have a Peanut Panic." Mmm, that's a good one. "Be glad it was Bally tonight instead of someone like Captain Crush." I call from the kitchen, "They'd be cleaning you out of the carpets instead of feeding you burritos." I hand him his and he starts chowing down, making a point of chewing slow, savoring each bite. "You know," he says as he turns to me, face starting to swell, "I couldn't've asked for a better last meal. Thank you." He finishes his burrito before his throat swells shut and closes his eyes, trying to still his body. Bally panics and searches him for an epipen, but to no avail. None of the cops have anything. Paramedics are too far away. He's dead. I shake my head and pull down my shade. Closing up early tonight. I step outside into the air and give poor Bally a hug as she cradles the dead man in her lap.

I never understood the general distaste for Mondays. Sure they tended to herald a distinct lack of sleep, but that was almost a godsend. When exhausted one often winds up with a singular focus for the task at hand, being entirely incapable of mental multitasking. In any event, it was Monday again, the first one that truly registered as such after the months of educational hiatus during the summer. Even I had to admit that things looked pretty bleak. It wasn't due to my own exhaustion, my want for sleep was actually distracting me from the problems at hand, it was the changes to school policy that brought on the feelings of dread as I took the familiar path towards the school's main doors. That was when I noticed the first change. There was a sign above the door that read " C entrance, groups U and H proceed to left and right entrances respectively ." I sighed. This was going to be a long year. As I began my trek towards the left side of the building, winding my way around the C students using the front entrance, I reflected that I had known that things would be different. I had known since the new Thirty First Amendment that things would be different, but it was only that day as I stepped through the left entrance for orientation that it truly struck me. As I stepped inside cardboard signs with arrows directed me to the room in which we would receive what could only be described as a half hearted pep-talk for the upcoming semester. I found myself in a dusty abandoned classroom with about a dozen odd students. One of my other fears was just confirmed. The only other people in group U were either idiots of political dissidents. I was neither. Why had my parents not just lied to put me in group C? This could ruin my entire future too, it was hard to imagine high profile jobs hiring a U class student. The really aggravating thing about it was that it would have been relatively easy to hide. It would be harder to lie about being in group H, but I knew for a fact that many of the students going into group C this year should have by all rights been in this dreary classroom with me. Just a week ago last Sunday I saw Malcolm Dodge drinking with friends around town. The whole thing was just degrading on so many levels. The instructor stepped in and began the expected speech about how important it was to take our education seriously in the upcoming year. It was all really standard high school bullshit, up until the end at the very least. He finished with a scripted diatribe about how the new changes were for the benefit of equality and every student. When he finished I probably would have laughed had my face not been frozen out of sheer horror as the the implications. It was amazing how much could change in a couple months. As I walked out of the classroom, preparing myself mentally for math, the instructor handed me my school ID. I glanced at it as I stepped into the hall. On the right next to my picture was the official seal of our Prime Minister and Holy Pope of the Catholic Church. In the bottom right corner there were three lines of text, with the bottom one being circled in red pen: C - Christian H - Heretic U - Unaffiliated Edit: formatting

The signals had been coming in for months before we finally got them decoded. The news, such as it was, was devastating. Millions were driven to suicide, unable to accept the apparent truths: We do have a creator, but they're not perfect. The creator wasn't even divine. Apparently our creator was a low-budget hack who decided to finally'come clean' to his creation by releasing what amounted to some combination of a readme.txt file and various Meeting Minutes defending his choices. Some of the highlights: - Reduced cost of'neck' structure by eliminating one redundant tube. Fuel and air now enter through same aperture. Cost savings justify slight increase in failure rate among humans. Operators will need to be careful in feeding humans not to jam the sole entry. - Removal of'Appendix' organ deemed too expensive. Requires reissue of engineered drawing. We'll just reduce the size of it, route function around it, and hope it doesn't explode too often. See attachment: Estimated failure rate of Human Appendix. - Request for additional bone around'Temple' in skull declined. If the upcoming nonviolence programming gets done before release, having a weak spot around the central processing organ shouldn't be a problem, and bone is costly. - Redesign of the eyeball to bury the nerves properly will not be complete until version 1.0 at earliest. All models V0.7 and below will simply have to compensate for blind spots with their binocular vision. Footnote: This may not even make it in until version 3.0, if ever. Humans unlikely to notice their blind spot unless they go looking for it, and the wetware guys have a neat trick in mind to cover the gap. - We're experiencing a lot of problems with their self-reproducing systems. The male systems are unreliable, but we're putting those on hold to look into problems with the female side of things. The systems work, barely, but have a chance of mortally wounding the unit in operation. Even when they're not active, they cause the carrier a lot of problems and discomfort. They can near-cripple some carriers for up to 25 of their uptime, and waste a lot of resources. - We had to route waste expulsion lines through the reproductive organs as there wasn't time to fine a better excretion point. Psychology is very, very far behind in their development and won't have time to test this before release. Hopefully it doesn't cause any weird side-effects. These logs caused mass hysteria in parts of the world with deeply religious cultures. Millions of lives were lost and the feeling of self-importance humanity once held for itself was stripped overnight. Only one good thing came of the whole thing. A final entry was transmitted and arrived on November 23rd, 2046: - We're implementing a recall program. Anyone with an older-model human can return to us at [ coordinates ] and receive an upgrade to our current model at no cost. Space programs have reached an all-time high.

It's not just that the Sun is missing. That would be bad enough on its own, right? The old and trusty ball of flames gone missing somewhere across the Pacific ocean. Yes, that's a big problem right there. Not the worst one we have right now, though. I glance at the clock on the bookshelf. It's been six hours now. Six hours since my brother-in-law left to get some supplies at the local mall. Water, food, batteries..... My wife is looking out the window, her eyes straining to see something in the darkness outside. I doubt he'll be coming back, but I keep my mouth shut. No. The worst problem..... the one that makes my hands tremble and my chest get tight is that..... I think it's getting darker. I know it because of the streetlights. I've been counting them over and over again for the last hours. I know that, back when my brother-in-law left, I could see all the streetlights up to the Fowlers house. Nine. Nine streetlights. I can only see three of them now. And the third is barely visible. A faint bright point floating in the darkness, as if enveloped by a black fog. I hope the Fowlers are safe. I place my gun, a Glock 19, on the side table next to the couch. It makes me feel safer, though I suspect it won't make much of a difference if..... whatever..... gets in. Better not to think about it. We stay in silence, listening to the soft static crackling coming from the TV. White noise, that's all there is to see now. It's a relief, after all the noise, speculation and babbling idiot hosts from the first hours. Three hours ago, I went outside. I had to let our dog, Zoey, back inside. That was back when I could still see up to the sixth streetlight. I grabbed my Glock, opened the main door, and stepped out into the darkness. It was..... strange. Not nearly as cold as I had expected, but there was a thickness to the air. Walking through it made me feel as if my feet were submerged in water. Sounds were muffled, and it was hard to breathe. Exhaustion started building up as soon as I had taken four steps out. When I got back, I realized there were thin tendrils of dark mist starting to creep into the house. I made sure to close every window and door, placed towels in every cracks. I didn't find Zoey. I glance at my wife. Her face is pale. I follow her gaze out the window. Only two streetlights now.

Twin figures, one a radiant figure of healing energy, the other a pale reflection of silvery death, entwined and poured their hearts out to each other. Once the passions of both had been sated, Narcissa turned to her lover and said "Dearest Tristan, what of your father? Surely a High Warlock does not want his son "involved" with someone like me, and certainly not with a Morningstar!" "Beloved Narcissa, it is the very arrogance and power lust my father extols as virtuous that drives me into your arms. His mad wars against your family and their allies have proven to me the futility of his methods. 20 years and not a single inch of land we fight for has been won. So yes, indeed do a edge myself to turn my magic against his forces and to end the cycle of bloodshed!" The scrap of a door down the hall sends the two lovers into a frenzy of motion, as robes are pulled on, hair is bunned, and enchanted arms and armor strapped tight. On baited breath the Coue waits as the click of designer shoes carries Madame Collette past their hiding place, and once the overbearing witch had gone, they slipped out into the corridor. With longing gazes, they parted, Narcissa to the Morningstar Necromancy Wing, Tristan to the Clerical Paladin Barracks, of the Pigfreckles School of Spellcraft and Sorcery.

I wasn't sure why my mother had never mentioned the VHS tapes she had stashed away in the bottom of her bedroom closet. I was only rooting around in there because I'd loaned her some shoes last time I'd come home from college and I wanted them back, but instead I found about a dozen unlabeled tapes stacked neatly in the back corner behind the pile of shoes and mostly hidden by some long dresses. At first I thought they were going to be weird sex tapes or something, but when curiosity compelled me to put one in the VHS player my parents still had lying around, I found that they were of a different nature altogether. The first tape started off with a grainy view of our living room. It was Christmastime according to the decorated tree beside the fireplace and the wreath sitting on the mantle, partially obscuring the large mirror behind it. After a few moments a woman came onscreen carrying a small baby. It took me a long moment to recognize her as my mother, and I was only certain of her identity when I heard her voice say "Look, Ashley, Santa Claus came!" Ashley is my name, so I assumed the baby in her arms must have been me. My birthday is in September, so this must have been my first Christmas. I watched transfixed as a part of my past that I had no chance of remembering played out before me. I got some new pajamas and a few baby toys that year, and most of the tape was just me snuggling in my mother's arms while she tried to get me to play with a stuffed elephant. Eventually I started getting fussy, and my mother got up and took me out of the room. After a few moments the living room scene went staticky, and I fast forwarded a bit to make sure that it wasn't just a blank spot in this homemade tape, but that seemed to be the end of the recording. I quickly popped the next tape in. This one started in the same manner: a view of our living room without anyone in it. There was no Christmas tree this time. The scene remained unmoved for longer than the first one, but eventually a toddler came running into the room laughing hysterically. It was me again, and close behind me was my mother. I fell to the floor, still giggling, and my mother immediately scooped me up and spun me around, also laughing. She played with me a bit, tickling me, blowing raspberries at me, and tossing me up in the air, all the while laughing with me amidst my screams of excitement. " Come on, silly girl, we need to get you dressed! " she said finally. " Noooooooo! " squealed the still pajama-clad toddler, but I made no moves to resist as my mother carried me back the way we came. Again the scene remained still for a time before going staticky, and again I found that that was the end of the video, despite there being hours of recording time left on the tape. I was starting to feel like something was a little strange about these tapes, but I kept watching them. Each captured between five to fifteen minute snippets of my childhood, not always in order. There was another Christmas scene, and a birthday party, but most of them were just regular days, always filmed from the same angle in our living room. However, something in the seventh one caught my attention. The large mirror above the fireplace was directly opposite a bay window looking out into the front yard. From the angle that the camera was at, I could clearly see the front yard through the window reflected in the mirror. The young me in the video was doing something in the living room as usual, but some movement in the yard drew my eyes up to the mirror. It was just our dog running around, but as I was about to look back to myself in the living room, the realization hit me like a ton of bricks. Where was the camera? From this angle I should have been able to see the camera in the mirror, but there was nothing there. I tried to convince myself that I was wrong, that the camera was shorter than the window and out of view of the mirror, but I couldn't. I had literally just finished my college trigonometry midterms the week prior and passed with flying colors. I had a natural talent for visualizing this stuff, and I knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that I should be able to see the recording device in that mirror. Fed up of having more questions than answers, I decided to text my mother at work. Hey mom, why did you never show me the video tapes from when I was a kid? The answer was not what I wanted. What video tapes? After I explained where I'd found them and what the contents were, she called me instead of texting back. " Ash, get out of the house and call your cousin Tiffany to come pick you up. Leave the tapes where they are. I'm calling the police now. I've never done more than take pictures of you with a polaroid or my phone and we certainly never owned a video camera. And I have never been aware of any VHS tapes in my closet. " I spent the rest of the day at Tiffany's house. The police confiscated the tapes, and despite repeated inquiries by my mother, they have never provided any answers. Whenever I'm home from college now, I don't spend much time in the living room anymore.

The Zorblaxian representative examined the document intently, as though daring it to reveal its secrets. As far as anyone in the room knew, he (not that you could really put human gender to a Zorblaxian) didn't read any Earth languages, though his spoken English was improving rapidly. Nevertheless he stared intently at the sheaf of pages, hastily printed out by one of the million assistants that seemed to be waiting outside the room. His proboscis absentmindedly sucked some mucus off his single eyeball, putting some in the room in mind of someone licking their lips, and putting many more off their lunch. The alien turned to Colonel Davies, who was really only there because he knew planes, and there was hope of some sort of a technology sharing deal on propulsion systems. The Zorblaxian had turned up his proboscis at medical and computer technology. But now, in reaction to a chance reference by Davies, who was too used to trotting out his classical education to those who dismissed him as a dumb fighter jock, the creature was examining The Odyssey. The alien began hesitantly, "So you say this..... O-Diss-I-Yes is returning from war. And meets many strange beings along the way." Davies nodded. "Yes, and then he returns to his wife and has to defeat her suitors. The other men trying to marry her, for they believe Odysseus is dead." The Zorblaxian gave the little wiggle that it used as a nod. "And this Odysseus..... is not real." "Well he may have been. But even if he was he didn't do any of these things." "Yes. Because none of these..... beings he meets are..... real either? They are as you said..... made up?" The creature sounded almost titillated! "Yes indeed, they don't exist. They're a fantasy." "So someone wrote this, but was not recording true events, instead just taking things from his own mind?" "Well yeah." A thoughtful pause. "And do others have this ability?" Colonel Davies tried and failed to read the expressions on his superiors' faces. With no lie instructed he figured he'd just tell the truth. "Some are better than others, but yes, most of us can write things down from our heads." A smug upcurl of the left skin flap. "Deception." "Not really deception if everyone knows." A scrunch of doubt in the fleshy top part of his face. "So you have more like this? More made-up writing?" "Yes, we have thousands of stories." "Thousands." The creature's proboscis was waving all around its face now, and its central arm-like appendage was quivering. Its giant eye looked at Colonel Davies, and then around the room. "I think we may be able to make a deal."

The tears had been with him through it all. Through math class, through chemistry, whenever he laid his head to rest at night. It had been coming for a long time, it wasn't a surprise. But that didn't make it easier. " We need to see other people, it isn't working. " He'd seen it, she wasn't talking as much as she used to, the Skype calls had grown more and more quiet. And here they were, when she was not. The tears came once more, breath catching in his chest in a huge swell as he fought down the guttural wail that filled him like a smoker's first cough. Looking down to shut out the shame of crying in public, he watched as the tickle of warm tears transformed into broad specks on the blank page of notes that sat before him on the table. Both hands reached up to cradle his head, squeezing harder and harder as the hoarse sobs fought to escape. It hurt so badly to be alone; even the misery of impending doom was better than the deep sinking feeling of inadequacy and disgust that now washed away happy memories of a summer past. He resolved to stand up, to close his eyes and march out right into traffic. Just a few steps it was, then maybe god could decide if he was better off alone- " Hey, are you ok? " A voice asked. He looked up, sniffing. His eyes followed a figure in a dark uniform as it sat down in front of him. Hi, my name is Krystal read the name tag.

Everyone knows that it hurts to die. What they don't tell you is how badly it hurts to come back. I see it all day long; the orderlies (isn't that cute? Call them'orderlies' when you hire them so they think they're wheeling living patients around instead of hoisting cadavers! Makes them less likely to turn around and quit on the spot!) place the client into the ReAnimus machine and do their little check -BPC; breathing-pulse-color; you have to be sure the client is well and truly dead before you turn the thing on or else there can be a lawsuit -strap'em in and at my signal the lights flash and suddenly the corpse jackknifes in his or her bonds. They died during a seizure? They're still seizing; won't stop until we get them clear of the rig. GSW? They leak. They're the reason the floor in the chamber is coated with anti-slip rubber; it prevents falls and is easy to hose down. Infarcts can feel their exploded hearts quivering uselessly in their chests. The ones that fell are hardest to look at; sacks of splintered bone wrapped in mushy discolored skin. Like human bananas gone bad. I can feel the familiar rush of chilled airflow. I know without opening my rolling eyes that this is the ReAnimus chamber. Just hours ago, I was lead tech on the revival crew. My job was to turn the machine on, help the'client' out of the machine, calm them down and then explain that he or she had been the beneficiary of a Death Insurance policy, meaning they had been revived for exactly twenty-four hours from the time of revival, and that it would be prudent to use this precious gift to set their affairs in order and say their final goodbyes to loved ones. Sometimes they want me to hold them awhile, cry with them, pray. One woman ran out of the chamber buck-naked, laughing and shrieking said she was gon na hunt down the sonofabitch that beat her to death, and bring him with her this time. When the retrieval crew got to her, she'd done just as she promised: used his own guns on her ex until his head was little more than strawberry jello. He didn't have a policy. Until roughly twelve hours ago, I didn't think I did, either. But now that the gloved hands are helping me free of the ReAnimus' plastic exoskeleton, I can feel the air whistling through the neat hole at the base of my skull. My teeth taste bloody as I smile at the unfamiliar crop of techs, nodding along with their questions so they let me go and track down whomever killed me.

Dear Merciful One, I beg of you to grant me one more day under your watchful benevolence for I am..... I need to..... I must go to work in order to recieve a salary so that my family doesn't starve..... An old excuse, but one I hadn't used in a while. I feel a trickle of sweat drop down my brow, but I feel that familiar tremor after the judgement has passed and breathe a little better. Another day. I'm 52 years old. When I was a younger I barely had to think about all the things I wanted to live for: girls, sports, learning new things, new experiences, getting to see the future, etc. It was easy back then, but now that I'd done all those things I'd reached that turning point in my life where there were fewer and fewer things to look forward to. And yet I must live, or my family of seven will starve. A valid excuse, but a boring one, and if there's one thing the Merciful One can not stand it's repetition. Today I see the man. The oldest man who has ever lived. He is 219 years old. He lives alone in the top floor of a private hospital where he is attended to day and night by a fleet of doctors and nurses. Many seek his counsel on the topic of longevity, but all who have spoken with him so far have left disappointed. How can such a man not want to share his knowledge with the world, so that all can reap the benefits of long life? I am angry, but I mask it well as I enter the hospital. It is very hard to get an appointment with him, and I should count myself lucky that I get one at all. It is said that he has not spoken to anyone in twelve years. When the elevator doors opened I smelled his husk, and the dry rattling of his breath from the otherside of the corridoor. I followed the dispassionate nurse who led me to his bed, and I saw what looked like a withered child contemplating the agony of his existence. He took notice of me in a detached kind of way, and closing his eyes, resigned himself to a conversation. "Assk...." he whispered. I cleared my throat, and keeping my tone even and neutral asked the question that so many before me had asked: "How do you do it? What reason do you give to the Merciful One above that lets him grant you such a long life?" His eyes remained shut, and for a moment I thought he'd fallen asleep, or worse. Then suddenly he choked and coughed, a faint spittle of blood decorating his gown in a manner that seemed to suggest that it was not his first time. Drawing breath, the old man answered me, and the words said that day I would take to my grave: "It makes him happy..... to watch me suffer..."

"The time I accidentally kickstarted Armageddon, or, how I spent my summer vacation" Danny Carriveaux AP English, 9215 Mrs. Gundrum My summer was totally boring. I made subs at Subway and tried to save money for college. When I wasn't doing that, I was out with my friends at the skate park or at house parties. Those were cool. One night in July, I was at a party and didn't meet any girls, so I walked back home. In my room, I turned on my laptop and played around for a bit. I thought I was looking at a Kickstarter page for Food For Sherman, one of my favorite bands, looking to finance their new album. Nobody had donated, and I wanted to be the first. I gave them five bucks, then went to bed. When I woke up, four dudes were standing around in my room. The tallest of them, wearing an awesome blood-red suit of armor, asked me "Daniel Carriveaux, arise and assume your place as the one who will bring about the destruction of man," or something like that. "What?" I asked, totally confused. He told me that the men in my room were the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse who had been waiting for an invitation into our world to do the end of the world, and I was going to lead them. And I'd given it to them when I donated to their Kickstarter. I told War that I thought I was giving money to a band, and he said "We know. We thought it would be a lot more popular." Then he showed me the page, and sure enough, as a reward for donating five dollars, you called in the Four Horsemen and oversaw the destruction of mankind, leading to the final battle between good and evil. I told him that sounded awesome, but there were some things that needed to be done first. Like, they needed to cover for me at my job while I slept off my hangover. Not my best idea. All the food got rotten and had to be thrown away the moment Famine walked in the door, and anyone eating a sandwich already got food poisoning and died on the spot thanks to Death. Pestilence violated a whole bunch of health codes, and War got into a fight with my manager and got me fired, which they told me when they showed up at my house an hour later. They wanted to know when the real work would be done, killing and sickness and starvation and all that. I told them to cool it. That's not really my bag. Instead, we all hung around and I brought them to parties. Chicks thought it was so cool that I was friends with the four horsemen, at least until they got super sick and started puking. They looked really out of place walking around with those horses, so instead I got them into skateboarding and taught them some tricks. After a month, we were the Five Shredders of the Apocalypse: War, Death, Famine, Pestilence, and Chill. They were seriously up on wrecking humanity's shit, so I was always telling them to relax. I managed to get them super into Breaking Bad on Netflix, though, so when they discovered that, they stopped trying to kill people all the time and they were some pretty alright dudes. Then, about a week before school started, we were skating down the street when the ground started to shake. I thought it was an earthquake, but everything went pitch black but bright at the same time. Was I having a stroke like my grandpa? No, it turns out that I was surrounded by a bunch of angels and demons. On one side stood the devil, dressed in this weird flowing robe, holding a sword and looking sort of like a chick, and behind him stood thousands of demons ready for war like a scene from Lord of the Rings. On the other side in a ring of light was Jesus Christ, who didn't look anything like my church says he looks, leading a bunch of angels dressed all in white with wings and halos and spears. Then Jesus and Satan stepped forward and they looked at me and the Horsemen in disbelief and shock. No one seemed to say anything for a really long time, so I broke the ice and said "Hi, I'm Danny. These are my boys. What's up?" "We know who you are," Jesus said, super disappointed. "This planet was supposed to be ruined! We were supposed to hold the battle for the fate of all men's souls this day, as had been appointed eons ago!" Satan hissed. "Oh. Yeah, my bad," I told them. "I wasn't really feeling the whole thing. I'm more of a chill kind of guy, you know?" Jesus scoffed. " 'Chill'? My Father, the creator of everything in existence, ordained this date as the day when creation would come to an end and one side would emerge victorious in our spiritual war, and you threw that away because you wanted to be chill? There was supposed to be a wasteland for us to wage our battle upon!" "A wasteland? Well, stuff's pretty shitty south of 12th Street," I offered. Both Jesus and the devil screamed. The devil said "You four, with me!" and I could hear my buddies behind me poof out of existence. Then Satan pointed a clawed finger at me and said "Say your prayers, bitch, because I won't forget this!" Finally, he looked at Jesus and said "Tell your dad to get back to me when he has a new date for Armageddon picked out. Unbelievable..." And then he and his demons all disappeared in a huge puff of black smoke, and I was left with Jesus and ten thousand angels all staring at me in disappointment. "How did this happen?" the son of God asked me. "You know how you turned water into wine? Well, I turned whiskey into drunk. The rest was all the horsemen showing up and wanting to wreck n00bs. I never asked for it." Jesus just shook his head, then slowly disappeared along with his angels, and I was back in the middle of the street, alone, with a car beeping at me to move out of the way. So that was my summer vacation, meeting the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, avoiding the end of the world, disappointing Jesus and Lucifer, and losing my job at Subway. All in all, kind of a boring summer if you ask me. I'd rather be like my friend Kyle who worked on an oil rig with his uncle outside of Mexico. At least he got a tan. The end. "Danny, Wonderful imagination! A"

Charlie's phone began to buzz across the nightstand. He opened a groggy eye and tried to catch the elusive phone to press snooze one more time. Press snooze one more time? "SHIT!" Charlie jumped out of bed and sped through his morning routine. He cut himself twice shaving, spilled coffee on his one good shirt and smashed into his trashcan at the end of the driveway as he backed out. If he managed to speed he might get to work on time. This would be his third day being late in a row, his manager already threatened him with firing yesterday. If Charlie lost this job he had no idea what he would do. He floored the gas pedal and prayed. Brake lights flashed in front of him as the entire highway came to a dead stop. The minutes on the clock slowly ticked away. Every passing second confirming Charlie's fear of being late, yet again. Traffic began to slowly move as cars worked themselves around a terrible accident. Multiple cars were tangled in a twisted mess. Charlie's heart dropped when he saw a white sheet covering a body on the street. He might be late but at least he was alive, Charlie thought sadly to himself. He pulled into the office where his temp job was located. He barely made it inside the door before his manager was yelling at him. Unsurprisingly Charlie was handed a white envelope with a check for the amount of hours he worked and escorted off the premises. He sat in his car and cried. He hated himself for being too incompetent to get places on time. His entire life he had been late, he couldn't handle it anymore. The cellphone in his pocket rang, distracting him from his self-loathing. The number read Unknown. Maybe it was the temp agency calling to make him feel worse. He picked up and said hello. "Mr. Bontemp? This is Avery Mason and I have a job proposition for you. Would you mind coming to an interview today?" a man with a southern gentlemanly accent asked. "Uh, sure? What time?" "10:14, sharp, at the Manas Hotel room 814. Don't be late," he said and hung up the phone. It was only 9:03, it would take roughly twenty minutes to get to the hotel. Charlie didn't consider that an interview in a hotel room was weird or that he had no idea how this person had gotten his phone number but he needed a job, and he needed it now. He threw the car in reverse and sped off. There was no way he was going to be late. A few miles down the road dark smoke began to billow out of the hood of his car. The car sputtered and squealed to a halt. "SHIT!" Charlie screamed in frustration. He jumped out of the car and began to run down the road. 9:22. Charlie wasn't in the best shape and sweat was running down his body in a thick heavy drops. He wheezed around the final corner and saw the large hotel looming over the street. 10:12. He sprinted across the street, a car swerved avoiding hitting him by inches. He pushed through the front door and raced across the lobby to the elevators. Desperately he hit eight rapidly until the door closed and the elevator lurched skyward. 10:13. The elevator came to a stop on the third floor, the doors slid open revealing an empty hallway. "What the hell!" Charlie shouted and hit eight again and again. The doors closed and the elevator began to move again. Until it came to another stop on the fifth floor. Again the doors opened to an empty hallway. 10:14. He was late. Again. The elevator moved again and stopped on the eighth floor. He pushed open the doors and raced down the hallway. Maybe their clocks were slow, Charlie prayed as he slid to a stop in front of room 814. He knocked on the door as politely as he could but to his ears it sounded thunderous. A young man in a fine black suit opened the door and gestured Charlie inside. An older gentleman was sitting in a plush red chair staring out the window. "You're late," he said in the familiar southern accent. "I know, I'm sorry, my car, and the man raised a hand silencing Charlie. "I know. It's fine Charlie. It confirmed our theory," he said. "Theory?" Charlie asked. "You see, you weren't actually late Charlie. You've never been late. You have always arrived to places exactly when you were supposed to. This morning if you had woken up when your alarm went off you would have died in that car accident. If you had arrived here Mr. Carter would have shot you. He had strict orders to kill you if you got here at 10:14 or earlier, but if you arrived at 10:15 you got to live." Charlie stared at the man in stunned silence. "What I'm saying Charlie, is that you are a very special and unique person, and we want you on our team." The young man in the black suit whom Charlie assumed was Mr. Carter handed him a black business card. "Call that number if you are interested. Mr. Carter and I need to be at another appointment." The man stood shook Charlie's numb hand and left the room with Mr. Carter following. Charlie looked at the card. A phone number was printed in white. He flipped it over. In the same white letters printed on the back was, "Together we're going to save the world." - [ Part 2 is up! ] (https: ) Thanks for reading! If you liked it check out rWritten4Reddit

I saw the old man push the swing, again. He had to be at least ninety, and as my aunt would say, "So close to death, he has the Grim Reaper on speed dial." He would sit for a while at the park where I worked as a ranger. Then, struggling to get up from the weathered, wooden bench with arthritic pain, he would rise, go over to the swing, and give it a few desultory pushes. At least, they seemed desultory to me. Each day since I started, for months: He'd sit with his cane, and stare off into nowhere. Then, get up, totter over to the swing set, and give an empty seat a few pushes. Often, that set was occupied by laughing children, challenging one another to swing higher than the rest, sure of their immortality and their ability to be just fast enough, or strong enough, to avoid mistakes the kind that, unfortunately, ended in a broken arm or twisted ankle for the ones who were not as quick, or as brave, as their peers. The old man would wait with the patience that only the elderly have, having known the passage of decades. When those children were done, he'd walk over to the chain-and-rubber child's playground toy, and give it one, two, three pushes. Sometimes four. Then, after a minute, he'd leave. ..... One day, I was overcome with curiosity. I approached him as he slowly made his way to the recently vacated swing set. "Hello?" I came up from behind him. Today he was wearing a yellow short sleeved shirt, the folds of his worn, aged skin moving shakily as he maneuvered his cane to support his frail body. He kept going. I don't think he heard me. "Hello!" I repeated, a little louder as he made it to the swing he traditionally pushed, lacking any child to enjoy it. He slowly turned and looked at me. "Pardon me?" He said with a thick accent. I would guess eastern European roots. "Hello!" "Hello, young man. How are you?" He extended a shaky hand, and I returned a soft handshake. I was approaching forty; I wouldn't say I was all that young. Compared to him, though, I was baby. I couldn't help but notice what looked like a bruise on his inner arm. Poor guy; they probably poked and prodded him for blood at his doctor's office. "Fine. How are you, sir?" I replied. "Oh, just getting along. I come here every day for wool-gathering, you know. Such a beautiful park, here." His voice sounded old, and tired. "It is, sir." "I think my brother and sister would have liked it, here." He said, eyes momentarily downcast behind his thick, Coke-bottle glasses. "Where are they?" "Dead." "I'm sorry to hear it." "Thank you, son." He looked up again, at me. "So, you have a question for me, Officer?" Heh. My uniform. Just under two years on the job, and I'm still not used to people addressing me as'Officer'. "My name is Dan." "Daniel?" "Just'Dan'." "Okay, Daniel. What's your question?" "Well, sir. I noticed you come and push the swing every day, with no children in it. May I ask why?" "You saw me do that, eh?" He smiled a little at this, like he was a child caught stealing from the cookie jar. "Yeah." "Then watch, and I'll explain." He turned to the swing, and gripped the chain with his right hand. "The soldiers took us my brother, my sister, my mother, and me when I was six years old. My father was probably at the factory; I do not know." He paused, his unsteady right hand shaking the chain, his left leaning on his cane. "The soldiers took us, and separated us. My sister and mother in one boxcar; my brother and me in another. I rode a night and a day, and when they let us out, we were herded into long houses. My brother and I stayed together. They put us children to work on machines where our little hands could get at smaller parts. Sometimes my friends' hands were crushed. My brother lost a finger..." He paused, again. "They gave me this to make sure I knew I was a number, not a person." He turned his arm, and showed me the bruise. Only, it wasn't a bruise; it was a series of numbers. Old, faded, but indelibly marked into his skin. "The Americans came and freed us, just a month too late. My mother and sister were dead from the gas chambers, and my brother died of pneumonia. I was ten when I left the camp. I was lucky, and got sent to live with my aunt here in America, where I got work in a bakery." He walked behind the swing, and steadied himself with his cane. "My brother, my sister, and me? We never had a childhood. We never played. We worked, starved, and did our best to avoid the guards' attention. So, I do this." And he pushed the swing. "One push, for my sister, Anna," The swing went out, and came back. "One push, for my brother Yosef," the swing went out, and came back again. "And one push for me, because no one ever did." And he pushed it again. ..... The silence was deafening, punctuated only by the creaking sounds of an un-greased playground swing, and a survivor's memorial to a childhood that was taken from him and his siblings.

They call me Cat's Cradle. I hate the sensationalized name that was bestowed upon me when the world first discovered two of my victims. It's too narrow and suffocating for one who takes such pride in his work, but I suppose it has helped to keep me from being caught. As far as police and the media are aware, I have only five notches in my belt; The first pair, and a trio that I arranged just to stir things up. Initially I wasn't sure that a human's tendons were strong enough to be used like string, and I simply had to know for sure. For the record they are quite strong, though brittle after a few hours. It was just an experiment, one of many, but people seemed to think it was my calling card. In truth I have stripped the life from nineteen men and four women, all of them a drain on our beautiful country. Vagrants, beggars, and drug addicts the lot of them, and not a one worth even an iota of mercy. Their kind suck the life from the world, tarnishing the natural grace of society and those that fight and claw each and every day to live a good life. They all deserved it. Every weekend is a new adventure, as I take a break from the daily struggle to live comfortably and bring justice to the dregs of humanity. It helps that with my career I can write the extra miles off on my taxes. One might call it tax fraud, but I prefer to think of it as financial responsibility. I'm still working, so to speak, only at my second job. On this particular Friday evening I saw my next mission along the side of the road before he even has his thumb out, fortune smiling on me before I even reached my destination. I would have this over and done with before the sun rose, and be in time for a hearty breakfast and a nap before catching a show. Flashing my lights once as I pulled to the side of the road, I unlocked the doors and waved for the stranger to get in. Now as a rule, I don't advise that anyone pick up a hitcher, especially not well past midnight. Some of them can be mentally unbalanced or dangerous, and none of them are worth any of your pity. I have experience, however, having removed many from existence for the betterment of mankind. Flashing the young man my most disarming smile, I waited patiently as he climbed in and dropped a backpack between his feet. "Where to?" I asked casually, putting on the mask I force myself to wear in their presence. "There's an old train yard just inside the city, that's as far as I need to go tonight." "It's pretty late, did something happen to set you behind?" "You could say that." Something was off about this man, though it took me a moment to place it. As I pulled the sedan back onto the highway, I watched him surreptitiously. Disheveled brown hair, a day's growth on his face, and a worn out jacket with the color pulled up. He looked like any other vagabond wandering the American Midwest, but I quickly realized he didn't smell like one. There was no scent of stale urine and dry sweat on this man, nor did he stink like an ashtray or rum can. Some other odor, sweet and very faint, drifted off of him. I knew it from somewhere, but it's origin escaped me. I drove in silence as I chewed on the scent that was so elusive, noting that the man was not jittery or sluggish. Another vehicle had fallen in behind me by the time I reached the first stoplight of the moderately sized Nebraska town, and as I sat at the red my mind finally put the pieces together. For four of my victims I'd played around with natural and artificial toxins, observing their effects and making note of the most interesting results. Many of the poisons had a distinct scent, and even months later I could recognize them. "Water Hemlock." I said aloud, turning to look at my passenger. "Now why on earth would your sleeves smell of a powerful natural poison?" As the man stared calmly back at me, he cocked his head a little to the side, and the traffic light turned from red to green. Immediately the car behind me blasted it's horn, impatient and annoyed that I didn't tramp on the gas the very moment the light changed. "Excuse me for one moment." The man said, exiting the car and leaving the passenger door open. I turned and watched as he approached the vehicle behind us, and the driver got out to confront him. As quick as that it was over. A flash of steel illuminated beneath the street light, a splash of crimson hitting the windshield, as my passenger quickly and efficiently slashed the driver's throat. The motorist fell to the pavement in a heap, as the hitcher calmly walked back to the side of the car. "You didn't leave." He said, wiping the blade of his finely honed knife with a strip of cloth. "We're not at the train yard yet." I replied, a slight thrill running through me. The man stared at me for a long moment, before concealing the blade in his sleeve once again and climbing back into my passenger seat. Somehow he had managed to avoid getting even a drop of blood on his clothes, which was no easy feat, and spoke volumes to me about my passenger. "I can not stand rude motorists." He said nonchalantly, sniffing at the scent of the poison on his sleeves. "They're just the worst, aren't they?" I replied with a genuine smile, thinking for the first time that I might have finally found a kindred spirit in my travels. "What's waiting for us at the train yard?" "I'm not sure. No doubt there will be someone there."

The permit weighed heavy in my pocket as I approached the apartment building. The gun rested painfully on my hip under my jacket. I took the steps up to the fourth floor one at a time. Looking down as if to inspect each step before ascending the next one. My mind raced through my past against my will. I remember every moment with her, and every agony without her. She was the one. Period. That was it. There was no one like her. No one who could ever replace her. She was so perfect. So beautiful. So kind and caring. She actually saw me as a person rather than something to be pushed aside or avoided. No one had ever treated me like she did. And no one had ever hurt me like she did. " I'm sorry, it just isn't going to work. I like you a lot. But more like a brother. I still want to be friends. I hope you understand. " The words echoed in my ears as I approached her door. The revolver cleared its holster and the hammer slammed back into position. I raised it to eye level, lifting my hand to knock on her door. She wouldn't feel a thing, she deserved that at least. And then a thought struck me. It hadn't been that she didn't like me at all. It had been that she liked someone else. Frantically my mind covered all the possibilities. All the potential " targets. " I stood frozen on her doormate. Arm and gun raised. Prepared for an action that I could no longer complete. It hadn't been her at all. It wasn't her fault that she was more attracted to other guys. It had been me. It was always me. I was because I wasn't good enough. And if I wasn't good enough right now, I never would be. The permit nearly rips as I yank it out of my pocket. Scanning it quickly I find the section that I need. The section on specifying who you want to kill and why. As I suspected, there is a loophole in this situation of love lost. ... BANG!! The sound echoes through my apartment. I spring to my feet, spilling noodles all over the floor. I run to the door to see what created the sound. The peep hole is covered by some kind of red paint. I listen for a moment more. Then, hearing nothing, I open the door slowly and peek out. The destroyed face of a young man falls into the room as I open the door. His head little more than a massive red hole. Viscera and gore splash over the carpet. Bile and vomit fills my mouth as I run for the phone to call 911. I scream into the receiver, " a man just shot himself on my doorstep! " My heart slams against my chest as I look at the body from down the hall. I see the permit clutched in his hand, and know that he was here for me. But even as I recognize him, I realized that I have only spoken to him twice.

The great censoring of 2070 removed former large websites and their history, replacing them with new goverment controlled websites. "We shared things called memes, which were pictures with weird texts and jokes and references only a few weird people would understand. The frog was one of them. I believe we called him Peep? Or Pepe? It's been a while. "I slowly reach for my wallet, a brown leather one. It had aged a lot. Most people didn't carry around wallets anymore, ever since all our information became digital. "Blinking in suprise, I let out a hearty chuckle and nodded. "It sure did. It sure fucking did. "

The pain was intense as I pulled into the drive. I could hear every part of my body begging for release. My hair clung to my forehead on a bed of sweat. In that moment I doubted I would make it. I had a few meters of path and the stairs to the front door to go, and now my body was screaming at me; my eyes were obstructed by a torrent of sweat. I got to the door; I'd left my keys in the car. I fell to my knees and let go a scream; a scream of mercy to my vicious bowels. This would not happen to me. I would not be another victim. I felt something in me stir, other than the churning of my stomach. The door would open for me. No locks. Nolocks.

It's the future. Okay, it's the present, but it seems like the future. It doesn't help that we slap the label on everything these days, and the line's a little more blurry than it used to be anyway. There's the Future Research Corporation, which started the trend. They're the number one discoverers of new technologies, as you'd expect. The other "Future" companies are similarly placed in their fields. We even have a "Future" branch of government. We probably have several, but only one is public: the Bureau of Future Crimes. No, they don't plot crimes. They send out the notifications. I got mine in the mail today. It's polite. Not a form letter, but still impersonal. They tell me to contact my next of kin to ensure everything is taken care of. They mention her by name. It seems vaguely threatening, but I know she hasn't received a letter. I can be thankful for that much. I contemplate running. I imagine myself on a beach on some sunny island where this sort of thing doesn't happen, where you can remain blissfully ignorant right up until the moment the locals murder you and steal from your fresh corpse. Sounds like paradise, right? But you can't run. It just doesn't work. I look through the rest of the package. I know what I'm going to find. The route plan. This is how I'm going to die: in traffic heading over the South Bridge, the one that leads out of the city. There's a time and a method. It says it's a gunshot to the head three hours from now. At least I won't have to pack a lunch. There's other things in the package. Forms to sign for listing my preferred method of burial, whether I want to donate my organs, a place to attach my will. Standard death stuff, with all the convenience that being alive grants. The last note in the package is the big one. It tells me that the cost of any reality correction events will be deducted from the value of my estate. I want to tempt fate. Maybe I'll leave the city from the North, instead. Let's see how reality corrects that! Except bigger corrections have happened. They usually make the news. And afterwards the family is destitute because of the selfishness of that doomed bastard. It doesn't feel so selfish from where I'm sitting. I get dressed in my nicest suit. I go out and have a coffee at my favourite joint, the one with the cute waitress. She gives me her number again. I hand it back. I'm a married man. The clock's running down now. I feel trapped, like the walls are slowly closing in on me. The sky is as clear and inviting as it's ever been but I still feel its weight upon my shoulders. If I want to make my appointment I have to leave now. So I do. As I drive I hit every green light. Ah, that's a few corrections there. Sorry, honey, I should have been more prompt. Still we're well off enough that it won't matter too much. I just know how much you hate wastefulness. There's the bridge. I look at the time. Just over a minute to go. I panic. I slam my foot on the accelerator. The car's engine dies instantly. I can't quite tell, but I think it stops on the exact spot the route plan specified. As if it could happen any other way. I see my wife. She's in the next car over, stopped as well. She hops out of her car and into mine. My blood is pounding in my ears and I can't hear anything, but I can read her lips. It seems like she's speaking in slow motion. "I'm leaving you." And then I see the gun. Fucking psychics.

Some hailed the first successful animal reanimation as "the culmination of mankind's collective labor." Others simply called it necromancy. The debate between scientists and philosophers bled into the public domain and engulfed society in such a polarizing chaos that human trials were delayed by nearly two decades. Almost twenty years of supporters and activists and terrorists all claiming they had the right answer (and often fighting to prove so). But it only took a few moments for the technicians to induce consciousness when they brought me back- no longer than it would take to wake me up on any other day..... just as if someone had pulled the covers off. I can still see the changing looks in their eyes. Hopeful and curious and scared; then complete horror as my body began to move. But I was just as much a witness to the terror as anyone. My consciousness had returned, but its vessel was no longer mine. The body began scanning the room, person-to-person, like a starving mad butcher- every few seconds erupting into a fit of crazed laughter, driving many onlookers to hide their faces. I wanted to hide too. I wanted to run and latch on to another soul like mine. I wanted to shout, "Oh God! Oh God! We're not alone! We're not even in control!" But, how do spirits communicate? No, I waited until the body discovered me inside and mounted my mind and preyed on its warmth.

Sitting on the bridge of the StarShip Hope I watched as one by one the stars around me blossomed into light and began to buffet the craft back and forth as the shockwaves, travelling at the speed of light, began to twist and warp the ship. It was hopeless, the sky a solid white and each wave rolling over us more and more powerfully and as I watched on the cameras, first one and then both of the huge engines were ripped from the ship and tumbled into nothing. We were wrong. The scientists had known that something was coming but we had been too egotistical, assuming that the tears in space-time were a local phenonema, that if we could just get away, to find a new home, that we could ride this out, but we were wrong, they all were wrong. Six billion pods behind me contained the frozen remains of earth and for the briefest moment I considered waking them, but it would only be seconds now until the vast forces at work shredded us like a bug. Supernovas, well, it was one of the guesses they had made about what would happen, but their guess was that it would be just Sol. From what I could see it was every star, the entire Universe was ripping itself apart and I was here to see the end of it all. I wondered if they had really thought that or if this whole exercise had been one to keep us busy in the final years as we counted down and watched the rips grow bigger and stronger. I was lucky, I'd drawn the straw to guide us, all by myself with the computer and now I was the only human who would see the end coming. We'd brought only the bare minimum, but I had smuggled aboard a cigar; I'd hoped to light on a new planet, but that wasn't going to happen. Now, as the end came near I popped it in my mouth, nothing to light it with but as a goodbye to existence and a hello to what came next. We'd all hoped we'd have more time, that this massive gamble would pay off, but it hadn't, this was the end and...

The severance packages aren't as generous in Hell as they are here." "Well, I'm sure the current situation can't last forever. The boss can't be very happy about it." "Perhaps, but to be honest, I'm getting a bit weary of the death business anyway." "At the moment, we have only entry level positions available." "I like working with my hands." " I don't know. " They were honest words- words that left my mouth desperately following the question and the eternity of silence. No- I wasn't stupid. They were words that I knew wouldn't be accepted. The courtroom was a pixilated rainbow. Sprites of various neon hues, meant to stand out against different, darker backgrounds, were jammed next to each other at random in the stadium. Looking at them all made my eyes hurt, so I looked down. Their eyes on me made my heart hurt, so I trembled. Boos echoed from the stand at this sign of guilt. The judge- Angra Mainyu, the dragon-king who preceded over the military, the senate, and the courts, allowed it to continue. He knew they weren't in a hurry. He allowed me to suffer. Then, if only to save his own, monster-sized ears and those of the jurors, the strike of his gable finally put an end to it. For now, at least. " Order- order in the court! The prosecution may continue... " " Thank you, your honor, " said a sleek, tuxedoed lizard named Afzal. His oversized, lambent-green body towered over me and most of the jurors in the front rows. Every vowel sound he made sounded choppy in some implacable, metallic accent, like he used tuning forks for toothpicks. For this reason, he had no speaking roles in his boss-fight level. His sheer presence was intimidating enough. " Now, Doppelganger Number 8A-277, " Afzal continued. More booing consumed the court, and he raised his horrible voice over them, " How else do you explain these incriminating circumstances?! " He turned his body 90 degrees to face the expansive jury, casting his shadow over my defense attorney and me. " That villain...that terrorist had not been seen in approximately three months, three days, twenty hours, eight minutes, and fifty one seconds. Are we to believe that, out of nowhere, that menace to our kind returned and not only completed the first five levels with unheard casualties, but also managed to find, operate, and successfully use our hidden, experimental powers up, our reality-breaking glitches, and our top secret warp zones? " He let a silence fill the court, only broken by the tittering mumbles of the braver jurors. " No! " Afzal said finally. " The horrible man from not even Angra Mainyu knows where had to have inside assistance! " " Objection! " my defense rose up. She was a blackbird: an air ally and one of the only monochrome characters in the world. Her voice had a twitter to it, and I much enjoyed it to Afzal's. " The prosecution engages in argumentative questions, which he himself answers. " " Sustained! " agreed Angra Mainyu. " Please, the prosecution must rephrase the question or move on... " " Alright... " Afzal turned back to me. " Doppelganger Number 8A-277...did you or did you not engage in treasonous acts and first-degree, intentional, and premeditated murder?! " " no, " a frightened voice answered. Only after the sound had dissipated, I realized it had been my own. " Did you or did you not leave your post during the invasion? " " no. " " Where were you? " " Buh-between the two cement pipes, patrolling left and right. As I was trained. " " Did you, or did you not, voluntarily let the invader through? " " I- " I stumbled, " He got through, but he was going very fast... " " Did you or did you not allow him through? " " No, I- " " Did he get through because of your own faults and culpabilities?! " " ...yes. " Afzal smiled- I didn't know the lizard allies could smile. " Then, " he continued, speaking to no one in particular, " is it so much of a leap to assume this was purposeful? " He turned to me, eagerly expecting an answer. " I didn't mean to- " " Is it not possible...? " " I would never endanger my comra- " " But you did let him through? " " Yes. " " And you did let him go on- presumably to slaughter your fellow comrades? " " ...yes. " " ...The prosecution rests its case! " The rest of the trial drove on. Too soon, I saw the judge sit up. He was speaking now- " The jury may confer..... " He exited. The rainbow before me dissipated. Sitting in the echoing, empty chamber, I tried to stop shaking. Afzal began organizing his papers in a small briefcase. My Defense Attorney patted my back. We had tried. There, together, was silence. Slowly, those jurors began to fill the room. And slowly, there, a rainbow was painted in the seats. They chattered among themselves. Finally, Angra Mainyu reentered. With that, a well-dressed turtle stood. " We the jury find the defendant, Doppelganger Number 8A-277, not guilty on the charge of first-degree murder. " said the turtle. " However, we find Doppelganger Number 8A-277 guilty of the lesser charges of culpable murder and negligent, militant treason. " My head hit the desk in front of me, and I glued it there. I'd never cried in public anymore- I'd never even been around this many people. But it didn't matter anymore. Angra Mainyu spoke thus, " Very well. Doppelganger Number 8A-277, I sentence you to the mandatory sentence for this thing you have done- and that is death. You will be detained indefinitely in maximum security. And may I have mercy on your soul. "

Now we're the boogymen, the nightmare that you fear, the danger nobody wants to face..... We're the terror of the universe, and for what, because we genocided a few worlds. Our price is very simple, let us loose, and you'll get everything you dreamed. We'll give you lasers, we'll give you nukes, we'll give you AM weaponry that really fucking rocks. "You really do keep in shape huh?" The nonchalant tone in that squeaky voice of my 60 year-old sister-in-law irritated me to no end. Her once beautiful features had been eroded by now, parting for the trenches that lined her face in the form of wrinkles. The web that seemed to restrict her eyes only served to make her seem more friendly in that old age though. Of course, to such a direct and awkward question, the only approach is to smile, nod and move on, and that was what I did for I myself had much to suspect in that regard. It wasn't just that I had aged well or anything. It was more like I hadn't aged. 70 years old, in the golden years of my life and yet I barely looked a day over 20. Truth be told, it creeps me out. My wife Layla's honey-glazed eyes flickered brightly even in the well-lit living room. They glanced over me, burned into my very soul, and all I could think of was their beauty. They had mesmerised me back in my youth, and continued to do so even in my "old" age. They creased into a smooth smile, her eyes forming thin lines that seemed to accentuate her features. She may not have aged as well as I had, but her everlasting beauty shone through even so. I walked over to her and sat by her side, feeling the gentle warmth that she always seemed to emit. Life felt good. - A year had barely gone by, and yet fate turned its gears in the cruelest of ways. I should have expected that love alone could not overcome the ever-looming threat of death. It had been so sudden. She..... she had died staring into the night sky, her petite body snugged comfortably into my embrace. Even if my arm died every time I let her do so, it brought me a certain peace and calm to let her do so. The nights without her were tough, were long, were an eternity. Where was the bright woman who always cheered me up? Where was the comedian who loved me with all the passion of a thousand suns? Questions, questions. They crept, snuck themselves into every facet of my thoughts, as I began to be plagued by my own seeming youth. Just as shadows sneak their tendrils into the corners of the light, so too did these questions begin to invade my very waking moments. - It must have been startling, seeing a 170 year old man look 20. His empty eyes betrayed no emotion behind them beyond a certain weariness, a despair that welled itself deep enough within his pupils, his consciousness that there was a sense of being unable to salvage the situation. A deep, brooding silence hung itself around him like an ever-tightening noose and yet his breath did not halt. His breath never ceased its steady pace, but it always seemed to desire a break. This was not a man who was satisfied with life. This was simply the impatient patience of a mortal man condemned to immortality, to a life without the quiet sanctuary of death.
