"Clarissa!" he yelled hoarsely but she didn't hear, "Clarissa" he repeated, voice straining, but it was useless. Everything was changing again. John hurried forwards through the street trying to focus on the retreating figure. New York looked just as he'd remembered only the colours were just off, a little too bright giving it all a surreal edge. Central park looked beautiful in the autumn sun though he barely had time to register it all as he followed her into it. His heart was in his throat and though he could never physically tire any more, he'd found the dreaming was wearing on him mentally and if he didn't focus hard enough he'd be lost in the shared psychosphere like an errant thought eternally adrift. The sky was loosing it's definition. Orange sunset was morphing into swells of rainbow starbursts that reminded him of the Arctic lights that..... he was cold and it was night and he fell ungraciously in a heap amongst the snow-drifts. John coughed and raised himself slowly, feeling the chill bite of the winds and fumbled for his torch. It was so dark out here and the others would be waiting for him, overhead the northern lights played a magnificent display of colour..... of colour that..... John stared at his hands. This wasn't right was it? He could hear the others calling to him to hurry up, they were going to lose the race if he didn't- His left hand was gloveless. He stared at it feeling terribly confused but felt his eyes focus on one thing, a symbol, a twisted circle, the symbol of infinity tattooed to his thumb that- "Clarissa" he mumbled, remembering. The snow around him started to melt away, dissolving and morphing. Clarissa. Focus. When he opened his eyes he was in the park again. Focus John begged himself, to let his mind wonder would mean losing her again and his heart ached so very much. Standing up he found himself next to a small pond and saw the figure sitting on the bench, soaking up the sun. She had her eyes closed and for a moment he admired that perfectly sculpted face as beautiful as he'd ever imagined. He settled into the seat slowly and watched her eyes fling open, those emeralds shining at him happily as she leant over and gave him a peck then hugged him. He savoured the embrace and, despite himself, cried. She pulled back in alarm. "What's the matter" she asked, "I've been waiting for your for aaaages" she said with a confused laugh. John looked around, remembering this day, and he laughed too, wiping away his tears. "I know" he replied, "I was looking for you for a long time."

"Jeff, my child, you've certainly earned your place among the stars." God said "I wasn't even a good Christian though." Jeff responded. "Christ? Yeah he was ok. Kind of melodramatic, but he was entertaining nevertheless. Yeah he's here, he told me to say hi." God recollected. "Are you telling me our place is determined by our entertainment value to you?" Jeff asked bewildered. "Ah'huh." God responded laughingly. "You certainly gave me plenty of laughs. Remember the time you brushed your teeth with the hemorrhoid cream? How does someone not taste as distinct lack of mint?" "It was early in the morning and I was running late. I just figured why start over?" Jeff explained innocently as laughter echoed in the distance. "That is the Jeff we have all come to know and love." God reassured. "Wait a minute,'We'!? Who else has been watching me?" Jeff asked in astonishment. "Why, everyone who has ever passed onto this realm, of course. Everyone you've ever known or loved." God continued. "You've been the star of the show up here for quite some time now." "Did my grandmother see me forget her first name at her funeral!?" Jeff inquired anxiously. "Bernice!? How does someone forget a name like Bernice!?" God laughingly jabbed, "Yeah she saw it. She thought it was cute you only ever knew her as Grandma. That was a pretty good episode." Jeff thought a moment before coming to a realization, "So my life has been broadcasted up here in the form of what, like some kind of TV sitcom!?" "The Jeff show has been quite a hit!" A large hand emerged from the white fluffy clouds and with a single wave an old style television set appeared and on it played a 90's sitcom style intro filled with clips of Jeff's past. A tune centered around the show's name "That's Jeff" played over one embarrassing moment after another. Jeff watched the clips play while standing still, mortified at the prospect of being a celebrity for his lifetime of embarrassing mishaps. "This..... This can't be happening." Jeff muttered to himself. Clip after clip of moments played on the set, many of which Jeff had not cared to remember for many years. The time he locked himself out of his car as he was changing into his swimsuit, leaving him naked from the waste down at the lake and forced to ask campers for assistance. The jerk-sock he buried in the backyard out of shame only for his dog Chester to dig back up and bring to the dinner table, triggering an investigation by the missing-persons department complete with DNA test. They had even highlighted his accidental flatulence during a recent dentist visit. The show was comprised of all of Jeff's most embarrassing moments, but nevertheless, the production value was still very good quality. "You've been giving us laughs for years, and in this horrible miserable rotten universe I created, laughter is the most valuable commodity ever." God explained. Jeff started to look on the bright side, "I guess it's not so bad. I'm a celebrity in heaven!" Laughter echoed in the distance and God's laugh boomed all around. "Heaven!? This isn't heaven."

"Are you ready darling?" Carolines mother carefully consuls her daughter just hours before the wedding. "I'm ready take them off" Caroline assured her mother as she slowly began to unravel the bandages covering her eyes. The bandages are completely removed and for the first few moments she simply sat there in quiet, until finally giving her mother a passionate enraptured hug with tears in her eyes. "So where's Steve?" She asks wiping a tear away, "I'd love to see him." Her mother looked hesitant but finally said "Honey Steve's right outside but are you sure you want to see him?" "What do you mean?" Caroline asks stunned at her mothers atitude. "Well you know how he went to Iraq and well dear he had a pretty rough encounter and well..... he's not the easiest on the eyes do you understand?" "Momma let him come in." Her mother quietly stepped out and complied with her daughters wishes. Steve walked in with a furrowed brow and the look of overwhelming anxiety on his half burnt face. Finally he stood face to face with Caroline and managed a half smile and after an awkward pause a very subdued "hello darling." Caroline didn't see his two missing fingers. She saw the long afternoons with her arms around Steve strolling the park. She didn't see the burns over the left side of his face but the moments when Steve had her next to his chest sharing insights into eachothers character. Any reservations she had about the man in front of her disappered as she heard the familiar cadence of his voice. She stepped forward and embraced the man she saw only as her husband.

The statue was something of heated debate among our panel of scientists, archeologists, and anthropologists that had accompanied our expedition. It was decided that this discovery was to be kept a tightly held secret from the public, so as to control any hysteria that might arise from this "monumental" finding. The ears and the eyes were all but gone, having been eroded away. Upon further examination, the statue though in very bad shape, resembled every sense of a modern cro-magnon, from the domed head and the proportion of limbs to the body. How a statue found itself 8 billion light years from Earth is incredibly mind boggling however. The material appears to be of the new unique metal found on this world which has been durable enough to survive the countless sandstorms, and it's dating exceeds the limit of our sensors, indicating that it would have to be at least 4.5 billion years old or older. The statue was but one of many. More were found scattered all across the dusty desert world, many housed in what seemed like gigantic underground tombs. Like the first, they were of similar human features, all bearing the same sword and shield. From what our panel could deduce, these statues were obviously built in reverence, but the lack of any recorded contact of humanity and these so called artists has proved to give our team only more questions Not only are there statues, but massive looming spires made of an incredibly durable black stone which extend all the way up into the upper mesosphere. They appear to have been covered in carvings at one point, but they have evidently all but faded now. . Who was this civilization that built these monuments? What happened to them? And what happened to us so many eons ago? Finally, after 3 weeks of constant searching and head-scratching we came upon a solid answer. On the 23rd day of our search, our buggies came across an impossibly massive structure that loomed over the grey sand that covered this world. This structure was different from the elegant spires and statues that littered the planet, this one was short, squat, and almost arachnid in style. Upon entering the structure, a deep chill took all of us, and we wandered through the looming tunnels of the structure. We shined the light on the walls and saw that they bore carvings in a yet undiscovered language. The incredibly intact carvings showed that this world was actually once covered in a diverse set of biomes with an equally diverse amount of fauna and flora at one point. Mountains, deserts, forests, and plains were among the settings discovered. Creatures that were yet unknown to mankind many were humanoid in shape were also depicted. Some were elegant, others were short and squat. As we examined these pictographs further, it was evident that a type of black shadowy creature began to show up on the carvings. Unlike the other creatures, these new shadowy ones were obviously predatory, bearing a wide variety of claws and spines. The next panel showed a massive almost piglike monster towering over all these shadowy beings, and to the right of them depicted a mound of corpses of these creatures from before. The shadowy creatures now bore a wide variety of wicked weapons now, such as pitchforks, scythes, and hammers. It was evident that this hoglike monster was the leader of these shadowy monsters, judging from his size and presence in the carvings. The next several panels featured scenes of widespread destruction and chaos. Burning cities and farms, as well as countless bodies, all the while presided over by the shadow monsters and the giant pig-thing. Finally there came an image of what appeared to be a fortress surrounded by the shadow monsters and their giant leader, who seemed poised to strike down the seemingly pitiful fortification. We all concluded that whatever led to this planet being in the state it was in right now, was because of these shadow things. Yet on the next panel, it showed a lone man standing against the horde of black monsters and their leader, a young man who bore a sword and a shield just like the statue we had discovered. Alone he appeared to turn back the waves of monsters in the now heroic carvings with his sword. In the final panel the man was depicted standing over in triumph over the slain giant pig monster. The same man from the statue, only this time, the carvings showed that this man was clad in green. The next hundred panels depicted the same theme, the rise of these monsters and their eventually casting down by this heroic figure, all the way down until the end, where the last panel at the end of the tunnel unlike the many others from before simply ended in pitch black darkness.

"We mean you no harm spirit." Josiah's lips turn up slightly hearing the slightly obese man yell from the foyer. "Spirit? This could be fun." Josiah had originally come here much earlier to see what he could take from the Arbuckle's while they were away, but this could be fun. He knew the house well having been a guest there in his youth, well, earlier youth. Josiah took out a marble. He used these often to distract people. Robbing these local homes never required much effort for him. The only requirement was that he be quick. So as soon as he let the marble go to roll down the stairs he moved. By the time the marble hit the last stair he was already in the room next to the foyer. The ghost hunters distracted, pointed their cameras at the marble falling down the top of the stairs. Meanwhile Josiah grabbed the bellows from the fireplace, and aimed at the oldest one. A guest of air gently hit her neck. "He's here. I felt him. Are you sure about this?" She said softly with a worried sound in her voice. Josiah struggled hard not to laugh. He had his marble. He threw it so it banked off a wall. That got them to think it came from elsewhere. With their backs turned Josiah moved with speed to the room across from him. Looking for new mischief he saw the radio and turned it on.Appropriately Micheal Jackson's thriller echoed throughout the house. Josiah climbed up a bookcase, through a hole in the floor to arrive in the study. He peered down to watch the ghost hunters. They surrounded the radio. "It's unpluged." One of the others pointed out. "I don't know if I can do this." The older one said as she backed toward the door. Josiah smiled, he hadn't noticed the radio had battery power, but it was a good turn of events. He was starting to drive these people out of their minds. He knew they never ran into a real ghost before so this must be a jolt for them. Josiah started wandering the rooms upstairs looking for what he could do next. He reached the study. He never liked this room. Of course he didn't believe in ghosts, but he felt if any room in the house was haunted it was this one. Glancing at the desk he remembered Mr. Arbuckle cleaning his gun on the desk. It scared him as a kid. Josiah put his hands on his knees and took a deep breath. The room started to shake. Books fell. An earthquake shook the house. Faintly he heard someone yell from elsewhere, "He's upstairs." Josiah didn't want to be caught, but he needed help. The big man crowned the stairs and turned towards the study. "Can we help you?" Josiah wanted to run but had nowhere to go. "Josiah we want to help you." He bent down a little. Looking straight at the boy. The quake started subsiding. Josiah was shocked, enough so that he was no longer having a panic attack. He moved past the door took a glance at the banister that had rotted away. "How do you know my name?" "Josiah you can move on now there is no reason to stay." "I'm not a ghost. I was just playing a prank on you." "Josiah what year is it?" "I don't..." "How are your parents? Are they well? Did you see them yesterday, last week?" The man started asking rather pointed questions. "Of course, I mean they are well, I think." "Josiah you need to accept this. You are in pain, but you can leave now." "I'm not dead" "No, not dead, just passed on." The man said with much sympathy in his voice. The others filmed the interaction, but the elder woman, she, put her hand on the banister as reaches top of the stairs. "You have suffered enough you may leave now. I forgive you." Josiah just stared at his hands, crying, he couldn't even see them through the tears. These people were scarring him now. "Josiah remember. I am Mrs.Arbukle." Josiah was surprised. She looked so old. "You struggled with my husband for a gun. Shot him and then fell through the railing in the confusion that followed. It's alright now. He has moved on and so should you." Josiah struggled to find the words. "Are you sure?" The lady simply nodded. Josiah smiled and disappeared in a small flash of light. "Thanks for everything." The lady appeared very relaxed now. The big man held out his hand for Mrs. Arbuckle as they walk down the stairs. "I am just happy I can help the spirits find rest."

Jenny calmly put down the knife after slicing her finger. She stared at the cabbage, wanting to pick up the knife and stab it. But something wasn't right. Her finger stung, but not a drop of blood dripped out. Yet she could see that the cut was quite deep - nearly a centimeter of skin jutted out. As she slowly pulled the skin back to take a peak, she gasped. Something disgusting was there! It looked like a worm. She nearly fainted. Flailing her hand back and forth she yelled, "Get it off! Get it off!" With an inhuman cringe, and her hand stretched as far from her as possible, she shuffled towards the sink, collapsing on it. Icy cool water ran down her finger. With eyes closed she furiously tried to rub away that nasty thing that was crawling out of her finger. But it was rigid and hard. She opened her eyes. It wasn't bone - what was is? She peeled back the skin. Vomit, refusing to be forced down any longer, erupted into the sink. The whole room smelled acidic. The was some sort of wiring inside of her. It was like a bad dream. Please, she prayed, wake up. But she couldn't wait for an answer. She ran towards the table, slapping the infuriating cabbage to the ground and grabbing the knife. Strip by strip, she pealed away at her skin. There was no flesh. No bone. No blood. Only mechanics. She jammed the knife between the wires and tried to pry them apart, but instead the knife bent. She looked at the crooked tip. A sudden influx of memories - if that word even applies - surged through her. Hundreds of years of memories. There had been a great war amongst men. Only onetenth of the human population survived. After using AI to win the war, they decided to destroy the technology. She was one of the few who survived, secretly hiding, ignorant to even her own existence. A sleeper cell that had slumbered for over a hundred years. It was her mission, she and the others who survived, to eradicate the human race. A voice interrupted the flood of data. Water poured over her robotic hand. "Jen! What the Hell are you doing? When's dinner?"

The wind whipping my face. Rain pelting my exposed skin like needles. Blinding light. Searing pain. Voices. Pain. Light. Pain. Darkness. I came to in a small room that looked like a hospital room furnished by an antiques collector. The weird, too clean smell of hospitals mixed with the musky smell of old furniture in a very disorienting way. My entire body was covered in bandages, several IVs in my arm, sensors and monitors attached everywhere. I cautiously tried to sit up, expecting pain, surprised to feel none. "Good, you're awake. How do you feel?" Startled, I whipped my head around to the doorway where a man stood wearing a well tailored suit. Lightning flashed in the windows. "Who are you? What am I doing here?" I started rattling off the usual questions one would ask in my situation, but was quieted with a gesture and a smile. Rain began to patter against the windows. "I'm sorry. How rude of me. I'm Jacob. And you were in an..... accident. But you're safe now. So I'll ask again, how are you feeling?" "I'm..... what happened to me?" The wind outside was picking up, whistling through the drafty windows. "Jaina, please calm down I can explain everything." My palms break out in a sweat and my heart starts to race in my chest. The rain is beating so hard I can't hardly hear myself think. God I hate storms. I wish it'd just stop already. The rain stopped so suddenly my ears rang in the silence. Jacob smiled slightly. I stared at him, wide-eyed and open-mouthed as he explained. "Jaina, you're aware how the Champions get their powers, yes?" He didn't wait for my response before continuing. "And you, my dear, by all rights should be dead." I picked my jaw off of the floor and tried to remember what happened. "I..... I was on a boat. I was on a sailboat. I got caught in a storm. What happened?" Jacob walked acrosd the room to a small bar in the corner and pulled two glasses. "You got the gist of it, really. It's hard to say exactly what happened, but when we found you, you were covered in burns from head to toe, floating in the harbor. I'll let you connect those dots." He handed me a glass, two fingers of what smelled like whiskey. I held my hand up and shook my head. "No thanks, I don't drink." He gave me the look everyone does when they hear that line, then shrugged and poured the contents of my glass into his, then promptly downed it. "Well then, Jaina, I guess the formalities are over with. So, welcome to the Clubhouse, you're our newest Champion." Thunder rumbled outside.

Mitzy and Don take shifts standing vigil outside of Greg's hospital room. They are watching for me. If I approach the room, they will call the hospital staff, who will call security, and I will be roughly escorted out. I know this because they have done this to me five times now. I have been informed that the next time it happens I will be charged with criminal trespassing. Every time I have been escorted from the premises, I have stated my case as calmly and as rationally as is possible when your husband is dying of late-stage leukemia and you are being prevented from seeing him. I reiterate: "He is my husband. I am married to him. I am legally married to him and I have a right to see him." As it turns out, in the state of Georgia, as of this date in 2007, I do not have a right to see him. I know this because I have been told so, repeatedly, by Mitzy and Don, and hospital staff, and security, and a number of attorneys in the tri-county area who I have phoned. Mitzy is all smiles when I try to enter Greg's room. Her rejection of my right to see my dying husband is cast in the charming lilts of southern hospitality. She offers to take me to the hospital cafeteria and have sweet tea with me and discuss God and pray for Greg. A real heart-to-heart. She will even connect me to a therapist in Atlanta who was doing wonders with Greg, when he was a teenager, before college corrupted him. When I try to force my way past her, there is Don, who is not so hospitable. He is 65, but 6'5," and probably something like 650 pounds, all muscle. He is not shy about throwing that weight around, when it comes to keeping me out of Greg's room, and I regret never having worked out regularly. I holler as he wrenches my arm behind my back and forces me to the ground: "Please, for the love of God. I love him. I just want to say goodbye." I just want to say goodbye. So now there is this, plan B: a not so charming kid named Jethro. I mean his name is actually Jethro, if you can believe it, and he looks like a Jethro too. Built like an anemic scarecrow and wearing a hooded sweatshirt in August may as well be wearing a neon sign that says "ask me about my track marks." I need Jethro because everyone on staff at the hospital knows my face and knows to be on watch for me. I need a confederate they don't recognize. So for the low price of 500, Jethro will don some scrubs he has stolen during one of his many ER visits, dose Don and Mitzy's midnight coffees with a sedative, and spirit Greg out of his hospital room. At 12:15 AM in a fetid alley adjoining Mercy General, I stand over Greg's gurney, crying like the world is ending, because in some sense it is, and this hick Jethro is the only witness to the last kiss I will ever share with my husband. Jethro jabs a needle into Greg's thigh. I can barely manage "what the f before Greg is awake, fully conscious, gasping from a sudden rush of pain and adrenaline. "Epi," Jethro says, and wipes his nose with the back of his palm. His skittish eyes are searching everywhere for nothing. "Thought you might'n wan na say somethin'. He'll be fine." "Are you okay?" I say, cradling Greg's face. His eyes bulge, his jaw sets, and he nods. He brings his breathing back under control. the fuck am I?" he breathes. "I had to get you away from those bitches you call your parents." His eyes roll and he swallows hard, trying to cope with the pain. He looks back at me. "I told them to let you in if you came. I told them." "I know you did." Jethro is taking this moment to piss against the alley wall. "Who the hell Greg says, noticing Jethro for the first time. "I hired him. He brought you out of your room." "Jesus, who did you get mixed up with?" "Listen," I say, "I don't have a lot of time. I need to tell you." I clasp his fingers in mine, but he breaks the grip. His bony hand strokes the cut on my cheek, the deep black bruise there. "Who beat you?" "You know who beat me. Don always hated me." Greg closes his eyes, mortified. I take his hands again. There's nothing to them anymore, none of the strength I used to love. "You're so bald," I say, laughing. I rub his head. "It's called chemo. You should try it sometime. Bald is sexy again." "Just what a baldy like you would say." "The weight loss is incredible, too. I'm never doing Atkins again." Jethro zips up, loudly. I bow my head and sigh. "I need to tell you," I repeat. "What I said in Boston, I didn't mean it. I didn't mean any of it." "I shouldn't have left," he says. "I shouldn't have let you go. I mean, Christ, we almost died just trying to get there in the first place. We finally got free of this stupid hick town. And I let it all fall to shit. I'm so selfish. I'm so stupid. I'm so "Shut up," Greg says. He opens his eyes. Bright teeth and warm smile. "You always get like this." "I love you." "I love you, too." "Uh," Jethro says. I turn. He's pointing down the alley at a police officer who is approaching us, his car parked at the alley's mouth, red-and-blues on. Jethro flees. For someone so frail looking, his ability to vault a 10-foot brick wall is impressive. I don't flee. I smile down at Greg. "I'll see you again," I say. "You better. I'll be waiting."

"Huh?" His acquaintance answered. "I'm crazy but I want out," he replied. "Don't we all?" "I..... huh?" "You think you're special? Do you really believe that you're one of the special few who are in this valley? Do you think yours is the only valley? Have you no thought to the mountains, the islands, the marshes, the steppes? Do you think people are happy with the kleptocracy? Do you think we're blind to the poisons and pollution, the wearing down of the lands? This clearing is not unique. I often wonder how many geniuses really exist. Look around you, next time you're out in public. People everywhere, streaming by, bustling about on the worthless minutiae of their everyday lives. No one challenges them. There's no dire, life or death need. Their requirements for survival are filled, they busy themselves with the tiny, unimportant, trivial details. They possess no roaring storm to transform their tiny flame of genius into a roaring inferno. So instead, that little flame gutters and eventually extinguishes itself. I look around at these others with dismay, sadness, because I used to be like them. Once, all my needs were met. I lived a happy life, relatively speaking. I worked at a good job, owned a good little house with a good little mortgage that slowly disappeared from good little payments, and celebrated every Friday with my good little friends. It all went well - up until the medical appointment. Just a lump. Just taking samples. Just a standard assessment by the lab. Just standard cancer, likely to respond favorably to treatment. Hah. Just another little flame, slowly burning itself into nothingness. I knew, however, from that first appointment. I wasn't going to have the happy ending, the triumphant little picture of me, a scarf covering my head, grinning and holding up my fist in victory. For the first time in my existence, I found myself staring at my own mortality. And faced with that chasm, the little flame inside of me sprang into life. I needed to beat this cancer, win the war of attrition against my own cells, but I knew that I couldn't rest easy after a win. Every single cell in my body held a ticking time bomb, threatening to go rogue and take me out in a suicide attack. I could fight them off, but not all of them. Not forever. I needed to escape. I turned to the wealth of humanity's knowledge, alternating my binges between the library and the internet. I crammed my brain full, as many facts as it could hold, and then pushed in still more. I read until my eyes burned, and listened to lectures and recordings until my ears were deafened. I spent my nest egg - what use would I have for it otherwise - and built myself a laboratory, a workshop, a forge. And I reforged myself. Milled aluminum and titanium struts, lightweight and strong. Banded polymer muscles, designed to contract when stimulated by implanted electrodes. Silicon relays, connected to selectively permeable sensory membranes to pick up on neurotransmitter signal fluctuations. I started with an arm. I ran as many tests as I could, but eventually, I had to go under the knife. I paid a man, a former surgeon, a man fallen on hard times. He saw my burning flame, perhaps sensed the heat of my potential. I instructed him, made him repeat it all back, did my best to teach him what he needed to know before he put me to sleep with the carefully calculated dose of anesthesia. I woke up, opened my eyes. I didn't turn my head. I felt for my arm, both arms. Slowly, first one and then the other, I lifted them up. My left arm looked flabby, sad, spotted with moles and imperfections. My right arm gleamed with the promise of a brighter future. I deemed the experiment a qualified success. It responded perfectly, moved smoothly, performed admirably. I soon began work on other limbs, building the body that would hold my future. I'm still working on the brain, however. Motor neurons are replaced by wires leading to intra-polymer electrodes. Sensory neurons are replaced by piezoelectric layered plastic, producing signals in response to pressure feedback. But duplicating the massive tangled web inside my skull will require a more intricate creation. Still, I think to myself as I lean back, watching the movements inside my limbs as they obey my mental commands. Made of organics or metal, I am no tin man, no automaton. I don't need flesh to be human.

" " Tony it has been a month, I don't want you coming back here living on my couch. " " I understand I managed to save up enough money for two months, but I think I can make it last for another if I honestly need to. " " OK, just as long as you don't end up back on my couch, you have an interview today, don't be late, and don't screw it up " " OK I won't. I'll talk to you later mom. Love you, bye. " I get dressed, then I get in my car and head to the interview. I arrive and they call me in there. " Hello Mr. Harris, we saw your job application, and we liked what we saw, although we had a question about your employment history. It say's you have worked at 5 places in the last two years, What is the reason behind all of this. " I explain why and then the interview continues, but now I feel that question alone has lost me the Job. " Well Mr. Harris, thank you for the interview, congratulations you're hired, you start your training as manager here next monday. " " Thank you so much sir " " you're welcome, and oh, by the way Mr. Harris " " yes " " Thank you for helping me and my wife find our child, you looked really familiar when you came in for the interview. " " You're welcome sir. " On my way home I was relieved I now have a job again, I can pay rent, and I have a solid income. But, then I realize, I had never been on time for anything important up until a month ago, and now I'm always on time. Was the curse from the story my grandma told real. No I don't believe so because even though I was late to work, I was on time to help a family find their child. -1st story

My mind twists around the slippery words, trying in vain to grasp, to understand. He's never given me anything. Ain't no such things as a free lunch, that's what he taught me. Ephraim gestures to the narrow, deep basket. "Go on." I take a tentative step forward, but I don't dare reach for the prized sweets. Is it a test? Will he hit me as soon at my fingers touch the wicker handle? Tell me not to take other peoples' things unless I'm willing to fight for it? "I ain't gon na hurt you," he says. His face is placid and warm, a rarity for the old goat, but his eyes are cold, a lattice of angles and black ice. Involuntarily, I cringe away. With a visible effort, he keeps his voice level. "Tessa, dammit, I'm telling you to take the cannoli." "But..... why? They're yours." "And I'm giving them to you," he says, exasperation edging into his words. "For shit's sake, didn't your mama teach you anything?" "Of course she did," I say, blood rising to my cheeks. "But she's been gone for six years, and instead I got you." His gaze hardens, but not in a mean way. Just sad. "I know." Splaying his fingers across the table, he winces, draws a sharp breath, and I swear his mind goes a million miles away. A shaft of late afternoon sunlight falls through the dusty cottage air, splashing across the right half of his face, and something shimmers in the corner of his eye. "I could have been better. I should have been better." Again, his voice slips through my mind like water through a sieve. This is the closest thing to an apology he's ever uttered, at least in my presence. Has he lost it? Has the inevitable breakdown finally arrived? "I've made arrangements he pauses and presses a hand against his chest. "Your aunt lives on the coast. She knows you're coming. You'll have enough food and water, and Rufous for company. You already have a knife. Keep it close. Pack your things, empty the pantry, take the cannoli, leave the gun." In a small voice, I ask, "Are you kicking me out?" His lower lip quivers, and the corner of his mouth pulls back in another pained grimace. "No, Tessa. I'm doing you a favor." A cold thought sends prickling fear across my neck and shoulders. His fingers running in circles over his heart, his wheezing throat, his staggering gait, sharp like broken glass. "It's the thing. The thing in your lungs." "It ain't just my lungs." Ephraim smiles bitterly. "Not anymore." He places a map on the table. A black dot marks our home, and a red line runs across the landscape like an open vein, leading back to the seaside I once called home. But that was a lifetime ago. "Keep to the main roads, since they have a lot of traffic. Lots of people to witness a crime. Don't walk at night. Don't trust anyone." Raising his eyes to mine, he leans close. "Above all, use your brain. I won't be there to protect you." I shake my head and tears blur my vision. "Where will you be?" The chair creaks as he leans back, absentmindedly pressing against his solar plexus. He doesn't look away, and my heart sinks. Softly, he says, "Leave the gun, Tessa."

The first time I noticed a ten was in High School. I never really cared that others could not feel them. I just assumed there was something wrong with my brain. Ever since I became aware of them, I've been trying to understand them. Most people range from one to five, with one being usually people with Down syndrome and the elderly. Most twos and threes are common people you meet every day at most places, from cashiers to truck drivers. People with fours and fives tend to be teachers, store managers, and small business owners. However, every time I see a six, I am almost positive it is a college professor, or some type of academic. The funny thing here is that I can not tell if somebody is more likely to be dangerous like a serial killer, drug dealer, or rapist just by looking at their number. In fact, I once met a three which had been in jail for shop-lifting shoes. My mind is still troubled by this fact. What could these numbers mean? Until I met her, I used to think the higher someone was in the social strata, the higher their number because they had more power and thus were more dangerous because they had the powers to more easily harm somebody. For example, every picture of a president I saw felt like a solid nine and almost all members of congress I saw on TV were eights or nines. This observation explained me why managers tended to be about five or six as opposed to a cashier which could be a two. The managers hold power over somebody. However, when I met her, I was dumbstruck. She was the first ten I ever had the pleasure to meet. More than her beauty, I was attracted to her number. What was so special about her that merited her the number ten? Were my theories wrong? That day I couldn't sleep. My mind kept going over everything I had learned. All the patterns seemed to follow so logically, so orderly. It all made sense without her. The rules were perfect. But she broke them all. I mean, she was not that beautiful. There were girls way more attractive that her, with better bodies, softer voices, and charmer personalities. What is it with this girl? I wondered for many weeks. Now, however, I wish I never had. In fact, I wish I was never born this way. You see, the first time I kissed her, my world collapsed. This girl's number made me wanted to know her, so I did. I started talking to her. I wanted to know her so well because I wanted to pin-point the exact reason for her magical number. But I ended up falling in love. And it was then that I discovered the reason behind her number. As I suspected at first, the numbers represent the potential for danger for a given individual. The more power someone has over you, the more dangerous they are. The piece of the puzzle I was missing though was the fact that this is all relative. You see, this girl was a ten for me, because I'd anything for her. And if I had stayed away from her, none of this would've happen. If I had stick to my theory, I would've realized it was a stupid idea to get close to someone that dangerous. But I didn't. And now I am rotting in this god forsaken place for killing those priests who molested her when she was a child. No wonder they too had a ten.

"You! Yes, you! Give me a story!" they demanded. "A story?" I asked. "Yes! A story!" "But I'm just a run-of-the-mill servant, All Might One. How could I possibly entertain you of all beings? I can barely entertain Writing Prompts redditors..." "Aye! But we the creator, in granting your lot with free will, have lost our ability to live inside your minds. We are curious. We are intrigued. What kind of mighty legends can one such as yourself muster? You are a storyteller, are you not? A wielder of tales? Try one on me!" "Very well..... "Once upon a time there was a mighty God. Their ability to conjure up great sums of creational energy pushed them to create an infinite universe. Within this universe, they exploded hundreds of burning lights, the fire of which lit up the void and sprouted countless masses of independent, living matter. This matter condensed and hardened into an infinite count of planets, moons, and meteors, each new creation wondrous and infinitely special in its own way. "What the God did not expect, was for some of these planets to produce life. And so the cycle of life began, producing cells, aquatic beings, large lizards, stupid bipedal beasts, and other distant creatures some of us will never encounter. All of this amused the God, but also terrified them, for it meant that what he had produced in jest would have to become a serious undertaking. "So they observed from a far, as the dominant beasts of countless unconnected worlds populated their dominions with countless constructions of their own making. Some were impressive, others downright frightened the God. And so they made their first attempt at dismantling creation. "This, however, failed, as creators are never truly able to destroy what they produce. So is the unwritten law of the universe. Therefore, they watched as centuries unfolded, hoping for a time when creation, as it is, would not be so stupid and blundersome. "And though they hoped, this wish seemed impossible, for the beings insisted on demolishing their world, piece by piece, fellow creature by fellow creature. In the end the God grew bored and wandered their universe alone, only interacting when the fancy most suited them." My narrative done, I stood perfectly still. Hoping against hope that the God would not be offended. After a long pause, the God responded: "Hmm..... yes..... I guess that was a horrible story..." "I did warn you! Maybe the next creature you meet will have a better one?" I offered, encouragingly. "I doubt it..." they grumbled, walkingfloatingor cloud swimming away as only Gods can.

God, one of those damn miners was coming. You probably don't know this, but I'm an NPC villager from the popular game, Minecraft. When players visit my town, I offer up 8 cooked chicken in exchange for an emerald. They're probably rotten by now, as nobody has ever wanted my trade. When I'm not trying to rip people off, I hide in a house and hope that the zombies don't knock down my door. Those damn players bring all the trouble. I was arguing with some shop trader from WoW when I got a call. I like to stay up to date with the latest fashion and technologies, but when the player comes, the village elders force us to wear the same stupid getups. "Sorry Ted, I got ta run. Some idiot just took all the torches out of the town and left; zombies will kill us any second." Ted looked horrified. "And-and you're just gon na let'em kill ya and yer family?" I nodded. "Well, goodbye for now. Forever, actually." As I warp back into my blocky homeland, I see zombies tearing apart the flesh of my son and wife. They're almost as unphased as I am, but they make little grunting noises. As two zombies attack me, I emotionlessly let them. I'm not programmed to fight back.

I've had a pretty rough life. Not only am I saying that but my friends believe the same. When I met them I had already gone through several foster homes, too many black eyes and abusive parents on top of an already confusing shuffling of homes in my life. "Maybe this is what life is." I would continually think to myself. "What would it be like to not exist?" I'd ponder the nights when I couldn't sleep from fear of being the object on the other end of a parent's hand. "I could have it worse." I provided as some sort of inspiration far too often. Each arrival in a new foster home I was greeted by new friends and friendly faces, constantly. The foster parents were always the ones I'd want to stay with. Was it not possible to simply stay there? Why not? How could I keep from moving about? No matter how hard I'd try to stay confined to my room or hidden behind the others, they'd seek me out. I could never hide my face. It's as though my silence and lowered gaze meant nothing to them. My foster parents would never understand me or my silence. I have no doubt that soon I'll be taken away from this foster home and placed in another situation where I can continue questioning my life and its purpose. I've tried running away, four times now, and it doesn't work. Seems the parents love me enough to call the police and have a search party locate me immediately. Only then to bring me back home and fall back into the deep trench of abuse and neglect. I'd thought that it'd get better after a display of worry and sadness upon losing me. Never. Now I wait. I wait for a new parent to take me away and..... I'm not sure, treat me differently than all the rest? Maybe even love me. I crept back upon hearing the front door open with its'creek, creek, thud' as it made its way over the jagged floor and impacting into the door stopper that was more of a punching bag for the doors weight. My foster parent called my name and I winced. Today was the day I'd been dreading ever since I'd got here. Here, to the comfort and love of another non-permanent parent. "How would I fair in this new home?" "Could I be treated without abuse, maybe just less abuse?" "When should I stop hoping and give in to the life set before me?" It was all too overwhelming and my head sank as though no words of joy could bring me out of it. No optimism could rest my soul and return me back to a happiness of playing in a field with clean open air, all worries away from me. I sat in the car onward to a new home and a new life without saying a thing. I stayed glued to the window in hopes of being anywhere but in this car. ..... Weeks go by and every morning I wake up, I'm greeted. Each day brings about more joy than I could hope. Every. Single. Night. I'm given hugs. I'm entertained and given attention. I get to run and play. I'm able to express myself. I..... I'm happy. I have never been treated so well. I have no words for my new life. I have only actions and a sore deep in my heart, healing from this blissful type of new living. Never have I been more carefree and excited for each and every new day. My new parent is exceptional. I let him know that I'd love to stay by giving him kisses constantly. By staying next to his side on every walk. By heeding his every word. Sit. Stay. High five. Shake. Speak. Roll Over. And I'm sure more will come but I dare not disobey this new, loving parent. I will do anything to hold on to this life. This beautiful life I don't think I could ever live without. And I have a feeling my new parent couldn't live without me, either.

The man was 120 years old. He was asleep when the demons showed up. Loneliness, a massive blue monster stared at his face. " He looks good for his age. How has he made it to this long anyway? " " We could wake him up and ask him, " Darkness said. His pale eyes glowed in the dark of the room. " What do you think, Silence? " Silence, small and grey, nodded his head. Loneliness reached out a claw and tapped the man. His eyes fluttered open, and he sat up in bed. He fumbled around for the light on his bedside table. With a click, the room was illuminated. He slipped on his glasses and gazed at the demons before him. He blinked, and rubbed his eyes, and blinked again. They certainly seemed to be real demons. " Hello, " he said, jovially. " I'm Archibald. What can I do for you? " Darkness looked at him quizzically. " You're not afraid of us? " Archibald smiled. " Should I be? " " We're demons! We have been sent by death to finally claim you, " Loneliness explained. " But, most people succumb to his clutches without us physically needing to get them. Tell him, Silence. " Silence nodded. " Ah, " Archibald clapped his hands together. " So, the little one is Silence, but who are you? " " I am Loneliness, and the third is Darkness. " Archibald stuck out his hand, and each demon shook it. " Well, it certainly is a pleasure to meet you all. Would you like tea? Or whatever it is demons drink? A brimstone concoction? That may be a challenge..... " " No, sir, we're fine, " said Darkness. " What we want to know is, how have you lived so long? " Archibald let out a hearty laugh. " You know, I often get asked that, " he chuckled. " You said you never physically claim a soul, right? And you work for Death, so I take it you are the embodiments of loneliness, darkness, and silence, correct? " Silence nodded, surprised that this human could catch on so quickly. " Well, " the old man began, " the secret is, I've never succumbed to those things, because I've never had them. " Loneliness looked surprised. " We have gazed upon your past. You sleep alone now, as you always have. And yet you've not been lonely? " " Oh, no. I have many neighbours, and friends, and the ducks down by the pond. I have all the love I could ever want! " Darkness was confused. " But has your life never been cloaked in darkness? " " No, again, my friend! There have been times of uncertainty in my day, where I was unsure of what to do. I was afraid, but no matter how dark the world seemed, I held my head high and was my own torch. " Silence walked up to Archibald's side and poked him, with a quizzical look on his face. Archibald chuckled. " And how could I forget you, Silence? After a long day of work, I relish in the silence. It comforts me. I turn the silence into poems and art and stories! But..... I suppose 120 years is quite a long time for a human to be alive. Your master wants me because my time is up? " Darkness lowered his head. No one had referred to him as a friend before. " Yes..... Archibald. The Master likes to do some..... spring cleaning now and then. Out with the old, in with the new is an expression I believe you should be familiar with. " " Well, if my time is up..... " Archibald murmured. He climbed out of bed and slipped on his fuzzy slippers. " I suppose it is time to make way for the new generation. " He spread his arms out on either side of him. He closed his eyes, and smiled a peaceful, yet sad, smile. " Well then, take me away, boys! This shall truly be a grand adventure. "

I gazed upon its tiny form. How had it broken my defenses? I would need to check my traps. It had been a decade or two since anyone had dared enter my volcanic lair. "I have a proposition for you, oh great and wise..... dragon? ahem..... forgive me, I don't know your name," it stammered. I let the insult pass since the tiny mortal had just contributed to my great horde. And it had peaked my interest after years of slumber. If anything else, I'd be able to have a nice snack before my mid day nap. "My name is not important. What is the reason for your trespass into my domain, mortal?" I lowered my voice to scare the morsel. It quivered and shrank back a step, "Well you see, there is another of your kind that has been terrorizing my people for many months now." "And why is that any of my concern?" I laughed. "Well, we found it's hoard..... I am willing to tell you where it is..." "If I dispatch the beast for you," I finished. "You are truly stupid, aren't you? We are the greatest beings in the world. Do you think me so stupid I don't know that information already?" I bluffed. In my later years I'd lost a bit of the lust for material wealth. The kind of wealth I now searched for was more magical in nature, but this little imp need not know. "Forgive me mighty serpent, but I know for a fact that the other dragon I speak of has also in its possession a glowing orb that the ancient books tell me that all of your kind seek." I paused, knowing about the powerful spheres that granted true eternal life. The expression on the little girl standing in front of me changed. She knew that she had piqued my interest. "Tell me where it is, mortal, and I will dispatch this other wyrm." She opened up her small pack and pulled out a small parchment with a faint glow about it. "Before that, there is only one way to trust you." She replied as she pulled a quill out of her pack. I knew it. A blood pact. This impudent little bitch wanted me to tie my fate to hers in exchange for the location of the orb. She was smarter than she looked. I let out a deep sigh. My twilight was coming, and I didn't wish to part with this world yet. She had me. "Beware the consequences of your magic, little one. A blood pact will forever tie us together. Do you fear that?" "I understand completely, and there is nothing left for me to fear, O mighty dragon. Do you accept my proposition?" The cost was great, but some things are worth risking it all for.

August 1st. The strange thoughts and feelings that I'd get around mom didn't start happening until I was about 12, so right around puberty (I think that detail is important; the psychologist would probably be interested in that). One night I walked into the bathroom to go pee, and mom was in there, mostly naked, doing funny things to herself in her private places. She jumped and moved a nearby towel to cover herself quickly, screaming in the process. I jumped and screamed too, and ran into my room. As I sat there, mom walked in and in a very calm but forced voice reminded me to knock whenever I was entering a room. Before I had thought this was a silly rule because it was just mom, me, and my little brother Sam, who was just a toddler. But at this moment I started to think that maybe some rules were very good rules. But after I went to bed that night, I couldn't stop thinking of the noises mom was making. I had heard her making those noises before, when she had her older man friends over and they would go to the room and do'adult things.' But as I approached the bathroom door that night, I heard her making those sounds so was curious as to why she was doing those without her man friends. This part may sound weird..... but hearing them for the split second while the door was open, I had one of those things call a..... dehza voo? Another weird part: she was saying dad's name. All the times I heard mom making those sounds with her man friends the door was closed, but this time I could hear her and I swear I had heard them before..... in that same, clear, unrelenting way. Along with the parts where she would stop and say dad's name. I think this next part is important too. When we took the train to go and see my dad's family back in San Francisco, I had that same dehza voo feeling as I was getting on the train. My heart beat got faster and I grew very very scared. The important part is, this is the train station where my dad had died. Mom did not tell the story until my last meeting with the psychologist, with me just outside the room but able to hear. She doesn't like to talk about dad, but I can tell she is still very sad sometimes. She told him that suicide was highly unlikely because there was no evidence to indicate that my dad was sad or depressed or wrong in the head. She told him that the newspapers said witnesses said they saw a man in a rush, trying to get to his train before it departed, but getting killed by a service locomotive while trying to cross one of the tracks. My mom was nine months pregnant at the time; he was on a business trip, she told the doctor, looking at moving to a higher position in his company, complete with a raise, better benefits, and lots of other things that sounded to complicated that I can't remember. But this was only a week ago, when she was telling the psychologist the story. I wish she was honest with me, because it feels like it's something dad would have wanted. It feels like dad wouldn't have wanted her to be so sad and seeing so many man friends all the time. But mom always tells me that she has to try and move on in whatever way she can, that she has to keep herself helping me and my brother and helping herself. I know I'm only thirteen, but mom's way of trying to help herself feels very wrong. I think I need to mention this part now, this is the part the psychologist told me to talk about. Last night I heard mom with one of her man friends again, but this man friend has the same name as dad. She kept saying his name over and over again. I don't know what happened to me but I got real horny and sweaty and I had to say mom's name. After it stopped, I started crying real bad but I didn't understand why. Then I had a dream, and I saw that I was holding mom, in my arms. Mom was much younger, and I was much bigger and smarter, I could tell. We were in a big field with lots of grass, a large park. Mom rolled over on top of me, then over me, and then kissed me and said,'You're it!' and ran away. I remember I smiled and got up and chased her all over the park until I finally caught her by the swings. I grabbed her through one of the swings and pulled her in close and I kissed her and then shoved her back, saying,'now you're it!' She laughed as she stumbled back and we continued to run around the park. I remember it was a very happy dream. That is all I have to say about these things for now. Maybe the psychologist will be able to figure something out from them.

The weather on the island was about 50 kinds of shite: Cold, rainy and windy were the first attributes the group noticed when they left the plane and hurried into the relative warmth of the airport. None of them had extra luggage so they immediately made it to the busses. In halting English, the people who lacked tickets rectified that problem with the driver: 3 Sol one way, 5 Sol return trip. Those, who needed sleep caught up on it, assisted by noise cancelling headphones, earplugs or just the superhuman ability to filter out loud, drunk soccer fans. The rest socialized in a loud, inebriated manner. Soon, they were at the stadium and after a lax security check, they could go to their seats. Despite not wanting to let it show, people were anxious: their team had not brought all that many victories home this season, which was why relegation loomed. Having travelled since early morning, the fans of this 6th league club were also somewhat tired. But when the teams entered the pitch, this all was forgotten! The fans cheered for their team, nicknamed the Billy Goats against the team with the Shamrock as a logo, which as a first time participant in this league after a surprising relegation from the 5th league, didn't yet get the honor of having particular chants about them. Even though the hosts had little to gain or lose this late in the season, this middle-of-the-league as they were, they fought valiantly but in the end, in vain: a late goal after a corner brought the Billy Goats ahead. The fans celebrated thus goal as if they had just won the world league. In German, they chanted: "Niemals 7te Liga, nie mehr! Nie mehr!" (Never 7th league, never again, never again!) (As an explanation: The 1. FC Koln is a perennial relegation candidate and a typical yoyo team. And I implied whether against Celtic or against Bayern, they will be a yoyo team)

Foreward: Been playing Stellaris a lot lately, so this was a fun write. Used a couple races I made in that as inspiration. It's been a busy day, so I've had to write sporadically. Hopefully I was still able to make something readable. Wolves Admiral Jenner scratched at the arm of his command chair compulsively, studying the movements of the people below him. The bridge of the U.T.S. Salamis reminded him of what the NASA control center had looked like five years ago, in form if not feature. The rows of monitors and equipment were the same, spread with efficient uniformity before him in the softly lit forum. But all of it had been advanced by a century at the least, courtesy of mankinds' new patrons, the Echysian Polity. Holographic projections, data feeds, and tactical assessment kept operators in a constant state of motion and information analysis. In place of a wall monitor, a view screen took up the entire north wall, floor to ceiling, giving the admiral and his crew a clear and vivid picture of a foreign star system. Otalp, the Echysian representative assigned to the Salamis, stood at Jenner's side, staring quite literally into space. This seemed to be an odd mannerism of the Echysians; they often stared straight ahead, expressionless, as if they were in a constant state of consideration. Even so, Jenner got the sense that his compatriots mind was absent. "Something wrong?" Otalp glanced down at the admiral from his revery. "What's the longest you've been away from home, commander?" He asked, his voice tinted with a strange cooing intonation. Jenner shrugged. "Well, I did a tour in the Second Korean War. I was gone..... I guess, five years altogether. I went on leave though, went back for visits. This assignment is probably the longest consecutive time I've been away." In fact, he'd been commanding the Salamis for nearly two years now, spending most of that time on board in space. He noticed then the fresh rivets he was scratching into the pristine sheen of his arm chair, and tucked his hand by his side. Otalp stared off into the view screen again, his eyes running over the barren, blue surface of a minor planetoid. "I boarded the J'Val over a decade ago as part of the Seventh Defense Fleet, right before the Blockade. My last view of home was out of a port view screen as we warped out of the system, away from the Appaq. It looked..... so beautiful..... I still remember the atmosphere's shade of blue, the reflection from the suns. That was eleven years ago. I'm not even sure I have a home there anymore." Jenner studied the strange being, his stoic features tinged with sympathy. He turned back to the view screen and answered softly "Somethings are universal. Greed, aggression, war. I think..... I think we always hoped it would be different, out here." " 'Fundamentally, all life remains as it was. Its aspects simply become greater, or smaller.' Setarcos the Seeker." "What's the first thing you're going to do when you get home, Otalp?" "Find my family." He responded immediately. Jenner nodded. "Of course." "What about you?" The admiral was silent for a moment. "I really miss the smell of lilacs." "Lilacs?" "It's a kind of flower, lovely aromatic. I had a garden of them right next to my porch. On a cool summer evening, the smell would waft right up and tickle your nose." He gave a small smile. "I can almost taste the sweet tea now." "Sweet tea?" "Hmph." Jenner replied, readjusting his focus as a metallic spire came into view around the horizon of the blue planetoid. "Hiris V shipyard coming on view screen, admiral." An ensign reported redundantly. Scaffolding extended out into space along a complex structure of metal extensions built around the kilometers tall spire. Hundreds of hulls and exposed skeletal structures could be seen hanging among the scaffolding, like metal insects caught in a spiders' web. The Hiris V shipyards were a challenging target for the fleet. A forward base of operations, its destruction would cripple enemy supply lines in this sector. Jenner was more than a little hesitant at attacking a target like this, especially with the fleet operating on experimental tactics. But he was more confidant that they needed a challenge; the validity of these experimental tactics had to be proved in a true crucible. Around the edges of the shipyard in a ring formation came the Fifty-Sixth Appaq Lance. The sharply angled vessels looked devilish in the light of the K-class star. Jenner began firing off commands, leaning forward in his command chair. "Comms, signal the fleet, battle order 104, engage on my signal. Helm, takes us in towards the capital ship, comms make sure the corvettes keep the fighters off our backs, we're gon na have a hard enough time as it is. Brace for contact in t-minus 17 seconds." The opposing fleets began to ungulate like a swarm of agitated bees. Fighters little bigger than terrestrial jets orbited the massive cruisers, as the two alien trained their guns on one another. While the enemy feet was still several hundred meters away, Jenner called out "Fire at will, battle protocol 104!." The humanEchysian ships lit up like a bank of fire works, pre-firing into the hostile mass. Few of the shots hit, but it allowed them to quickly adjust their shot into the enemy inertia. Energy beams followed soon coming from the Appaq ships. The energy weapons were built to carve up allied armor, but the humans modified kinetic weapons easily penetrated Appaq shielding, which energy weapons would have been ineffective against in any case. Still, the dichotomy meant that the human ships had to strike a crippling blow within the first few minutes, or be forced to fall back; and if an Appaq ship was able to strike the first blow, more likely than not it was the human ship that went down. The view screen of the Salamis could see little of the battle raging around them. It's electric eye was focused firmly on the Appaq capital ship, a massive vessel with a crew compliment of over a thousand. Compared to the graceful, aerodynamic design of the smaller ships that surrounded it, it was a bulky behemoth, designed to take a beating as it carried the highest ranking officers in a fleet. Jenner stared the ship down from his seat, rocking as an energy blast glanced off the Salamis's hull. "Engaging the capital ship sir." An ensign reported, swiping furiously though holographic displays. "Target the shield array, we need a clear shot for the missile pay load." Energy discharges slammed into the hull, ripping open holes into open space. The bridge shook violently with each hit, the room vibrating with the report of recoil guns returning fire. A bridge console overloaded, exploding in a shower of white hot sparks. Fire containment crews rushed in while console officers pulled away their dead and wounded. "Scans report generator down, sir!" "Missile bay, activate Greek Fire, target the thinnest layer of armor, on my mark..... fire!"

Huh. I just wrote this story for a different prompt, but I feel like the story of a mad Shopping Cart Attendant is right in line with what this thread could use. The Lexus driver didn't even see the cart until it was nearly too late. She had been distracted trying to get her daughter settled in to her car seat. Alan had been two aisles over when he saw the reverse lights flash on and the car began to move. He rushed as fast as he could. It wasn't enough. The car and cart collided. The carted skidded and fell over, scratching the paint job of the sedan as it fell. Alan arrived on the scene as the driver, a middle aged woman, and her elementary school aged daughter stepped out to examine the damage. The plastic of the cart had rubbed a red streak across the back bumper. The cut in the paint was two inches long. It would take a lot of work to make the car look new again. " Look what you made me do! " The woman was clearly distraught as she shouted at her daughter. " You couldn't just put your seatbelt on like a big girl! " " Ma'am, " Alan interrupted, " don't blame the girl, I should have moved that cart be- " " I'm sorry, who exactly are you? " " My name is Alan Quixano, ma'am. I am in charge of keeping these cars in control. I should have moved that cart, instead it hit your car. It was my fault and I am sorry. Don't blame the poor girl for my mistake. " The woman took a moment to compose herself. " Ok. Mister Quixano. I accept your apology. If you don't mind, we need to be on our way. " " M'lady. " Alan responded. He picked up the cart as the woman and her daughter climbed back into their car. As they drove off, Alan was sure he saw a tear of joy in the young girl's eye. The carts were dangerous. That's what no one else seemed to understand. It was Alan's job to keep the carts in line. And Alan was good at his job. . After his shift, he jumped on the number eight bus. Roxie was driving today. Roxie always had a big smile on her face. Alan told her all about the Lexus and the woman. " Its that new wind farm their building north of town. " Roxie said. " Bringing in all these folks with their fancy cars all obsessed with development. You're probably going to have more fancy cars to protect from them carts soon. Anyway, Mancha Street is coming up, this is your stop. " This gave Alan a lot to think about. Roxie was right that there had been more and more fancy cars in his parking lot in the last few months. The whole neighborhood was changing as more and more of the wind turbines rose just north of town. It wasn't just fancy cars though. There were also more big trucks from the guys building the turbines. While the fancy cars needed to be protected from the carts, the carts needed to be protected from the big trucks. If a truck hit a cart it would send it careening wildly through the parking lot where it could hit anything. It was getting harder every day to be a cart attendant, and it was harder because of the giant windmills north of town. . Alan and his roommate Sancho liked to watch Netflix and smoke pot in the evenings. Today they were watching Daredevil. It wasn't as good as the comics, but it was entertaining nonetheless. After a few episodes, Alan told Sancho about the woman in the Lexus and how the new wind farm was bringing in new vehicles that were bad for the carts. " Dang " said Sancho, " What are you going to do about it? " " What can I do? The carts have to be kept safe, and that's my job. " " Oh come on man! What would Daredevil do? He'd find a badass way to beat the crap out of these guys. Let's face it, Donna would think that's pretty hot, too " " If I beat the crap out of a guy, my manager, Miguel, would fire me on the spot. " " True. You'll have to find some other way to keep the carts safe though. " . Over the next weeks, things got worse and worse for Alan. People left carts everywhere. It almost seemed like there was no point in using electric cart pusher the store owned. Carts were too scattered to keep in a straight line. At the same time, the contractor building the turbines made a deal with the store where they could use the back of the parking lot as a staging area for some of their work. All of a sudden Alan had half as much room to work. Then came the day of the storm, when everything changed. Winds blew carts to and fro through the parking lot. At the same time, the rain made it harder for cars to see the carts, meaning that if Alan didn't stay on top of it, another accident was inevitable. One cart got away. The wind blew it to he back of the parking lot. As the bulldozer pulled in, the driver didn't even notice the cart until it was too late. The worst part about it was that Alan wasn't even the first one to learn about the crushed cart. The construction worker went into the store and alerted management of the crushed cart. Miguel was the first employee to see it. Alan thought that Miguel didn't really even care about the cart. He did care about looking like a big shot. In the same day Alan, the greatest shopping cart attendant you would ever meet lost his first cart and got written up for his efforts. Something had to change. He could do like Sancho said, and try beating the crap out of the construction team, but he new that would do no good. He needed to aim bigger than that. . " You're crazy! " Sancho exclaimed when Alan told him what he had planned. " You're going to get caught for sure if you do that. " " They have cameras, yeah. But that's why I want to use that horse mask of yours. " " That's not a horse. " " Well, what is it? " " It's a donkey " " A donkey, okay. As long as it doesn't look like me it should do the trick. " . Two news stories would make the rounds in the following days. Security footage captured a mysterious donkey faced figure stole all of the shopping carts from the local department store and drove off with them using the automatic cart trolley. The second story was the power outage that turned out all the lights in the Mancha neighborhood for several hours. Later investigation would reveal that a shopping cart was pushed into a transformer in the Mancha wind farm. The resulting short caused several of the batteries to stop collecting power, setting back construction for several months. What never made the news was the missing persons report filed by Sancho Panza. His roommate had gone out that night and never returned. However stories kept filtering in of people seeing him wandering from town to town, often with several shopping carts in tow.

"Yeah but, I mean, I need more notice than that," I point out. Right, yesterday was a busy day. No time to go grocery shopping, what with your action-packed schedule of Counter Strike and masturbation. Chucky's always giving me shit. "Not in the mood today," I say as I hop into my work pants. "This is gon na be a good week, I can feel it." You finally gon na ask a girl out this week? "Oh, you got me," I said. "Pow, right in the feels." Earth log 1 2075 AD. I wake up this morning to an apocalypse more horrifying than any conceivable. Not zombies, not machines, not aliens..... no-one. Nothing around, absolutely desolate as far as I can see. Supplies for survival are not the issue, everything is as it was. But sanity is something I think will be an interesting challenge to maintain. Nothing but time; time to think. Think why? Why am I the only one? Have I been chosen for some task, or have I been simply left behind. Where was I when this went down. What is special about my 2 bedroom flat on the 4th floor down this side of the hallway, that literally every other place on earth appears to have been evacuated. I guess time will tell.

"Hi" I said, cheerfully sitting on the bar stool next to him. He looked at me warily, obviously wondering who the fuck I was and what I wanted. "My name's Mason" "So? Fuck off." He drained his whisky and called the bartender for another. "So what's your name?" I continued, not letting his attitude get to me. "Look, whatever your selling, I'm not interested." "Well you don't know that" I replied conversationally. "Know what, that your selling or that I'm not interested?" "Either, both." I asked the bartender for a beer and turned back to see him glaring at me. "How about you fuck off and let me drink in peace. I'm sure there's plenty of other people in this bar that are interested in hearing your shit." "But you're the only one I want to talk to." I protested. "Really? And what'd I do to get so lucky?" He snarled. "Well if you'd tell me your name I could tell you that." He sighed. "Alex. My name is Alex." "Oh, good." I slid off the bar stool and leaned in close to his ear. He smelled like grease and sweat. "You raped my mother" I said and left the bar. Outside it was dark and I waited on someones car for him to follow. Sure enough a few seconds later the door opened and he came out. He was big and it was all muscle. "What the fuck are you talking about?" He asked angrily. "Almost 20 years ago. Then 9 months later I was born." I said cheerfully. "Oh, that." He said and walked closer to me until he was only a couple of meters away. "I suppose you want to talk about it." He said warily, staring at me with dark eyes. I shrugged. "If you want to." "I don't." He replied shortly. I was relieved, I didn't want to talk about it either. "Then what do you want to talk about?" I asked. "I don't know. We'll figure that out. Let's go." I followed him to his truck, a dirty but nice hilux. I got in the passenger seat and we left.

"We are currently experiencing technical difficulties. Please be patient and normal service will be restored shortly." "Hello?" No response. "H-ey?" My voice breaks. It hasn't done that since I was in high school, trying to learn how to talk to girls. "I think there's been a problem." I press 0 on my phone, in a vague hope that maybe it will get me an operator. Instead, it just produces a god-awful blaring tone and before I can stop myself, I instinctively hit the button to end the call. My breaths are coming faster and my chest hurts now. I'm afraid I might be hyperventilating. Is that even possible? Shouldn't the air be as frozen as the picture on the TV or the cars I can see out of my window? Maybe things I touch still function normally! I seize on the mad hope and dash outside. It's the evening, but I still have to jog more than a block before I find a person outside. It's someone I don't recognize: a balding man in a wife-beater and shorts, watering his lawn. Sluicing gems of water hang suspended in the air, shattering the fading sunlight into infant rainbows. The waterer is wearing a pair of fuzzy pink house shoes that look several sizes too small for him. My first instinct is to seize the man and shake him, to demand that he share this frozen world with me. Instead, I reach out and touch one of the gravity-defying globules of water. I push it around and it breaks up as my finger passes through it, but it otherwise behaves nothing like a liquid should. Now I'm scared, haunted by images of my fingers passing through the man in similar fashion, flesh and blood offering no more resistance than pudding. I can't bring myself to- "What the hell are you doing!" The man shouts at me as sound and sensation come rushing back. Water sprays all over my legs before he can jerk the hose away. I'm standing in his garden. I run for it, laughing as his shouts follow my retreating back. Whatever it was, it's over. But..... my phone must have the number I was called from saved in it. There are mysteries to be solved! "Normal service has been restored. We thank you for your patience." It was a message left on my voicemail. The number for both calls just shows up as . Even when I try to call back, I just get the blaring tone. In the year since then, I've decided it was all a daydream. I think its better that way. After all, if it was just a dream, I can still pretend to be sane, even if my heart skips a beat whenever everything goes quiet. Like now. There is no sound, except the ringing of my phone.
