Training day. I always hated training day. We took in a few million dead kids, told them how the job works and told them that they didn't have to go forward into " the great unknown " if they weren't ready yet. Big surprise, we get a lot of volunteers for the job. I had a good kid with me this year, his name is Greg. Greg worked as a cashier at Safeway until he was robbed and shot between the eyes by the robber. The first thing he asked me when the shock wore off? " Who the fuck robs a Safeway? " That got a chuckle, which happens once every founding of a great nation, so I liked the kid from the get-go. I had to show Greg how to do the job, and it was pretty simple. You find the recently deceased, you explain their predicament to them, and then you carry them onward. Pretty simple, very straightforward, but Greg was a good kid, and I still hate myself for dropping him into the deep like I did. It was a scene like out of some girl's nightmare. She'd been walking home, sparkling rock on her finger, skirt swaying with the subtle breeze. She had a smile her brunette hair just couldn't hold back, even when it blew in her face. It was probably the most infectious smile either Greg, or I had ever seen. She walked with the confidence only love can give a woman, and like that, it was all taken away. She was grabbed by a bunch of thugs, literally dragged into a nearby alley and violated in every possible way you could think of. I still don't like thinking about it, and I've been at this a long time. Greg surprised me. He looked almost... eager. " How's it work? " he asked, ready to go to work. I was disgusted, but I managed to ask him what in hell he was talking about. Y'know what he said? " Well, how's she gon na kill one of ' em? " That naivety... that innocence. It broke my heart, really. I put my hand on Greg's shoulder and told him in the nicest way I could that we weren't here for the thugs. As soon as I'm done talking, one of those thugs pulls out a big knife and cuts the girl ear to ear. I wanted to cry. Not because it was sad- I'd seen plenty sadder- but because I wanted to let Greg know that he wasn't alone. The poor fucking kid, he just stood there. I'll bet he wanted to be a superhero as a kid so he could save people, and now he's just idly watching them get murdered, drown, kill themselves and every other way to off yourself you can think of. I could see in him, watching his tears stream down his cheeks, that he figured out the enemy of a hero isn't a villain, but rather it's passivity. It's doing nothing and standing back while the horrors go on around you. We took the girl in, explained to her what happened, and listened to the same hundred excuses and same hundred questions they all had. They all insisted that it wasn't their time because they had things to do, and they all asked us about heaven, hell, reincarnation and everything in between. One guy actually asked if we could give him an extension on life so he could return a porno he'd rented, and make it look like he didn't have a heart attack while beating off. People, man. But after the girl passed on, Greg told me he wasn't cut out for the job. We both knew he wasn't, but I didn't want to be true. I wanted Greg to keep doing this for my own selfish reasons. I wanted a friend- I wanted someone witty, who could make me laugh, even if it's just with a pinch of cynicism. I've got too much of the latter, not enough wit. I don't laugh so good anymore. But Greg was adamant. He didn't know what was on the other side of that door, but it was better than sitting back and watching the world die. He told me that he couldn't stand by and do nothing. He told me that maybe on the other side there would be something he could do for people, even if it was just a gust of wind, and even if it only worked once in a million years. It was better than watching. And y'know what? The kid's right. Please consider this my formal resignation to the Mortality Bureau. It's been an honor to serve you for the many decades I've been around, but it's time for me to move on. Thank you.

"Who wants this?" He holds up the bronze token in the air. Its about an inch long and half an inch thick, made of dull metal that somehow still manages to glimmer in the morning light. There's a roar of muted approval from the shambolic crowd below. Buck pushed past the man on his left who was missing part of his ear and stood his ground. Someone shoved him and he shoved right back, eyes fixed firmly on the small token that the foreman held between his skinny fingers. Buck grimaced as the crowd around him jostled and cried out. "Please! I've got three kids at home." "My wife's ill!" "Please, please. I haven't eaten in two days." Buck didn't have a wife, or children. Yesterday he'd dumpster dived round back of McDonalds. Cold french fries are delicious when you're starving. But he hadn't worked since mid-October and the pile of cash he'd got under his mattress from his last non-tokened'job' was steadily running out. He needed to do something legal for a change. But that meant getting up before the grey light of dawn and trudging, hands in armpits, down to the local lumber yard, where the foreman would hand out ten tokens to the ten most desperate and dangerous men. The foreman holds the disk up a little further and the moans of humiliated men grew louder. Buck felt two hands push into the small of his back. He momentarily lost his balance before turning back round and punching the offender square in the face. Then, before he'd even realised it was happening, the foreman flicked the token and it went soaring up into the air. Down, down it tumbled, towards the dozens of outstretched hands. It fell and ten men jumped after it immediately. Buck launched himself into the fray, refusing to give quarter. An elbow hit him, and a starburst of pain above his eye told him his eyebrow had split. Again. He kicked out at a man scrabbling on the ground. "Give it to me!" He grunted, throwing himself down beside the prostrate man with wild abandon. He gripped the man's hands and turned them over, revealing the little disk. He ripped and clawed at the man's hands until he started screaming with incoherent pain and rage. There was an awful tearing sound which ripped through the noise of the screaming crowd. The man dropped the token and backed away, holding his bleeding hand. Buck had torn one of his fingers off. But there was no time to think about him. He picked the disk off the floor, now smeared in the man's blood and held it aloft. "I get work!" He cried out, his voice hoarse. "I've got the disk!" The crowd of men drew back, glowering at him with a mixture of jealousy and anger. Buck stepped up next to the foreman, doing his best to wipe the blood from his sliced eyebrow and from him hands. He handed the token back reluctantly and the foreman took it with a handkerchief. The gates to the lumberyard opened. Buck was going to eat well that night.

I grew up in fear. Honestly, it's amazing I lived as long as I did, as our numbers dwindled more and more, every year, to their endless numbers. They weren't just a force, they hunted, they consumed, they thought and fought us, every moment, of every day. The only thing that kept us alive was their tendency to rip their victims apart, before they could be turned. Of course, now I understand. Only the weak couldn't escape. From the moment you're bitten, it hits you, like a bucket of ice-cold water, it hits you, fills you with fear and adrenaline. If you can't get away for half an hour for it to happen with that in your system, then you're not worthy of surviving, you're just more food. You're not capable of this. I get it, now. When I got infected, I was the last. Nobody is left in this part of the world, as far as I know. And now, I see why they did everything. Those of us who are clever, are fighters, who can be hunters, we're the only ones who survived being bitten, or survived attacking the remaining humans. Natural selection at it's finest. Of course, some of us they chose, like me. I asked the one who got me, the same day, once I understood I had nothing to fear. He could have followed me, hunted me down and kept trying, but he understood. I'd proven myself getting as far as I did. "You had the instinct and the ability, all you needed was to be one of us." My heartbeat is gone, my lungs quiet and dead. My skin is cool to the touch, though it is intact, solid, like that of all the others' I've seen. And yet, for all those things I lack, I've never felt more alive than now. Now, I understand. I'm a predator. I am a Hunter. What I hunt doesn't even matter- so long as I can sink my fangs into its flesh, rip it limb from limb with my claws, stalk it in silence as it walks, unaweare, and fill myself with its meat, its flesh its blood. This is all I've required. I am not prey any longer.

There were four of us on a trip to collect soil samples. We had our collection positions all plotted out on a map, five kilometers apart, each. By the time we made our trek toward the last spot, we were on the brink of collapse, by thirst and by exhaustion. I turned on my GPS and we moved to the final point. We walked in silence. About 30 meters away, I saw a rock. The rock sat at the exact coordinates of our final sampling location. We could move the rock, but we were tired. My assistant suggested turning around, but we had come too far. We approached the rock. It turned. The rock was wearing a grey suit with a black tie. It had matted hair and dark skin. Its face was half-flesh and half-dirt. The rock had a manila folder under its arm, also half-dirt. We stood and stared as the rock approached us. It was not well. Its jawbone was visible through the paper-thin skin tightly bound around its skull. Its arms were broken pencils taped together by an elbow. It walked like one foot was two pounds heavier than the other. Nonetheless, it grinned like it had reunited with an old friend. Out it stretched both pencils and bestowed upon us the weathered folder. I took it. The rock nodded and turned away. It sat down in front of us and watched the sun dip behind the mountains. The cover of the folder was painted in meticulous fashion. "FOR YOU," it spelled out in bold, white lettering. We opened the folder to find old, dirty papers with what at first appeared to be the drawings and rants of a schizophrenic. What was actually written was the exact opposite. The cover did not lie. The papers were for us. Each page was a piece of a map of the surrounding area, with the pH level of the soil of 30 spots around a 20-kilometer radius. The pages included local vegetation reports, sketches of wildlife with proper Latin names, everything. We were astonished, to say the least. I crouched down next to the rock. "This is incredible. How did you get this?" "I'm just the messenger." "For who?" "A friend." I stopped and stood up. The land was flat all around us, with only my team and the rock in sight. "Would you mind clarifying exactly who that might be?" "Don't think too hard." I examined the rock. I had seen it before. It was tall, nearly 2 meters in height. It had aged from the cold arctic weather, but something told me that it hadn't always been this weak. I looked into its brown eyes and it looked back at me. At that moment I came to a realization I have never experienced before or since. This man was not just the rock we had assumed he was; he was The Rock. We checked the bottom of every paper. They all said the same thing in the lefthand corner. "D. Johnson 2014." Only one thing was left to find out. "Hey Dwayne Johnson, also known as The Rock, why are you wearing a suit and starving in the middle of a tundra?" "Well, to answer your first question, I was returning from an awards show. To answer your second question, I decided to take a hike and got lost without a cell phone. I would appreciate your help in getting me back to my home in the United States of America." "No problem, Dwayne Johnson." We brought him back to America in our van and he thanked us profusely. I thanked him back for his help in getting us this extremely useful information. And that's how I met The Rock. I really need to learn how to end a story.

Austin was far from an expert chef and had never prepared a single Mexican dish his life, and yet he still told that chick he met at the park the other day that he could make some mean tacos and guacamole. This small lie had convinced her to pay him a visit tomorrow night for dinner, so now here he was at the grocery store, with the highest rated guacamole recipe he could find online, searching for ingredients. " Check, check... oh I'm an idiot! I almost forgot the avocado! " He made his way to the produce section, and slowly walked up and down the aisles reading the names displayed above each pile of fruit and vegetables because he was clueless as to what an avocado looked like before it was cut open. When he finally came upon them, he sighed and said, " Now how do I know which one is a good one? " Suddenly, his eyes were sucked in by the vacuum of transcendence created by perhaps the single most satisfyingly shaped object (other than various part of the female anatomy) that he had seen in his life. He reached for it, lifted it up to his face and whispered, " It's the perfect avocado. " The produce section went silent, and he could feel his words reverberating off the walls. He looked to his right and saw a rather attractive young woman staring in his direction. He smiled and awkwardly brought the avocado down from his face. She gave him a flirty wave and moved on. " OK. That should be everything, " he said as he turned around and smashed his face into the chin of a tall older man standing directly behind him. " Ahh! Excuse me. Do you want something? " he asked the man. " That rather luscious avocado you just careless dropped into your basket. I'll give you all the money I have in my wallet for it! " " How much do you have? " " Nine dollars. " " No, I'm sorry. I've got a date tomorrow, and I want it to be perfect. " The man scrunched up his eyes into thin, horizontal slivers and lifted his hand so that his index finger and middle finger were pointing directly into Austin's eyes. With his fingers still judging, he backed away proclaiming, " You are not worthy of that which you possess. " Although at first startled, a pride began to swell up within Austin. He started towards check out and patted his Avocado saying, " Thanks to you, I just might be able to pull this off. " While the cashier was ringing him up, the pretty woman from the produce section queued up behind him. He felt his heart race just a little bit, but decided he already had one cool girl he was meeting tomorrow, and this one here was probably out of his league anyway. Abruptly, his thoughts were broken by the heavenly sight of the avocado as the cashier pulled it out of his basket, but rather than scanning it, she stuck it underneath the counter. " Hey, what are you doing? " " It's not yours until it's bagged. It's mine now. " " What? You can't do that! " " This is my turf! I can do what I want! " " Your... turf? " was all he could muster up to say in his confusion. " Give that back to him or I'll talk to your manager. Everything in this store is for purchase. You can't take it away from a customer just because you want it, " demanded the pretty girl. " Bitch, " the cashier mumbled under her breath as she pulled out the avocado and rang it up. After he paid, Austin headed outside and waited for the helpful, attractive woman to thank her. He began thinking maybe he did have a shot with her, and it wasn't like he was committed to the Mexican food loving chick yet anyway. The supermarket doors opened, but before he could say anything, she laughingly remarked, " Well, that was strange. " He chuckled and said, " I know, right? I was a little speechless. Thanks for handling it for me. " " Don't mention it. Where's your car? " " Right over there. " " I'll walk you to it. " " How about I walk you to your car? It's the least I could do. " " No thanks. I'm actually about to head back to work. It's not far from here. Let me help you with one of those bags. You've got more than me. " He declined, but she snatched one out of his hands anyway. They began walking to his car, and he said, " Since I can't even walk you to your car, how about I take you out to dinner sometime to thank you for your help today? " " I'd like that. Let me give you my number. " He punched in the number on his cellphone and asked, " ...and what's your name? " " Call me later, and I'll tell you, " she said as she winked and began walking away. His heart fluttered and he started getting into his car, when he realized she still had his bag. " Hey! Excuse me! You've got my groceries! " She didn't seem to notice him and kept going. He yelled a few more times, but she still gave no response. Then he realized that it was the bag that the cashier had placed the avocado into. " It's not in there! " he shouted. She stopped and looked in the bag. Then she spun around with a look so angry it wiped all of the beauty from her face. " Looking for this? " he asked as he pulled the avocado out of his coat pocket. She let out a bizarre, little giggle and began spinning his bag of groceries like it were a sling ready to fire a stone. " Hey! Don't do that! " She released the bag, and it went flying towards him. He jumped to the side, and it just barely missed his head, smashing through a window of the van behind him. " Jesus Christ, " he squealed. Then she let out a horrid scream, and began charging at him, not running upright like a human, but on all fours like a mother bear ready to ravage the perceived threat to her cub. He immediately flung his card door open, hopped in, and slammed it shut. The girl, who just a moment ago sent his heart aflutter, now caused it to pound with intense fear. He fumbled as he stuck the key into the ignition and was just about turn it, when she leapt over his car and landed in front of it, standing upright and facing him. He froze and took a deep gulp. She raised her hands into the air and slammed them down on to the hood. Her fingers penetrated the metal and she twisted her arms, ripping the hood straight off of the car and flinging it behind her. He watched as it soared through the air and smacked into the tops of some trees at the edge of the parking lot. With hair in her face and her mouth hanging open, she slowly lifted her right hand into the air, in what he assumed would be a fatal blow to his car engine, and he immediately lifted the avocado above his head and shouted, " Wait! " He rolled down the driver's side window, and she casually dropped her hand and walked over to him. She stuck her hand out and he placed the avocado into her palm, but for some reason when she tried to pull it away, he couldn't bring himself to let go. Instantly, she hissed and launched her other hand at his throat. He promptly let go, and gurgled an apology. She released his neck and smiled. As she skipped away, she said, " Don't forget you owe me dinner. " " God help me, " he desperately muttered as he sank into his seat.

" Shit, we've still got ten to intercept. I must have burned too early. " " Well, like the old saying goes, ' The Devils in the details '. " Mick managed to convey his eye roll through the gold mylar reflector and shatter proof glass visor of his suit, " Oh Christ, Gerry, shut up. " Gerry's laugher crackled in over Mick's suit radio. " I don't know if you should say that, man. He might hear you, " more of Gerry's laughter. At this, Mick cracked a smile, turning his head to look off the side of the work sled they both clung to, and stared down at the growing speck in the distance. He was confident Gerry couldn't see him grinning through the visor out here in the solar glare, but he wasn't going to risk giving him the satisfaction. Hard vac was no place to screw around. After a moment, when Mick was sure he wouldn't slip into laughter and encourage Gerry, he said, " So what if He does? If he's willing to ignore the billion and a half of us not on Earth then He's probably not gon na pop out here just cuz I told you to cram it. " Gerry chuckled again, " Yeah, shit, He's probably not even listening anymore since he sucked up all his chosen and booked it before the Red Bastard filled Earth up with all those face eating tentacle things. " Gerry floated gentle against his restraints as he hand enunciated quotations around ' Chosen '. Mick frowned, " Seriously? I don't want to think about those things. I still had cousins on Earth. " Gerry's chuckling died down, and in a more serious tone said, " Ah, shit, I'm sorry. I suppose I should have asked if you were a second gen spacer or not. " " It's fine, let's just focus, the next rock's coming up, is the drill ready? " " Yup. " " Booster pack? " " Yup. " " What's the running total up too? " Gerry checked his wrist read out, " We're up to 10,721 objects ready for thrust. " Mick whistled into his helmet, " I wonder when we're gon na make our move? " Gerry chuckled again, " I don't know, but we'll sure show the bastard how to really rain fire when we do. " Mick cracked another smile, and this time he didn't care who saw.

Everybody died on their birthday, nobody knew which one. Society made birthdays a solemn day for reflecting on the past year. Which was good, in a way, but for some poor souls that reflection became suicide. Taking your own life was the most cause of death in the world. Maybe it was the anxiety of never knowing if this was the birthday. Maybe it was the waiting, watching the minutes creep by. Many thought the remorseful just let death come and take them. I was old fashion; I believed in fate. You can cheat at cards, or on your wife, but you can't cheat death. My beliefs, however, are in the minority. Most subscribe to the philosophy of prevention. Entire industries have cropped up to placate the need. Everlife is the biggest company on Earth. I work for them. I am a life pod district engineer. I, from this tiny office, monitor thousands of people who paid millions of dollars for a one day stay at our facilities. I watch large blocks of individual pods on my computer. Each one the size of a coffin, completely sealed off from the outside world. All air is sterilized before being pumped in. The patients are sedated and vitals are constantly monitored. The doors will not open for a full twenty four hours. All threats are kept at bay. Sure we have had a few deaths, but those are usually massive organ failure. We can't cheat death, but our numbers are pretty damn good. Everlife has become so successful that the world elite use our services. Heads of State, Presidents, Kings, and Queens all trust us to protect them, from themselves. As with every other thing on this planet, the Everlife system started noble and was slowly corrupted with money. What once started as a way to protect humanity, eventually because a haven for the elite and wealthy. Pod rentals are so expensive that only the very rich can afford the privilege. Average Joes, like me can only dream of using the same pods. If I made the rules, I would award pods on need. Then again I could be biased. My father turns 72 in three days and his life's work is six months from completion. It will be a nerve racking day for the entire family. He has devoted his life to isolating the birthday gene, the very essence of life and death. He is so close. If he can just make it through that one day, all of society could change. That's why I am killing a President today, on her birthday. It's not that I have anything against the lady, far from it. I even voted for her, but the French have offer me a lot of money, and I need money. One catastrophic software failure and a city block of pods will be shut down. I have come to grips with the fact that I will have to shut down 330 pods, an entire sector, to make this work. I will be the cause of all those deaths. They are all just numbers on my screen, except pod 126. That number will allow my father to buy another year. Death should be quick. Oxygen should be depleted in thirty seconds and suffocation in less than three minutes. I have timed the crash for 19 minutes. That's the exact amount of time it takes to process the French payment and reserve a pod for my father. It shouldn't be traced back to me. It should look like an accident. Sure there will be an investigation, but that will take weeks. I only need a few days. Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday madam President.......

For my first thirty sum odd years of existence I never really gave any thought to the notions of God, the supernatural, or even extraterrestrial life. I was the kind of person who had to see something happen right before my eyes to believe that it actually happened. I grew up in a small Alaskan town near the coast that you've probably never heard of. The town was relatively close to a nearby oil rig and it wasn't uncommon to see drifters come and go looking for employment on the rig or one of the many fishing and crabbing vessels. The people in my town were as rough as the strenuous life they lived. Like I said, it wasn't uncommon to meet people from all over the world searching for work. I became friends with many of them and even enemies with a few. However, one drifter in particular left such an impression that he changed the very fundamentals of everything I thought I knew. Larry arrived in our town in late February that year. Earlier that year there was an explosion on the oil rig that was caused by some natural gas or something, I don't really understand how all of that stuff works, and the whole thing was pretty much destroyed but miraculously the crew had survived. I ran a little bar in the town, not much to look at, but it was the only watering hole for 50 miles in every direction. One morning as I was sweeping outside the bar, cleaning up from the night before, a face approached me that I had never seen before which like I said isn't at all uncommon in my town. "Can I help you?" I said, "Sorry to bother you this early, but I'm new in town and recently unemployed." He said. "I was just wondering if maybe you're hiring, I'm not too proud for any job that you could give me." I actually wasn't hiring at the moment and to be honest I couldn't really afford to hire anyone else, but I really felt sorry for the guy. "I guess he can help out bussing tables and bar hopping." I thought. The military had also recently moved into the area doing some kind of weather research about 20 miles north, and the soldiers had begun to flock to my place. I figured maybe I could use the extra help. He was a pretty big guy as well, about 6'4 and looked strong as an ox. Every now and then a drifter would come in who thought he was a hard ass so having this guy around to settle a few scores wouldn't hurt either. "We'll I could use someone to help out around here as a matter of fact." "I can't pay you very much, but I do have an extra room above the bar that you can stay in if you'd like." I said. "That'd be great." He said. "When can I start?" "Well first I need to know your name." I said. "Larry" he said. "Nice to meet you." Larry was a better worker than I had ever imagined. He was hard-working, polite, and the guy never seemed to get tired. All of the regulars loved him and we became pretty good friends too. I decided to take Larry with me to a mechanic that I knew in a town about thirty miles east. My truck's transmission light had been on for a while and I decided to have it looked at. The night before there had been some really heavy snowfall and the roads were in terrible condition. We came around a curve in the road and saw that someone had missed the curve and ran their truck off the road about 50 yards into a healthy pine tree. The truck was completely wrapped around the tree and the tree had fallen on top of the truck as well. We pulled over and ran to the truck as quickly as we could. In the passenger seat we saw and older man slumped to the side and bleeding pretty badly, but he was breathing. The way the truck was wrapped around the base of the tree and the way that the rest of it was on top of the truck there was no way to get the man out. The man was seriously injured and losing blood fast. "Go back to the truck and close your eyes." Larry said in a tone I had never heard before. "WHAT?!" "Do it." "Now." He said. Dumbfounded, I reluctantly walked back to the truck, both angry and confused, and did what he said. Well, not completely. I watched. What I saw, I could not believe. Larry walked over to the truck and like you or I might lift a 20 pound dumbbell, he lifted that massive tree trunk off the top of the truck. I was in disbelief. What he did next was even more remarkable. He then proceeded to unwrap the truck from around the tree WITH HIS HANDS. When Larry walked back over to my truck holding the barely breathing man in his arms he could tell by the look on my face that I had not done as he said. After he laid the man in the backseat of my truck he got in on the passenger side of the truck and and with an inexplicable look of almost shame in his eye said, "forget what you saw, and never speak of it." At that point I knew that Larry was unlike anyone else on this planet. Over the next few months feats like this continued to occur. Each time Larry seemed more and more reluctant to perform them. We never spoke of any of them and I could tell in eyes that he appreciated my silence on the subject. Larry began showing up at work In the mornings having not slept the night before. I knew this because he was never at his apartment above the bar. I watched him from my house across the street take off north every night. On foot. To the north there was absolutely nothing but an old, dilapidated road for the next 20 or so miles. Every morning as I was cleaning up from the night before I would see him come walking down that road towards the bar. I still don't know exactly what he was doing or we he was going but I suspected it had something to do with that military research going on up north. I will never forget the last night I saw Larry. A trucker hauling freshly cut timber stopped in to have a few drinks with his buddies that evening. This guy had come in a few times before and he was a real asshole every time. I had recently hired a new waitress and he decided to make it a priority that night to harass her as much as possible. Both Larry and I, were ready to throw this guy out but she told us not to worry and that she had dealt with pricks before and this guy was no different. The next time she went over there the guy decided to grab her ass and that was it. Larry was steaming and looked over at me and I have him the "throw his ass on the street" nod. Larry walked over there and said "Thats enough." "What are you gunna do about it?" Said the trucker. "Well then I'm going to have to ask you to leave." The guy then took his glass of beer and threw threw it in Larry's face. Larry never budged but, the guy wasn't through yet. He became angry and shoved Larry as hard as he possibly could. Larry didnt move an inch and in fact the guy bounced back off of Larry. Larry then turned around and began to walk off when suddenly a beer can came hurdling in and hit him in the back of the head. Larry walked towards the door and before he went outside gave me a wink that I will never forget. That was the last time I ever saw Larry. However, when we walked outside something unimaginable had unfolded. The truckers truck was 20 feet in the air, impaled by a string of telephone polls. I can not begin to accurately describe what we saw out there. I do know, however, who was responsible. I walked up the short flight of stairs to Larry's apartment and everything was still there but I knew he wouldn't be back. But before I left I noticed above the doorframe someone had carved, more like burned, two letters. It looked like a set of initials and it read C.K. Was here.

The summer sunset peeks from behind trees to my left, a river runs slowly and calmfully to my right, its animal life getting ready for the night. It was a good day today, I caught almost a dozen fish, five of which I'm taking home. Its warm, its calm, life is good. I almo- - Hey! someone says and interrupts my train of thought - What the fuck? Where are you? I look around but see no-one and then suspect someone to be above me, sitting on a tree or something - Well not up there, that you can depend on. His tone of speech is half-humorous. - WHERE THEN? This is not funny. Is there a recording device somewhere or some shit? - Nope. Just me. What's a recording device? I can barely say: - "What's a recording device"? What do you mean what's a recording device? Who are you? - Ben. - Ben? Well, Ben, could you please be polite and TELL ME WHERE THE FUCK YOU ARE? - Calm down, friend. I hope I haven't upset you? - Just tell me where you are - Down here. I begin a search, even looking under my feet (?), and finally come to stare at a..... frog. I look around myself, confused. - I'm right here! Do you seriously not see me? I turn around with horror in my eyes: - You're a - - I'm a...? - You're a frog. - Pffft. That's irrelevant. - It is? REALLY? - You've never seen a talking frog before? Sarcastically, I respond: - Oh yeah, all the time, yeah, fuck yeah, I have a talking dog and a talking parrot - oh shit that actually exists - anyway and I have a..... I have a talking fucking..... worm, or some shit. Yeah I always talk to animals. Every day. The frog - Ben, I guess - just stares at me. Then it starts a new topic, as if the old one has never happened: - Hey yeah, so I was meaning to ask you something. A silence occurs. - So...? I ask, waving my hand. - So is it okay if I ask you? - Of course its okay - what the fuck why wouldn't it be okay to ask me - you know what this whole situation is too absurd, I'm going home. The sun is setting. Bye. Fuck. - Hey! Don't leave! Then, when I'm a few meters away, a voice comes from among the grass: - Do you want to be a princess? Can you get injured by confusion? Like can enough confusion in one moment just cause health issues? Because if it could, I would've been DEAD. - Wh....WHAT? I say as I turn back slowly. - Do-you-want-to-become-a-princess. The frog named Ben asks, as if I'm retarded. I can not get myself to say what one more time, even though I am double dared, motherfucker. - First: you're..... a fucking frog, and then you ask me..... if I want to become a..... princess? - Exactly. Now, answer quickly for time is of the essence. - I'm not even a woman! - That's irrelevant. A silence. - So, what do you say, human? The frog asks. I play along: - Yeah okay, turn me into a fucking princess. Do it. - HAHAHAHA! It's just a prank bro! Why could I turn people into princesses? Are you fucking stupid? Lmao dude. - WHAT? - Stop saying what dude, the frog says as it jumps toward the river: now get the fuck out of my forest, bitch. I am left standing until the mosquitoes rise from darkness and force me to leave the forest with my fish. Two weeks later I kill myself.

Telling tales of telling time, Stared at by two bright eyes, Ears open and mouth dropped wide, At the sight of this watch of mine; Young as him some time ago, An old man with a face I know, Passing on from his short life, And passed on to me this watch of mine; Time wore on me as more time passed, I saw to the wrist where this watch sat, The hands no longer tick, the band was thrashed, Still on my slit wrist, sat this watch of mine; As my time ends, yours now begins, Only you and this watch hold on to my sins, As my father did when it was time, I pass on to you; this watch no longer mine.

So then God says to me, "My child. You've been struggling." I look down in shame. I manage to squeak, "Yes sir." I can feel Him staring at me. Not in anger, not in annoyance, not in disappointment, but He looks at me in love. But of course, He is perfect. I'm the one who fucked up. I'm the one who let others get to me. I'm the one who danced with the devil. I'm the one who should have asked for help. But God understands. He knows everything. And yet He loves me anyway. I try to look up, but there is a weight holding my head down. "No child, don't look. Just listen. Don't worry. You are here for a purpose. I have a plan. Trust in me. Have faith in yourself. I am always here for you. I love you. And I want you home, in due time." I meekly respond, "But why not now? What am I supposed to be doing? Why am I still here?" I hear a quiet laugh. "Instead of always wondering what is is you should be doing, you should just do." I muster up the strength to look up. I see a light off in the distance. I let out a sigh and go on my way.

The slightly balding man with over-sized glasses takes his seat next to the young attractive host. He clears his throat before exposing the audience to a melodic French accent. "Tissue samples." he says, "We took small samples from a large number of people afflicted and tested out, oh, one thousand iterations of our medication." The host adjusts how he's sitting and leans forward, he clasps his hands together before continuing the interview. "And how many people had to volunteer before your lab started seeing results?" "Oh, more than I know how to count, haha." the esteemed doctor joked, "Everyone was so excited to sign up when they heard a cure was in development. Not treatment, but a bonafide cure. I think that's the reason we were able to find so many people." The host leans back in his chair. "And I'm sure the craigslist post helped too!" The audience laughs and the studio band plays a short riff. "I don't know what that is." the guest responded. "But there was one volunteer who came out of nowhere. A lot of people use the phrase patient zero for those who start diseases, but this was a patient zero who would eventually help us cure the disease!" "And is he here now? Could we talk to him?" "Unfortunately no. Although research and development has concluded, he will need more time to recover." "Recover from being cured?" The audience laughs and the studio band plays a short riff again. "Well we initially only needed small tissue samples from many people. But when we found our, how you say, the golden goose, we had to take many samples from one person." The audience is silent as is our handsome host. "By the time we were able to bring the drug to a useful level," the doctor went on to say, "I'm afraid we had used all the tissue equal to one of our volunteers legs." "And he was okay with this?" "He knew that what he was doing was for the greater good..... We think..." "You think?" "It's hard to gauge willingness when the patient is etherized upon the table." "Uh-huh. But he's okay now?" "Well after we moved to clinical trials, we still had a few bugs to work out. By the time our drug was marketable, our volunteer had donated his other leg as well." "Oh my..." the host mumbles, imagining the horror of the situation, "He sacrificed so much that we could rid the planet of one of the most infamous diseases. I'd like to shake this man's hand." The audience cheers in agreement. Even the band leader is tearing up. "We also had to use his arms..." the doctor added. The studio is silent as the mood is brought down further than ever. The host tries his hardest to regain his composure. "So this man," the host started, "Is now a paraplegic for the rest of his life, so that your labs could develop a cure?" "That is correct," said the smiling doctor, "And I'm happy to say he no longer has AIDS!"

It was a long time since my adventure began; I can't remember how many years. It has been a good time but now, wearily, I lay my head down on my pillow to take me to that destination, where all quests end. I dimly notice that I have friends, relatives, aquaintances everyone around me. They don't want me to go, they think I will be lost, that I have no guide, that I will be alone. There is only one way to find out. I close my eyes A tunnel appears before me with a great, blinding, light at the end, it calls to me, wants me. I feel pulled towards the end like a moth to a flame. It is not forced, nor painful, but rather a desire, to discover to find what the light holds in store for me, to find what is in that great beyond, to finally know the secert - the ultimate answer. I find myself falling gently to wards the end when I hear a voice. It is a child, about 2 years old I'd imagine, shouting and sceraming for me. "Grandpa, Grandpa. I don't want you to go" There are others now to, dozens of them, some sob and whimper while others yell and cry but they all penatrate. The tugging is gone. I see them now. They look so sad. Do I have to go through with this? Is the answer that important? The answer will come for me eventually, whether I look for it or not but these people, they need me now and I don't want them to fade just yet. I take one more whistful look to the light before making my way back.

The clacking of his nails filled the tiny hall he walked down. These buildings were so odd to him. It was nothing like he had experienced before. He arrived at the end of the hall way and stood in front of two humans holding long metal devices. Both of their eyes grew wider than he thought possible when he approached them. " These beings are so...odd looking. " He thought to Gen'ralis. " I agree sir. They look like little Norrogs. " Gen'ralis thought back to him. The image of the furry-topped little minions from their home planet crossed his mind causing him to grin. Yenfelda in the back must've caught a tail of the image because she too grinned. The two humans let them through the door. The door was too low, requiring them to duck under to fit through. Morthinji folded his wings in to avoid the thinly spaced door sides. He stepped into a room full of humans glaring at him. He held a calm disposition; this wasn't his first time confronting a new species. One of the humans in the middle spoke first. " General Morthinji, welcome to Earth. We are a species governed by multiple different authorities and governments. " As the human talked, Morthinji was busy talking with his comrades behind him. " What is a government? Yenfelda, did you read anything about that? " He thought to her. " I tried but I couldn't get my mind entirely around it. Basically, they have laws that the people must obey or they will be punished for it. " Yenfelda thought with a hint of disgust. " Laws? " Morthinji thought to the both of them. Gen'ralis had nothing to add. Morthinji took the question to the human talking. " Human, what are these laws you have created? " The human was taken aback. It was a question he clearly didn't expect to be asked. " To which law are you referring general? " " To these laws in generality. What are they for? " " Well, society can not function without set laws for people to obey. Without order, there is chaos, general. " Morthinji wanted more. " And you punish your people for disobeying laws that another equal man put in place? " " In our system, it is the only way society will function properly. " Morthinji was met with extreme disgust upon hearing the human's explanation. His frustration carried over to his companions who tried to block it out of their minds. " Human, I will tell you this. Of all the places I have been across the galaxy, you are the first to require such things of your own people. " Morthinji said, now looking down upon the human in front of him. The human was now frustrated as well. " You come from a completely different civilization, with different functions and different ways of life. It is not your position to judge us when you come from a differing society. " The air in the room changed with his statement. " You call this life? If you call the act of limiting your own people to the point of being reprimanded for acting freely a definition of living, you may be the most vile society I've ever come across. " Gen'ralis sent wave after wave of calming thoughts to ease the situation for him. Morthinji finally calmed down and thanked Gen'ralis. " My apologies. Maybe if I explain how it is within my society it will give you a better idea of why the idea of limitation is so wrong to us. In our society we are all equal, no one male or female is above another. Even in jobs we are equal. We do not believe in limiting ones right to live freely. We were all created to live freely, were we not? " " That is a very touching idea general Morthinji, but lawless society has been tried here before and it has failed over and over again. To implement something that historically does not work would be a form of insanity. You came to us general, not the other way around. What do you want? " Yenfelda sent a thought to him, " Maybe it is the people themselves. We knew they were of lower intelligence. It could be that they don't possess the ability to naturally form limitless society. Gen'ralis seemed to agree. " These humans can not be farther from redemption than we were at the beginning. We must try and help them Morthinji. General Morthinji expected another one of the humans to speak up but the rest remained silent in front of him. " Our job is to make this world a better place. We are here to abolish leadership and create an equal and free world. We intend to recreate the experience of free, limitless life that our home society is able to enjoy. If you are willing, we would require your help in achieving this goal. " While Morthinji meant it as a positive thing, the humans reacted extremely negatively. All of a sudden, they were all very nervous. The human in the middle got off of a device held to his ear and looked back at Morthinji. " I thought this might be the case. " He said as he nodded to someone behind Morthinji. While Morthinji was fast, getting taken by surprise was something he did not expect. As soon as the human nodded, projectiles fired from both sides. Electricity flowed through his body rendering it useless. Men were on top of him attaching metal circles around all four of his hands, joining them together by links. With a last mental cry, Morthinji called out to his people. " Help! We are being taken captive! Come to Earth, free us! " The man above him lifted the long metal device and slammed it down on Morthinji's head, enveloping his mind in darkness. Her hand trembles as it strokes my head. I can feel the blood flowing weakly through her skin, and I look up at her with concern, my eyes wide. She says something strange, I can never understand her, but her smile lights up my world. I let out a little bark of excitement and wag my tail. She loves it when I wag my tail. I get the reaction I wanted, and her smile widens, and she begins to stroke me even more. After an eternity she stops. I howl my disappointment but she doesn't continue. She tries to get on her two feet, that's how they normally walk, but rises and then sits back down. Perhaps she decided to play after all? My tail begins to wag and excitement fills me once more. But when I look at her I find though that she's not smiling. Instead there's a grimace on her face, she's in pain. Worry shoots through me, and I jump on to her chair, and begin to lick her. Usually this gets a laugh out of her, but she can only manage a weak smile. It's okay, I tell myself. She's been sick before. Like that one time she was in bed for a one sunrise, and when she was in that scary place with the white walls and beds for 3 sunrises. She always came back, she's always okay. I whine a little, mostly to reassure myself, but I just can't shake the feeling that there's something wrong, something wrong with her. Suddenly I feel the muscles under her skin contract. Oh no. I don't know exactly how, but I knew something was wrong. Something even licking couldn't help. She started breathing in short gasps. I had to get help, find someone. I began to run around her very large kennel, barking as loud as I could. The doors were locked so I couldn't go outside. But someone had to hear me..... someone had to help. After several minutes of this, no one arrived, and then I heard it. Heard her. She was calling my name. Softly yes, but my hearing is sharp. I heard her. I ran to her, and jumped on her soft chair and licked her. There was some bad tasting water near her nose and eyes. She was weak, very weak, her breaths were getting shallower and shallower. She said something again, but her words didn't really matter. I could tell by the smile and her sad looking eyes what was about to happen. Even though everything I knew told me it couldn't. Humans were supposed to live for centuries, so why now? Why me? She had looked after me and my dad and his dad and his mom and on and on. Why did I have to see her die, and why couldn't I do anything? But despite the despair I felt I stayed strong for her. I pressed up to her and licked her as her breaths got shallower and shallower, as her hand stroking my head got weaker and weaker. She had taken care of my family for seven generations, the least I could do was stay with her in her last few minutes.
