Rain and Jason ran down the narrow, dark tunnel. All around them, engravings and graffiti on the abandoned subway's walls displayed humanity's art; depictions of love, hope, philosophy and crude genital outlines were momentarily lit as the pair rushed past them, deeper into the darkness. With every breath, every step and stumble, they listened for sounds of pursuit. "Here!" exclaimed Jason, breathing heavily. He aimed the flashlight at a large, forked crack running from the vaulted ceiling toward the ground. Inside the fork a hand outline in purple spray paint could be seen, made in the same fashion as could be seen in ancient caves around the world. In the palm of the hand was a stenciled triforce symbol in the same color. Stepping off the rails, they approached the strange picture, making their way over and around the litter and debris that evidenced the tunnel's prior use as a shelter from the attacks. Rain moved to a hole formed by a piece of concrete that had broken out on the right side of the forked crack and reached inside, grasping a short section of exposed rebar in the gap and pulling with all her weight. Slowly, the slab moved out as if it were a drawer, moving on a salvaged set of rails on the other side. Jason's flashlight showed a tattoo of clouds and raindrops on her arm, muscles tensed and defined, as she strained against the weight of the door. As soon as the gap was large enough, Rain slipped inside, then took the pack from Jason as he passed it in and followed her. Jason moved the flashlight over the room they were now in. Immediately behind the door was the rail system that allowed the slab to move in and out; beyond that was a mural against the back wall, depicting events in an extremely colorful and vivid palette. The room was otherwise almost completely empty. Rain set down the pack and grasped a handle on the inside of the door they had just come through, pulling until the slab was back to it's former position. "OK, let's get started," Jason said as he began going through the pack, taking out a digital camera and an additional flashlight. Rain turned her attention to what they were here for: the mural. Spread over the length and height of the long wall, the incredibly detailed artwork showed many shapes and figures, most of them in conflict with each other. Rain saw a linear time progression from left to right: the rise of powerful corporations, the acquisition of each, one by one, by the largest corporation, AllCorp, which swelled in size and importance until it was more powerful than any government. How that corporation invested trillions in exploring every avenue of science to exhaustion. The rise of the Altered, and the havoc unleashed when some of the Altered rebelled against their creators, using the unnatural gifts and powers given them to escape and aid those oppressed by AllCorp's iron grip on the world. The devastation as AllCorp's army bombarded the city because of the rebel Altered headquartered there. Now it depicted the room they were in with a bearded man surrounded by white cubes, painting the mural and then sealing the door. Then it showed more. "All set," said Jason, swiveling the camera on a tripod. "Let's get a panorama of this thing and get somewhere safe to analyze it." Rain nodded slowly and turned away from the newest end of the mural without studying it. She'd have time later, and didn't want to be distracted from focusing on survival and getting out of danger once they left. She moved out of the camera's field of view, over to the darkest corner, and shone the extra flashlight on the mural to give the camera the light it needed. As she shifted in position, her foot tapped a sealed plastic canister. Stooping to retrieve it, she flipped her hair out of the way of her eyes, revealing that one-third of her throat, face and scalp were bald and scarred on the left side; the same side as her arm tattoo. Holding the flashlight up to the small, transparent container she found it to be full of sugar cubes. Wrinkling her brow, she tossed the container back into the corner. Maybe the old man had simply been a deluded crazy person instead of the powerful Altered that he claimed. Still, he had put on a pretty good show of foresight before they parted ways. Rain refocused the flashlight on the mural; their plan wouldn't change now: get a copy of the mural and get to safety. That's all that mattered right now. Jason panned the camera over the mural several times, directing Rain where to aim her flashlight for best exposure. Eventually satisfied with the result, he began packing the things back into the pack. They had been down here for half an hour; the next patrol would be along in the same amount of time. Rain handed Jason the extra flashlight and stepped away, moving to the very end of the mural, where a small figure was depicted with some text underneath. Jason's flashlight was focused on the pack, which made it difficult for her to see what it said. "Good to go," said Jason, closing the last zipper and shining the flashlight toward Rain. "Let's get moving." Rain froze in place. Now fully illuminated, the figure and text were clear to see. A female, with hair missing on the left side of her head and a tattoo on her left arm, was in an action pose, facing off against a menacing AllCorp T.U.R.F. battlebot. Underneath, in neat, clear capital letters the artist had written: "SHE WILL DETOY THEM ALL." First part of my first ever prompt response! This is my first draft, forgive my errors, but also give me the feedback!

Now You See Me Today was the day Jerin did what he did everyday. He woke up, turned the TV on, and caught a bit of the local news. "Good morning Arnaville! In local news, more home burglaries in the Candish area. Please remember to lock your doors and be vigilant for any suspicious activity. Here are five sketches and screen stills created from video surveillance in victim's homes. If you recognize any of these people, please call the police department's number which is on-screen." Jerin smiled and thought to himself, "Ha, 5 individuals shown, and there of the pictures are me. I guess my simple disguises are working well." He put his headphones in and left for his jog. He didn't always take the same route as he used it as part of casing good prospects, but he always passed through the same area of his neighborhood on the way out. Of course, he ruled out any of these homes for working, but he always noticed that one home in particular was especially enticing. No visual security implementation, 1960's design, and of course, no dogs. He had never even seen the owner and assumed it must have been a part-time home for someone. Maybe it was a parent's home who's in a nursing home now. The draw of the home was a visible set of jewelry not at all obvious to anyone except a trained eye. Through the thinning bushes of winter on the first floor's bedroom they were visible through bay windows. Jerin had grown confident in his abilities, and decided he could bend his own rule. Tonight, he was taking an easy hit. Making his way home after the rest of a regular jog, he formulated a simple plan of entry. He let himself into his home and took a nap. - 14 hours, a few meals, and a movie later, Jerin put his face on and left for his solo job. Her arrived at the house in the same exact condition he had seen it every other day. Regardless to the obvious lack of any presence, he stayed routine in his precaution as it had become second nature. He surveilled the surrounding area and surreptitiously moved the the back side of the house where he pulled out his lockpicking kit and quickly made work of the back door. He was in the kitchen. It was nondescript with nothing of note, and he continued to make his way to the bedroom with his silent footfalls in handmade supple leather shoes. Everything was going so easily. The door to the room was open, and he found the jewelry presenting a necklace of pearl on top. He put his hands, which were cloaked in thin cloth gloves, on the necklace but could immediately tell they were fake. He opened the box, and it was filled with plastic trash imitation jewelry. Usually imitation jewelry was not presented in such a way of pride, so Jerin was a bit shocked by this. Having already changed up his routine a bit, he decided he felt a bit confident and was going to do a quick check for anything else of value in the home. He was sure no one was here, and if there was anything he had learned about the generation that bought and lived in homes kept in this traditional way, it was that they hide their jewelry in the closet, so he walked to the nearby walk-in. Upon opening the door, Jerin sees that it's actually a staircase leading up. Intrigued, he silently crept up until his head peered just over the floor of the room. It was dark up here, but he could discern that the room was an art studio of some sort filled with canvases. Almost certainly there was nothing of value, but seeing as no one was around and the nearby cot was empty, he produced his compact flashlight and clicked it on to scan the area. Jerin froze. Of about 50 visible canvases, he was on all of them. Many of him jogging..... many of him at home..... and many of him at work.

"You cheating bastard" St.Peter stared at me as the queue of the dead grew exceedingly long. A great presence of light floated above him and without any words I knew I was safe. "Okay, 12 it is. Follow John over here and he'll set you up with the Veil" I cautiously followed "John" over to a wall covered with black robes. One of them stood out as being special, it had a yellow glow to it and seemed to fly on to my shoulders. It lightly descended over me. I sat it the darkness until an unknown force sent me out into a light. " ..... So what your saying is you remember the moments right before your birth, that's all I can interpret. It's just a weird dream, maybe you want another baby, or perhaps afraid of death. Talk to me tomorrow if you remember anything else" I walked out of the therapist office and on to the rocket pad where my ride was waiting. It wasn't exactly the greatest visit. Oh sure, I found my IQ had doubled in the past year and the therapist offered me all his wealth by me asking about his carpet but I was still unsure of my dream. The asteroid belt was particularly beautiful at this rotation. It's one of my favorite sights on the trip from Europa to Phobos. It's a bit of a long trip, 10 minutes, but who am I to argue. I know my place in Solar society. I was born the child of the Duke of Ganymede. Through deft arranging I attained the affection of the Empress of Neptune. The marriage happened within hours of meeting her. At that point I was a few diplomatic steps from becoming the first pick for the Secretary of the SUN. The ship landed on the footsteps of the Phobos division of the Martian Federation. I had a meeting on Space-Time disarmament. I also had to give a speech on the pedestal of the Deimos memorial. Deimos, once the culture capital of Mars had been attacked by a Pluto planetarist movement by a Space-Time bomb. The dimensional interference led to a Pandemic of cross-universal tumors. I had been effected but I got the extremely rare strain that advances brain power. Thus the doubling of IQ. With my increased intellect I was able to find loopholes in the SUN manifesto that basically allowed me to keep my position indefinitely. That's where I've been. I'm kinda a celebrity. Mars, with it's democratic republican government, sees me as a voice for stability and peace. Jupiter, as the son of two half-Deity leaders in the monarchical society, worships me. Neptune sees me as the brains of their aristocracy. Uranus, with their typical proletariat nature, hails me the defender of the worker. Lastly Pluto..... hates me, but I guess you can't win them all. After the speech I returned to my ride. I had a lunch planned at SUN headquarters on Mercury. As simply the bureaucratic hub of the system, there are no permanent residents. As I approached the SUN an emergency signal appeared on the display. It said an unknown gravitational force had been founded and was dragging the ship toward it. I looked out the window to see a gray sphere getting larger and larger. I blacked out. "Hey guess what bastard. New laws have been put in place nullifying any extra dices. In order to return balance we set both rolls to 0. Welcome home."

Warning: Half Life fanfiction ahead They say Gordon Freeman doesn't talk. And they're mostly right. I don't talk. Not to them, anyway, and not since the Incident. I have no idea why they insist on calling it an Incident. That makes it sound like someone, I dunno, miswired the coolant system and one of the tanks blew, not like they supercharged a giant quantum physics manipulation machine and the entire space-time continuum blew. More than that, though, I also have no idea why everyone insists on calling ME either the hero of the day or the devil incarnate. All I did was push a button and move a cart, and then not get killed. And then I disappeared for twenty years. A fat lot of good I've been doing humanity this whole time. But that's not the point either. When I took my job at Black Mesa, I was your average nerdy scientist, and I thought myself incapable of ever harming another living being. I felt there was an inherent goodness in all life and given a chance it could manifest itself. I was what you might call a bleeding-heart. Then I beat my first headcrab to death with my crowbar and saw Carl get headraped by another one, and my heart began to bleed out. By the time I had finished defendingescaping from Black Mesa, there was no blood left. Only ice. You have one chance, I'll tell you now. One chance to prove to me that you're on my side. You blow it, this is my world, and my world has no use for you. I am not proud of the ruthless machine I've become, and I wish I didn't have to be it. But my enemy was the one who flipped the switch, and until every last one of them is gone from this dimension, the switch is locked, the power's on, and all you can do is hang on for the ride. end Half Life fanfiction

Freddie and Helen Kissinger had lived on 15 Elm Street in the small town of Nottingdale, Indiana, for the last forty-five or so years of their lives. Freddie was a school principal at the local elementary school, Helen taught music at the same school. Freddie had advanced cirrhosis of the liver that was expected to be untreatable at his age, and Helen had been coughing up blood from the tears in her stomach lining that had come up as a result of some parasitic infection or another. They were ready. Sort of. Helen squawked from the bed, " Did you leave the letter for the kids? " Freddie quavered, " Yes, dear, it's behind the screen door. " " What about the dog? " " The dog died two years ago. " " Leave some cookies out on the porch for the kids when they stop by. " " I did at noon. " " What-what about the garden? " " Helen, who gives a shit? We're going to die. " It was a beautiful day outside. The petunias swayed in perfect formation, the sun beat down through the windows of the little isolated house on the lonely road coming out of town. Freddie kicked the dog on the way upstairs, with his sleeping pills in hand. Four of them would kill an adult human, and Freddie wasn't exactly sure if either of them still qualified as either of those things. He wore his dress blues, while Helen wore her Sunday best. He had to coerce her into taking off the plumed hat before she settled down. He gave eight pills to her, and eight to himself. Little nuggets of death lying in the dusty bowl of his time-worn palm. He was ready, and looking at Helen, his wife of sixty-three years, he knew she was ready too. They mouthed the words together. One. Two. Three. Freddie palmed the pills. They lay clutched in his hand, and he sighed and leaned back as if he had done something momentous. He stuffed them under the covers. He lay down and waited for his wife to die. Fifteen minutes later, he heard his wife's breathing slow. It was time. He carefully got out of bed. He didn't have cirrhosis. He just drank a lot and hated his wife. He looked outside. He was ready. He stepped out of the room with a boundless energy he hadn't felt since he graduated high school. He clattered down the stairs and clicked his heels. Suddenly, " YOU DICKLESS BITCH, I KNEW YOU DIDN'T TAKE THOSE PILLS. " Fuck. He grabbed the shovel and went upstairs.

"You ever seen anything like this before Agent Emerson?" the young Sheriff asked. "No. Nothing this," Emerson paused, "savage." The face of the corpse had been smashed open like a rotten watermelon. They had found the gore covered claw hammer a few feet away from the corpse in the brush. "This was personal. Help me cut the rest of his shirt away." They cut the blood stained shirt that used to be white, off of the body, then placed it into a large plastic evidence bag and sealed it. The Sheriff gasped when he saw the man's bare chest. Faces of women were tattooed across the man's torso. Each portrait perfectly capturing their likeness. Beneath each tattoo was a name. Beth, Amber, Tiffany, Candy, Emily, Karla, Jeanne, Jess. Emerson took photos of the tattoos as he worked his way around the corpse. As he got to the shoulder he realized the arms told a story of their own. A length of chain was tattooed around the bicep, a cheap one use camera, a stained mattress, a ball gag, knives of various sizes, a meat hook. With each photo Emerson took, the pieces began to fall into place. "How many women are there Sheriff?" "Thirty three." Damn. More than we had estimated. "But there's space cleared for at least one more," the Sheriff said pointing at a freshly shaven patch of skin. "Someone fought back. Search the woods there's a survivor!" Agent Emerson said stepping away from the corpse. Emerson found the trail quickly. Broken twigs and branches led him deeper into the woods. He would have walked past the small brown log cabin tucked into a thick growth of trees if he hadn't heard a low buzzing sound. The old wooden door was slightly ajar, Emerson drew his pistol and pushed inside. The cabin smelled like wet rot and butchered meat. Bile rose in his throat, not because of the smell, but because he knew what it belonged to. Floor boards creaked underneath his feet as he walked toward a closed door on the back wall. With each step the buzzing grew louder. He pressed his shoulder against the door and took a deep breath. Gently he pushed the door open holding his pistol at the ready. A young woman sat in a folding metal chair, tattoo gun held in her hand. "Miss, I'm Special Agent Emerson. I'm here to help you," Emerson said calmly lowering his pistol. She lifted her head, her wide blue eyes met Emerson's, they were a mixture of fear, confusion, and anger. "Why do I need help?" she asked genuinely perplexed. Emerson took a cautious step forward and held his hand out for her to take. "Just come with me please, it's not safe here." She nodded, dirty strands of blonde hair fell into her face. "Where did this come from?" she asked Emerson turning her arm so he could see it. The large portrait of a man stared at Emerson from the woman's forearm. Although Emerson had never seen the man before he knew exactly who he was. - Thanks for reading! Check out rWritten4Reddit for more stories!

The flickering of the dim florescent lights illuminated the room as Thalia stared with emotionless eyes at the ceiling, while the ticking of a clock sounded in the distance. She couldn't remember how long she had been there, and she lost all interest in figuring it out. Nothing seemed to matter anymore, ever since he was taken from her. " 23,996..... 23,997...23,998.... 23,999...24,000. " Thalia sighed " There are 24,000 holes in the ceiling. " She whispered to herself, with a momentary lapse of sanity uncontrollable laughter bubbled up escaping her lips. The episode lasted for several minutes before subsiding into a soft sobbing, they had been so close to fleeing the country. " Oi! Up with you, time to see the Doctor. " The asylums guard demanded banging on the visitation window. Thalia's bitten, bloody nails dug into her mattress gritting her teeth. Sitting up she swung her legs over the side of the bed. Raising her hands above her head she stood up stretching her stiff muscles, she could feel the burn gaze of the Guard scanning her naked body. " Hurry it up would you, the Doctor has requested you showered and groomed before you see him. " He grinned with a crooked smile, what was left of his teeth blackened and decayed. Thalia walked out the door he held. She passed a long hall of rooms that resembled her own, male and female alike and everyone stir crazy and nude. Women's screaming muffled by the padded rooms and men punching or banging their heads against the hard stone wall. She walked through the dark shower room and covered her stinging eyes as the motion sense lights blinded her. The guard walked in behind her and turned on the hot water; striding to a cabinet he unlocked it pulling out a bar of soap, washcloth, towel and razor. Thalia reached out her hand expectantly, the guard's expression morphed into a dangerous glare. " You best be putting those hands at your sides darling, new rule. You stand there and keep your mouth shut while I bath you. The last bitch tried to slit my throat with a razor, I'm not falling for that shit again. " Thalia nodded turning her back to him stepping into the welcoming spray of the hot water, she moaned she had since forgotten what it felt like to shower. Turning around she saw the Guard's impatient glaring, her shoulders slouched stepping out of the water towards him. His glare extinguished, lust sparking in his dark brown eyes as he skimmed her body. Wetting the washcloth, he lathered a generous amount before slowly taking the soapy cloth to her skin. Closing her eyes, she thought back to the first time she had really made a connection with Him, after her chip malfunctioned. Gray clouds swirled in the sky, lightning flashed illuminating the street in 3 second intervals. They had just successfully pulled off their first supply run, avoiding the Canadian forces that patrolled the streets at night. They brought their car to a slow stop in front of their camp in the middle of the woods, where they had built a cabin with others like them. Others whose chips had malfunctioned, those who were aware of the corrupt society the word was becoming. He hopped out of the truck excited about the spoils they had acquired. " Thalia! You were amazing, I have never seen anyone handle the husks the way you did! They thought you were one of them. " " Oh stop it Jeremy, it was nothing. " Thalia blushed starring at her feet shyly. He stepped closer to her tilting her chin up to look into his eyes. " I'm serious. Don't sell yourself short, Thalia you are the most amazing woman I've ever met. " He whispered stroking her cheek with his thumb, Thalia gazed into his glacial blue eyes and her heart seem to pound in her throat. " You...really think so? " She asked hesitantly making no effort to pull away from him. Nodding Jeremy put his hands on either side of her face and leaned in pressing his lips to hers. Thalia melted into him winding her arms around his neck deepening the kiss. His tongue swept across her bottom lip requesting entry, she parted her mouth slightly her tongue darting out to entwine with his passionately. " Hey! Are you even listening to me? " The guard demanded snapping his fingers in front of her face. Thalia blinked a few times snapping back to reality. " Huh? " She asked confused looking up at him. He huffed annoyed shaking the towel out in front of her. " I said dry off damn it before we're late. The Doctor doesn't like to be kept waiting. " He repeated throwing the towel at her, she began drying herself as slow as she possibly could just to piss him off more. Once she was dry he pointed her in the direction they were headed and she walked in front of him like instructed. How had the world gotten so fucked up? Thalia thought her bare feet thudding on the linoleum floor. Damn the scientist who invented the chip. Research plans were discovered that dated back 50 years of the chip's design. The chip was designed to be implanted into the human brain that shut off a person's free will, and was replaced by programming that controlled every aspect of a person's life. The United States had been secretly taking over the world, one Canadian at a time. The chip was made to make people obey the government's commands, to take up arms to infiltrate other countries for world domination. It 2016 was the year of the new President, when the United States had turned into a tyranny. The people were given a false sense of security by the Prime Minister of Canada, warmly welcoming anyone who wished to escape. Little did they know it was a trap, lured into the main testing ground for the chip. This wasn't the first time she had been experimented on, when she first entered Canada with her parents she had been implanted though she didn't remember how. Thalia had subconsciously been aware of the chip's programing without being able to do anything about it, that was until Jeremy came along. It was Jeremy that helped bring her consciousness forward, destroying the functionality of the chip giving Thalia control over her body again. Her heart thudded painfully in her chest when she thought of him. He was the love of her life, and she'd never see him again. She was meant to spend the rest of her days as a lab rat, while the " doctor " tried to figure out how to prevent the sub conscious regaining control over the body. Thalia neared the end of the hallway, she squared her shoulders and marched into the testing room. She stopped on the yellow line like she had been instructed to many times, glaring daggers into the back of the man responsible for all her heart ache. The man leading the chip epidemic, the one who prodded in her brain constantly trying to break her and find answers. The guard cleared his throat announcing their arrival, the " doctor " pivoted in their direction his glossy white lab coat whipping around him. With a huge grin he strode over to them, his black dress shoes clonking on the cement floor. He stroked the side of her cheek, turning her face left and right inspecting her. " Hello Thalia, glad to see you've recovered from last week's procedure. " That wide smile void of all emotion remained plastered on his face. With eyes that matched his own she glared up at him " Hello, Father. "

There's no way Terrence could tell how long this existence had plagued him. Days? Weeks? Hard to know when every few seconds an alternate universe presents itself; shocking his senses, catapulting any awareness he has into a sea of confusion, and damaging the reputation of, if only for a moment, his parallel self by noticeably profound bewilderment. Ironically, his curse is his parallel's advantage: Invariably, every alternate reality Terrence finds himself in, the people around him begin to question him and ask why he is behaving so oddly. Without an answer, his parallel self probably looks like a complete moron. Then Terrence blinks out of it. Such is his life though, since he woke up some time ago and found himself hopping from one universe to the next. He figured a worm hole must have somehow found him and transported him to these alternate realities, or something to that effect. What else could explain this phenomena? He kept waiting for the right universe to blink into..... but alas, each one had eluded him. Most of them were scary, dreary, or unrecognizable to his understanding of life. While most appeared miserable, the few that seemed tolerable or even good never provided him the implements to stop this horror. He estimated he'd seen 100,000 universes by now. But this one looked right. He blinked into a luxury home, surrounded by family members running about the large mansion. Everyone looked exactly the same and his family seemed generally similar their home was perfect and the backyard even had a pool! Terrence stretched his eyes open and started searching as furiously as he could. His mother questioned him, "Terrence! What on earth are you looking for and why do you have that look in your eyes?" "I need a knife Mom, NOW!" Looking frightened, Terrence's mother left the room, presumably to find Terrence's father. She called to him, "Stay there!" Terrence's eyes were starting to sting, this was the longest he'd lasted without blinking and his eyes desperately needed to close. But he willed them open. He grabbed onto a sharp paring knife and found a reflection. Carefully he outstretched his right eyelid. He cut it off. The pain was immense, but the focus he had committed to keeping his left eye open was all the distraction he needed not to pass out. He outstretched his left eyelid. One quick swipe and he was free! In pain, of course, but free! Terrence wiped the gushing blood from his eyes and executed the familiar muscle movement of blinking: he was still there! In this luxury home! Where he knew his parents and siblings would be, at the very least. He called for his parents to bring him to a hospital. "Mom, Dad! I'm hurt! I can't explain why, but please bring me to a doct Terrence was gagged and thrown to the floor. Between spaces of the blood in his eyes he could see his father and brother tying him up. His mother was looking at him, undisturbed, and his sister was entering something into a small computer tablet. "What's going on?" he tried to mouth through the gag to no avail. His father and brother picked him up and started shoving him towards the basement. They went down several flights of staircases, easily the deepest basement Terrence had ever encountered, when he saw the most terrifying thing he had ever seen: dozens and dozens of bloodied bodies, all tied up. Some were wriggling, some lay motionless. A few were trying to scream through their gags just as Terrence was now. This was not the most terrifying aspect, however. No, what curled Terrence's stomach was that all the bodies were..... him. Nearly one hundred duplicates of him, all with severed eyelids. Some standing, some lying down, some dead. All bound at the hands and feet, all with missing eyelids. The father and brother threw him into the pile. Terrence looked at the head of the stairs, the light from the kitchen shining down the long staircase. He saw himself, free, with eyelids, calling down to his brother and father, "Dad, Jay, there's another one in the backyard now. He's using the hedge trimmers to cut off his eyelids. We have to get him!" Terrence watched as his father and brother ran up to meet his doppelganger. Terrence looked around at his other doppelgangers. He wanted to be away from this hell, from this nightmare. He tried to close his eyes, but he could not.

30 Years ago, I had left the tribe I was now about to see again. Isolated in the depths of the jungle, which was becoming smaller every week, they were unique in many ways. They valued intelligence more than strength and had their own little strategy game - a mixture of go and mancala. Their heroes were the ones who could get lots of food for the tribe while barely lifting a finger. They did not value technology much - only had a shrug when I showed them a knife, explained guns to them, or such. But when I taught a few of them how to read and write, they got much more interested - though mostly in things concerning biology, chemistry, and such. They were really clever - quickly managed to produce their own soap after reading about it in one of the books I brought along with me. And after the first such successes, everyone wanted to learn to read, and everyone tried out everything in the books, often with funny, and sometimes with scary results. But they quickly learned to be careful when things became dangerous. I left the tribe once every week or so, and brought more and more books - all areas of science, at first simple books like encyclopedias and school books, in the end the most prestigious affordable scientific literature. When I went back home, I made sure they'd get the most important published papers - in full detail, as I knew they were already past the pop-stuff. For a few years, I received a letter every once in a while from one of the kids I taught how to read and write, with funny stories of their newest exploits. Later, when she married, the letters became less, and more about herself, her feelings, and her relations. She mentioned how grateful everyone was for the books and journals. Not much more. Now that I was a pensioner, I wanted to see what had become of them. So I traveled to them. I was greeted with a lot of laughter and friendliness. There were some comments how much I had changed, which sounded strange, but I couldn't really sort them in. The kids I had taught how to read and write were now grown ups - but looked more like 20-somethings than the around 40 year olds they should be. There were a lot of others I didn't recognise at first - all of them looked as if they were 20-somethings, except the kids and youth. They still despised technology to some degree - living in simple but now very big huts. They also showed me the labs each of them had. Some of them in tents inside their huts, apparently to keep them clean. I didn't know what they did in those labs - they were not fooling around and showing off like they did when I left. Nor was it a big thing for them to talk about. Only when I recognised one of the strangers did it occur to me: the woman, a mother of two of the children I taught, and who I had liked a lot back then, had not changed the slightest bit. I looked her up on my computer, where I had stored digitised copies of the photos I had made back then. I showed her the picture. I asked her whether it was her mother, not wanting to believe what I saw with my own eyes. Until I realised it was undeniably the same person. Relationships were in flux in this tribe. And so she stayed with me. But when I wanted to kiss her on the evening of the second day, she held me back. She led me to a section in a large tent in one of the larger huts which looked like an operating room. She asked me to lie down. They gave me something which made me fall asleep. The next day, when I woke up, I felt really good - full of energy, like after a really good night's rest when I was 20 years younger. I couldn't see much of a difference in my body, except that my skin seemed to be a little tighter, and some scratches and other blemishes had gotten less. I asked what had happened, and they were astonished that I was unaware. Didn't I send them all the books with all the knowledge which they applied? Over the next few days, my skin got elastic again, my eyesight and hearing went back to what they were in earlier times, and even my brain felt quicker. And then the shocking parts began: I could hear distant people talk when I paid attention, feeling my ears move a little to focus the sound into my hearing channel. I could make out leafs on trees in distant mountains when the weather was clear. I somehow knew which direction was north at any time. And when a fog came, I knew exactly which direction the sun was - because I could see the polarisation of the light. Every day, I discovered new abilities within me. It was like finding out how to move a muscle you never knew you could control. Or like seeing color for the first time. A small black dot formed on my forehead - I had barely noticed it on the darker skin of the tribe. And thought it was an ornamentation. But it enabled me to see longer electromagnetic waves - turning the milky way into a bright spectacle, making the far away cities look like fountains of light when watching them from a mountain, and making my phone glow with every call I made when I was near a cell tower - the closest of which was a day's journey from the tribe. It also gave all the humans a little glow from their heat. Then, when my body looked barely 30 years old, the skin modifications which I had seen on the tribespeople, stripes on the chest, appeared on my body, too. Everyone was happy seeing them, while I was puzzled what they would be good for. Eventually, some kids of the tribe led me to a nearby lake. They told me to dive, some of them leading the way. When I was under water, I realised I could hold my breath longer than expected. And when the oxygen level went down enough that I thought I should get up again, the stripes on my chest opened up and started filtering water! I could move my lungs, and felt that I had something like a water sack between the lungs and the ribs, filtering oxygen out of the water. Then one of them spoke. While under water. His speaking sounded different, but was understandable. It wasn't caused by air moving out of the lungs, but by a new muscle close to the voice cords, which would vibrate against the water like a speaker against the air. And I could do it, too! - after some trying. They had houses in the lake. Their tribe was at least twice as big as I thought. The lake also had a very deep cave, which apparently was a mine providing a few useful minerals. An underwater river connected the cave to another lake further up a nearby group of hills - which was also the reason why there was always enough oxygen in the lake. A feat of brilliant natural re-engineering, as I was told right then. I thought about what would happen if anyone found out about all their achievements...

"They seem to be nice people, Fred. I'm sorry that I didn't believe you. " , muttered Dilip as he walked towards the open lawn outside the room after dining with the royal family of the tribe," I should've came here a long time ago. I apologize I didn't trust you." "It's okay, Dilip. " , Fred replied with a graceful smile, "Who would have believed that I found an isolated tribe in these dense rainforests of Slavia. And that these people are more advanced than our race." "How did you learn their language?" Fred looked into the sky," I was searching this place for two years. My dad found them but when he returned, he died in the plane crash. I tried telling about the tribe he found to the people but they always ridiculed me and called me a daydreamer because I only had as proof, some letters, my dad had written me which everybody called fiction." he sighed," But I knew that one day I'll find this lost tribe. When I met them, they also treated me with respect and love, unlike my expectations. They speak Chyurda. Initially, we tried to understand each other by facial expressions and signs and hand movements. They are pretty smart. I also developed a fair understanding of their culture and language." The tribal leader came out to the lawn and gestured a calm smile towards both the guests. He said," Ded ra reda sra kuud?" "What is he asking? " , Dilip asked out of curiosity. "Did you liked the food? " , Fred translated, "After spending so much time with them. I feel one of them." "Tell him, I'm blessed to honor His Majesty's presence." Fred looked towards the tribal man and spoke with a gratitude, "Ra'k brakkad su rumur aeuir vrakamca." The tribal leader looked happy with his hospitality and went back to his stone room. "I thought about what you said, Fred, these people are more advanced than us not at macro-technologies but micro-technologies. One of them escorted me to one of their labs where they can literally program the features of a new sapling using their computer-type machines. Maybe they were isolated for such a long time because they were more focused on exploring at micro scale than the macro scale. Together they and us will revolutionize the biotechnology industry." Dilip glanced at the sun as it went beyond the horizon.

The breeze carried the scent of rust with it. Rust and flowers. Two tired feet at last rested in the grass. It nestled around her toes, quietly tickling her ankles. The sky was large and barren today. She laid down. Corrosion and death had plagued the world. Everyone she had ever known was dead. People were tiresome anyhow, their mouths full of ulterior motives and brimming with subtext. Secrets, traditions, culture, and sex..... They never knew up until the very moment they destroyed one another that they were all, in fact, the same. No matter now. She closed her eyes. She was the last of humanity and grateful for it. We were a hateful breed. The day the silence came she was sure she was done for. It was night when the final attack was made but daylight halfway across the world where her tired feet laid to rest. The rage was launched twenty one miles south of her and landed with hateful accuracy. It destroyed everything in a blinding flash of white and dust. She prayed that it'd be the end of her torture - the end to her inexplicable existence and her even more unfathomable curse. She knelt as the white flash wrapped around her. She opened her arms to embrace it. Finally, peace. But peace was far from what the light brought. Searing pain tore through her entire being as she came to. Her skin and bones had shredded and melted into a viscous mound of sinew and sticky, bloody tissue. She saw only blackness and felt only pain. She had no mouth to scream. Weeks and weeks passed. Months. A year. She no longer knew how to tell time. Ever so slowly her cells regenerated. One by one proteins were reconstructed and reabsorbed. Thousands of times she felt her body dry to a brittle crumble before the rains came and rejuvenated her growth once more. Soon after a year and another rainfall she was able to open one eye. She blinked furiously and in a panic. She had convinced herself she had been in hell the entire time. She had rested, albeit in unquantifiable pain, thinking that there would be some semblance of an end at the end. She had no such luck. Her curse survived what human kind could not. She survived. Today the sky was barren but the grass was warm. It swayed and breathed with the wind. She had long since forgotten all the pain. Just as she had long since forgotten all the people. She lay there, forgetting everything she knew one by one. Memories faded into a blank canvas. Eyes closed, she cared not to think. Her skin lifted off into the breeze in weightless ashes. She never knew what she was. She never understood why she was. She'd never know that her existence was wrath and hate manifested into organic life. It would have been incomprehensible to any, even her. She was the last remnant of human emotion left behind by our kind. The only thing that survived us. But now, after all this time, there was nothing left to forgive. So she forgot, and faded out of existence.

My gaze stayed glued to the ground. I trudged along toward the last of the evac ships. We would have had a chance - we had massively greater strength, more durability. In infantry combat we massacred them in droves. There was nothing we could do about the artillery, though. And when they launched that massive, final round - well, the whole planet shook. The planet of my ancestors, and their ancestors, and those before them. Gone. Under new management. I could hardly stand to leave Earth - I doubted any other planet in the galaxy would have its oceans, or lush forests. Some of us were staying, of course. Well hidden. They'd be ignored or unnoticed, and would probably adapt. I had nowhere to hide, however; I had no choice. A guard kicked me in the direction of the ship. "Get moving, stupid fucking dino. Earth belongs to the mammals now."

I felt the tug on my body. I hadn't felt that in ages. Slowly I felt myself dissipate through the lamp and out into the real world. Everything around seemed so strange, so different than the things I'd seen before. It made sense seeing as though the last time I had a master was a couple thousand years ago. The old, familiar look of shock and terror lit up the woman's eyes. My previous masters had always been men, so this was a first for me. I made my usual spiel and waited for her three wishes. " Hey, do you think I'm that stupid? " she asked. " You're going to twist whatever wish I make and then I'll be worse off than I was before. " At this I had to sigh. When will people understand that I want to grant them their wishes. I don't want to twist and mangle them to harm the person. " Miss, I'm not going to manipulate my wish. I'm not that kind of genie. " I wasn't very surprised when she didn't believe me. My last master didn't either and he attempted to bury me as far away from human civilization as possible, but someone must have dug me up. " You'll remain as my master until you use all three wishes or die, whichever comes first, " I said to her. She crossed her arms and looked me up and down. It didn't look like she believed me, but I saw the greed that I'd seen in others eyes sprout in hers and I knew she was going to give in. " I wish for ten dollars, " she said. I made a ten appear in her hand. It figures she would try to test her luck first on something supposedly safe. " Nice, " she said. " Alright, I still am not sure about you, but I think I'll go ahead and use my wishes. Actually, I think I came up with the perfect wish. " A smile crept upon her face and I knew something bad was about to happen. Anyone who thought they could game the system inevitably paid the price. " First, I wish to be the richest person in the world. Second, I wish to have another genie. " Her first wish was no problem. In the flash of an eye, her bank accounts filled with untold riches. Unfortunately, her second wish required summoning my brother, the only other genie in existence. His lamp appeared on the table next to mine. I watched as he came out of his lamp while I was sucked back into mine. Our lamps are supposed to hide themselves after each master, but my brother used his magic to pull me back out and keep me around for a few minutes. I found that I wasn't able to talk, though, only listen. " Wow, it worked, " my old master said. " Yes, you have three wishes, " my brother replied. " I wish for immortality, " the lady said. " Excellent choice, " my brother replied. " I also wish to become more powerful than any other human. " " No problem, " my brother said, a devious smile creeping upon his face. " And finally, " the lady said with a smile, " I wish for another genie to appear. " I had to rub my eyes when she said that. I knew she was already in deep with the first two wishes, but the last one sealed her fate. She definitely worded it wrong. I watched helplessly as my brother waved his finger in the air and worked his magic, all the while floating back into my lamp and being sent to some far off part of the world. It is because of my brother that genie's get a bad rep. I'm the nice one, though no one believes me, and those who do always seem to somehow find my brother as well and then make some ill-fated wishes. So, that's my story. Us genies can communicate while we are in our bottles, even when separated. My brother hasn't stopped laughing yet, although my old master hasn't found the humor. There use to only be two genies in the world, but now that she had been turned into one, there were three of us. The good news was that my brother had already burned his bridges with her, so it means that I might have a female companion after all of this time. The bad news is that I think that she will be worse than my brother. I don't think anyone will ever understand the plight of the nice genie. -163

It was odd that such a tiny hunk of metal felt so heavy in Davis'pocket. It was his ring (well, as " his " as anyone's could be), but where it used to be light, almost forgettable, now it hung like a weight from his neck, an albatross to bear. He fidgeted, uncomfortably, on the bench - his hand often darting to the pocket to make sure it was where he had left it, though he knew he could feel its every move against his skin - and eyed the time, nervously counting down the minutes. Almost five. Soon he'd know. He had wondered if today would be the day they'd get out late, if today would be ' his'day, but, just like the last painful, dragging, searing weeks, he sat in silence waiting for someone who wouldn't come. Maybe it was best to do like Sarah said... maybe he needed to move on. He couldn't make a difference sitting here, every day, never living. He couldn't make her proud. He knew, somewhere deep in the pit at the bottom of his stomach, that he'd never have a chance to, now. From beyond the door, he heard movement. Davis sat up, eyes darting around the room as if they had something to look to, and he strained his ears against the echoing, deafening quiet of the hallway. They were coming. Standing, Davis withdrew the ring, holding it in the crux of his hand. He spared a glance at it; it was a dull, tarnished bronze, his father's ring before him. Davis swung on the balls of his feet, side to side, waiting, this few seconds feeling a lifetime. As the doors swung open, there he was. Behind the leading line of journalists and groupies, each group vying for his attention more than the last; behind the bailiff in his starched, stark white shirt and tepid demeanor; behind his slimy, slick-haired lawyer and his overpriced suit, he stood. He was sharing a now-common story about the number of Enragement Rings he had been given over the last few months, bragging about the records he had broken, and was pointing to them, gold and shiny all, swinging from a makeshift necklace slung around his neck. As the group came upon Davis, they didn't seem to notice him until he and the man stood almost nose to nose. Davis wanted to accuse him of all the things he's done, all of the pain... just like the other fathers had done before him. Davis couldn't remember his name, though. Every thought now was of her. Willow. With a flick of the wrist, Davis'ring slammed into the man's chest with an imperceptible thud and, unseen, fell to the floor. As Davis raised the pistol his father had also given him, he managed to bark, " I want my daughter back you son of a bitch. "

I feel like I'm drowning in work. At times like this, I can't help but think back and ponder about how I came to hold this position. I stare with resentment at the placard sitting at the edge of my desk. Brian Colms - God of Oil - Divinity Corp. I took a position here at Divinity as an intern in my senior year. I was a political science major; simulated evolutionary engineering was nowhere near my radar as a potential career path. The opportunity at Divinity arose because I knew a guy that knew a guy. I figured it would be a good way to beef up my CV. Twelve years later, and I hate my life more than ever. I know what you're asking: "If this job isn't for you, why did you continue after your internship?" Fair question. Allow me to elaborate. Divinity is a leading innovator in the global evolutionary engineering sector. Basically, we create multiverses; simulations of millions of constantly evolving universes at a time generating thousands unique worlds that harbor simulated life and we harvest the technological outcomes of these worlds for real-world applications. When I began as an intern, I was tasked with cataloging a subset of hydrophobic substances. For the most part, the work was pretty minimal. In fact, the brunt of it had already been done before I got here. I simply had to keep an eye on the development of new oils as they popped into existence in each simulation. After graduation, I was looking for work. As luck would have it, Divinity was now hiring demi-gods to be in charge of its expanding oil sims. So I applied for the position and I got it. Initially, the job was similar to my work as an intern; some mineral oils here, a few triglycerides there. I couldn't understand why they wanted a person to take on this position full-time. But I wasn't complaining. The pay was decent and the work was manageable. So I stuck with it and gradually worked my way up the ranks over the years. As this area began to expand, so too did the workload, and I had to take on some interns, myself, to help get some things done. But it wasn't until my fifth year that things began to snowball out of control. I know the planet that was the source of it all. I know it well. It haunts my dreams. When I close my eyes, I see the architecture of their damned oil refineries with vividness. They use it daily; some of it for cooking and some of it for transportation. They wage wars for some of it. Entire political battles revolve around the stuff. Fucking Earth. For the previous decade that Divinity and other evolutionary engineering firms had been operating, never had a single simulation found such extensive uses for the stuff. But Earth had, and it was like they were addicted to it. When I realized what was happening, I tried to change the source code for the program to try to get them to use something else to drive their civilization. I gave them nuclear. Let one of the administrator gods deal with the issue. But they only used it as a deterrent to help keep their oil businesses running. I strengthened the coding of their wind turbines. Jim, the asshole God of wind could take care of it. Nope. Solar, I figured, would surely provide a strong enough incentive for them to switch. After all, it's pretty much what every simulated civilization as well as our own seems to gravitate towards once they realize the potential of it. The big-wigs at our solar division, Helios, could certainly manage that. But time and time again, the occupants of this planet found reasons to reject all of my alternatives. Sure, some portions of it managed to stick, but mostly, they were swatted away. It was as though the renewables I was offering them was water and they were all, well, oil. I've sent a formal request to my superiors about pulling the plug on Earth, but so far, they want to "wait and see what happens." I've asked them to hire more personnel, but they seem to think that I should be able handle it. So here I am, neck-deep in a viscous adversary from an anomalous world among thousands, that won't let me have a moment of peace. I hardly have time to see my family, anymore. I don't have time to get my personal affairs in order. If the higher-ups won't help me, then there's only one thing to do. A little climate change should mitigate the problem.

"Not even if you were the last man on the planet!" How many times have you heard that phrase? For someone who enjoyed the clubs of New Mombasa its something I heard a lot, but I never considered what that might actually be like. Lonely? Terrifying? Maybe even fun? Well when you've had 10 years to think about it while the population dwindles around you, it becomes a surprisingly peaceful time. In 3135 the global population had fallen to just 11 million people, and we had mostly given up. I shudder to think what the people of humanities peak in the 21st century would think of us now, the glorious human race defeated by a simple virus. Perhaps they would think less of us if they could see the great monuments we built, and the scenes in the streets as we celebrated our history. Ill never forget the great feasts of the early years when food was still plentiful, 11 million people across the world in song is a sound to behold. So. Our funeral. My task as the last of us. It seems wrong to have such a thing after so many years of joy, but how could we not mourn such fall. "Okay ready?" I gather all my composure, im preforming for one person but really, but I feel all of the eyes that ever watching me. "Yup, go for it!" "I know none of us were really religious but I had to addr..." She interrupts me impatiently "Get on with it already!" Shes still making jokes. I truly couldn't have asked for a better companion for the end of days could I. "Okay." Well here goes nothing. "To the creator, whomever you may be, I stand here today at the end our time. We have risen above the animals of this world and held dominion for thousands of years, and now we return it to them. While the land will reclaim much, our mark will never be expunged from it; our monuments stand tall and strong and our history is preserved forever. Should you look back upon us, please do not judge us by our actions. Our intention was pure, as were our hearts, we can only apologise and ask that you remember us. Troy dug his fingers into the rain-soaked soil, raking his broken body across the mud; his essence congealing with the Earth's. "Haha! COME OOOOON! Roll over and die like the dog you are! Aha!" Sergei's abrasive Russian accent rises above the clamor of the pattering rain. The two men to his immediate left chuckle in amusement. "Why do you keep trying? You're dead already, huh?" Sergei steps forward, leaving his colleagues behind. He scoops a tire iron from the ground and waddles towards Troy, his rotund form rippling with each stride. Troy whimpers as he hears the footsteps get closer. "Should have paid money back, Mr. Nealy." Raising the tire iron above his head, Sergei huffs a pig-like grunt as he brings it down full force on Troy's calf. The dull thud of metal on flesh is accented by the crisp crackle of a bone shattering. Troy screams out, his voice hoarse with agony. His body begins to shake, half from fear and half from shock. He tries dragging himself forward, but he can feel the bone in his leg scrape and stick into the mud. The pain is instant and horrifically sharp. He screams again, nearly passing out. "Just keel him already," one of the other men bellows in an ever thicker Russian accent. "Fine, fine..... no fun for Sergei." Sighing in disappointment, Sergei tosses the tire iron to the ground and takes his pistol out from under his trench coat. He struggles to pull the slide back as his fingers slip across the polished metal of his Baretta. Troy, still clinging weakly to consciousness, is suddenly snapped back to reality by the telltale metallic click of a hammer being cocked back. He knows his time is up. "Pleeeaaase..... I...... I have a f-family..." Troy's voice, barely a whisper, sputters through the raindrops coursing down his face. But Sergei is unfazed. He'd heard every desperate dying speech ever concocted, and he had lost the ability to empathize long ago. "Sorry, friend." He wasn't sorry. "This is what happens when you take from client and never give back." As Sergei trains his crosshairs on the back of Troy's skull, Troy employs the last of his strength to roll partially on his side, screaming, "For eight fucking dollars?!" A thundering gunshot ripples through the construction yard, nearly drowning out the rain. Troy's body goes instantly limp and ragdolls to the ground with a muffled squilch. His blood begins to form a crimson stream slowly meandering through the mud. "Eight dollars?" Sergei grunts to himself. "Fuck..... movie is expensive these days..."

"Do you have any road-crossing experience?" Steve the chicken bad been conducting interviews all day. His current applicant was a frog. "I have some, but really, it's a big part of my family," the frog replied. "They even made a video game inspired by my grandfather." Steve glanced down at the frogs resume, finding it lacking. He knew it was really going to come down to the final interview question. "And why will you be crossing the road?" The frog looked surprised by the question. "Why? Well, I suppose because it will be my job to." He was nervous. Steve stood and extended a wing. "Thank you for your interest, we will be in touch if you are chosen for the position." He wouldn't be calling the frog. Several roosters applied, a snake, a goose, and a few mice. None of them could answer Steve's question correctly. He had been doing this for years, and he needed to find a replacement. But how could he pick someone that couldn't answer the simplest of questions? The final applicant of the day was Jerry Buttercup, a small cat. His application showed that he grew up on the streets, and therefore had significant experience in crossing them. The interview went better than Steve expected. Jerry was the perfect replacement; he was aware of his surroundings, he had superb reflexes, and an air of mystery. Steve almost didn't want to ask him, but he knew he had to. It was far too important. "Alright, Mister Buttercup, I have one final question for you. If chosen for this position, why will you be crossing the road?" Jerry smiled, and reached for a pen and paper. He scribbled on it, and slid it across the desk, face down. Steve picked up the paper, smiled through his beak, and sent it through the cross-shredder. "You're hired, Mister Buttercup."

It was there again, the rabbit hole which ruled my dreams. Try as I might, I can never get to it. Every step I take pushed it a little farther away, a secret just out of reach. Tick, Tick. A ringing tick marked the rhythm of my walk. My heart pounded faster. Tick, Tick. It was the same tick I'd heard from the strange rabbit on that cool, Fall afternoon. Almost like the sound of a clock. But that was absurd, a rabbit with a clock? I must have been mad. Why would a rabbit need to tell time? The hole stopped its retreat. Adrenaline surging, I ran to it hurriedly. Tick... Tick... The ticks slowed down. Suddenly, my legs were pushing through some invisible lake, their progress slowed. Tick... I couldn't breathe; the urge to run spurs me onward, but I'm frozen in whatever trapped me. Only a few more meters and I could find out what's down the rabbit hole. I struggled in vain before snapping back to reality in a cold sweat. " Oh, rats! " It was the closest I'd been to seeing down the rabbit hole. Tick. Tick. The clock? Surely, my mind was playing tricks on me. Tick. Tick. There it was again, but this time accompanied by the sound of a quiet thump, and a small voice, " Oh, so very late. Maybe too late. " Fear invaded my entirety. Sneakily, I made my way out of the bed and towards the door, grabbing a heavy book on the way. Tick. Tick. I forced the door open. " AHHHHH! " Despite the shock evident in the rabbit's scream, there was no matching the surprise I felt. A look of uncertainty colored the rabbit's face before he dashed around the corner of the hall and out of view. Recomposing myself quickly, I chased after him. This must have been a dream, so I intended to explore it. It was raining out. The sound of each drop splashing against the cobblestone street helped to hide the hurried sounds of the rabbit, but I was too fast. The stones scraped my feet, and grime squeezed between my toes. My chest felt heavy, and my knees hurt from running. I was very tired for being in a dream. The rabbit darted into a shrub, then into the woods. I followed unwaveringly. I heard the rabbit up ahead, " Go back, Alice, it's too late! " There was no way I could turn back, he just didn't want me to get to the rabbit hole. My nightgown was soon torn by thorns and stained by numerous cuts before I burst into a clearing, finding the rabbit. He was slowing now, looking for something in particular. After getting his bearings, he darted towards a tree next to a stream, and disappeared. I knew where we were. My dreams were always from the other side, but I'd been in this field plenty of times. Excitement pushed me forward, now that there seemed to be no magic keeping me from my goal. The rabbit hole was dark. Some part of me urged me back, but it was only a dream. Why shouldn't I continue my adventure? How often did I get to hold a conversation with a rabbit? And I had to know why he made me listen to that infernal TICK! Even as I thought it, the sound echoed out of the hall. A single, solitary click. " Mr. Rabbit! I'm coming after you! " Ignoring his earlier warnings, I gathered myself up before crawling after him. The crawl soon turned into a fall, and I lost any sense of direction. Colors and laughter surrounded me. Strange, disembodied eyes watched my uncontrolled descent. As soon as I thought of what dream death might await the end of my fall, I entered a room of blinding light. I closed my eyes, expecting the worst. Instead, I felt myself slow and ungracefully land, face first, on a large box. Shaking off my embarrassment at being so uncoordinated in my own dream, I looked around. A whimper caused me to focus my attention behind me. The rabbit was there, but his eyes were teary, his nose running. My eyebrows narrowed as I wondered what was wrong. The box below me shook. Concerned and frightened, I looked down. The box was a deck of cards! The end shot open and cards as tall as lampposts flew out. It was hard not to smile, so silly was my vivid imagination. They swirled around me, only showing their backs, forming a circle around the box. A haughty laugh boomed through the room and I saw a door with a large face on it open. The cards landed, standing vertically, before they turned to reveal their faces. All red. " You're too late, Alice. " Her voice was shrill, and gilded with glee. There was no care or mercy in hers eyes. They scared me. I heard the rabbit begin crying behind me. This dream wasn't fun anymore. I wanted it to stop. " OFF WITH HER HEAD! " I want it to stop!

First contact had come when we least expected it. The world had been too busy, too active, it hadn't noticed the ships slipping in from the depths of space until they were already here. Sure, we thought there were aliens out there, but with the need for smart phone camera proof, the ease of internet debunking and the absurdity of all those UFO sightings we just hadn't thought they'd be coming here. We pretty soon picked up radio transmissions running to their ship as they picked up feeds from all over Earth. For over a month now they had sat up there watching, waiting, analysing. They had sent a small message letting us know they would make contact via computer to the United States President. We think they may have watched too many films but still..... They had remained very silent up until now. I was one of the very few reporters allowed in on this momentus day, the day humanity finally spoke to the rest of the universe. How many others were there, what knowledge and technology could they bring? Finally we weren't alone in the universe anymore. The screen on the President's computer fuzzed then patched through to a patchy image of a room and a face, it was definately a face. The picture started to move, the President opened his mouth to offer greetings and..... Laptop Battery Low. Automatic Shutdown. Call Ended. No one got their return number...

A mechanical eye was suspended in the sky, quietly hummed in solitude. In the distance, an orange sun set through a dusty haze. The sleek grey aluminum airframe ran through the irradiated, crisp air, far above the smoldering skeletons of a city. The MQ-15 was an prop-driven, solar-powered observational drone of a bygone era. Brought to service in an unlikely war, it became the unlikely evidence for proof that people were once here. The stressed vessel survived the great flashes that vaporized a civilization below. Periodically, the drone's solar powered batteries whined as they sent another bleep to satellites that hung above the sterile continent. In the distant vacuum of space, the eyeless prophet floated in the place where the blackness of night met the ashy hue of day. The satellites meticulously trawled through the PGP encrypted list of counterparts of manned bases on the ground and dispersed a request for orders. There was a lack of a response. No matter, they would continue onto their destruction, forever looking for a reply that will never come.

"Come close children, and listen." The children gathered around the withered man, even the older ones. They enjoyed the stories of Before. It wasn't often that they got to see the world Above. The radiation had toasted the land and what creatures remained Above were twisted husks of what they were, violent and aggressive. "Are you all seated? Good. I will tell a story that I haven't told before, of the Time Before and of a family and the struggles they dealt with." The children whispered excitedly among them, it wasn't often that they got to hear a new story. "There was a family, whose name was Griffin. There was a father and a mother and two sons and a daughter. They also had a dog they kept as protection from the many dangers that roamed in the land Before. The Father worked with nuclear energy to help power the world. He was the Provider for their family, similar to how your fathers are the Provider's for your families." This excited the children, to know that the people Before had parents who cared for their families too. "How exciting it must have been in the time Before," the said to one another, "I bet the father was a good Provider." "Hush now, be still," The old man said, "One day the Provider was on his way to his duties and he heard a song wafting through the air. It was an amazing melody and he knew that this would be the anthem for his family. He followed the noise and found the source. A radio speaker that was seated on the porch of a house he wasn't familiar with was playing the melody." "Excuse me, Elder?" A small boy from the back of the audience raised his hand. "Yes son?" "How did the song go?" the boy asked excitedly. "The song preached about the Great Bird is the Word and how we all shoud know of the Bird and his Word." the old man explained with great care. "Does that answer your question young man?" The boy nodded and sat down, excited to have learned the words and lesson in the song of the story. The Elder continued, "The Griffin man knew that he had to have this wonderful tune, so he did what was illegal and stole the radio with the Song in it. He ran and ran down the streets and through back alleys and taking twists and turns and doubling back to ensure that anyone who might have seen him would lose his trail. Before too long he made his way back home and placed the radio on his own porch, and played the song for all of his family to hear. The rest of the Griffin family came outside and all sat and enjoyed the pleasant soothing melody the drifted from the speakers of the radio." Here the man stopped and took a drink of water, and evaluated his crowd. It had grown now to include some adults and was much bigger than it was when he had started the story. "After about an hour of the Griffin family just sitting in peaceful quietness listening to this song a Mutated walked up the porch and before any one of the family could react, he struck the Provider in the face. Shocked the family scrambled up and stood ready to fight the Mutated. The Provider stood up and appraised the Mutated, and saw that it was a six foot tall chicken, and was very angry. Before the Griffin man could strike back, the chicken pulled hand cannons from his pockets and slew all the Griffins where they stood and took the radio and walked away." The man looked up and saw the shocked expressions from his audience. Normally his stories were light and humorous. Nobody was expecting a family to be slain. He saw the little boy in the back raise his hand again. The boy asked what the moral of the story was. "The moral is, don't skip your duties and you won't be attacked by Mutated. Now everyone, back to work."

Tom walked through the security check. It was a scrutinous check, but considering the power that he had as a weather forecaster, it was perfectly understandable. In countries that were more unstable, criminals often bribed and threatened weather forecasters. The ability to control the weather is one of the highest powers known to mankind, and a power that was once reserved for the gods. That power then became available through a college education. With the increasing number of students studying meteorology, the weather forecaster profession has become much more exclusive. On top of the physical check, forecasters also have to pass a mental check, both before they get the job and every month after that. In light of what has happened to Tom tonight, he probably would have failed. As he walked into the newsroom, he heard the doors behind him lock: another safety measure that left Tom uninterrupted. Although he had a relatively massive responsibility, his job was simple. Most days where sunny, farmers got some wet days, and Christmas got snow. Simple enough that a robot could have done it, but robots aren't meteorologists. " Good evening, my name is Tom and I will be your weather forecaster tonight. Tomorrow, the Orlando area will be experiencing another sunny day with temperatures around room temperature, whether you like it or not. " A tiny, familiar smile appeared behind the bulletproof glass, on the face of Tom's weather supervisor. Everyone hated that pun. " The air will have its trademark Orlando dryness, but there will be a storm in a certain area in the city. " Tom could feel the shocked gasps, coming from the mouths of the audience. " Yes, a powerful storm will roam the city tomorrow, thankfully localized to a small area, right above the head of a certain woman who decided to cheat on me. " Now the gasps had spread from the audience, to Tom's weather supervisor and producer. They'd probably start the lengthy process of entering the newsroom any moment now. " Yes, it's quite a dreadful storm. In the best case, it might mess with someone's hair-do, but everything here points to worse consequences. " As quickly as a hurricane, Tom's supervisor sprinted out of her chair, and Tom wondered when his fat producer would follow. " I'm also afraid that there will be quite the brutal hail, with each ball of ice being about the size of a key. This storm will take place above a certain red Toyota Yaris. I bet you viewers are wishing you had a garage right now. " Although the producer and supervisor where out of sight, he could hear them shouting and banging on the door, ready to storm the room, and subsequently fire Tom. " Lastly, be sure to bring your dog inside, because the monsoon period has arrived... in the backyard of Longbirch ave. 742. " " Thank you, and good night. "

She was in her late thirties, perhaps early forties with brown hair curled tightly as it cascaded down just past her shoulders. Her attire would suggest that she worked an office job, a white unblemished suit coat paired with a form fitting pencil skirt. Wealthy without a doubt, a stupendous way to start the day. I inched closer to her, pretending to be interested in a large ruby bracelet. Now was my time to shine. " My wife would absolutely love that, " I said hoping to pique her interest. " Her attention shifted slowly from a bright diamond necklace to the little girl in the stroller. " Oh yes, " she said bending over to pinch the infant's cheeks. As she slowly descended towards the face of her child, I did it. Quickly and quietly I reached my hand deep into the folds of her gargantuan purse. My hand seized a rectangle of leather, a wallet. As she straightened back up, my hand returned from the void that was this woman's purse and slipped the spoils into the right pocket of my pants. Too simple. Not wanting to stay longer than needed in the presence of this woman, I rocked on my feet a while longer, commented again on the appearance of the youngster, muttered a quick, " Have a nice day, " and walked casually down the street. As to not cause suspicion, I continued down the street looking for the right place to review on my success. There was a cafe about two blocks down that would do perfectly. As I neared the establishment I felt the adrenaline start to dwindle inside of me. So smooth. I unlatched the buckle that held the leather together, taking in the smooth feeling. As the full size of the leather was unfolded I examined the upper opening of the holder. The girl at the top of the page was a young blonde girl, about two years old, with bright blue eyes, the same girl who had been with the woman. Each day you'd pass me and offer a "good morning." I'd catalog the outfits you wore. Seventeen times I've seen you in the yellow and white sundress, three of those times your hair was up. Those were my favorite, I marked those days with a heart and a plus plus sign. The other fourteen times, your hair was down. Beautiful put not as pretty. It has been six months, nine days and give or take, five hours since you've worn it. The winter came, so I excused about four months worth of mock necks, pants and blouses, but it's now been more than six months. Six months, nine days, and give or take, five hours. Why aren't you wearing it? At first I decided you'd retired it, donated or otherwise lost interest. Supplanted it with maybe the lime green skirt and white blouse you seem so fond of these days. Never could I have imagined you were simply refusing to wear it, for thinking it made you appear anything but beautiful. Now I understand, shhhh...... If you try and scream it will only be worse. See here? In your closet? This is it. Why don't you wear it for me? Do you have any idea how that makes me feel? What do you have to say for yourself? They say the worse kind of pain is a paper cut, but they're wrong. This. What you've done to me. Imagined me some kind of monster. This, this is the worst kind of pain. I can not eat. I can not sleep. I've been banned from entering the building, from seeing you in any manner, let alone the dress I adore. I had a daughter, she loved me. She had a dress, just like this. She would be your age by now, and surely just as beautiful. Here's her picture, don't you see it? I see it. I love you. I had moved on, it was hard. My wife, my job at the time, I sacrificed it all but I moved on! DO YOU HAVE ANY IDEA HOW HARD THAT IS? I'm sorry. Stop sobbing. I moved on, I functioned again, her memory began to fade, and then you. My lovely dear, you strolled in wearing this. Do you see the picture? She looks just like you. But I know she isn't you. You are a monster, not me. This is torture. I know this will be hard to understand, but until you're gone I'll never really be whole again. Goodbye, princess.
