It's not so bad, having a dud power. I am a ward of FISH, the Federal Institute of Super-Humanity. We are the lucky ones, our guardians tell us: our powers were discovered when we were still young enough to contain them, before they destroyed us from within or turned us megalomaniac Super-villains. This remote valley of New Mexico is our only home. The Clairvoyants here predicted when and where we would be born, and then other supers whisked us away as various psychokinetics and reality manipulators worked to erase any memory of us on the outside, digital or organic. We were raised inside this compound, and slowly everyone came into their own, discovering their own brand of telekinesis or super strength or prestidigitation or transformation. Or well, almost everyone. "Oops." said Jenny, a thin wisp of a gal one grade below me. A gust of air knocked the soda of my tray over my clothes. I looked up, trying to show disgust instead of despair. "No harm no fowl," said Ryan, a handsome jerk with an intimidating build and icy grey eyes, "She'll just get another." I grumbled and wandered back to the soda machine, filling my styrofoam cup back up with stale cola. This is the the Superpower Mediation, Elimination, Limitation Learning center. Yup, FISH-SMELL. It's for the kids who just didn't make the cut, super powers like the ability to cry rosewater or grow orange body hair while singing Middle-English rotas. This place is where the powers that be put the young supers they wish they could tell, "Sorry we ripped you from your loving families for nothing, please enjoy this imitation of normal high school while we figure out how to reintegrate you into society," except the powers that be never apologize for anything. Even here, though, I'm the dunce. Jenny has aerokinesis, but it only works if she's right near an air conditioner on full blast, and Ryan has precognition, supposedly. As fair as I can tell, he can only predict events that are painfully obvious outcomes already. And I? I make free refills. No, I can't make any liquid come from nowhere. If I am offered a beverage, or buy one, and drink it all, I can make the same amount I got before come from the container I originally got it from without depleting it. If I drink it straight from the bottle it doesn't work. That's it. I take my tray back to the corner of the cafeteria and pull out my sketchpad. I'm used to lunches alone. I refill my mechanical pencil from the only box of leads I've ever bought and draw the mesas in the distance. I'm cross-hatching the shadows when I smell roses coming toward me. Ana. The freak with the rosewater tears I mentioned earlier. Ana is actually short for "Rosana" because our guardians have a sick sense of humor sometimes. "Hey, Faye, you got a sec?" I look up. Ana's eyes are bloodshot, and the fragrance is overwhelming. I sigh and put down my drawing. "Sure. What happened?" "Balthazar went rogue." Balthazar had classed into Super Elite Specialist Forces, just called'Elites' because SESF is unpronounceable. They were our opposites, kids with such glowing powers they were fast-tracked into prestigious active positions and given new names to match. Balthazar had the power to transform into a ten foot tall molten-metal wolf at will. He'd been a shoo-in for Elites from day one, and he'd never been anything other than an insufferable brat because of it. "Oh dear. If he stays out too long it'll cause such a media mess," I replied sarcastically. The existence of Elites was supposed to be a secret, but when every day is spent within the same three square miles, eventually everything get around, Even to the losers in the SMELL center like us. Leaks of its existence to the few dusty towns nearby, however, was a much bigger deal. Speculation caused by rogue supers was even worse, and sometimes it triggered an all hands on deck call to make it seem like whatever caused it never happened to the normals. Ana wrinkled her nose. "He didn't just ditch," she replied back, "Psioniqua and Rhiannon tried to stop him, and they got hurt." I took a sip of my soda and asked, "How do you know?" "Nique is telecasting it to me, right now." She looked down at the table, uncomfortable, and then whispered, "Rhiannon is bleeding to death." "Oh holy fck," I shouted, "Why is she telling you this? She needs to telecast to the infirmary or security or something!" Ana shook her head. "Rhiannon's physique makes her immune to normal super healing, and Balthazar's training means his timeline can't really be chronologically altered. She needs you!" I gulped. "Me?" I croaked out. Ana nodded. "Rhiannon will give you the blood she's losing," she answered, "If you refill her veins."

"Imagine you're in a field." Green extends in all directions. "You're alone, the earth is flat, and the blue sky touches the horizon." Blue shoots from the ground, arcing overhead. "The sun appears, tiny in the sky." There's a bright light, rays casting shadow behind me. "What color is it?" "Yellow." It burns so brightly, winking playfully. "Good." She licks her chapped lips, the sound distorting my tiny sun's light. "Look ahead of you. There's a sheep." Something soft and downy wanders across the green, its shadow stretching far beyond the horizon. "What color is it?" My brows crease. "Uh "What color is it?" The green wavers. Baa baa black sheep, have you any wool? "Uh." Mary had a little lamb, its fleece as white as snow. "Um." The sheep wavers, cotton fuzz shifting from dark to bright as its shadows remain inky. "What color is the sheep, Jess?" Black and white race across downy fluff, one after the other, again and again. "Um." I see the black sheep, blending into its shadow. "Um." In the same blink of an eye, that sheep is white and contrasted against the verdant grass. The term verdant applies here because I'm in the countryside, you see. "Jess?" If I were in a park in the city, it would probably not be verdant, because the term approximates the countryside. But I suppose one could argue a well-tended city garden could be very similar to rough rural hills, provided there's adequate insulation from all the racket of urban life. "Jess! " You couldn't have a sheep in the city, no matter how well you tend your garden. It would have to eat too much, and poop too much, and cities produce so much waste as is so really you'd be doing a disservice to the environment if you pulled livestock into a concrete jungle where people commute and hail taxis and buy street tacos in their work clothes trying to catch the last train to their office after they overslept by 7 minutes because it was daylight savings' time and they couldn't get out of bed because it was too dark- "Jess! " -because the clocks shifted back an hour and I think I've been here for an hour at least because my wrists hurt and my fingers are cold and I might have a headache or maybe I've been thinking really hard sometimes it's hard to tell the difference- "Look at the sun, Jess." -between thoughts and headaches because thoughts are thinky and headaches are achey like how your head feels when you look at the sun because it's so damn bright- "What color is the sun, Jess?" -and so damn "yellow" sitting so damn high and- "Where is it?" -mighty in the "sky" like a teardrop- "What color is the sky?" -rolling "blue" down my cheek because I can't- "Where are you, Jess?" -go "home" because I'm so fucking- "Where are you, Jess?" "Hopeless!" The grass is gone, and with it any sense of calm I've had. I tense, feeling the straps bite my wrists. The more I struggle, the more they hurt, until sweat beads on my brow and my lungs scream. "No, no, you're okay. You're here, you're okay." A cool hand braces my forehead, holding me down. Ants chew my skin. "No!" My eyes snap open, taking in the broken sink in the corner. Porcelain jagged, water dripping down the wall. We fixed that. Papers litter the floor, turning translucent like fish scales. "No, no Fish can be freshwater or saltwater, but we drink freshwater. "Jess, honey, look at me." The cool hand forces me away from the freshwater fish scales and into a pale face, slit pupils and golden eyes. "What color is the sun, Jess?" I shudder, arching my back against the steel table I'm bound to. In that moment, I'm back in the ruins of Rashelle's basement. In that moment, I'm listening to the water bubble in the walls and the gas stream through pipe. Her face hovers over me, aquiline nose sloping up to those stony eyes. "The sun, Jess." Blue tears roll down my cheeks as I fall into those eyes, surrounded by burnt gold. "Yellow."

I always tried to do the right thing. My parents raised me to obey the rules and respect authority and, in general, love my fellow human beings. And nothing has changed now that I've gotten older. I still try to live the same kind of life. And it's not to make them proud any more. They've been gone fifteen years now. So when I heard a voice tell me that was strike three, I didn't have a clue what I could've done. I didn't even know about the first two. I was so distracted and disturbed that I almost missed my stop. I had never been late for work in my life. My boss usually let me work through lunch and leave an hour early, so she was a bit shocked when she saw me walking with the rest of the office. "Brix, you ok?" "I have to take care of something that can't wait till 4," I answered as I headed for the stairs. No way I was riding in a crowded elevator with my mind reeling like this. I flopped down onto a bench in Montgomery Park and sighed. The next..... I'm not even sure how long it was, but it felt like an eternity. I just kept trying to figure out what I did. I was startled by that voice whispering, "It's time." A shadowy figure grabbed my arm and led me away from the park. Nothing was right. What should've been my office building now looked like an old courthouse. He shoved me up the steps and into a large room. A booming voice shook the walls. "Next!" The shadowy figure pushed me to the front of the room and stated confidently, "This is the one known as Brix, whose third strike was committed this morning." The judge peered down at me with contempt. "You? Seriously?" "Your Honor, I believe there's been a mistake..." I began. "Silence!" she shouted. The echo of that one word bounced around in my skull seemingly forever. "Read the charges. You tell me if any of these are a mistake." The owner of the whisper voice pulled a thin stack of papers from the bench. "Strike one, June eleventh, nineteen seventy-seven, four fifteen in the afternoon, defendant Brix poured half a bottle of mint extract into the meatloaf mix his mother was preparing." The judge cleared her throat and asked, "Do you deny this?" "No, ma'am, but..." "A recipe is a set of rules for cooking. You broke that rule. Strike one. Next charge." "Strike two, October thirty-first, two thousand nine, eight o'clock at night, defendant Brix continued to hand out Halloween candy to trick-or-treaters for an additional fifteen minutes, in violation of the town ordinance." The judge asked, "Do you deny this charge?" I was stunned. "Do the parents of those kids get a strike also? They violated the ordinance just as much as I did, maybe more!" "Do you deny this charge?" "No, ma'am, but I request..." "SILENCE!" Just when I thought she couldn't get any louder, the whole earth seemed to shake. "You willfully violated the town's rules. Strike two. Next charge." The shadowy voice stumbled for the first time. "Apr..... April nineteenth, two thousand seventeen, five thirty in the morning, ummm, defendant Brix, ummm, left the toilet seat up, causing extreme discomfort and embarrassment to his twelve year old daughter Janie." He looked up at the judge and, echoing my thoughts, said, "Really?" The judge's cruel grin turned downright evil. "Yes, really. Do you deny this charge?" I was dumbfounded. This was my third violation? I couldn't remember if I had put it down or not. I saw this morning that I had forgotten to clean out the cat box before I went to bed, and I wasn't going to leave it since it was my responsibility. That messed up my morning routine, but only by a minute, and was that enough to cause me to forget..... "I honestly can't confirm or deny it, Your Honor." "Well, I didn't certainly didn't expect this from you, but rules of etiquette are still rules. Strike three. You are hereby banished to the netherworld for a period of no less than six hundred years and no more than eight hundred years. Send him away!" The evil smirk on her face made me, for a second, wonder if she made up rules to get rid of certain people. "But..... but..... what about my family?" I pleaded. "They deserve to know what's going on!" As the shadowy figure led me out of the courtroom, I glanced back at the judge in disbelief. Her smirk had been replaced by a stern frown as she yelled, "Next!"

Blood trickled down it's remains hitting the floor in a rhythmic, yet eerie tone echoing out in the cold Silence of the night. Beside it lay a gleaming object it's reflective surface catching the faint light of the window illuminating the bloody remains with the moons dancing light. It to was caked in blood. Was it provoked? No. The dismembered corpse had done nothing to deserve this fate the gleaming object had bestowed upon it. The act of violence was a mere predatory reaction. Are we all not prone to violence? Do we not crave the satisfaction of superiority and power we get from these atrocities I and so many others have committed? But as I sit here now typing my confession, staring impassively at the carcass that lays only a few feet away I can't help but wander if I am the monster that my victim must have believed me to be. Was it true? Did I care? Repressing these thoughts I stand and make my way to the nearby bathroom to grab supplies. A damp cloth, some disinfectant a lighter, a garbage bag and mop are cradled in my arms as I return to the room. I make my way to the body, it was still as I had left it. A pool had formed on the floor it's faint aroma making me feel slightly sick. Was this regret? Perhaps. With the skill and speed honed from doing this many times before I mopped up the pool as best I could and sprayed the discoloured spot with the disinfectant. Than I pushed the body aside and wiped up the renaming blood on the counter and surrounding wall. With a look of mild interest I give my victim a final glance pity washes over my face briefly to be replaced by disgust and resentment as I reach across the counter and grab the creatures tail tossing it in the garbage bag with a final flourish as I gave the counter one last wipe and lit a well earned cigaret letting the bag fall beside me. Fuck I hate rats.

[ ] (dropcap) "AUGH! Sonuva James wasted no time in grabbing his rifle and opening the front door. At the side of the house was a man wearing a blue uniform with a red-and-white nametag. Paul. He stayed a safe distance. At least ten feet. Not that Paul was going anywhere. "Who are you? What are you doing here?" "Don't shoot, don't!" The man cowered behind his bloodstained hands. "Do you live here? Please, can you get me out of this bear trap?" "Answer my question." He sobbed, trying to wipe away tears and smearing blood on his face and shirt. "Look, I'm just here to check the gas meter!" "No one touches that gas meter without my say so! I have called that company seven times! " James' hands shake with rage. "Has ANYONE in that company seen Highway Man 3?" "I can't die here! I can't die, I can't die..." He rocked around in the fetal position until a new outburst of blood poured from his thigh. "AAAH!" "You've been following me!" "What? No." He did not sound at all convincing. His voice sounded weak. Pathetic. "You are! You're here to kill me!" James switched his grip on the gun. Paul's breath was fading, and his eyes began to flutter. But Jason was not going to let him have the satisfaction of dying. Not yet. It took some time to drag Paul around to the cellar door, and even longer to take him down the stairs to his workstation. James put a tourniquet on his leg to stop the bleeding. Then he tied Paul up and waited. Paul awoke, immediately straining against the ropes. James noticed, and picked up a rusted handsaw. "What kind of killer are you?" "What?" "Why are you after me? Is it demons? Or are you just some sick, twisted monster?" "Please. Let me go. I have a family. I have kids." "It doesn't matter." James ripped the saw through Paul's elbow, and he screamed in pain. "You're a killer. You're getting what you deserve." I watched the entire ordeal through the small window at the base of the house, which peeked into the cellar. He never saw me. It was easy to check the spot for traps now that I knew what I was looking for. The scene unnerved me. It wasn't right. James was not supposed to kill people. I was supposed to kill James. He'll be more alert now. Paranoid, yet vigilant. This will not be fun at all.

I've been with her as long as I can remember. There's a vague notion of others before her, but they don't matter. She means the world to me, and I to her. She tells me I'm her " favorite boy, " and such a " handsome gentleman, " and I swell with pride. I love you, I tell her. I wasn't able to work. I can't remember if I had a job before, but she made enough to feed us both and did so happily. Whenever she came home, I'd eagerly greet her and listen about her day; comfort her if she seemed sad or her day seemed rough. I'd never interrupt, just let her speak and idly play with my hair. I loved that, found it so soothing. In turn, I would protect her. She didn't need to ask, I could tell if she was anxious or frightened. Sometimes, when she got food delivered, I'd stand behind her and stare at the delivery kid, just in case he got any funny ideas about my girl. I'd also perform a sort of inspection of any friends she'd bring over. She trusts them, so I'd trust them... I just verify. I heard that phrase somewhere before and always liked it. Anyway, her friends were a little odd. She'd tell me to give them one of my standard greetings - " pound it " meant she wanted me to bump fists. Her friends tended to delight in this one. One tall dude immediately gave me a hug and said, " Can we be best friends?! " I looked at her; she raised an eyebrow and shrugged. I looked back at that guy and snorted as if to say, You wish, then joined my girl at her side. We used to take nightly walks around the lake. This was very exciting for me but I tried to restrain myself for her. She's not as fast as me, so I have to remember to slow my pace. But I can't help it sometimes. I have a very sensitive nose, the world is full of such amazing smells and she barely notices them. I mean, it's fine that she can't, I just wish she could experience this with me. I look back at her at try to convey what I've learned from every tree, every shrub, every blade of grass. She doesn't get it, but she smiles lovingly, and that is all I need. When I started getting sick, she took me to the doctor. A lot. I didn't understand a lot of what was discussed, but she was always there, always offering a hand to hold. When we got home, we'd sit on the couch quietly, and she would speak in soft, comforting tones. I'd lay my head in her lap and she'd gently run her fingers through my hair. Sometimes, I'd lie on my back and let her rub my belly. I know it's weird, but I like it. It triggers something in me and my leg spasms. It's not painful or anything and it makes her laugh - my favorite sound in the entire universe. Then one day, my legs started giving out on me. It was a little frustrating, to not know if you were going to be able to stand or not. I was coughing and sneezing more and more. I started losing my appetite, but was always thirsty. My sight was going all... funny. I was always tired. Part of me wanted to just go to sleep forever, but I couldn't leave her. She called the doctor, went over my symptoms. I watched her face crumple. Watched her eyes well with tears before she stood to leave the room, to go outside. I tried to get up and follow, but she said, both gently and firmly, " No, you stay. " I was worried but waited where she told me to. She always came back, of course, but I still hate when she goes. I hated that she was alone. Did I somehow wrong her? Make her cry? I hoped this wasn't the case. That was the worst offense in the world. The door opened and she appeared. She was sobbing now. What did I do? She threw her arms around me and wept into my shoulder. " My sweet boy, my favorite boy. " She repeated the phrase, again and again. I rested an arm on hers and nestled her. She kissed the top of my head, wiped away her tears. I locked eyes with her, waiting patiently. She told me, " We have one week and I'm going to make sure it's the happiest of your life. " I couldn't really imagine anything better than being with her, but I accepted her offer. I'm not really sure what she meant by a week, or what one left was, but if it would make her happy, it's what I'd do. She wasn't wrong. One night, she made me this thing she called bacon. I'd never had that before. I perked right up like I was young again. Bacon?! Why aren't we eating this every day?! She laughed through tears at me reaction. She also took me to our lake. We haven't been here in ages! I thought she'd forgotten about our spot. She let me smell everything as long as I wanted. I started to get tired, though, my hips and back started to ache. I longed to keep going, but she was understanding and just helped me back to the car. We also tried to paint together. I should stress tried - I ended up getting paint prints all over her apartment. She was laughing the whole time, took me to rinse my feet and her hands. While scrubbing my prints off the floor, she began to cry again. I bowed my head apologetically, resting at her side. " It's not your fault, " she said through the tears. Then who's fault is it? I asked, but she didn't respond. Every night, we would curl up together on the couch and it was pure bliss. - She shows me our painting this morning. I guess it's just my eyes going bad, but our prints don't look the same. I can't quite figure out why. They're just different. Funny how I never noticed before. " Come on, my sweet boy, it's time, " she calls. Her voice is shaky. I am so tired, so she comes to me instead and takes me to the car. I watch and smell the world go by, and it's such a beautiful blur. She walks with me, and I recognize we are at the doctor's. She has to fill out a form, and suddenly breaks down. She's crying hard now. I try to comfort her, and she just holds me. I look at one of the nurses, she seems to know what's going on and lets us go into a side room. We are sitting on the cold floor, the two of us. I never noticed before, but this was abnormal. Usually she is perched on something off the floor. A chair, a stool, the sofa, the bed. But today she is on the floor with me. The tears won't stop. What can I do to make it better? They still don't stop. She reaches for me, so I sit with her. The doctor comes in, but I choose to ignore him. He doesn't matter. My pain doesn't matter. Only she matters. She tries to compose herself. Wipes away her tears. She's picking me up now. She's so strong. She lays me on the table. The doctor shaves away some hair on my upper limb. I never notices before, how hairy I am compared to her. She's so smooth. She's holding my head now, her face pressed against mine. She repeats, " You're such a good boy. You're my nice, strong boy. I love you. " I'm a little scared, if I'm honest. And suddenly... I can't feel the pain anymore. I can still smell her, faintly hear her. She's still telling me she loves me. Suddenly it doesn't matter than I haven't been able to breathe very well, I feel nothing beyond my love for her. I try to lick her face, but I can't. I love you too, I try to tell her, but I can't. She means the world to me, and I to her. I just wish I could tell her-

Mr. Jones absently stared at the four round patches of ash in his perfect lawn. He had sworn to keep his old friend's lawn beautiful when he became President of the United States, and accepted a life of near constant surveillance to do it. A trifle to some in this age, but a hard sacrifice for a freed-loving man from the mountains. His loyalty to his friend and pride in his work were what kept him going. Now, he hardly noticed the procession of giant insects solemnly walking towards the White House. He had failed in his duty. Resistance was futile. Arnold, chief of security, had already lost two men trying to stop the steady advance of the aliens. If you stayed out of their way you were fine, but attempt to stop them and you were toast. Literally. The halls smelled like burning hair in some places. They were clearly here for the President. At first they (slowly) made for the Oval Office, but when the President was evacuated they changed direction to follow him. He would have been flown or driven out by now except that all approaching vehicles had been immediately destroyed by the alien landing craft. The invaders themselves and their ship seemed resistant to all forms of attack. President Reed was a very nice old man, and very honorable. When faithful Arnold had run to him and desperately tried to say everything but "I can't stop them," Reed calmly shushed him and said, "It's obviously me they want. If I go they may leave the rest of you alone." He began to walk towards the aliens, who had just rounded a corner in the bunker and entered the long escape tunnel. "Sir, will you at least leave your cat here?" Arnold pleaded. "Mittens has kept me company all three years of my Presidency, and I will certainly want him wherever I go now." President Reed, you see, had the one eccentricity that he always kept his cat with him, to the dismay of all his stricter staff members. Mittens was in his arms now, a regally purring pile of white fluff. At his command all of the President's company stayed behind. Reed approached the aliens at the same pace they approached him. He showed no fear. When they stood about a meter away the aliens stopped. The President stopped as well. There were five of them, one in front and four double-file behind. The one in front was carrying a golden box with red hinges in two of its little arms. It reached forward, opened the box - And revealed catnip and a beautiful salmon fillet inside. President Reed decided he was going to get along with the aliens very well.

His appearances upon the mortal plane have always been brief, conspicuously powerful but ultimately harmless and miniscule. Teachings of altruism and empathy, supplemented by His divine intervention had been enough to bring thousands upon millions of billions of worlds to a world of peace, kindness and charity. The threat of damnation brought the rest to unity, ultimately conquering over their darker natures. And then he left for the next, returning only to gaze and not intervene. This world, however, was demanding something different. The poverty and hatred in this world smothered its dregs, as the uncaring masses brought their charity and unknowing faith to leech-lords that claimed to exalt his name; even as these false prophets gorged themselves on the lard of the land and the bones of the least. His teachings have been subverted to corral the spirit to unthinking obedience and ignorance of the fates of their fellow men. Never before had anything like this happened, and He had decided on how to make anything like this never happen again Even as his consciousness seeped through the billions of this world, he could feel their animus as if they had been in His loving presence. He could feel their consciousnesses flowing like a great river of thought through time as it moved their bodies and operated their minds. This was something he treasured deeply in His creation, and it pained him to subvert their will to His liking. But they will never know. He had no need to take a breath, but he found himself doing so as he prepared to steer this river to where it needed to be. Where it had to be. He raised His incorporeal hand and Snap. And that mighty river of thought shut off.

Another? No, I'm done. Good to see you though! We should do this again some time. He smiled, a little out of focus (both ways). Sure, I'll let you know the next time I'm in town. You coming out? Nah, I'll stay for a bracer before I go. OK, then. We shook hands and I headed for the door. Outside the air was brisk, giving my that little wobbly to my fuzzy head but with the promise of clarity to come. We'd picked a popular bar, so the curtilage was quite generous, a few hardy souls were hanging around by the gate line. I walked up to the gate to the street and reached for my credit pass holder. Not there! I checked my other pockets, with a growing sense of unease. Coat, inside and out, nothing. Trousers, side and hip. No. I turned to head back into the bar, and stopped. The doorman eyed me. I, er, I left my pass holder in there, can I just... No, sir, you can not. We appreciate-your-business but entry-is-a-privilege-not-a-right and requires-a-credit-pass-image or as-required-by-law-a-cash-deposit. Words he'd spoken many, many times before. The look in his eye said, go on, have a go, see how far that gets you. I turned back to the gate line onto the street. Ten feet high, smooth metal. You really aren't supposed to be able to get through one without a credit pass. Or, as my bulky friend reminded me, as required by law, cash money. There was the slot in the ticket machine at the end go the gate line. It might even be working. Did I have any cash? I survey my pockets again, feeling much more sober. No cash. Of course not. So, he'd said a bracer before I go? How long could that take? I could just wait here. I adopted a nonchalant pose. The folks over by the gates finished whatever conversation it was they were having and went back inside, swiping their passes over the door's sensor. Could I? No. The doorman was watching me very carefully and anyway, if there's one class of establishment that has a good paywall it's a bar. I turned back to the gate line. I could feel the weight and heat of the doorman behind me. Sir, do you have business with this establishment? Well, I was drinking in there a few minutes ago, so... Sir, do you have current business with this establishment? The curtilage-is-provided-for-the-benefit-of-those-with-business-here and is not-a-public-right-of-way. I looked around again, feeling very sober and slightly panicky. There! A help point, on the ticket machine. I stepped over and pushed the button. A synthesised voice, hardly less expressive than the doorman invited me to wait. I look back at the doorman, caught his eye and then pointed to the yellow line on the floor - I was on street property. He shrugged and looked away. After a long seeming cold time a voice called to me through the chain link fence above the ticket machine. Two revenue support staff stood there, one a few paces back with one hand on a stun gun, the other eyeing me up. Oh, yes, hi! Um, I left my pass holder in the bar, silly me, and so, I need to get home and I'd like to take a penalty fare for the street, and then I can claim it back once I have my credit pass again and it'll all be fine. The revenue support staffer smiled a smile that I didn't like at all and said ID. I tapped my empty pockets it's inside with my credit pass. U-hu. Name and address, date of birth, registration number. I recited my details while they were tapped in to a tablet. What do you need all that for? In case you have form, in case you're a repeat fare dodger. I'm not a... a hand was raised in my face. This is not your address. Yes, it is, that's where I live. No. We do not have anyone of that name at that address. The stun gun was now out. Not pointed, but out and ready. Oh, wait, I moved there a few months ago, maybe your database isn't up to date. I gave the name of the previous owner. The revenuer looked down at the tablet again. We do not have anyone of your name at that address. Some heat rose from within me. Well, how is it my problem that your database is out of date? That is where I live! I'm trying to do the right thing here, and take the penalty fare! The stun gun was pointed now, and the doorman was hovering close to the yellow line. Fare-evasion-is-a-very-serious-matter, sir, our-customers-pay-our-fares and fare-dodgers-both-reduce-the-profit-of-the-company, which-is-theft, and reduce-the-amount-available-to-invest-in-the-service. Well, I looked around at the door of the bar again - how long does " a bracer " take? Edit: typos

I woke up, with the the sun shining in my eyes. It was a bright light, which was what made me think that it was the sun, of course. I later learned that it was, sadly, not. I lived in Oregon, in a small village on the coast on the pacific ocean. This was not my house, it was a cottage that I lived in during the summer. Now, as I woke up, this bright yellow light shone through the large window frame at back of my room. Even with the curtains partially closed, it seemed bright as day. I lifted myself up, almost collapsing at first, my legs still asleep. After regaining balance, I managed to open the curtains, squinting my eyes to see this sun. I looked out, grunted and closed the curtains again. It was nothing special. Then, my brain processed what I had seen and I jerked the curtains open again. " Holy god, " I said, my mouth open. " Please, let this not be what I think this is..... " It was the sun. Rising above the horizon, it was bigger than ever. Taking up nearly half the horizon while it was only rising. After looking at it for a bit more, I took my eyes off it, knowing that I could be blinded soon if I continue. Hell, I probably needed glasses after staring at it for that long! I put on a shirt and threw on some pants, wanting to go outside and see if the neighbours were witnessing what this. I took a step outside and immediately went back inside. It was hotter than an oven out there! I quickly closed the door, all of the precious cold air escaping into the inferno. I'm going to die, I thought to myself. I cranked up all of the air conditioners in my house and waited for them to provide some cooling to my boiling body. Nothing came. I realized the power was out. Going to the cupboards, I took all of the food I could find and brought it down to the basement with me. I knew that was the only place I could last the longest at. As I sat down in the corner, slightly cooling off, I took the first thing that came into my hand. It was a mars bar. I opened it and bit it. How I wished I could be living there now, if only we had colonized it earlier...

No one remembers exactly how the thing got so big. Of course, I'm talking about the 4th of July Parade. It started out just like you'd expect, an hour of floats, men in silly hats driving tiny cars, local businesses throwing candy, that sort of thing. There were speeches from the local politicians, picnics, you know. Being a small town, everyone had a good time. But somehow it got bigger. Longer. More floats. More trucks for businesses (some with strange names that no one had ever heard of,) their beds full of the King and Queen of every concept imaginable. More clowns, more funny cars, and worst of all - more Parade Officials. The first year it happened, the Parade went on for hours. The Officials knocked on doors, suggesting that everyone should come watch. Most did. Some didn't. A few never showed up again. But the Parade was over, we all went home and went about our business until the next year. This year, the Parade Officials didn't suggest. You came to the Parade. You watched. It drug on for hours. Then days. If you didn't come and watch the Parade, you became part of it, some King or Queen in a cage in the back of a strangely designed truck not made by any auto company we had ever heard of. We never heard from those people again..... The town came to a halt during the Parade. Things just stopped. Things broke. The mess left behind was often compounded by the candy thrown at the crowd. No one knew where the stuff came from, so it all went to the local dump. The town fell apart during that week. The Officials had gone from simple door-knocking neighbors to uniformed guards with guns, dragging people off to join the crowd. Watch the Parade. The town fathers despaired. How do we stop it? No one knew. Except me. You see, even though the Parade had become this massive beast, the organizers still dutifully filed their permit each year. As the person that was elected to approve permits this year, I simply stamped it "Denied." I found out where the people in cages went. You don't want to know, trust me. But the town was never bothered by the Parade again.

Probably not what you were looking for, but here is what I came up with: "We can't keep doing this." she said. It was becoming too difficult for her to keep running. She was still dressed for her 9-5 life, and not adequately equipped to run for her life. I wasn't sure how she want on for weeks like this. She had abandoned her high heels a while back, and we haven't had the time to stop and grab a pair of shoes for her. Her feet were callused and bleeding. Propped up against the wall, she reached down to rub the bottom of her feet, trying to massage out the pain. Her eyes were looking up at me, searching for some sort of reassurance. We stood there, frozen, for what seemed like enough time for me to think of any combination of words to console her. I couldn't think of a damn thing worth saying. I could hear them coming for us. Their movements echoed in the staircase below. They were maybe, if we were lucky, four sets of stairs beneath us. I grabbed her, delicately slinging her arm around my shoulders and dashed into the hallway. Two apartments down I could see an opened door. We found refuge inside. They were getting closer. I turned the lock on the door, attempting to find a sense of comfort in my now anarchy driven world. You weren't safe anywhere, but somehow twisting an inch thick piece of metal, separating me, from them, made me feel a lot better about my situation. I helped her make her way to a couch in the living room. The television was still broadcasting the same message it was when this fiasco started, a haunting reminder of what our lives had become. " This is the emergency broadcast system. Marshall Law is now in effect, due to an unprecedented breakout of the D4 Lunar Virus. Symptoms may include: Fever, chest pain, nausea, dilated pupils, discolored skin, and uncontrollable muscle spasms. If you notice a loved one with these symptoms, distance yourself and seek assistance from your local Emergency Medical Station. If you yourself need medical assistance, please seek aid at your nearest Emergency Medical Station. Stay in your homes. Food and Water will be provided to you shortly. " The television echoed on. "What a load of Bullshit" she said, wiping the tears from her eyes. "Those weren't medical stations, they were execution lineups." She was right. She didn't have any evidence to back up those claims, but she was right. I tried to convince her otherwise, denying the cruel reality myself. I tried to suppress the memory of my brother's visit. He needed antibiotics, badly. My brother was stabbed in a shopping mall the day after they initial outbreak. The city had become so polluted over the years from our new supply of oil, his wound became infected in a matter of minutes. He stiched himself up, but the infection discolored his skin. People found it unsettling. He walked up to the medical station with the hopes of seeking refuge and getting the supplies he needed, but that wasn't the case. I found him a few weeks later, in a pile of bodies behind a medical tent. They didn't even put a bullet in him. Maggots were crawling out of the hole in his neck. They were at the door now. I could hear them trying to ram it down, but they didn't have the strength. Savages. A few weeks back, someone had the bright idea of spreading around the rumor that if you drank uninfected blood, it would grant you immunity from the virus, and clear you of all symptoms. What a load of bullshit. They started at the blood banks. When that well was dry, they started finding live hosts. The latest innovation developed soon after they realized it was a waste of blood to kill someone and let their blood drain onto the ground. Blood farms were set up. I saw my first one a week ago. The victims were strung up on bathroom walls, above bath tubs. I couldn't count how many incisions were made on their blood stained body even if I tried. The ramblings of witch doctors polluted the area around the bodies. They were still alive. I ended their misery. I looked over at her, as she sat on the couch, staring hopelessly at the image on the television. Tears were casually strolling down her cheeks, and she remained indifferent to their presence. I was only able to imagine what thoughts were running through her mind. Did she regret pairing up with a stranger a few weeks ago? Did she never get to tell her loved ones goodbye? Did she, a shareholder, feel guilty about funding Lunar Oil Missions? Perhaps. But perhaps, like so many of us, she was trying to find the answer to a poorly timed existential crisis. I told her we needed to climb down the fire escape, but as I motioned to the window she remained motionless. "What's the point?" she finally said aloud. Her words crushed my spirits more than any others could have. She was the last humane person I knew, and would most likely ever know, and she wanted to opt out like so many others before hrer. I tried to tell her we couldn't, and she said we could. She reached into her backpack and pulled out an apple. I loved apples. It hadn't ripened yet, but had been growing after the virus filled the air. We didn't need to examine it under a microscope to know that the apple would kill us. The apartment door was beginning to crack. I could hear the witch doctors preaching about how they were going to gut us, and drink the most blood. She put the apple to her lips, kissing her life goodbye. "This is it." she said. I was panicking. I was struggling to say her name, let alone an awe inspiring speech to save her life. "I can't believe it took me so long to finally let go." she said, opening her mouth wide. I wanted to tell her that although the world had gone to shit, we couldn't take a bow before the show was over. For all we know, we were the last hope humanity had to reclaim its former glory. We were human beings. Our entire history was comprised of people fighting uphill battles until the very end. I wanted to tell her that if she gave up now, she would be leaving me to fight alone. I wanted to tell her that the only reason I was still alive, is because I didn't want her to struggle alone. My only reason for waking up in the morning was to ensure that someone else was doing alright. Her suicide was hurtful, because it meant that the feelings weren't mutual. She was fighting for her own survival, not mine. I remember her telling me she was an atheist, too. Her wanting to oprt out wasn't her looking to find paradise on the other side, it was her declaring her existence null and void. She bit into the apple,, smiling with delight. Juices dripped down from the corners of her mouth as she chewed. Her skin quickly darkened and her pupils grew wide. She turned to me, as if she had one last secret to share. The words never made it off her lips. Her eyes showed no regret, but were screaming that she was sorry. The apple hit the floor. She was gone. I turned my head, starting at the door. I was defeated. A miserable existence was waiting for me on the other side of the door. Opting out wasn't an option. It never was. Even though, as I sat there, knowing I had no reason left to be alive, all hope of a happy ending gone, I couldn't help but feel proud. I survived longer than most, compromising none of my humanity to do so. The show was finally over. But just as the curtains of my bleak life were closer, and the hinges on the door were almost off, I heard a voice. "You're not my dad." came out of nowhere in a high pitched voice. I turned my head to see a little girl, frightened by the events I brought to her. I stood up and walked over to her. She was terrified. Kneeling down, I took her hand and smiled. "Where is your dad?" I said, trying to seem more curious than scared. They were almost through the door. "He went to get me some soup." she said, holding her stomach as the words left her mouth. I put my hand on her forehead, she had a mild fever, was it a common cold or something worse? "Well, let's go find him." I said. I grabbed her arm and walked her over to the fire escape. "Ok!" She said, filled with delight. The door was finally broken down just as her and I climbed out the window, making our way down the fire escape. My show wasn't over. Yet.

"This is brilliant, who else knows about this?" "Just us, the agent who reviewed the brief, and the think tank boys who submitted it." A vault with no radiation shielding would still ensure the relative safety of it's inhabitants while giving us a chance to monitor the full effects of the bomb's radiation on living organisms." "I think you're going to like this one too, Sir. It's a Vault with a virtual reality simulator inside. Dr. Braun actually took the time to submit this one himself!"

"What the fuck is that?" Nobody was surprised by this exclamation, and the visit to Australia had already prompted it several times. When Chotzavsimilols'vim first vistied Earth, he was, admitteld, bad at blending in. Thankfully, by befriending outcasts in the first place, his friends didn't really care when he revealed his true nature to them. Referring to him as male was, of course, just a formality based on the human form he'd adopted, as his species had twelve sexes and thirty-six genders, but he'd gone for the white male human form after studying the power structure of the dominant species of Earth. Still, his friends were surprised when he had continued to make the same exclamation. "Dude, Zim, calm down. It's just a platypus. Honestly, it's one of the safer things in this place." Zim was the nickname that James had given him due to his poor skill blending in, as well as the green hair he had chosen upon joining the group of outcasts. After learning the origins of it, he had to admit, it fit. "Yeah, you've seen the footlong spiders and exploding trees in Australia. Why is the platypus so shocking?" That was Sharon. She had a point, but he still couldn't let go of his shock. Sure, the platypus was tame by the standards of his own world, but this wasn't his own world. As a scientist, a xenobiologist, studying this planet, he couldn't help but be shocked by the creature. It just didn't make any sense. It was a mammal, as they called this subgroup of life, but it had the characteristics of avians, and the males had a poisonous foot. A poisonous foot! He'd seen plenty of different things be poisonous in his centuries, but this might have actually been a first. "Why? Was this some experiment that got loose? A prank played by rogue scientists? Why does it exist?" Chotzavsimilols'vim couldn't believe that evolution was responsible for the creature. Earth wasn't old enough for a clusterfuck of a species like this to evolve naturally, at least, not in his experience. "Nah man, at least not as far as any of us know. It's older than mad scientists on this planet." James said, in his typical laid-back tone. Were it not toxic to his species, Chotzavsimilols'vim would have gladly sampled some of the "weed," as the man called it, that gave James his personality. "What's the point of it then? It's got a beak! It doesn't even look attached! It just looks like someone stuck it on the thing as a joke, and if you pull hard enough it'll come off!" Chotzavsimilols'vim still was unable to understand how a creature could be. "Well, it would come off if you pull hard enough, but I'm pretty sure that's called animal cruelty." Sharon, with her usual snark, made Chotzavsimilols'vim smile a bit. Sarcasm and snark were considered some of the highest forms of humor in the galaxy, and she could have made the comedians of Zogfaf Rog Erusha die laughing. Her pale skin looked far too warm in the Australian heat, and he was afraid that she would come down with the "sunburn" if she didn't get inside soon. She was, as their species called it, a "goth," and did not handle the sunlight well apparently. "It lays eggs for Eomhawy's sake! It's one of your mammals, but it lays eggs! Okay, I've got to check this." He pulled out a gadget that lit up. Due to prior experience, James and Sharon knew it was basically a space iPhone. He typed in the Galactic standard language, and explained he was looking up the creature on, as he put it for them, "the space Google." Some pictures popped up, and Chotzavsimilols'vim sighed. "Right. That explains it. It's not natural. None of this continent is. Apparently, it was created for exiled Cardaler-Koner." Chotzavsimilols'vim smiled, relaxed in his assumption being proved right. "Still, the species have mutated over time, and some of them have gone extinct. The poison foot is new." "What are the Cardaler-Koner?" Sharon asked, curious to know about whatever aliens were sent to the down under. "And, funny, that's what the British used Australia for as soon as they found it. Looks like it was built to last." "Well, let's see here..." Chotzavsimilols'vim trailed off, doing some work between the "space Internet" and the human one. "Ahh, there we go! Apparently, they stopped being sent here millions of years ago after a revolution. Your species has discovered their fossils, and I must admit, having met them, your name for their species fits. Apparently, your species nicknamed them the'Demon Duck of Doom'." James and Sharon laughed, amazed that, of all things Australian, that was the one that came from another planet, rather than being created for the job of being a prison. AN: The Demon Duck of Doom is a real historical animal. The head was the size of a small horse. It ate meat. It was a giant duck.

"What the...?!" I said to my wife. "There's an ambulance, a fire truck, and police cars outside our house!" "WHAT?!" she screamed. "That means someone is going to get hurt, something's going to burn, and there will be a crime here! WHAT DO WE DO..." "Oh relax," I said, always the sceptic. "They can't predict the future based on their silly little crystal balls. I'm going to go make some bacon and eggs." I went downstairs to make my breakfast, but the knob on the stove was jammed. This was frustrating, it never usually happened. I tried to twist it harder, but it still wasn't budging. And harder. And harder. And harder, when suddenly the knob turned and the stove erupted in a fiery burst, singeing my hair. I screamed and leapt back from the stove, only to bang my head against the kitchen bench. I thought I was concussed, so I began crawling to the door, when two paramedics "See, this is why we need to be clairvoyant!" one of them yelled. "Now let's get you out of here..." Before they could put me on a stretcher, a chunk of the ceiling fell down and crushed them. I looked around, the stove fire had spread to the rest of the house and was burning everything. I mustered the strength to stand up and looked around at the stove, the source of the fire. While I tried to figure out how to stop it, I noticed that a gas pipe had burst and was leaking near the stove. I knew what would happen next. BOOM!!! I tried to run, but the explosion was bigger than anticipated and I was burst through the place where the front door originally was, but had burnt down. As the firemen put out the blaze, a police officer came to me. "Sir, we need to ask you some questions about how this fire started."

"I'm pregnant, and we need to talk" In hindsight she looked more stressed than I expected from someone I have just dated for two weeks. The people at the next table stopped talking, and started pretending not to listen to us. I stirred my coffee one more time, hoping it made me look calm, and that she wouldn't notice the screaming and yelling behind my eyes. "Listen, "I started, "I know we have only been seeing each other for two weeks, but know that I am fully committed to this no matter what you choose to do." Wait, was that a smile on her face? "Nick, don't get me wrong, I like you, and it's been a fun two weeks, but I don't have much of a choice here." She looked at me, poking her cake a little, then she shoved it aside. "The thing is "she started to look more uncomfortable, " ..... The thing is, that this is a first for me too, and it's not going to be easy, I mean, my parents will freak out, just not as much as yours." "What is that supposed to mean? " , I ask her. I realize now that I am still stirring my coffee, so much for trying to stay calm. There is just something about the way she is shifting in her seat, the way she is ignoring the people around us, she is just so intensly looking at me. And what does it even mean that my parents are going to freak out even more? "Lucy, it has really been a wonderful two weeks, from what you're saying it will be another who knows how many weeks. Perhaps even years. " , I hope that sounded mature. "Shouldn't we at least talk about our options? I'm still at school, you're living with your parents, I can hardly afford this date. " , that sounded less mature, but it had to be said. She rested her head in her hands now, shaking her head in what looked like disbelieve, at least that is what I told myself at the time. Her eyes met mine again after a minute or so, there were no tears, and there was no anger. Yet I felt really uncomfortable, I knew that things were going to be very different now. Lucy got up from her seat. I caught a glimpse of her belly. Is she showing already? We didn't even have sex until after a week of going out. She opened the door of the cafe, looking back at me. "See you soon Nick. Just let it sink in a litlle." She kept walking, and I didn't get up. I just sat there. I didn't even get up when this huge blue bus came out of nowhere, the driver's face was in horror as he saw Lucy in front of him, and I'll never forget the sound the tires made. It felt like forever before I finally mustered the strength to get up. The cafe was empty, everybody had run outside to see what happened. A crowd gathered in a circle, I tried to get closer, it seemed impossible, and it felt like I was moving further away. I heard some people asking someone if they were okay, and the answer came in a mutter. "She was there, I hit her, I know I did." A light tap on my shoulder stopped me in my tracks. I turned around. "I told you, I don't really have a choice."
