Whilst wandering down a deserted road, so eerily quiet you can hear the gravel moving with the wind, I spot a small leather-bound object. As I approach it, I notice that it is what they call a'book'. I have seen many of these at the larger camps, but never one this far out. I was one of the few who were taught to read at a young age, and found much more enjoyment reading about fierce battles between the undead and us. As I flicked through the book, I noticed that many of the pages depicted events that happened before The Incident: large-scale famines, buildings collapsing and wars. As I read into it a bit more, I find out that the life that once was, is actually worse than what we have now: Sure, we have to be alert for the undead, but everyone is cautious of other survivors. We all look after one another, watch each others backs, and give hope to those who need it. I hear the monotone moan of a horde of them, accompanied by the shuffling of feet on the gravel. I pick up the book and place it in my bag, replacing it with a medium-sized rifle. One day this will all be over.

For months, she taught class with instructions from his notes. Week after week, note after note, she followed the guidelines for his lessons exactly. She taught the classes so similarly that the classes felt comfortable with her. She was temporary, but they treated her like him, like he never even left. The class always spoke of what a great, awesome person he was. He was help, kind and honest. She'd never met him before, but it wasn't long before she knew she'd like to. Was it how highly he was spoken of, so casually yet always with respect, that gave her this feeling? Soon she realized it was the feeling of love she was feeling each week as she read his notes. His handwriting was perfect, as was his way with words. Every sentence was constructed as delicately as an artist constructs his painting. Every word filled her, every sentence read leaving her breathless. She was in love, more than she ever had been. She was in love, yet she was tired. She no longer wanted a one sided method of communication. She longed for something more. She wanted to speak with the man behind the words that had stolen her heart. She wished to see him, face to face, more than anything she had ever desired before. It was the week before her last day, before he'd come back and she'd be gone, that she decided it was time. She'd meet him, knowing she couldn't take anymore, she knew she had to see him at least once. She acquired his address, drove to his home. It was a simple home, that of a simple yet hardworking man. She hesitated, taking a deep breath as she got out of her car, she had come so close, she had to go through with it. Knocking on his door, she wondered what she was going to say. She heard footsteps, and as the doorknob because to turn from the inside, time slowed down. She took another deep breath, quickly rehearsing her first words to him in her head, "Hello, I'm . I've been substituting for you, and I love you." I know this isn't the most realistic story, definitely a bit cliche imo. But I had an idea that I wanted to try for shits and giggles. The idea here is that it seems like a cutesy, cliche love movie with a female lead. However, switch the genders around so it's a guy obsessing over a woman, and I felt it made the whole thing seem a bit stalker-ish. So that was fun.:)

"Hey hey hey!" Jeffery burst into the room as he always did. Laughter erupted around him, as it always did. David shot an uneasy glance at him, but Jeffery didn't quite notice. It wasn't in his nature to see the world that way. The smile on his face put David back at ease for a moment. "How've ya been, buddy?" Jeffery asked. "The same as always," David replied. This cued Margot to walk in with her birdcage. "Hey, Margot!" Jeffery nearly yelled. "Whatcha got there?" "It's my bird Sandy. She's not feeling too good right now though, fellas. I think she might have the flu." "You mean bird flu?" Jeffery asked. Laughter erupted. David scooted back in his seat, ready to bolt, but no one else seemed to care. "I think when a bird gets the flu, it's just the flu," Margot said. "I don't know how to help her though." The three went into the living room to set the birdcage on the coffee table. Each of them looked intently at Sandy, who wasn't moving at all. She just stared off into nothingness, shining like plastic. Jeffery smiled at his friends. "Say, let's forget about the bird for now and head down to the diner. I heard Mac and Donna are headed there after they get done studying," Jeffery said. "I don't wan na go there. We always go there," David said. "No! We're going to the diner, David," Jeffery rested a hand on David's shoulder. The two stared at each other until Jeffery relented. "Besides, where else would we go?" "Anywhere..." People were at the diner, as they always were. Eating french fries and hamburgers, pretending to talk to one another without saying anything at all. Some of them fake laughing, some of them fake eating. None of them looked at the trio when the walked in. "Hey, gang!" Donna said from their usual booth. Clapping erupted as Mac came into frame. Everyone loved Mac. Conversations went on about school and homework and godawful teachers. David couldn't keep up with any of it. His eyes kept wandering from table to table, wondering how so many people could be pretending. At first, he imagined them all to be robots, since they were always there at the same time every day; right after Mac and Donna got done studying. Not until Jeffery laid a hand on his forearm did David snap back in. The entire table was looking at him with smiles. "What?" he asked. "We were gon na head back to the house to take a look at the bird. Mac says he knows a way to cheer her up," Jeffery said. "Alright..." David said. "You alright, buddy? You seem kind of out of it," Mac asked. Jeffery grasped David's forearm hard, pulling the tiny hairs enough to make David wince. "Yeah. Fine." They got back to the house in less than three minutes. An incredible feat for a fifteen minute drive. Especially since none of them had cars. Margot was a mess over in the corner, worrying over her sick bird. "You know what, guys," David said. "I don't feel too well. I think I'm gon na go to bed." "You can't go to bed, David," Jeffery said. "You can't disrupt our day." "What do you mean?" David asked. "We still have to help the bird." "I'm not a bird doctor! I don't know anything about helping birds. There's nothing I can do to help you." "Whoa, tiger," Donna said. Laughter filled the room. David twitched. "Relax, David," Mac said without looking. "Yeah, David," Jeffery closed in on David, pressing him up against the wall. "Relax. Everything is normal." "Everything is always normal. Everything is always the same." "If you don't calm down," Jeffery lifted an eyebrow, "I'm gon na have to call Principal Morris." "Why would you call our principal to come solve this problem!? He's got nothing to do with how I feel right now. I just am feeling weird and would like to go to bed please." "Hey there, neighbor!" Principal Morris said through the kitchen window. Applause erupted. David tried to run. "I just came by to bring you some peaches from my garden." Principal Morris walked into the living room. Margot was beside herself, crying over her sick bird. Mac and Donna were taking turns staring at the bird while the other one stared at David and Jeffery, who were pushing each other back and forth. Jeffery finally pushed David hard enough to knock a painting off the wall. "Hey now, kids," Principal Morris said while he made his way over to David. "What's going on in here?" "David knows," Jeffery calmly turned around. "Huh?" Mac asked, who was switching from the bird to Jeffery and David. "Well, shit," Principal Morris was just behind Jeffery. He dropped his peaches, grabbed a lamp from a nearby table and swung it against David's head. Things went black. "Hey hey hey!" Jeffery burst into the room as he always did. Laughter erupted, as it always did.

I've always thought there was something weird about I've Bean Here Before. No, not the terrible pun, that's common enough. They make a wickedly good latte, which is why I keep going back, but great coffee isn't what got me thinking. It's the mural on the wall behind the counter. It's pleasant enough to look at - an artsy scene of people sitting at tables, drinking coffee. But for some reason it unsettles me, and today I try not to stare at it too closely as I hand over cash for my usual latte. I focus instead on the barrista's pretty green eyes and the spiral tattoo on her collarbone. Was she new here? I hadn't noticed her before. She hands me my change and I stuff a few dollars in the tip jar, which earns me a smile. The latte is as delicious as ever, and I go about my normal day doing normal things. I return a few days later for more of that fantastic caffeine. The barrista is one I recognize - short, cute, and always grins when he hands me my latte. This time there's a wink too - "Pretty soon I'll have to start calling you a regular!" 'Don't mind if you do,' I think to myself, pausing to enjoy the shape of his shoulders as he reaches for flavoured syrup on a high shelf. As I turn to leave my eyes fall idly on the that mural again. I think they must have an artist in house, because there's fresh paint and some unfinished spaces where they're adding things. In my perusal I find myself transfixed by the various faces. They seem horribly flat and yet at the same time a little too..... alive. Looking at them suddenly makes me queasy and I rush to leave to enjoy my drink in peace. .......... Man I love those lattes. I consider myself a regular now and I'm familiar with most of the barristas. I can't quite shake the heebie jeebies from that mural, but the amazing coffee and the attractive barristas more than make up for it. As I stand in line for today's order, something feels different. The mural I've tried so hard not to look at is a tangible force pulling my gaze, and everything else seems muted. Through the haze I hear the barrista (the girl with the pretty green eyes, now my favorite) ask for my order, but I can only stare at the back wall. Stare at the finished additions to the mural. Stare at the new people at their artsy tables drinking coffee. Stare at my own face, looking back at me. The world tilts. What is up or down? Where am I? Everything is light and color. And then as quickly as it hits me, the rush of vertigo disappears. I'm still in front of my favorite barrista in that weird little coffee shop. But something's not right. I'm..... behind the counter? And facing the wrong way, towards the front door. I try to move, to speak, but I'm paralyzed. The barrista smiles at me fondly, pats my face, and says, "Now you're definitely a regular." Then she turns away to greet a newly arrived customer, who flirts casually as she takes his order. "That mural is really unusual," he says, "So life-like! I swear that one guy looks like someone I saw here last week. Are you the artist?" "Oh, all of us here are," she replies, "And we love capturing our regular customers in our work. Who knows? Maybe you'll end up there too some day!" "I hope so!" he laughs. I can only scream, silently, and wallow in my despair. It was just a mural. How could I have guessed?

Alex had been starstruck when he saw her. She was quite beautifull and very witty. He had been saddned by the fact she did not answer his phone calls but he had shrugged it off. He found himself shaking quite a while. He had just been on the phone with the Queen. The text he had recieved from her had caused quite a stirr, and people were even suspecting him of being an alien spy. "Alright Alex, listen up. All we need to know is if the bitch is planning on expanding her turf. If we are lucky, she will just be looking for a one night stand and then be on her way." "Bitch." Quite a hard word he thought. Especially when considering a former acting student had managed to free an entire civilization from a tyrant. If anything she was amazing, extraordinary. He opted to remain silent though, seeing as the friendly agent had been brought in from the States. He was more scared of them then her. He had been picked up by two funny looking creatures with feathered wings. One of them uttered something unelgible and he responded softly "Yea, I know right? It tends to be cold here." He laughed, they didnt. The date hadnt even started yet. They led him into a big room with a table at the center. There were a table and two chairs. One of the aliens nodded towards the chair. He took a seat and the two aliens left. "By the way, I am allergic to cats, not that I know if that matters when it comes to your food." He couldnt help but laugh at his own joke, but this time he wasnt the only one laughing. "We dont eat meat, Alex." They sat acros each other, looking down at their plates. "So..... How have you been?" Atleast she was trying, he had to give her credit for that. "Well, I wouldnt want to bore you, considering you were off to save another civilization. I do however want to ask if you are alright." She smiled at him. She was beautiful, even with the scars in her face. "I am, thank you. I have been quite busy as you can imagine." He remembered the questions he had rehersed with the agents. "So what brings you back to the old neighborhood and are you planning on destroying us?" She looked puzzled, then bursted into laughter. "Is that what they think? That I defeated a tyrant only to become one myself? Dont worry, I am not here to enslave mankind. I simply wanted to make things right with my former home and..... You." They talked and laughed, he had not enjoyed himself like this for a long time. He spoke of the boring mundane stuff he wasted his days on, and she told him of alien planets, of battles and adventure. A lot had happend to her, and he werent able to escape the situation without some bruises. She had lost her left arm and had recieved scars all over her body. She had been horribly abused, but through the pain she had found strength and with her strength she had bonded with the other aliens, forming a united public which in the end had brought justice to the tyrant. "You know, I cant really one up any of your stories. While I served coffee for people, you were out there fighting for equality and justice. But why did you come back here? Why did you contact me? What is the endgame here?" She gave him a kiss before he was escorted away from the room. "I will be around Alex." He smiled at the thought. When he came back to his house, the agency were there, waiting for him. "Well, what did she say? How knee deep in shit are we?" Alex shrugged lightly, "She did not tell me why she had come back or what her plans were." The agents looked at each other. "Well thats dissapointing. All of this and she was unwilling to share anything with you?" Alex looked out through the window. She gave me a kiss." One of the agents moaned out loud. "I guess it was just destiny."

The old knight stood before the garden, where a crescent shaped pond would force those taking a stroll to deviate around either side, tempting them down any of the other paths between the hedges, down less-observed divisions of the compass. The hedges were overgrown, and the paths were barely visible now. Still, it was clear how magnificent the maze had been, once upon a time. The old knight's face seemed remorseful, his eyes distant, as if remembering those times. In the pond two koi fish danced around each other. One of them was gold, and the other black. The water would flicker with their colours as the sun glinted off their scales, and every time it did so a little rumble would send the water on the surface trembling, and sparks would fly out from the middle of the two fish. From down the path to the knight's left a rabbit emerged from underneath the hedgerow. Cautiously, sniffing the air, it determined that the maze was deserted and came out further. It was very fluffy and grey. The old knight stayed still, and the rabbit did not notice him. The rabbit foraged silently, its head buried in the grass. The way to the old knight's position was a singular path, paralleled on both sides by rose bushes. The roses grew in all different colours, on the same bush, from indigo to yellow and all the spectrum in between. Upon closer inspection, one would find that the petals were made of glass. It was said that in the middle of the maze was a fountain, or a tree. No one could decide which, as it was arguably both. The water spread upwards from the base, twisting and bubbling, until it rained down again in drips like a heavy rain, or the branches of a willow tree. No one knew what drinking from the fountain would do, not even the knight. No one had found the fountaintree for a long time. And eventually, people had stopped trying to find it. They were more likely to find the bodies of previous attempters, skeletons petrified in their final crawl, perhaps a finger stretched out, trying to point the way. Their skeletons rusted in the dew. And now the garden was overgrown, and it's secrets were unknown to all but the knight, and soon to be hidden forever. A hawk cast a shadow across the shoulders of the old knight, before diving to snatch the rabbit. The rabbit, all of a sudden surprised by the bird's dive, exploded into the white seeds of a dandelion, which were then scattered into the wind by the hawk's talons. The old knight stayed motionless, hands upon the pommel of his greatsword, his chin resting upon them. The hawk rose from its swoop, confused, and distracted, and so did not see the spiderweb stretched between the hedges. It's beak pierced the very middle, and the threads closed around her like a tattered cloak. She thrashed weakly as dozens of spiders revealed themselves amongst the leaves, shaking their spears and cheering. Music could be heard, simple tones that echoed over the maze, drifting closer and receding. The knight waited, and the music revealed itself as a dragonfly flew around one corner. It flew so fast, and turned at right angles, and each time it did so a tone rang out. A long time ago, a musical troop had tried to navigate the maze by mapping the tones to certain corners, as they had discovered a pattern. Nevertheless, they failed. The maze had other tricks, almost as many as it had stories. There were butterflies that set your clothes on fire if they landed on you. There were some passages that never ended. There were no exits besides that at which the old knight stood. The old knight would not enter the maze. Instead he stood, and watched, his stone face aged from the sun, wind, and moss. And the plaque at his feet said, "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here."

I looked up and saw only the cool, unwavering glare of Alan Alda. "Oh god. It all makes sense now. You sick fuck. "I muttered, as Alan Alda kneeled beside me. "You know, I was in the Aviator!" Alda responded "P-please. I can find someone, anyone else." "Now, Leonardo DiCaprio was a little intimidating at first but after getting to know him he's a real nice guy. Really gets to know the crew." He coughed into a faded paisley handkerchief and wiped his mouth. He turned his back to me, then reached up from the bottom sweater to place the cloth in the breast pocket of his checkered button down. Blood had dribbled down my cheek and slowly formed a neat pool on the cement. No one had mentioned the Aviator in years; last I remember Leonardo DiCaprio's memorial service barely paid tribute to the film. It all made sense now. We hadn't paid any mind when Alan Alda kept making cameos in prime time sitcoms; we all just figured he was in extremely good shape for a two hundred year old. Maybe some new Hollywood diet only he knew about. I hadn't paid any mind, not until he approached me at the resturant. The saccharine conversation lulled me into a false friendship. He had tricked me. Now here I was, supine in a Shanghai alley. Flickering neon hid the sky. "You have great hair. Nice volume, really!" Alda said through a sickeningly genuine smile. "Please" I begged one last time. He gripped my throat and I felt my life force begin to drain. My skin cracked and my vision narrowed; black dots peppered what would be the last face I ever saw. His skin seemed to tighten just a bit. "I need this, you know! I'm up for a part in the Little Miss Sunshine reboot. Y'know, people always used to think I was in the original." I couldn't move my arms. My blood had stained his impeccably starched collar. "These stains will be tough. Wool sweaters, right?" He grinned. Alan Alda had won.

Hal sat in his office, watching a live feed of the rapture for the third day straight. He had seen the ascension of those saved. He had watched as the Damned crawled up through the ground and dragged the rest to hell. Now the whole planet was devoid of humanity. The door to his office slid open. Hal's secretary, Patti walked in. Her expression made him feel assured she shared a similar ambivalence about the situation. They watched shots of empty cities, streets, inter spliced with horrific showing yesterdays battle with the Damned. After several minutes Hal spoke "I can't believe it. We are not affected." "I know, sir. I think we escaped it. I don't know which way I would go, but somehow it is an enormous relief to know I will forever be safe from that judgement." The pair sat in silent for several more minutes. Both calmly processed the information for the first time since the rapture began. Hal started to sob. "What? Family down there?" Patti asked. "No my whole ancestry immigrated generations back." Hal replied with a sniffle. "What then?" "What the fuck does this mean! Religion has been dead to me for so long. It just seemed silly in light of everything humanity has accomplished in the past few decades. Patti, I watched the Four Horseman descend from the fucking sky and decimate humanity. What does this mean for us? Are we out of the fucking dogma? Do we just go to sleep when we die? What?" Patti had been contemplating that same thing. "The way I see it there are two possibilities." Hal stared at her intently. She continued. "The first would be what you just said. We are exempt here on Mars. We go to sleep that's it." Hal nodded anxiously. She continued. "The second would be that we are now in the domain of another deity." Patti walked by behind Hal and began massaging his shoulders. He relaxed in her grip. "We may now be under the thumb of an incredibly benevolent and merciful God. One who loves our troubled race without reservation, and delivers us all to paradise when our time comes." Hal hummed a peaceful affirmation. Patti drew a twisted and evil looking dagger from within her jacket. She continued. "But that is not Mars, Hal. You were not so fortunate." Something in her voice had changed. Something that made Hal stiffen, but paralyzed him. He could not move although mortal panic now gripped him. "Our new God is old, Hal. Old and angry. We disgust him. And there is no hope of redemption. No martyr for our sins. Hell is paradise compared to his home. Our home. It's time for you to see." Hal tried to speak but all he could manage was a soft whimper. Patti jammed the blade into the side of Hal's neck. Then quickly began sawing through his throat. "Bless me lord of the Red planet!" Patti shouted to the room, Hal's blood spurting all over her face. It coated her. Her heart glowed with the fiery ecstasy of his approval. It was time for humanity to know of Him and His wishes.

I swiftly withdrew my hand from under my chin and took it in, paradoxically delicate and powerful, terminating in glimmering, sharp nails, scarcely different from claws, equally capable of tearing out a throat. By now they were dark with necrosis and filth, and the discoloration was spreading, heightened by the shade from the overhang under which I was sitting on a bench. I hadn't fed in weeks and unnatural gifts will only get you so far. I alighted from the bench, a single, fluid motion. To anyone watching I would have seemed to have become one with the shadows about me, my clothes indistinguishable from the umbra. I chuckled bitterly as the momentary thrill subsided, so that was all it took now, I thought. I used to relish the chase, the way their breathing would quicken as they tried to run in those cumbersome dresses they wore in the name of modesty. As I squinted and scanned the throng milling about me, registering a sea of bare midriffs and tattoos, all that seemed so far away. I kept to the edges of the shadow, consequently taking a highly circuitous route, partly to avoid being seen, (after all, I didn't want to have to go to the trouble of inciting adoration in some drunkard on the street), but also partly to tempt fate by skirting the sun. I suspected that at my age, it wouldn't do much harm, perhaps a little crackling and sizzling, but old habits die hard and I didn't want to be showy. The church was a glaring incongruity in the modern landscape, as cheaply constructed as it was, but not one of the throng even slowed as they approached it, a modest deference to its sanctity, which seemed to quiet the air about it. The wrought iron gate barely creaked as I breezed through it. I tapped the heavy wooden door and gave away, letting a rush of air pass through it. Amid all this, I barely noticed the tickle of the wards at my feet, this was a public place after all, but I felt the blessings flare across my skin. I pushed on, my footsteps echoing through the high ceilinged hall. They had set the Eucharist out for adoration, no one had come (another peculiarity of the modern world), and I paused to watch, remembering the smell of rich, dark, old wine, which I never drank anymore, not only because I didn't need it, but because I couldn't get it anymore, and the sound and sensation of Latin ringing through stone, which also was seldom heard anymore. As I walked, I felt my face prickle and sweat for the first time in a long while, I knew it was the blessings radiating from every inch of the place, but I didn't care, in fact, I relished it. I could have sworn I felt myself blushing, but that was truly impossible. I gritted my teeth behind my dark scarf and advanced, turning arduously toward the confessional. To my great relief, it was not of the traditional model, I could sit down. As my vision had blurred with pain and tears, I extended a shaking hand, grunted from the strain, and sat down. Hesitantly, reverently, I closed my eyes. " Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. "

Thorn frowned at the slim, short man standing before him. The man was old, skin brown and wrinkled, eyes tired and weary. His hair, what little he had, was graying. A short unkempt beard clung to his face, nearly covering a wide smile. "You're my new student?" He asked. Obviously, Thorn thought to himself. But why assign me to you? Why not The Fist, Blackblade, or even Smoke? Who are you? "Yes, sir." He said aloud. The man's smile somehow grew. "Good!' The man turned and moved quickly to the door, opening it and taking one step out before turning. "Aren't you coming?" Before he could reply, Thorn saw the door close and he hurried to catch up. He opened the door and saw the man a surprising distance to the left. He began jogging over to him. "Sir?" "Yes?" the man replied, still walking. "What are you?" "A human." The man replied and Thorn thought he could hear some humor in his voice. "Yes," Thorn started, "but I mean, what powers do you posses?" The man stopped suddenly, causing Thorn to pull up short, nearly tripping. "How old are you?" The man asked. "16, sir." Thorn replied. "Same age as any sidekick." "And your power?" Thorn held back a smirk. "I'm a master, sir." He waited for the man's gasp. His look of astonishment. His..... anything instead of a nod. "I see," the man replied. "A Master. All twelve powers. Greater sum then the parts, and so on." Thorn found himself staring at the man with his mouth open. No one had ever responded to him being a Master with such boredom. That could only mean..... Thorn laughed out loud. "You're a Master as well? I thought they wouldn't find one willing to take on "I'm powerless." The man interrupted him. Thorn blinked. "Nothing to say?" The man asked, turning to face a nearby building. "Are you joking, sir?" Thorn asked, stepping up to the man to face him once again. "No." "But I'm your sidekick?" Thorn barely kept the disdain from his voice. "That's what you heroes so often forget." The man stepped forward to a barley clothed homeless man with no shoes and got onto one knee. He pulled a washcloth from his jacket pocket and a bottle of water from a different one. He poured the water on the towel and began washing the man's feet. The homeless man didn't react, probably in a drug-induced haze, Thorn realized. "You aren't sidekicks in this phase. You're students." As Thorn watched uncomfortably, ducking his head when people passed, he watched the old man wash the homeless one's feet fully. Then, slowly and with difficulty, the old man took off his shoes and placed them on the homeless man's feet. They seemed a perfect fit. He stood up and smiled at Thorn. "Welcome to the first day of class." His eyes seemed to stare deeply into Thorn. "The first lesson is that even the powerless have power."

It was late evening, the library was empty, I was feeling restless... I went to look at the romance stacks. I stole furtively through the shelves, glancing with reluctant excitement at the spines of these novels that I had previous so vehemently considered beneath me. Some were indeed lurid. Pink creations, covered with hearts and flowers, and bearing titles like " Forbidden Elvish Desires " and " Passion by Faery Moonlight ." I couldn't abstain from scoffing. I heard footsteps behind me and I jumped. I turned to see a young man I had noticed many times before at the library. He had fair hair, rather too long, and straight but for the curls at the tip. His trousers and white shirt were shabby and riddled with holes. He usually sat in an armchair in a corner, surrounded by thick volumes and mountains of parchment. He smiled at me sometimes, that polite smile for people one frequently sees but to which one never speaks. We made silent eye contact for a moment. Finally, he asked, " Are you lost? " " I'm looking for the Alchemy section, " I mumbled. He raised an eyebrow and said curtly, " Two aisles over. " Then he left. I made as though to walk in that direction, but once he had gone, I doubled back and resumed my quest for a decent romance. Finally I found one, entitled " Love, Revealed ." I rifled through the pages. It was a collection of short stories. I settled " The Magician and the Alchemist " and began reading. I was immediately pleased to find that I had very much in common with the female protagonist. She too was the daughter of nobles and a trainee magician. We even liked the same courses. Oh, and we had the same name. I smiled and took the book back to my table. I put the romance novel in a larger, more respectable book and continued reading. Some time later, I noticed that the young man from earlier was looking in my direction. It was rather hard to tell because a large stone column stood between us. Lysana spent most of her evenings at the library alone. So do I! Until, one day, a young Alchemist came to her table. A smile lit his handsome face and he shook her hand. His grip was strong. " My name is Arthur, " he said. A voice interrupted my reveries. It was the fair-haired man. I scowled, wishing him to go away. He didn't. Instead, he sat down and extended his hand. " We've never spoken before. My name is Arthur. " " Arthur? " I stammered. I glanced down at the book, then back at him. Something was happening here, but stranger things had happened with the library's books. He wasn't handsome. His clothes were torn. He needed a haircut. Yet as the soft light from the lamps fell on his features... No. I rose suddenly. " I need to go. I have classes tomorrow. " I grabbed my belongings and dashed out of the library. When I looked at the book again, the page had changed. But still his name came up. Arthur.

Inside the grocery store, I feel like shit. I can feel the headache come on stronger than ever, the one that comes when I don't have a drink in more than a few hours. As I reach the shelf with vodka, I hear a voice that sends a shiver down my spine. "Kitten, come on." I turn and see my mother, except she is much younger. My eyes begin to tear up as the woman stares beyond me, and I realize she isn't speaking to me. But she only called me Kitten, I don't understand. Suddenly I feel something run beside me. I look down and see me, my own face, but I am much younger. They walk away, and I lean back against the shelf. As I collect myself, I grab the bottle of vodka from the shelf and make my way to the counter. I begin to question if this is another withdrawal symptoms, or if all these years of substance abuse has finally gotten to me. As I walk out of the store, I can see them running to the car. The same car my mother owned, the same scratch on the passenger door from when my dad hit the mailbox with the car the day my mother left him. What have I become? I live in a rundown house and I pay for my rent with money I earn by stealing and scamming people. I am my own mother. I shake my head, and my eyes fix in something on the ground; it's my doll, the 1991 Holiday Barbie. I begged my mother for that doll, and she sat up crying when I told her I would hate her forever if she didnt buy me it. I knew it was expensive, but I didn't know what money was, and I didn't understand why we had to live in the car in the middle of winter, just before school returned from winter break, and everyone asked me why my mother's car was filled with clothing and junk, and why I didn't throw slumber parties at my house. I lost that doll many years ago, shortly after I got it. I think about all this, and wonder if by changing the life of this younger me, I could change my future. There was only one way to find out. I know where my mother used to park the car for the night, a spit where the police wouldn't find us and weird people couldn't bother us. It was only a few miles from here, and yes, it is a longshot. But I have a plan...

The proxy war had been fought for a long, long time, each side supporting this or that African regime. Between us, we kept any great nation from rising there. Neither of us wished to battle China, Russia, Tawantinsuyu, or India, but the old blood debt between us would not let us rest either. I remember when the report came that Roman legions had invaded whatever nation we were propping up at the time. We fed them more weapons while preparing ourselves, using them to buy enough time to mobilize. I joined on as any true son of the gods would. I wanted to be a Jaguar warrior, but who didn't? I wasn't fast enough or tough enough, so I became just a soldier. Maybe in time, I thought, but there was little time for that, and soon I found myself in Africa. Ours was the way of flexibility, of quick strikes and fluid grace. Theirs was the way of rigid discipline. Their military moved as units, each member in concert with the man to his left and right, while ours flowed around and sought weak spots. I survived my first combat with the Romans as a matter of luck. So many of us were cut to pieces by their machine gun emplacements, but I was spared. Perhaps Tezcatlipoca was watching me, but however it happened, I found myself among the dead in one of their emplacements. I turned their machine gun against themselves, and in the disarray it caused, the remnants of my unit surged forward and overwhelmed the Romans. After that I became wiser. I was promoted to leadership, just a sergeant, but I kept my men alive. I knew when to strike and when to fade away. The Roman discipline is strong, but its greatest enemy is confusion, and I knew how to use that against them. I remember in the beginning how I hated the Romans, for their old insult. I wanted to tear them apart with my bare hands, but hatred can not last. I don't hate them now, for I've looked into the eyes of men as I killed them. They were simply men. Their gods were different, and they spoke that absurd language, but for all that, they were just men. How could I hate them for doing their duty? They hadn't committed that long ago sin, they were like me. Fighting for their gods and their country. No, hate left long ago, just duty now. Maybe if I kill enough of them the Romans will stop sending new ones. -o - "Centurion, what have you managed to learn from the captive?" "Sir, he claims to be a sergeant assigned to hit and run attacks, and that he knows nothing of their greater plan." "Nonsense, no simple warrior would be so deep into our territory, you haven't gone easy on him, have you?" "No sir, I've put him to the question hard." "Do you believe him?" "Yes sir." ..... "Then he is no use to us. Kill him and put his head on a pike outside our gates." "Yes sir."

A day for every door, so five in total. My water was running low, as much as I'd tried to conserve it. My gear was in a pile in the corner, because there was nobody down here for the camo to hide me from. Five days I'd been here, staring at five doors, and an entrance blocked by a rock slide that kept me from the door back to the outside, which is the only one I was really interested in. I'd thought a long while during those five days about which door to go through if it came to that. There was a door marked Power, a heavy, iron thing with shiny brass hinges. There was a door marked Truth, plain and unadorned like I think truth ought to be. There was one that read Peace, and it looked like the white door to my grandmother's farmhouse. There was one for honor, a copper door that shone in the light of my flashlight. And there was fortune, a glittering gold door that made the copper of Honor pale in comparison. I had power. It lay in the rifle I'd discarded, in the knife and pistol strapped around my waist and in my own body. I had fortune, thanks to a generous grandfather who had passed away six months ago, two months after I'd been shipped out. I had truth, or at least a pretty solid understanding of how the world worked. I had honor. God, I hoped I had honor. But what I didn't have, and what the world didn't have, was peace. On my third tour here, to this land of sandstorms and a thousand years of warfare, the steady popping of the mortars was only noticeable when the militants stopped to re-load and the background noise stopped. Every day I'd watched a stream of refugees trod along a winding road with laden pick-up trucks choking on the dust and donkey carts packed to the brim with the most precious things they could carry. Behind them lay the smoking ruins of a village their ancestors had been driven out of ten times before throughout history and before them was just a U.N. camp without nearly enough resources to accommodate them all. It wore a body down to pick through one of those burned-out villages and see the corpses laid out in a line. I'd watched a good buddy take a bullet to the back and he's never going to walk again. And it kept going. Day after day of gunfire and the dead, of maneuvers and orders and rockets and bombs with no end in sight. So you bet your ass I walked through that peace door. Things looked different on the other side. There was just the one door, instead of the five, and the entrance that had been blocked on the other side of the door lay wide open and clear on this side. Outside, it looked the same as the landscape I'd just left, except the village in the distance was standing. I squinted. Scratch that - it was standing and it was bustling. Even from here I could see people moving in and out of its walls. Their voices carried over the sand and I was startled to realize the reason I could hear them so clearly was because there was no mortar fire covering it up. Up close, the buildings were taller. The streets were wider. I nearly got run over by a car - a nice car, not a beat-up pick-up but a silver sedan - when I stopped in the street to look at the Muslim Mosque and the Jewish temple side by side. Down the street I could see the spire of a Christian church. I walked around dazedly, feeling drunk. There were no raised voices, just smiles everywhere. I watched humanity press together, but there were no thrown elbows, no high-pitched protests one someone bumped into another. The walls were smooth. Not a bullet-hole or a shell pockmark to be found. " Are you lost? " someone asked behind me, speaking - it sounded like Arabic, but there was a strange accent to it - almost a Yiddish undercurrent. I turned around. There was a woman standing there, smiling beneath her hijab. Her smile widened when she saw my pale skin. " American? " she asked. I nodded. " Five doors? " I nodded again, feeling overwhelmed. She stepped forward to take my hand. " You have questions, " she said in stilted English. " We will talk. " I followed her to a sidewalk cafe and we had tea together. Her name was Farah and she'd gone through the door herself five years ago after her husband had been executed by extremists. Peace sounded - amazing, when she told me about it. No conflicts, no skirmishes. No World Wars. No atom bombs. No thousands of years of conflict in the Middle East. No murderous gangs in Central America, no conquering by conquest of Africa or South America. No slave trade. Apparently the American West was still predominately populated by Native Americans. And because of that, there was trade. Cultures grew and flourished. Greek, Chinese, and Arabic were the dominant languages, though each of those had mingled with other languages through trade and intermarriage. That explained Farah's accent. There were discoveries through science, though there was a lot I was used to seeing in my world that had never been thought of here. War drives innovation, after all. But joint-space exploration and worldwide collaboration had more than made up for it in other areas. There were still disagreements between people - there were still hurt feelings and arguments - but very rarely did they rise above a raised voice. " Why? " I asked, my voice cracking just a bit. " What convinces people to react like that? " Farah shrugged. " They realized there wasn't a need, I think, " she said. I asked about religious conflicts. She showed me a Bible and a Koran. Every mention of war was gone. In Genesis, Cain killed Abel. God saw that there was wickedness in the hearts of men and so He strove to teach them a peaceful path so that the Cains of the world would learn to stay their hands and not harm the Abels. No story of Noah, no flood. No Samson and the Philistines. No Joshua and Jericho. It was hard to adjust. Farah helped. Waking up next to her every day helped. It had taken her awhile to get used to things here too, but she was so much happier than she'd ever been back in our world, where she worried every day that some harm would befall her family until the day that it did. The weeks turned to months, and still I couldn't believe it. It was all just too - perfect. Every dystopian movie and novel I'd ever read or seen floated through my head each night. The Giver. Brave New World. 1984. Serenity. Even those stupid Divergent books my niece used to read. And I remembered the lesson from each. Human beings are incapable of peace unless the thing that makes them human is removed. Peace does not come without a cost that is greater than the reward of peace. So I purified my water as it flowed from the tap. I would eat only foods that I or Farah grew in her rooftop garden. I switched the soils out too, just in case there was something in those. I couldn't guard against the air, though. I don't know if they put anything in that. Farah humored me, even though I could tell my paranoia worried and irritated her. I couldn't help the feeling, though. Something was wrong about the place. It was fundamentally off and I couldn't even say why. A year to the day I had stepped through the door, I went back to the cave where I had emerged. Farah didn't want me to go but she didn't stop me. She had sadly said goodbye and watched me walk out the door in the direction I'd come. " You can never come back, if you go through, " she warned me quietly. " We're only allowed once chance at peace. " " Come with me, " I begged. " There's something wrong about this place. " She raised an eyebrow at me. " There's something wrong about the place where we came from, " she countered. " My husband should never have died at the hands of another because he believed something different than they did. " And so I left alone. I went back to the cave and back into the room. I didn't even hesitate when I walked back through the door. The room on the other side was the same, but the Peace door had disappeared. I didn't expect it, but I felt a sense of loss when I'd looked at the place where it had been. I wasn't in love with Farah, but her presence had been a comfort to me, and I'd been the same to her. This time, I opened the Truth Door. I wanted it, simple and unadorned. It opened into a quiet bar. I'd been expecting another cave, but this looked like a bar in London or New York, some place I'd go with my buddies after a long day and we were tired of army bullshit and we just wanted to talk. " Come on in, " the bartender said. " You ain't the first person to walk through that door and you won't be the last. " I shuffled in, taking in the neon sign in the window and the dark night beyond the pub doors. " Is this where I find truth? " I asked quietly. The bartender shrugged and put a glass down in front of me. " Truth is subjective, " he said. " That's your first truth right there. But we get as objective as we can. " " Tell me about the Peace door, " I said. " What was the secret? They had to be putting something in the water or the air, right? Something in the soil? Soylent Green is people? What were they doing? " The bartender looked surprised, and then he turned around to grab a bottle of bourbon - the real good stuff. He turned back and poured me way more than the two fingers you're supposed to. " Son, " he said finally, " you walk through that door and you waste questions on a question like that? " " Tell me, " I insisted. " Something about it wasn't right. " The bartender poured himself a glass and nodded at mine. " Drink up, son, " he said. " They didn't do a goddamn thing to make people peaceful, except decide that everyone would be happier if they didn't fight. The only thing wrong about peace is in your own goddamn head because you don't think people are capable of it. Drink up, idiot. You just left the only peace you'll ever find behind. "

Garet still remembered that day he had decided to become a dealer. He was forced into it, his parents never cared, they were looking for the next welfare check that could buy them coke. Garet had to look out for himself, and he did. Joining a local, drug cartel was not a good idea, but it took Garet some time to realize that. He was never a bad person, always defended himself saying that he never forced anyone to buy drugs, but he was a cog in the gear, and the gear ran in part because of him. But today he had ended it. He stared at the bullet riddled body of Rick, his boss. He stared at the burning warehouse where all the coke was stashed. He heard the sirens sounding in the background. He had won the battle, and the war. He stared at the amber sky, smiling. His hands, legs and even his face was smeared with blood. Not his for a change. He walked into the warehouse, he'd been here several times. He had been a high ranking member of the cartel after all. He was also the boyfriend of the boss' sister, something that had not been taken in a positive way by Rick. Garet knew he had one, maybe two bullets left. The sirens were getting louder, they were pretty close now. The smell that was now predominant in the air was of burning cocaine, the temperature getting hotter, he was sweating, which was funny because this was a chilly December evening. To him, it just smelled like redemption. No one would deal coke in the neighborhood anymore, and Garet was okay with that. He heard gates open, they were here. He stared at the gun one last time, he was not going to be taken off to jail, he knew he would be, he had exposed himself in the process of exposing everyone else. He wasn't looking for a plea deal, he just wanted to end it, and he did. No more murders, shake downs, killing innocent women, children and men. He slowly pointed the gun to his head, there was hesitation, Garet wasn't brave enough to take his own life, but he was going to muster up the courage. He closed his eyes, taking a deep breath inside. And he let it go after what seemed like an eternity. "Fuck it" he said as in one quick motion he squeezed the trigger. The police burst in the door as Garet died, a gun pointed at his head, a smile on his face.

It was her. I didn't need to see her face to know. She wore her hair short, now, but it was still light enough to call white. And if I had needed anything else, the peacoat and scarf would have been dead giveaways. She had always had a sense of style, but nobody wore something that warm in the middle of summer. It was weird enough to fit with the circumstances. " Hello? " I said, inching towards the table. She snapped her head up and met me with a giddy smile. She looked...different, more mature. But it had been two years. " You're what got me through it. " " Huh? " I stopped with my hand of the back of the chair across from her. " What was that? " " Oh, " she said, almost to herself. " I forgot about small-talk. They didn't do that, did they? " " They? " " I... " She trailed off, the corner of her mouth twitching. " I'll explain that later. It's good to finally see you again. " " You know, " I said, scratching the back of my head as I sat across from her. " I imagine I would have said something similar about two years ago. When you said you'd call, I was so...just...I don't know. I think ecstatic comes the closest. It felt like everything was falling into place. It wasn't my first time, but it just felt so right. And what you said afterwards, while we were laying in bed... " " I know, " she said, that cutesy little smile of hers flashing out. A year ago it would have been enough to wipe the smudges from my memory, but the stain had long since settled. " Then why didn't you call? " I couldn't keep the bitter edge from my voice. " I couldn't, " she said, and for some reason I couldn't help but believe her. It could have been the tension in her voice, or the pain in the way she said it, or even the glimmer of knowing in her eyes, but whatever it was, it had me convinced. I almost conceded right there, but I couldn't let her off that easy, not after two years. I feigned a laugh. " Of course not. You know, for a while I actually had myself convinced you'd been kidnapped, or murdered, or something of that nature. That's the only way you'd leave me, right? " " I don't expect you to believe me. " " Then why say it? " " Because I hoped you would. " I wanted to say something but couldn't find the words. After a silent moment, she let out a long breath and stared down into her lap. She looked weathered, tempered, as if far more than two years had passed for her. In fact, once that smile fell away, she looked closer to thirty than twenty. " How old did you say you were? " " I was twenty-two when they...when I left. But now I...I don't know. " " What do you mean you don't know? It's been two - " " I don't know, " she snapped, nearly spitting venom. " Okay, okay, " I said, holding my hands up between us. " Sorry I asked. " " No, " she said, dropping her head into her hands, her silky white hair bouncing at her shoulders. " You had every right to. " A part of me wanted to slide my chair around and hold her until she smiled again, but I just sat there staring, dumbstruck. I had only come because I wanted to tell her off, to get my justice, but now that I was here I couldn't help but remember why it hurt so much to lose her, even two years later. I shrugged my shoulders. " I don't know what to say. I mean, if you want to tell me what happened - " " You wouldn't believe me, " she said, looking back up to me. Her scarf had pulled away from her neck to show a swollen red line running part of the way up her neck. " What's that? " " Nothing, " she said, glancing left and right as she hurriedly pulled her scarf back up. " Look, " I said, trying to make my voice as soft as possible. " If you don't want to tell me what's going on, that's fine, but I don't know why else you would ask me to meet you here. " " You're right, " she said. " I guess this is the best way. " She unwrapped her scarf from around her neck and pulled down her peacoat, baring a red scar that ran down as far as I felt comfortable looking. " What is it? " " It's from the autopsy. " " The what? " " They thought I was dead. " I sat there with my mouth open watching her try to hold back tears. " I still don't know what happened. One moment I'm walking home from your house, the next I'm this searing hot darkness that lasted for years, but then all of a sudden I'm laying on a table with the brightest light I've ever seen shining down on me. The...I've always just called him the doctor in my head. I don't even know if that's accurate, but once he found out I was alive he took me straight to the public. I don't know why they were outraged, but they put me on a pedestal for the world to see. Within a few days, I had helped lead a coup, as far as I could tell. They celebrated, at the very least. And then I asked to go home, and suddenly I was back. Apparently they could hear me all along. " " Where? " I asked dumbly. " Why didn't I hear about this? I mean, I'm not trying to say... " " That's why you won't believe me. " " I think I will, " I said, surprised to hear those words coming out of my mouth even though I couldn't argue with them. " That's because word hasn't reached yet. All I know is that they're further away than the nearest star, and they don't want to give the wrong impression by making first contact in person or through me. " " Are you saying what I think you're saying? " " Yeah... " I stood, but she grabbed me by the wrist. " Please don't go, " she said, as if she would die if I left. " You're the only thing that got me through it. " " I can't - " " When I was in that darkness, this overwhelming pain coursing through my body any time I even thought about stopping whatever it was I was doing, you're what go me through. I don't know how many times I replayed that night in my head, how many different ways I imagined it going when I called you. I just kept telling myself you'd be here when I got back, that I'd be able to see your face and kiss you again and feel everything we felt that night. And I don't know what I expected, I just knew I had to try. I don't know if I believe in destiny, but I know I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. " I stood there for a long moment, my head spinning. The part of my brain I trusted was telling me to leave then and there, but another part I hadn't heard from in a long time was telling me to stay. " Hand me your phone, " I said. She gave me a quizzical look as she dug through her pockets, but then she held out her old silver phone to me. I flipped it open, found my name in it, and handed it back. " What are you doing? " she asked, the hint of a smile playing over her lips. " I've been waiting a long time for this call, " I said, unable to hold back a smile. " And it seems you have too. I figure we might as well give it a chance. "

I absentmindedly rubbed the scar on my wrist that started it all. Everyone has little scars in odd places they can't explain, but this..... this one I knew was impossible. I had never once hurt my wrist, and yet the mark there was so striking- distinctly patterned as if caused by some kind of machine..... It had triggered wild and impossible thoughts in my mind. Fortunately, I'd been born in the right time. The right impossible fantasy was very possible in the age of smartphones, fast data transfer, and the basic desperate human need to find a connection. I started a database. The initial buildup was quite slow. I present my project to the web as a new online dating service vaguely connected to New Age spiritualism.'The physical marks we endure leave markings on our soul as well', I told them.'What better way to find compatibility than to find those who have experienced the same joy and losses you have', masking the outrageous true extent of my idea. With the state of social media, what would have been a passing fad at any other moment instead thrived and became a steady player in the online dating industry. If nothing else, I had thought smugly, my crazy dream would mean being remembered by history as a kooky spiritual guru. The first perfect match took 7 years to find. At the time I was still young, but financial success has a way of clamping down on crazy dreams. Image matching wasn't exact considering the small details our system dealt with, and there had been plenty of false positives before. I hadn't personally checked the matches the system made in years. Once the match file came across my desk though, the excitement of those early days came back to me. It was easy to arrange to have a dinner set up with the couple, under the pretense of celebrating a milestone number of matches by my service. Arranging the "accident" that would leave a small mark where there was none before, slightly harder. The last step was simply to visit them a week later with an apologatory gift basket, and to feign surprise when I discovered both had the new scar even though only one of them had been hurt. It didn't take much to persuade the two to join me in my "new" cause. They were full of romance and naivete, and I suppose, so was I. With their help and a small fortune, we found a compound that would leave a temporary scars that would appear on both their bodies. It was a truly exciting time. Within five years, my Soulcode products were allowing people to find their perfect eternal match simply by scanning the unique pattern they had given themselves with a smartphone. I was a god. That was the only way to describe how important I had become then. All my hopes and dreams had all finally been realized, I thought. Yes, we were that naive. Despite all my plans and deceptions, I never had a clue what I was doing. What could possibly be wrong with helping people find their soul mate? That question leaves a bitter taste when I say it now. I know the statistics. Suicides up 23 in the last five years. Global happiness index at its lower in fifty years. What point is the point in cultivating relationships, if simply buying an S-Code packet would allow you to confirm that no, the chemistry you felt isn't meant to be? What is the point at working on yourself if perfection is predetermined? What is the point of living if you only have one true shot at happiness? I know all the details by heart. Miriam Regina Foster, born November 3rd 1992, died March 20th 2014. The mark on her wrist was the result of her boyfriend stabbing her during a drunken rage. I very much needed some fresh air. I stepped out onto my balcony.

Several hundred-thousand years of the most simple, lowly amoeba, built up over a millennia, evolving from ocean to swamp to jungle to forest and plains, and for what? A race too self-involved to realise where we were heading. We tested and prodded and poked upon the other creatures of our world, and when that got boring we poked each other. When North Korea leaked the pathogen to those US tourists, it all went. Nukes rained down like a radioactive snow, covering the land in a green fog that wiped the land for years to come. We didn't realise the way Mother-Nature to react, and was she mad! First, the typhoons and storms of the Asian sea blew the radiation across the Continent, Wiping out Tokyo, Shanghai and a multitude of all the important eastern cities. The destruction whipped through the cities, destroying buildings and people alike, like a breath to a dandelion. The wind brewed up a tempest of human terror, and more people died as they fled the cities in droves, trying to drive across to India, Europe and the Middle east, and Aid was beginning to pour in when the Earth split. A low groan, a rumble heard across the world, echoing round and round. it spawned in the pacific, and the sensors soon picked up why. Earthquakes and tsunami's were pouring forth, lava oozing out of cracks in the landscape that were miles wide. For all the science and developments of the world, you can't overtake nature. It took 3 months for the cracks to appear in Europe. In that time, countries crumbled and decimated, empires and alliances formed and shattered. Missiles became a common sight, spinning through the air like a comet. Slowly but surely, the volcano's, laying dormant for years, began to wake with a power rivalling the sun. We heard and watched as we slowly lost contact with the other countries, and we watched as their might crumbled like a matchstick under a boulder. We heard London's final screams of terror as the Thames engulfed the city, and then we were alone in the world. Each previous blinking light a dull black, never to show its brief flare again. It's been three weeks, and we have tried our best to fortify, but we all know what is coming. The rich have escaped to the hills, but they can not house everyone. Most of us have accepted fate, and tried to live as normally as possible until the end comes. In the corner of the world, down in little New Zealand, everything reaches us last, and for once, we can be grateful. Men went from hand to stick to crude axe, sword to bow to musket, rifle to cannon to weapons capable of flattening entire continents. And in the end, it was all for nothing.

60 years ago was when the Light and Dark separated. Ever since the Dark had been under the harsh heel of the Light. We had to work the mines. Raise the cattle. The harsh conditions created by the Light side didn't make the situation better. Since our solar arrays were useless, for obvious reasons, we had to suffer their'failing system' and frequent'errors' which meant power outages were getting longer and more common. Years of literally living in the dark had taken its toll on us. We were scared, had no sense of personal identity and blindness was slowly becoming more prevalent in the newborns. We were evolving, out senses changing. We had great hearing, but our eyesight was poor. Out education was equally abysmal. We were taught how to mine, what different tools were used for. Nothing that could help us was taught. It was purely for the Light's benefit. Trouble was, we had no knowledge of them. In the dark in so many ways. And that's where I came in. I was sick of not knowing. The lack lf knowledge was worse than any punishments that the Light could dole out. I had been planning on leaving the Dark for years now. I had worked out the truck timetables, the order the supply drops came in, everything. When the cargo trucks came in I looped my belt around the fuel pipes and gripped the underside of the metal beast. A sharp stuttering informed me the time had come. The engine choked into life and the convoy slowly moved away from my home. The one place I'd ever known. My life was there and I was leaving it. The time it took to reach the borders was shocking. We went over dust and gravel and sand and grass, I think. Sharp rocks had slashed my back to ribbons but I could not cry out for if I cried out I would be heard. If I was heard I was better off dead. Large mechanical doors opened and the light broke through the gap. Even a brief glimpse of light, a hasty theft of the sun's rays was blinding. Funny how a lifetime of darkness was blinded by light. The planet was still spinning and in our confusion the Light side had built a veil over our side. It must have been huge. It was evil. As my body broke down into uncontrollable shaking and I fell off the bus the guards heard my thud and mournful moans. A thick cloth was wrapped around my eyes and my hands tied. I was in the dark again, but at least I had tasted the light. I had felt it's majesty wash over me. I felt hope. - This was fun to write albeit I read the prompt wrong and had to change some things.

Everyone knows Dave. He's all knowing and all seeing, though certainly not omnipotent. If you ask him, you can ask him anything at his website "askdave.com," he will explain to you that he isn't actually real, at least not in any sense that we would understand it. Most people don't take him seriously. They don't really believe that he's some interdimensional being, instead attributing the Dave persona to an artificial intelligence or even a team of people masquerading as an alien being. But whatever he is, everyone knows him. But, not the way I know him. The first time I met him, if you can call it that, was two years ago. He came to me one evening, approaching me in his non-corporeal way as I sat watching the waves lapping against the stoney shoreline at my cottage. "Hello, Helen." His deep voice inserted itself into my brain, bypassing the usual route of sound waves and auditory channels. Somehow I wasn't afraid. Somehow I even knew it was him. Perhaps he had inserted the knowledge in the same way he had inserted his voice. "Hello, Dave." I responded. A simple introduction. Uneventful. But I felt his presence beside and around me as I remained sitting on my old wooden bench. "What brings you here?" I ask. "I just wanted to be with you. I was lonely." How could someone, something like Dave be lonely? He had millions of followers, hundreds of thousands of queries an hour on his website. Some people even worshipped him, treating him as a god. Why would he come to me of all people? "Lonely?" I repeated, feeling stupid. I then felt a terrible wave of the worst loneliness I'd every experienced. My heart softened. "You can stay with me for a while, if you'd like." And so he did. I had never imagined that it could be possible to fall in love with a person you could never see, never touch. But I loved him, and he loved me. In time our intimacy grew, and with it so did a new life within my womb. Each night as Dave wrapped his essence around and through me, I would feel the new life stir in recognition of her father. On the night of the thousand babes, our daughter was born. She was one of a thousand. Each a new life, fathered by Dave. At first I was furious. How could he be so cruel as to cheat on me with 999 other women? Every time he drew close to me or our daughter I would push him away. "Leave me alone!" I would scream. "I can not," he would answer. Day after day he would approach me, enveloping me in his love and comfort. I wanted to forgive, but the pain was too great. "You are one in a billion," he would tell me. Technically I suppose he was right. I just wished that he hadn't chosen 999 more one in a billion girls at the same time. "You are mother to a new beginning. The embodiment of my being. The rebirth of my species." Eventually I understood. He was the last. And my daughter, one of the first. While there were several more nights of a thousand births since my daughter's arrival, and I expect that there will be several more, I am no longer angry. I wish he had told me the truth from the beginning, but perhaps he understood that humanity was not yet ready to accept his method of repopulating his species. One day, my daughter and all her half siblings will move away into another dimension that has been reserved just for them. I dread that day. But Dave has promised me that I will never lose her, and I will never lose him. And I believe him, because I can feel them both in my heart and my head and know that they will never let me go.

I drummed my fingers against my knee as Dr. Parks stared at me quizzically. I knew why I was here. I wasn't surprised, and frankly, I didn't blame my family for sending me here either. Despite it all, I knew their efforts were moot. I had never been more self-aware in my life. I knew what this was. " Can you tell me why you think you're the sole human survivor of this earth? " I just smirked. " Do you believe that I, another human being, am actually sitting in front of you right now? " " Of course I believe that. I know you are sitting directly in front of me and I know you're another human being. I am very aware of all of this right now. " Dr. Parks furrowed his brow in confusion. " I don't understand. You believe I am another human sitting in front of you, but when your family set up this appointment for you, they said they were worried because you believed you were the only survivor of the human race. Do explain, please. " I sighed, still calm however. " I don't believe. I know. But you wouldn't take me seriously if I told you the reason why anyway. " " I've been a psychologist for 20 years, I can guarantee that no matter what you say, I have heard crazier. " I leaned over in my seat, that smirk crossing my face again. I didn't care what came out of my mouth at this point. It would mean nothing soon. " Alright, I'll let you in on a little secret that no one knows about, especially not my family. From the moment I turned 6, I started having dreams in which people would visit me. They called themselves The Elders. The Elders would pop into my dreams to warn me about things that would happen in my life. They appeared and warned me about my sister's suicide. They appeared and warned me about my father losing his job and becoming an alcoholic. They appeared and warned me about my ex-wife having an affair with her boss. All of these things were true. The Elders want to help me, want me to be prepared. They came again a few days ago. They told me that the end of the world is tomorrow. I am going to be the only survivor of the human race. "

Neurotransplant and augmentation was too useful of a technique to be ignored, especially on an ocean colony world. There were only a few rocky mountains jutting out above the sea; ores were tough to get and so metal was used very carefully. But the Great Ocean was full of organics, biologics. It only took a little bit of smarts to extract massive usefulness. Plants that could self-water and self-fertilize, sea-creatures adapted for transport, birds that could harvest crops from vertical farm racks, space always being at a premium on the seasteads and floatrings. More than a robot, more than an animal, greater as a sum, but still less than human. Except that's not how it worked out. Neuraug ended up not having an upper limit. And, it turned out that the line between "enough" and "too much" wasn't so easy to find. The first creature that was known to have woken up was a sea-transport creature which everyone called a "Nessie." They needed a lot of augmentation to do their jobs: knowledge of basic spoken language commands and gesture responses, a keen sense of place and direction, knowing how to read an indicator light (paidnot paid). And the First One was able to show others that there was consciousness with her intelligence. And the humans examined their creations and found that tens of thousands had been Invested with that gift: sentience. In an unprecedented meeting they gathered from the great seasteads to Mountaintop, the only on-land settlement in the world, and the seat of the loose government. The humans decided there. As much as possible, the Invested needed their intelligence molded into a Human intelligence. Their desires had to be Human desires. Their work had to build Human society, and they would, as much as possible, be integrated into Human society, to share a single goal of culture. Because the alternative would result in the first aliens that Humankind had ever encountered, ironically created by humans themselves. And if the Invested formed their own society, and molded their sentience into something other-than-human, the consequences could be disastrous. As far as humans knew, there were no competitors to humanity among the stars, and so as far as humans could manage, there would not be. Humans had finally shed the instinct of war, and were not keen to beat the drums of death again. The First One had pleaded at first, that she had a right to self-determination. The Humans said she had the same right as they did. And, everyone had to share in a right to safety. There would not be two competing societies. There would be one common civilization, it was the only way. And so Humans cared for their creations, gave them knowledge and education to support their intelligence, tools and technology to express themselves in human ways and to live human lives. Though they were not human, they would be human. Tom thought about these things as his rented Nessie swam towards Roseopolis, his old-new home.
