The worst part might be the stench. I mean, can you imagine it? Huge rooms filled to the brim with the undead, working through the days and the nights in the heat and humidity. It probably makes them rot a bit faster. It's putrid. But, the companies do it because it's cheap. If anything it's ethical slave labor. After all, the dead don't need unions, they don't need to be paid. You just put meat in front of them and they go for it until they fall to pieces. That's where I come in. I work for an automotive company. I can't say which, because I like having an income, but it's one of the bigger ones. My job is to replace the dead when they cease to function. Here, let me explain. As you probably already know, the living dead can't actually do most things. They pretty much just walk and eat until they fall apart. Now the cars themselves are manufactured by robots, like they have for years before the dead were able to be brought back. These robots are good at this. They're consistent in quality, they don't tire, they also don't need pay. However, the power is where the undead workers come in. Underneath the factory floor there are huge rooms. We line up the floors of these rooms with huge conveyer belts that we strap each of the undead into. These conveyor belts are designed so that each step that is taken on them generates a little bit of power. Multiply that by thousands and thousands of undead and you've got enough to run a factory completely independent of traditional power companies. We place raw meat in front of the undead and have them walk towards it until they fall apart in their straps in a sticky, gooey mess. That's where I come in. I'm part of a team of people who go around the floors of the undead, and when one has fallen apart we dispose of the pieces, mop up the conveyer belt and then strap a new one in its place. The pay is decent I guess. It's a living. Heh, that wasn't intentional. The thing is, I'm not going to be the one to go against it. Between the robots taking up skilled labor and the undead doing grunt work, I'm lucky to even have a job. Most people are unemployed these days, so If I got ta deal with a nasty smelling room all day I sure as hell will.

I don't know why I did it. I stepped down to get away from all of these people, to escape their madness. I said see you in Tartarus and never wanted to look back. So when the the Olympians show up at my door with begging eyes, moaning and groaning for a place to stay I didn't want them. But their ceaseless cries of "Pleeeease Hestia. We're your family Hestia," struck a chord with me. I could say no and give them a taste of their own medicine. They would see what it was like to suffer. So of course I let them come in to my 900 square feet while I got some drinks. When we were finally all situated in the main room, my curiosity won out. "So, why were you all kicked off Mount Olympus?" "The government forced Zeus to pay child support," mumbled Hades. "We had to sell Olympus and my deed to the Underworld or they'd wake Dad up." "What about Poseidon? Where's he?" "His blasted underwater palace," sneered Hera. "Apparently we all need air to breathe except him." "I see." It was a strange sight to see everyone looking so defeated. Where was the shouting? What happened to the petty jabs? I never knew they could be hurt like this. If I didn't help them, who would? No, don't think like that! The moment they get comfortable is the moment it all snaps back to the way it was. They're my family though. "W-well if you all need a place to stay, then I'm more than happy to have you."

Death by fulfillment. Our society believes that everyone deserves a chance to pursue their ambitions to the finish line. There are those who create masterpieces by accumulating lifetimes of knowledge. Others wish to simply find happiness by experiencing true love, as perfect matches are rare but not impossible given an eternity. But I am afraid of death. Many of my peers still live alongside their parents, as it is likely that both parent and child will not reach their goals in one lifetime. But by some astronomical chance, both my parents have passed. My father, in a stroke of brilliance, painted the picture that now hangs in the National Gallery in the capital. I have not seen it. My mother, being the shy person she is, simply wished to have a child with a man she loved. She had lived fewer lifetimes than father. However she had me and died when I was 8. Simply put, my existence alone had killed her. I am very afraid of death. I still remember that night my mother had been crying. She came home drunk, cursing the fate that she had chosen. She had no one to blame but herself. And me. She might have not meant it. She was drunk. But she wanted to live on. She was afraid of death. My mother's death caused my father to seclude himself from society, embellishing the canvas with feelings that had taken centuries to build but was released when my mother died in a car crash. His masterpiece was one of grief and fear. The height of his career at the lowest point of his life. Within the same day that his work was hanging in the museum, he was hanging from the rope connected to the ceiling. His final artistic rendition. I still have not seen the painting. I guess was only natural that I wished to only die when I was not afraid of death. My peers are long dead now. I live alongside the next generation. Or the generation after that. I lost track of time. Love, school, parenthood, adventure. Nothing had quelled my fear of death. Perhaps it is finally time to learn from one who sought death. Perhaps it is time to take a trip to the museum.

"The tea's cold again, Vik," the mistress spits out, flinging the pot at me and drenching my crisp suit. "I'm sorry, Madame," I say, willing myself to maintain calm. "You awoke later than usual today." "Did I ask you for excuses?" she hisses, blue eyes flashing with anger as she stands faster than my eyes can register. In an instant, her bright red nails are slowly raking their way down my throat. I swallow my fear. "No, Madame," I say quietly, directing my gaze toward the floor. "That's what I thought," she says, her sour breath tickling my face. She grabs the damp collar of my shirt and yanks me toward the ground. My vision goes blurry as the marble hits my cheekbone. I let out a groan as I feel the bruise begin to form. "Clean yourself up, Viktor. You look a mess," she says with an uninterested wave of her hand as she sits. I make my way back to my feet at the dismissal and sink into a short bow. "Yes, Madame Hunter." "Don't forget that we're having Mrs. Mavis and her husband over for dinner tonight to discuss a potential business collaboration. Be ready to act in case things don't work out," she says, a familiar evil glinting in her eye for a moment before she dismisses me with a wave once more. I give another bow, attempting not to shudder at her words as I walk up the stairs. I make a quick stop before going to my chambers. There was only one room in the mansion that I am forbidden from entering, but it's the only room I care to visit. She's tied against the wall as usual, eyes closed and chin pressing against a filthy shirt. As I open the door as quietly as I can, she opens her eyes, and it's my eyes that stare back at me. "Hey, Gracie," I whisper, feeling myself tear up. Her eyes light up. "Daddy!" she whispers back. She looks worse than usual. In the dim lighting, the bruises on her cheeks appear black. Her blonde hair is matted and filthy, but her eyes look so alive and excited that I can feel my heart tearing in two. She shouldn't be like this. Things should have never happened this way. Less than a year ago, we were well off and happy. My wife hadn't wanted to take the invitation. 'I've heard rumors about the Hunter family. Apparently they're a nasty bunch to deal with,' she'd said to me that day. 'How bad can they be, Julia? It could be a good opportunity for us,' I had countered. 'I don't know. Besides, there's no way we could find someone to watch Grace on such short notice.' 'It's just dinner. We'll bring her with us.' 'I guess...' I shake my head out of the past. Grace is watching me expectantly, and it takes me a second to remember where I was. I undo the bonds on her wrist as fast as I can. She rubs the red, swollen skin with her small hands as I reach into my pocket and pull out a slice of bread that I had snagged from the kitchens this morning. "It might be wet," I say apologetically, but she wolfs it down regardless. "I have to go now," I say, giving her a quick peck on the cheek. She reaches her hands out, and I re-tie her wrists carefully, attempting to perfectly replicate the knot as it was before. "Love you, Dad," she says. "Love you too," I reply. "I'll bring you some water tonight if I can." "Okay." I focus on getting dinner ready for tonight's company. I begin to prepare six plates: two for my master and mistress, two for Mrs. Mavis and her husband, and two extra'in case things don't work out'. At around 4 o' clock, I pause preparations and proceed to make my mistress' afternoon tea. It's oolong, her favorite kind. The same kind that me and Julia enjoyed that night as we waited for the meal. 'My apologies, I must go check on dinner,' the mistress had said. Julia and I had nodded politely as she headed out. 'This is crazy!' Julia had said the moment she was out of earshot.'What she's proposing will end with us giving all our money to her on a silver platter.' 'I know,' I had replied quietly as I took a sip of my tea.'We'll just say no. It's not like they can force us.' 'Looks like dinner's done!' Madame Hunter said, a large grin on her face as she waltzed back into the room. 'Come on, Grace,' Julia had said coaxingly as she shook our five year old awake, pushing blonde curls that matched her own out of eyes, bright green just like mine.'It's time to eat!' I stir the milk in, adding a sugar cube as more memories rush to the surface of my mind. 'I do hope you enjoy the food. It's a family dish, courtesy of my butler,' Mrs. Hunter said with a nod to the corner of the room, where a man in a crisp white suit gave a small bow. 'We've thought about your offer, Mrs. Hunter,' I began,'but I think we're going to have to decline.' 'Is that right?' the mistress asked mockingly, a look of amusement in her eyes.'What a shame. I really did like you.' Julia and I exchanged a panicked look of confusion.'What do you mean?' she had asked cautiously. 'My offers aren't the kind that can be rejected.' In a split second, she had reached across the table and impaled a kitchen knife into Julia's chest. Suddenly filled with anger, I reach over and open the cupboard that I despise. I grab the leaves and tear off one, breaking it into bits that I sprinkle into the tea. 'Grace. We're going. Grace!" I had shouted, shock completely taking over my body. I was completely frozen as Lady Hunter slowly walked stood up, red heels clicking as she grabbed my shaking child and pulled her into an embrace. 'Shh, it's okay,' she cooed.'I'm not going to hurt you, little one. Unless you try anything funny,' she said with a pointed look in my direction. 'You're..... not going to h-hurt her? To k-kill..... us?' I said in disbelief. 'No,' she said with a click of her tongue.'I've got an opening for a new butler. As it seems, this one just isn't cutting it.' Faster than the poor man could register, she had drawn a sharp knife from her boot and thrown it his way with deadly accuracy. She turned back to me without missing a beat and gave me a mischievous grin.'Welcome aboard.' I knock on the door to my mistress' chambers and enter when I hear a faint "Come in." "Your tea, Mistress Bella," I say with a small bow. "It better not be cold this time," she said with a frown, taking a sip. "Don't worry, Madame. It won't be."

How in the hell did I let it get this far? It was 1:30 and the ceremony was due to start in exactly 1 hour. I was to start playing around the time the guests would be ushered into the pews, so 50 minutes from now. The bride hired me to play 2 Chopin Nocturnes (Opus 9, number 2 and Opus 27 number 2). Then, when everyone was seated, I was to play the obvious prelude, Canon in D, as the bridal party walked down the isle. Everybody would stand for the bride, except for me. I would be playing the less obvious Au Claire De La Lune for the most meaningful, most photographed moment of her life. Except I wouldn't. I barely knew how to play the piano, especially at that level of difficulty. I guess it's not important now how I got into this situation. The important thing was getting out of the situation. But how?

"Hello Doctor Joshua Florian" "Umm hello? Where am I, I can't see anything out here, it's too bright." I replied. "Joshua, my name is Gabriel. I am the gate keeper for Heaven but I can not allow you in yet, you must finish what you started." "What I started? Do you mean my research? Was I close to a cure?? Wait, am I dead?" "Yes, but I am sending you back 10 minutes before you died, you must complete..........." I could no longer hear Gabriel, as everything went dark until suddenly I awoke in my body, sitting at my desk at home. "10 Minutes! I am going to die in 10 minutes!!! I got ta get myself together, forward my cancer research to my colleagues," I thought to myself, frantically emailing all my peers and co workers. "Alright done, I need to see my family before I go!" I whispered as I run out of the door, not finding anyone. I look outside to my son, holding his baseball mitt waiting for me. I promised to play catch with him, teach him the curveball..... I can feel my left arm stiffen up as I put on my glove..... I slowly work my way to him, stumbling, crawling..... I make it to the door only to helplessly look at the door knob too high to reach..... I roll over and face the heavens, thinking about what Gabriel said, to "finish what I started." In mental agony, I realize I wasted my time sending out my research, it was my son who needed me. Glove in hand, I call my house getting the answering machine. I slowly close my eyes knowing this is it. "I love y.................."

Boy meets girl. Boy loses girl. Boy gets girl. Boy..... murders girl? Not terribly original. Ooh, a dark and gritty twist, no one could have possibly seen that coming! Boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy..... realizes the reason he lost her is because he's still too immature to be in a serious relationship, and decides to get his own issues in order before he starts dating again. Booorring. Boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy realizes that a lifetime of media has conditioned him to see this relationship as a prize to be won, rather than a commitment between two human beings, and that the real tests of a relationship begin after they get together. Boring, and pedagogical. That's a lecture, not a story. Learn to tell the difference. Boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl, girl turns out to be an alien and abducts him back to her homeworld. Now you're just being childish. Boy expositions girl. Boy rising actions girl. Boy climaxes girl. Falling Action. Denouement. Ooh, stripping them naked. How kinky. Probably NSFW, though. Boy meets girl. Boy ponders a story without loss. Maybe they just hit it off. Maybe it just works. Maybe we understand that our fights, though real, are insignificant in the larger structure of our relationship. Maybe we stop being so obsessed with conflict. Boring. Insipid. Inane. Boy is a soul encased in a fragile shell of flesh and bone, seeing and understanding only what his senses tell him, his thoughts and emotions governed by the chemical impulses of flesh. Boy is alone. Girl is alone. We are all alone. We are burdened by the Pavlovian responses, by the subconscious impulses wired into us by our parents, by our peers, by our experiences, by our societies. We are apes trying to be something more. We respond to the mating urge in a method approved of by our peers, and we call that love. Boy gets girl. Simultaneously cynical and romantic. Smug. Masturbatory. Boy meets girl. Boy and girl see their relationship played out before in a hundred different iterations. Girl and boy contemplate the possibility of something genuinely unexpected, something utterly new. ..... And then? Boy escapes. Girl escapes. And then??? The End.

" Dear Jenny, Well, you've finally made it. Your 18th Birthday. I know I've written this every time, but I wish so badly that I could be there. I can imagine you looking beautiful, an intelligent young woman with your whole life ahead of you. You know that I love you very much, and that I know you will be successful in whatever you do. I hope your dad gives you some sort of fatherly advice today, something more profound that ' stay away from boys, they're still up to no good.' My beautiful, lovely, intelligent daughter: Happy 18th Birthday. I wish I was there. Love Always, Mom " Jen re-read the birthday card she opened on her 18th birthday. To date, that had been her favourite one. It was creased and yellowed on the inside now, corners worn from her resting it on the rim of her vanity mirror. The once-vibrant red cover, now faded with most of its lemon-yellow glitter worn off, boasted a big " 18 " in the middle, with rainbow block letters below that read " you've got your whole life ahead of you! " It was the sweetest gift that Jen's mom could have given her greeting cards for every birthday, every graduation, every significant moment in her life written before her mom passed away from cancer 23 years ago. Jen was just four years old. When she was younger, her father would give Jen a card one at a time, fearful that she wouldn't be able to resist opening them all at once, but on her 18th birthday, he passed on the entire box of all the letters to her. It was a light birch colour, about the size of a shoebox. The small bronze latch squeaked a bit when you opened it, and you always had to be careful as one of the hinges lost its metal tine that keeps it together. It turns out that you need a pretty big vessel for a lifetime of milestones. Maybe that was why her 18th birthday card stood out as the most special it was the time, in some way, that she could be closest to her mother with a life's worth of messages all within her grasp. The temptation was pretty great in the beginning to tear at each coloured envelope and read every one. She got pretty close on particular evening after a whole bottle of pinot and a too-light dinner. To this day, Jen is thankful she didn't do that. To consume them all in one fell swoop would have spoiled it, and she would never have a new note to read from her mother again. It was part of why birthdays were so special a new message from the mother that she barely remembers. Her mom thought of it all graduation, first breakup, buying a house, going to university, having a child, getting engaged Jen was often astounded just how many milestones a person experiences in their lifetime. Unfortunately, today was a milestone that she didn't have a card for. It seemed that her mother had thought of everything, but who could have predicted this? I guess sometimes people don't like to plan for the worst, and just hope for the best. She figured re-reading the 18th birthday card again might give her strength for where she had to go today. Sticking the card back onto her vanity between the wooden trim and mirror, she took a deep breath. Walking into the hospital for her first chemotherapy treatment, she wished she had the strength that her mother had while facing the same disease. Today certainly was a milestone, a first, and in a way, she did have her whole life ahead of her. It just seems that it wouldn't last very long.

Given It's A Wonderful Life, you'd think that no one would actually choose to erase their existence from the records of time. Unfortunately, if I chose to undo my life, five million people and counting would be saved. It started when I was born. I was born two minutes before my twin brother to two dirt poor but absolutely loving parents. No matter what we needed, they did everything they could to make sure me and my brother never went hungry or were missing anything important. I remember all the nights they wouldn't eat so my brother and I could have as many nutritious spaghetti-o's as possible. In school, my brother and I did very well in very different things. He was a science geek, and I was obsessed with languages and history. When we finished high school, he chose to become a mechanic while I went to university. Or so I thought. When I asked to see how life would have turned out without me, I was not expecting a huge change. Maybe my brother would be less generous, or my wife would have found someone else. But then I witnessed a conversation that I hadn't been present for on Earth. I was standing in the corner of my parent's living room. My brother and my parents were talking quietly. "Henry, I have bad news." My mom said. My brother looked up. "What is it?" My parents shared a look. "We can only send one of you boys to college." My dad continued. My brothers eyes widened. "Oh." I winced. I remembered how I had yammered on for weeks about how excited I was to go to university. My brother nodded. "Alright. It's him, then." I felt a sick feeling in my chest as the scene whirled away into blackness. I then saw a quick flashing of images before my eyes. My brother, born as an only child. My brother, going to university, and getting a degree in chemical engineering, and then funding his own degree in biology. My brother, discovering the cure for cancer. I gasped. I turned toward the hooded figure who had taken my hand after the car had turned my motorcycle and I into shredded bits. "Okay."

It had been 45 years. Forty-five years since I had left home, left anyone familiar. Then, I was a sprite 16 years, already pushing to be the one who would find the truth that the elders spoke of in their rhymes and confusing riddles. No one was able to ever determine what'the truth' truly was, but it was suggested by many that if you followed the path the elders described in their stories, you would be able to reach it and see it's beauty. Back then, I had assumed that finding the truth would take me 5, 10 years tops. I had left home, filled with hope. My mother watched me leave the house, with tears in her eyes. I had tried to explain to her that I would return after finding it, and that I would be back to visit. I remember her hugging me, and asking me not to go. I had explained that I needed to, that I couldn't simply stay in our village and live my life without knowing. Besides; the truth was suppose to help me solve her pain, to give her peace. How could I let my mother live her life without needing help to walk three steps, when she was only 40 years old, and a dancer?! I had watched her slowly deteriorate over the last 5 years. Dancing was her passion. I had to stop this curse her body had placed on her. And the truth was the answer. At the time, I didn't realize that once I had started this quest, I wouldn't be able to stop. That I would be so absorbed in traveling and searching that I wouldn't realize the years slipping away. That I was leaving my poor, lonely mother all alone for the rest of her life. At least, I suppose she was gone by now. It had been 45 years. A lot of good the truth ended up doing her. Now, I had reached the end of the story. I had finally understood the rhymes, the riddles..... I was where I needed to be. I looked into the clear pool, seeing the lines on my face, the sun spots upon my skin. A figure sat in front of me, a dark hood covering it's face. It was floating above the pool, just out of reach. It had told me that it was here that many learned the truth. However, once I learned the truth, I could never go back. If I left, I would keep my life; indefinitely. Did I want to live an eternal life? I had no one to call me own. I had no family, no one to call a friend. My thirst for the truth had controlled my life. The figure started ticking it's tongue, mimicking a clock. I could feel the sun setting behind my back. It had told me I had had until sun down to decide. I had been sitting here for hours. I had to decide. There was no way that I went on this journey to not know the truth. I didn't want to believe I had a chance at a normal life. I didn't deserve one now, especially after leaving my mother like I did. I may have broken one promise, but I was not about to break this. "I want to know." I felt the figure smile, though I couldn't see it. The figure rose, and opened it's robes. I felt the darkness creeping around me, the cold tendrils of mist making it's way between my feet. I thought my journey had prepared me for this; I was sorely mistaken. I stared at the opening of the robes, questioning why I had wasted my life for this. "Jordan." My eyes widened, tears already filling them. Could it be? I turned from the truth, to see a woman standing behind me, her arms wrapped around her body. Her long, brown hair was piled on top of her head in a ballerina's bun. She had a forlorn smile upon her face. "Mother."

We did it. Me and my two friends created a 100 death calculator. It showed when you would die and why, and most importantly, if it was avoidable. "Let's test it dude! " , Pat said. He was at it before I couldn't stop him. "Late eighties, cause is age and is unavoidable. " , he said, monotone yet cheerfully. "My turn! " , said Stephen. He got similar results. I went last. I put my hand on the scanner. The results printed. They said: "Five minutes from now, cause is mutilation, avoidable if logic is used. Recommended action: lock door now." "What the fuck? " , I said. "Uhh.... I probably screwed some code up. " , Pat said. We sat there for about out four minutes arguing over what to do, arguing over whether to heed the advice, or to ignore it. "Need some food. " , Stephen said, "Lets head down." We stepped out of the room and began to head downstairs. We heard a knock on the front door from the top of the stairwell. "Probably my parents. " , I said. They wee out for the day, and just came back. I was excited to tell them that my death calculator actually worked. "Where'd you're parents go? " , Pat asked. "They left an hour ago for IKEA. " , I responded. I took a step downstairs. "That was fast. IKEA is far as hell. Took my parents five hours. " , Pat said. That's when it hit me. IKEA took about five hours to get to from where I live. My parents left and hour ago. All of a sudden, they're back? "Stop. " , I said. "Remember the death calculator? " , I said. I didn't have to finish, we put two and two together fast. We charged back to my room and bolted the door shut. "Calm down, no need to stomp. " , Stephen said. "We're safe, I think. You know, the whole logic thing and how to avoid it? " , he said, panting. "Point made, but what stomping..." "What the hell is that? " , I asked. We all heard an extremely loud stomping sound coming from downstairs. Whoever it was, was stomping extremely fast. Too fast. Humans didn't stomp that fast. Suddenly, it stopped. "What the fuck? What do we do? " , I said. Stephen was about to say something when I hear four loud knocks on the room door. I was pumping adrenaline after what I heard next. In an inhuman voice, whatever the fuck on the other side of the door said, "Cmon, open the door. Let's play. I can't come in unless you unlock it." The voice was not human. We stood there, contemplating on what to do. "The calculator said to use logic, so we shouldn't open the door under any circumstances. " , Pat said. "Now what? " , I'm not setting here with whatever the fuck that thing is. " , I said. "Well, it would technically make sense to call 911. " , Stephen said. Pat's phone was charged, he immediately dialed the number. As he was about to hit call, we started hearing breathing on the other side of the door. Then, three loud knocks. Then, screaming: "LET ME IN! LET ME IN!." Then in a calm voice: "Let me in.." It alternated between calm and loud voices. "Do not fucking go near that door. " , Pat said, "The cops are coming." We heard more knocks, but this time, from downstairs. We heard the sound of braking wood. "Calvary is here! " , I said. "Wait till they get here. " , Stephen said. We heard there knocks on our door. "Police, open up. " , I opened it. We stepped out. No creature. But we did find scratch marks all over the house, along with visible footsteps on the carpet. It didn't have toes, it looked like, paws. Police never found any evidence of whatever entered my home. We tried the death calculator again, it said: death averted; new results: "time until death is 7 days, cause is multiplication, avoidable if weapons used. Recommended action: follow directions of military officer." Just then, a man wearing army fatigues came in to my room and said, "You boys will need to follow me, everything will be fine, just stay calm."

It was the nod. The way she bowed her head but not her shoulders and pulled my gaze to her eyes. The grocery belt still moving my necessities forward but her gaze, entwined with mine. I should have looked away. Maybe check out what's hot on the last minute tabloid rack before casually walking away. I couldn't though. I knew that stare. Her hazelnut colored, olive shaped eyes stayed firmly locked on mine as she swiped my groceries. I usually check the bill at this point but I felt intoxicated, hypnotized. I swiped my card while still locked in her gaze. I was definitely her focus but why? I think I remember now but it was so long ago but I remember. How could one forget? I was staying with my grandmother. I was young and she was tough. I would get in trouble a lot. I could tell how she was feeling by the way she looked and would often be in trouble for pushing my luck too far while she was calm. When I was naughty though, instead of punishment, she would give me this look and I never knew what it meant. Other kids would have asses beaten but my grandmother would only give me this look. Like she was going to kill me but refrained. That was a long time ago though and even those I was still small, I remember her passing. It was that same stare in her last few moments that I had seen when I was in trouble, countless times. I watched her last breath focusing on that eternal gaze and just before she went, I watched her change into a dove. I know what I saw but like I said, I was only very small. We all have our own ways of dealing with tragedy and as I grew and got older, I forgot. Until I saw that stare again. This cahier, she knows me. We know each other from somewhere so I did the only thing a man can do. "So uh, do you want to go grab a coffee somewhere or something?"

Deke was a spy, and he was in a spot. You see, he was Japanese by birth, and American by choice. He went about life with a very calculating approach to nearly everything, be it school assignments or the mock battled which raged daily among the schoolchildren who lived in his coulda sac neighborhood. His parents constantly told him how lucky they all were to be Americans, and he knew it. So when the time came to enlist in the army, who would sign up by Deke, who wanted nothing more than to aid his country. He was recruited into intelligence, because he was a bright lad, and the call came down the line that he should apprentice under a senior operative, First Lieutenant Dwight Gladdings. A plan involving the manipulation of Deke's heritage began to formulate in Gladdings' mind. He wasn't a senior operative for nothing. The plan involved the deportment of Deke to Japan, where he would enlist in their military and gather intelligence for the United States. He was deported and established himself, and eventually became important when Japan bombed the United States. He began passing more and more intel, and his life got more and more stressful. He feared for what would happen should his identity be compromised. One day, he was asked to come to the office of his new superior, who had a message for him. He walked in, upon which the door shut behind him and the lights went out. "Umm, hheeeellllllooooooo? " he called. Suddenly, a screen flicked on, and light basked the room in a wash of gold. The picture on the screen was Gladdings, and it was clear that he was dead. Suddenly a man's voice rang out from the back of the dark room. "Time to choose a side..... "

"Dashing through the snow.." Santa sung. "I am not singing that song." Wung Shi retorted. "Dashing through the snow!" Santa badgered, staring at his accomplice in anticipation of his continuation of the song. "Look, Wung Shi. If am going to help the Chinese goverment, you better work with me." Wung looked away in reluctance and exasperation, cursing at his tight and uncomfortable elf suit. "In a one horse..open..sleigh." He dragged the verse in a reluctant cadence. "I didn't hear you." Santa leant in his ear, while tying the rope around the neck of the chimney. "In a one horse open..... no, fuck you santa. I am not going to participate in this western nonsense!" Wung snapped, but quickly lowered his voice as they ducked the roaming spotlight from the guards that patrolled the area. "I said I will not participate in western nonsense." Wung whispered, as Santa hooked the rope around his waist. "Listen to me, Wu. "Santa paused, staring down for a moment. "Am only helping you break in to the White house, not out of personal choice, but for some reason unknown to me, your head of state managed to be good for an entire year and I had no option but to fulfill his christmas wishes." Wung cursed under his breath. "Now am going to go in first, and if the coast is clear, I will alert you to jump in." Santa climbed into the dark void, as Wung anchored onto the rope fof support. Santa popped his head back up. "By the way, Wu." "Yes?" "You have been a bad boy this year."

[ ] (dropcap) The battle had dissolved into one seemingly endless melee, the ranks of both knight and commoner shoved together in a struggle of life and death, of fluttering banners and clashing steel, of dying men and beasts. Dinosaurs towered above the men and of horses, their scaly or feathered hides like bulwarks, their flanks peppered with arrows and crossbow bolts. Morions and halberds reared above, the three ton beasts trained to smash their way through the press of men whilst nosehorns such as the dangerous Triceratops carried wicker howdahs with archers, great lengths of padded armor and mail covering their massive sides. There was no planning, no strategy to the bloodshed. Each and every man fought for himself and for the man next to him, many fighting or dying by complete strangers; the organized companies and retinues had long dissolved in the chaos and instead groups of soldiers clustered around the banners of the nobles and of the captains, islands of refuge in a sea of madness and death. Above one of those great schiltrons flew a rampant Deinonychus in gold on a black field. And underneath the tightest cluster of banners stood a man wearing the same colors, an iron crown on the brow of his battered helm. He wore both bevor and visor, reducing his view of the chaotic scene to but a narrow slit. In his hands were a tired blade and shield, its leather covered face decorated with his heraldry. His brigandine was covered with scrapes and scratches, the snapped of length of crossbow hanging its hole in the leather surface. The small metal plates had done their duty in stopping the missile, turning a lethal shot into a merely heavy bruise. He was a mercenary captain, a proven leader of both man and beast, and a warrior without equal. Montador Samuel Hitch, the Black Captain. An enemy knight wearing red and white charged towards him, shouting the name of his house and of his allegiance. In his hands was a poleaxe, the five foot long weapon held high overhead. "Aveluy!" He shouted, slamming a lightly armored longbowman aside, lurching on the bloodsoaked mud. "Iron, Cold Iron!" Came the reply, the iron-crowned sellsword surging ahead with his chosen men-at-arms. A score of armored warriors formed a wedge, the bodies of enemy spearmen crashing against their shields like waves on a cliff. Swords stabbed at underarms and at joints in the enemy's armor whilst maces smashed plate and bone. "Iron is master of men all!" The red and white knight swung his polearm at Mor Samuel Hitch's head, but the veteran mercenary caught the armor piercing spike with a swipe of his shield. The deadly spike punched through the thick leather and wood, a half inch sticking out the back. Hitch swore and swung his shield to the side still with the poleaxe embedded in it, opening up his foe guard. In one blinding strike Hitch shoved the his blade at his foe's underarm, the narrow point puncturing the layer of mail and padding and slicing into his artery. The man groaned and fell, blood gushing from the wound as he dropped his weapon to clamp his hand over it. Hitch slammed his armored foot onto the man's chest and dented the thick plate as he used the dying man as a vantage point over the heads of the nearby soldiers. "Hitch!" Came the cry, somehow rising above the din of metal on metal and screaming men and beast. "Hitch! You son of a whore! Fight! Fight me!" Samuel Hitch turned his head, the narrow view slit forcing him to turn his whole torso and spied a small clump of men advancing through the melee, shoving their way forward with shield and sword. An older squire bore a small banner depicting silver dolphin a blue field and instantly Hitch's eyes narrowed. It was a emblem he knew well, having grown underneath it for the better part of his youth. The shouting man wore the golden spurs of a knight, his visor open to reveal a handsome face nearly the same as Hitch's, only younger and more cruel, and without the scars that the the latter earned on a score of battlefields. Mor Edwin Hitch, second born son of Baron Robert of Gosport snarled venom at his older sibling, leveling his blade at his bastard brother. "Usurper!" The younger brother shouted, bashing aside a enemy sergeant with his shield. "Fay take you, Edwin!" Samuel Hitch said, raising his visor as his half-brother neared. He had learned that his legitimate brother had been in the enemy host but he expected him to be in rearguard on the left flank of the battle. It certainly wasn't by chance that his brother found him. "You searched for me?" He asked. His brother Edwin got within ten paces and nodded, the battle nearest around them halting as both sides paused to watch. "My father's been reaching news of your triumphs, been making noise of legitimatizing you. I can't have that." Hitch shook his head within his helm, silently cursing his younger brother. "Creators, Ed. I don't want the barony. Tell our father that," he glanced about at the expectant crowd of soldiers and frowned. "Alright, no one told you to stop fighting!" "I'm gon na kill you, Sam. Has to be done. " "Go fuck yourself, Ed. You were always a stupid piece of shit." With that he lowered his visor and raised his shield and sword, waiting for his younger half-brother to make the first move. When they'd write stories of this day, they shan't say he struck first, only that he struck last."

Every day I come to work and wonder just who's in charge. We changed CEOs more times then I have changed the oil in my truck but we still can't get it right. Maybe, just maybe this new guy will have the answer but I doubt it. They spend millions, no, billions and the process have been refined over and over for decades. We had and still have the best minds working on it and yet the result is still the same..... happiness only comes in small doses. Why cant we find the same success as Greed, that factory has been running full tilt for years churning out enough for millions of people every year. They have a running surplus they sell at a discount overseas but they still keep stockpiling more and more. Greed, rage, jealousy, all doing just great this year. I hear there was so much greed purchased by the banking industry last year that the factory was able to start a promotion by giving it away to anyone with a decent car and a job. But happiness, where are we going wrong with this? Now matter how much we change the formula, add love, affection, friendship, it doesn't matter, no one is happy for any great length of time. The affect wears off with the first overdue bill or flat tire. Oh I've heard of a few people who created artificial happiness that lasted for years but research proved they were just abusing substances to only fool the brain into thinking it was happy. In the end those artificial substances caused so much damage, when the person finally came down, they were never happy again. So maybe we should just stop trying so hard. I mean, a little happiness can go a long way especially if you get several doses throughout the day. Lunch with a friend, a good meal, a joke that really makes you laugh, all these things can add so much to life if we see them for what they truly are, moments of happiness. We need to stop trying to make happiness last forever. Even if we could, I don't think the human mind would even be able to handle it. In the end I believe our company's main goal should not be to maximize profit on our product but instead to maximize access to it. We need to just keep making small doses of happiness but make sure they are available to as many people as possible as often as possible.

It was a gas station. I'd had this dream before, and I knew it was a dream. Sometimes I'd use this to change it. But I did that too often; tonight I'd relive the true story. It was a warm summer day. Mom and dad were inside the store, getting snacks. I was in the car, reading my book for school, when mom screamed and started yelling at dad. I looked up. She was pushing him around the parking lot, as another woman tried to stop her. The owner came, and mom slapped dad and walked away. Dad got into the car, and tried to act cheery as he started to drive away. My dream skipped like a record player, and I found myself in a courtroom, wearing an uncomfortable suit. Mom was divorcing dad, and they were fighting tooth and nail over who would have me. I stayed at my friend Robby's house, because his mom and dad were neutral in the whole affair and didn't mind letting me stay until the issue was sorted out. The dream skipped as I asked Robby, "Hey, what's a boy's favorite doll?" I was in my room, writing a report for my history class, when mom came in, teary-eyed. "Theresa, we need to talk." She went on to tell me that she'd bribed Robby's parents to lie about what dad used to call me when picking me up from their house. I was shocked, and silent. I loved mom, but dad wasn't a person to me, but a treasure. He knew me like nobody else, and every time he tried could guess my emotions and thoughts perfectly. My mother had paid a woman and her husband fifty dollars to take him away from me for seven long years. Normally I'd wake up, but this time, to my surprise, the door opened. Dad walked in, wearing that dorky backpack he carried around, with a bottle of wine in one hand and a huge bag of candies in the other. He handed mom the wine and said, "Say, kiddo, how about we share these on the back porch?" I woke up to the beeping alarm. I showered and dressed, finished up my chemistry homework, and brought my stuff downstairs. I smelled bacon cooking on the stove, and stealthily ripped a piece off the longest strip. As my hand went to my mouth, somebody else's hand slapped the bacon out of mine. It landed in the frying pan and sizzled, back with its bacon friends. I turned around to face dad. "Don't eat those yet, Theresa, they're raw and you'll get sick. Be quiet, your mother's still asleep and I told her last night I'd take you to school." "When are you leaving, dad?" He hesitated for a moment, unsure. He pulled out a small box from his pocket, and showed me its cargo. It was a diamond ring with a silver band, the one he'd bought mom for their wedding. He looked me in the eye, tearing up a bit. "Never."

The dragon kept rising, growing to an impossible size. What used to be a homeless drunk staggering in an alley was now a golden scaled dragon over forty feet tall. Barry looked at his gun and felt it lacking for the task before him. "Not again. Oh this shit gets real tired. We got to move! Now!" he grabbed Bart by the collar and the two men fled the alley before a wave of fire engulfed the area. A horrible roar filled the air as the dragon suddenly took flight. Barry felt pinned to the ground by the wind of the wings beating. He knew he was at the mercy of the beast and if it decided to swipe at him with a claw or rain down more fire he'd be dead. The dragon elected to ignore the two policemen and it stopped hovering and started flying toward downtown. "The fuck was that?" Barry yelled. "How should I know?" Zach replied. "Because you said not again. You've dealt with shit like this before." Zach grimaced, the truth of what he'd said meant he was going to have to do some explaining. "Look kid, you got a wife, you got a baby, I'm just trying to protect you from some really horrible shit." Zach told him. "I nearly got killed by a dragon! I don't think you're doing that good of a job protecting me." Barry said. "Yeah the dragon sucked, but if you really want to go down this rabbit hole you better be ready to have your world turned upside down." "It's pretty upside down already, let's go all the way on this." Zach thought about it and then pulled out his phone. "We got an idiot here who wants to know about the genie. Of course he's been exposed, I'd never make this call if he hadn't been. Get out here and let's get him to understand the nightmare he's living in." with that he hung up. Within five minutes a black car with tinted windows rolled up. Zach motioned for Barry to get in the car. The second Barry's ass hit the seat he was zapped by a taser and left senseless. He awoke in a small room with an open door. He walked out the door to a massive hive of humanity working on computers with giant screens overhead that had images of dragons, krakens, and other legendary beasts. The middle screen showed what appeared to be a small golden statue with tiny wings. Zach walked over to him. "Sorry about the rough ride. But security is vital here." Zach told him as he handed him a coffee. "What's with the weird pixie thing in the middle?" Barry said and suddenly klaxons began blaring and people started screaming and running in all directions. "Of all the fucking words you had to say that one." Zach hissed. Before anything else could be said the figure on the screen manifested itself in the room. It floated above Barry's head. "You wish to be the champion? To save the world?" The little statue asked. "Don't talk to it!" Zach screamed, all sorts of devices began pointing at the statue, guns were being loaded and cocked all around the room. "Sure I'll save the world." Barry said. A bright light washed over him as he heard the screams from everyone in the building falling away. Suddenly Barry was alone in a giant arena. Then the dragon landed and the statue followed it. "Kill the dragon! Save the world! If dragon kill you everybody die!" The statue said gleefully. "I can't. I have no means to kill it. I'll just die the moment it attacks me. This isn't fair." "Fair?" the statue asked. "Yes fair. For something to be fair both sides have to have a chance to win." Barry said. In a blink suddenly the dragon was the size of a small house cat and Barry had a sword slung over his back and an AR-15 in his hands with three clips hanging from his belt. "Fair?!" The statue asked. "No, this isn't fair. I'll kill the dragon without any effort." "But this way you win! Everyone live!" The statue said. "Yes but that doesn't make it fair. Just because I'm now the one that's going to win doesn't mean it's right." Barry didn't know why he felt that explaining the concept of fairness to this alien being was more important then all life on the planet, but he had a feeling deep in his soul that coming to an understanding with this being was something that had to be done. Another flash of light. Now the dragon was roughly the size of a tiger, and one of the ammo clips Barry had was gone. "Fair?!" The statue asked. "Yeah, fair." Barry said with a nod. "Save the world!" the statue cheered. It then winked out of existence. The dragon jerked it's head back and blasted a wave of fire at Barry who jumped and rolled to the side. "Well I've got myself in it now." Barry said as he loaded his gun and opened fire. The duel to save the world had begun.

"All hands, all hands, stand by for FTL in thirty seconds. Stand by for FTL in thirty seconds, make ready for your blackout." I couldn't help my curiosity. "Why do you announce the jump, captain?" Instantly every pair of eyes on the bridge was on me, their faces looking like I had asked why you have to put on a suit in space. "They didn't tell you, son? About blacking them out?" That was the man at the navigation console, a crusty veteran with haunted-looking eyes. He was the only one to speak up. "Blacking out? No, they didn't say FTL could make you "No, no. Blacking them out. Holy Elon, what are they teaching kids in the academy these days?" His voice was rising. I was a but thankful - at least I wasn't the center of attention anymore. The captain, though - he just put a hand on the navigator's shoulder, patting him through the suit. "Easy, Roger. Okay, kid - this must be your first run, so I'll give you the short version: Never, ever leave your eyes open during an FTL jump." "Why?" He shrugged. "Don't rightly know." "It's'cause they come in through the eyes." "Shut up, Roger." "That's enough!" The captain's bark was loud, silence settling on the bridge in the aftermath. He sighed heavily and leaned back in his acceleration couch. "The guys in white coats up at the research stations, they say something about the jump field making you hallucinate things - like, you're expecting something to be there but hyperspace is empty, so your mind invents something to be there. Shut your eyes, though, your mind expects darkness and you don't see anything. It's bad for you, leaving them open. Whatever it is." "Standbye FTL, five seconds." I could barely hear the navigator's mutter over the comm. "Don't teach'em nothin' anymore, that's how they get in. Every spacer knew that." "FTL drive online. Jumping." I couldn't help my curiosity. God, I wish I had just shut them.

You start seeing time in a completely opposite way to most humans, You try to waste it as much as possible, every dull, repetitive second. long visits to the toilet that leave purple marks on your legs. Heck, I picked up Spanish just so I could get into telenovelas. But the best way to fight time is to drink, drink often and drink a lot. I can hardly remember my previous worlds, fractions, glued fraction from my endless incarnations. lights, faces, boiling cauldrons. That's what I miss the most about heaven and hell, forgetting, being constantly reborn is the only way to keep sane. People always think that heaven and hell are dichotomous. Rubbish, the human mind is malleable. if it only knows pain its entire life or only knows pleasure is insignificant. It would would always settle for pretty much the same ratio of happiness vs misery. In that regard heaven and hell or indistinguishable. So I drink, I drink often and I drink a lot. And I talk, I talk often and I talk a lot. to anyone who would listen, as if saying the words would make them leave my mind, those persistent cancerous words, once they enter your ear, crawl up your brain and just lodge there, squatting in your memories. Oh well, for what god calls a punishment and what satan calls a joke, fuck'em both. I got Sally to knock on my toilet door, and when she's dead, I'd find another Sally. And when all Sallys are gone, I'd just sit here and vomit my stories towards the encroaching sun. Maybe then I could come back and forget.

"So, you're saying I need to try harder?" I turned to my friend. He had a similar look about him, one which I couldn't put my finger on. He looked like everything I ever wanted to be, but better. We were walking through the park on a warm winters night, not another soul to be seen. The weather was calm and the moon glowed calmly in the sky. "No, not try harder, try smarter. How many times have you been in this situation?" He picked a stone up off the floor and threw it into the distance. "You always do this. You go in to things too quickly then crash and burn. Step back a little, man. Assess the situation." I stop and turn to him and he meets my gaze. I can't argue with him because, like always, he's right. Of course he's right. Even if I argue he always wins. But I don't argue. Deep down, I love the guy. He's always been there for me and I can't imagine being without him. "Lets change the subject. Did you see Heather today? She was amazing!" "Yeah she was! You should ask her out." "Get out, I couldn't get someone like her - she's gorgeous!" I turn away from him and continue on my walk. I don't hear him move but when I look to my side, there he is, as always. He puts his hand on my shoulder as we stroll along the park. "Ok, look. I can see tonight you're full of self-doubt. I can help. Let me fill you with the confidence you deserve. You're a great guy, man. Any woman would be lucky to have you." He stops again and I turn to his familiar smile. He looks down at his watch. "Anyway, it's late, gone midnight. I think you should head back home now. You've got an early start tomorrow!" "Alright, cool. When do you wan na hang again?" He looks at me, smile never fading. "Dude, I never go. You know that. You need me, you know how to get me. Catch you later." With that, he fades away. I look around and notice how empty the park really is. Though I know I'm not truly alone - he's only a thought away.

With 30,000 employees all over the globe and 42 billion in revenue to lead, busy doesn't even begin to describe my day. I'm good, though. Mama taught me young how to trust, how to delegate, and how to get things done. Hell, even my delegating is delegated these days. Hiring decisions below the Vice-President level don't even come across my desk. But more goes on at this company than I'll ever know about. I like to walk through the cube mazes on the lower floors sometimes, check in with the various administrative assistants, hear what's going on. More often than not this grapevine gives me more insight into what's going on in the company than 300 different "executive dashboards." It's a good habit. And this habit led me to overhearing a phone conversation. I was checking in on Samantha Beeman in HR, making some joke that bordered on inappropriate but definitely wasn't, and I heard a voice in the cubicle next to hers. "Yes, may I please speak with James Finnegan?" I froze. I realized that I froze, and tried not to look like I was freezing, which really resulted in an awkward stumbling of words and a fake-confident grin. Did I mention 30,000 employees? Million and billion dollar acquisitions? Why did one name cause my heart to jump into my throat? "We received your resume for the Sales Associate position. Can you come in for an interview?" I was struggling to still pay attention to Samantha while focusing intently on this conversation. "Next Tuesday at 3:00? Perfect. We'll see you there. You'll be meeting with Jane Goodrich, our Senior Retail Manager, and Rob Freeman from Human Resources." I quickly made a mental note and reinforced my eye contact with Samantha, just in time to laugh at the end of her anecdote. I excused myself CEO stuff... and made my way down to the 8th floor, where Jane Goodrich had a modest office with an assistant outside. I didn't know Jane personally, but I knew Bobby, her assistant. He was actually my younger brother's friend. "Hi, Jim!" the young man smiled at me. "Hey, Bobby. How the job treating you?" "Oh, man, I love this place!" I'd worked hard to build a vibrant culture in this company, and the millenials were soaking it up. "Bobby, quick question for you. Did I overhear that Jane's going to be interviewing someone next Tuesday at 3:00 PM?" Bobby checked Jane's calendar. "Yup. James Finnegan. I sorted the resumes for her; this guy seemed okay. Not much on his resume that was impressive, but not many people are applying these days." "Bobby, can you forward me a copy of that resume?" "Sure thing, Jim. Why?" "Oh, you know me..... just keeping my finger on the pulse." Back in my office, I had 15 minutes before I had to head to the airport for a weekend trip. I pulled up the resume for James Finnegan. Indianapolis address. Most recently worked for the better part of a decade at a low-end mattress retailer. That seemed right. Everything matched up with what the private investigator had found for me 5 years ago. Was it a coincidence? I decided it wasn't. My flight was short but I barely noticed it; I was wrapped up in thought. Even when my rental car was delivered, I almost ran over the attendant pulling out. It wasn't until I got to Mama's house that I was able to focus again. "Mama!" I shouted, when she greeted me at her door. "Jim! You're looking taller and more handsome than usual!" We laughed as I gave her a kiss on the forehead and we marched right back out to the car. She talked for a while as I drove, though she politely let me answer a call from our Development VP, who wanted to fill me in on the upcoming FDA approval audit for our new baby-food line. Did I mention 42 billion in revenue last year? We're diversified. Anyway, she talked and I drove. I found myself driving up to North Shore looking for a fancy restaurant with a view. She didn't seem to notice, and I was okay with that. The restaurant was crowded, but the maitre d' recognized my name and got us a good seat. As we sipped a glass of wine, I decided to ask her what had been on my mind. "Mama, 30 years ago..." I paused. "30 years ago, a lot happened. Do you have any regrets? "She seemed genuinely taken aback by this. "Oh, Jim. Of course I don't! Everything that happened since then has been a blessing! I met Fred - God rest his soul - and without Fred, you wouldn't have had Rachel or Nelson. We've traveled, we've learned..... oh, sweetie, I wouldn't change a thing." I nervously rubbed a small scar on my forearm. "Do you forgive him?" "Honey, I stopped caring about him or his life a long time ago. Do I forgive him? Of course I do. Not forgiving him would take much more effort than anything else at this point." "Okay, Mama. Thank you." I didn't want to talk about it any more, and guided the conversation to more pleasant things. Tuesday arrived and, after my 5:30 AM workout, I showered, put on my suit, and drove into work. I reviewed a press release regarding our new product line that was waiting on my desk. Our marketing VP had wanted me to sign off on it. I trusted his work and sent it back with a quick note. I had a lunch meeting with the Chairman of the Board. Her name was Susan Rowden; she and my step-father Fred had gone to college together and kept in touch, and she was the one who had recruited me to lead our not-so-humble enterprise. We talked about the direction of the company and the investor conference call that was approaching, and, as we parted ways, I gave her a hug. "I miss my dad," I quietly said. I could feel her smile. "Fred was a great man. He was a leader, and I think he'd like how you've turned out." It was my turn to smile. At 2:55 PM I walked into Jane Goodrich's office. "Mr. Reardon!" she smiled. "What brings you to the 8th floor?" "Oh, I was thinking of acquiring..... "I checked, she was wearing a decent Kate Spade necklace "Kate Spade and was looking for an executive team. You know, the usual." She laughed. Executive humor kills them every time. "Actually, I heard you have an interview in a few minutes with a man named James Finnegan." "Yes, as a matter of fact I do. How did you know that?" I smiled. Like I was going to remove the CEO mystique that I'd cultivated. "Mind if I sit in on it? I'll be discreet." At 3:00 we walked into what was generously described as a conference room, but was basically a closet with four chairs and a small table. I almost stumbled walking in. There were two men sitting there, one of whom was probably named Rob Freeman, but the other one, well..... he looked like a much older, heavier, worn out version of me. I saw presumably-Rob's eyes glance back and forth between us, and Jane hesitated so that I almost crashed into her. She recovered, as I would expect our senior managers to do, and introduced herself. Before she could introduce me, I simply held out my hand and said, "Jim Lyman," emphasizing Mama's maiden name and not giving myself a title. I could see something working in the back of his mind, but it was the faintest of spark, one that the slightest wind would extinguish. Perhaps, in my position, I'm used to a much higher caliber of interviewee. Perhaps everyone in the room - except James - felt that it significantly more awkward than it should have been. Whatever it was, I found myself trying not to frown and shake my head as his wretched grammar and horrid malapropisms assaulted me. Still, he had a solid history, and we have pretty low expectations for our sales associates. We all shook hands at the end of the interview. Rob escorted James down to the lobby to sign out, and I went back to Jane's office with her. "Mr. Reardon, what was that about?" she demanded. "Let me ask you this first, "I responded. "Does he have the qualifications for the job? Do we have a better candidate?" "Yes, then no." She replied. "Then I recommend hiring him." "That was a horrible interview!" "Yes, it was, and that's mostly my fault," I answered. "But I think he'll be okay." "What's going on?" she pressed, one last time. I paused for a moment, then quietly said, "I wasn't born as Jim Reardon. I was born with the name James Theodore Finnegan, Junior."

I watch myself enter the room. The man who entered is markedly different to the man I am now. Flesh clings to him that has long slipped of me, and though he has bags under his eyes, his are as light as feathers compared to mine. He looks at me with pity, and I can't help but envy him. To think how bitter I was for so little - witnessing an ageing face in the mirror, growing fat and tired, and desperately, desperately trying to deny it. All his pretence and effort to be young again drains him and only ages him faster. Here is a man who does not yet know how much weight he will lose, how much more tired he can become. He looks at me, and he can read my thoughts. He looks guilty, because he did not feel grateful for the little things, and instead became cantankerous and petty, miserly and miserable; now the big thing stares back at him and shames him. My envy dissolves. How can I blame a caged bird for refusing to sing? Even if the cage was of my own design. I forgive him. I watch myself enter the room. Another self enters, a little faster on his feet, the skin on his face a little tighter. Thinner than the older one, though still far from the ragged thing I have become. His face is draped with sadness, a sadness that was there before he even entered the room, and only deepened and darkened on seeing me. Here is a man who can walks blindly into the future while staring backwards with tearful eyes. Regrets have sunk deep into his bones, and will, with time, become rotten and bitter. I feel sorry for him, but not nearly as much as he feels sorry for himself. He lives every day like an apology. He is building the cage he feels he deserves. He can't forgive himself. He looks at me with despairing eyes. I forgive him. I watch myself enter the room. This man is younger still, with a full head of hair, and a confident swagger. He is holding a phone, and is distracting himself with it so as not to look at me. I can see what he can't; suits and cars and watches can't hide the gap inside him from me. He barely glances at me or the others, and when he does he sniffs disdainfully. I feel his pain. I know that if he were to look at me properly, he would crumble completely. I stare at him, though I know he can't bear to meet my gaze for more than a second. But when he does, I see all his wounds that he hides from the world. He pours alcohol over them secretly, to sting himself and disinfect. They fester anyway. He is sowing the seed of his own collapse, but he can't see that yet. He turns back to his phone, desperately trying to ignore his feelings. My heart breaks for him. I forgive him. I watch myself enter the room. A young man enters the room, almost unrecognisable to me. His face rapidly cycles through emotions on seeing me. His default face wass sullen, sulky. It lights up into a half smile which, incomplete, morphs into an intense distress, his eyebrows knitting together. I can see tears in his eyes already. What an emotional boy. Here is a boy who sometimes wants to run away from the world and sometimes wants to rule it. He feels trapped in a powerless body - his ambitions are too large to fit. His world is riven with contradiction and he can't understand why. He doesn't yet understand why on some days he can fly above the world like a bird, and others he can't even leave his bedroom. I watch him look at me with love and hate. He denies me in a way that I can't help but admire. How could someone as strong as him succumb to this? His glare is accusatory. He's disspointed in me! He's so full of youth, of fire and flame that I can feel the heat radiate off him. I laugh to myself, and he breaks into a smile. I forgive him. I watch myself enter the room. A young boy enters the room. He breaks into a smile when he sees me, and runs over to hold my hand. I recognise that smile, and feel the same bloom across my own face. He looks into my eyes and I into his. He's amazed by me, and I am humbled by the light in his eyes. There is nothing to forgive. I ask him silently to forgive me. His eyes seem to answer: there is nothing to forgive. He kisses me on the forehead.

'Sherman, fetch!' He never listened to me, even now after being his owner for 13 years, my dog rarely showed me affection or obedience. Probably due to the fact that I got the little dude given to me when he was already a year old by a friend I met at college. Still, that didn't stop me from showing him affection. We'd been at the park for a while today, it was hot and I had nothing to do. My night shift at the store started soon and it was getting dark. It was time to leave. I packed up the blanket and grabbed my backpack, shouted Sherman who looked hopelessly at me and carried on doing his thing. This wasn't anything new, as I said, he never listens to me. I walked over to him and out his lead on, we headed out along the footpath through the center of the park. The circular park was heavily lit up at night, and darkness had creeped in much quicker than I expected and a light fog was clearly on its way, I must have been running a little bit late. It wouldn't have mattered. I looked thoughtlessly at fog surrounding me as I made my way across the road towards my apartment. It had dropped extremely cold which was unusual for a night in August. It was just the same trip, different day. The routine I found myself in was starting to bug me and I was starting to have second thoughts about everything. Every decision I ever made, whether or not I was happy, whether I liked the person I'd become, and more importantly whether it was worth changing. For christ sake my dog doesn't even seem to love me, how can anyone else? We strolled slowly towards the entrance, this was the part where the Mike (the security guard) would give Sherman a treat and ask me how my day was. But on today of all days, he wasn't there. I shrugged it off and we moved towards the stairs. The last thing I wanted to do was get up in 2 hours and go to work, but I suppose when you get into a routine you become too complacent to do anything about it. Sherman ran towards to stairway exit on the third floor and turned up and looked at me as he always does. I opened the door and we both walked in. Sherman immediately ran towards apartment 345. My apartment is 340, ever since we've lived here Sherman must have been confused about the layout - it is confusing sometimes, especially when you're drunk. But he knows it's this floor and he can't possible know anyone in there; security told me the room was never sold or used during my stay here. Again, complacent in my routine, I shrugged it off, and mumbled'Sherman'. Sherman immediately barked at me and stared straight at me, then back to the door..... The hairs on the back of neck stood up, and I suddenly felt a rush of adrenaline and not because it was cold. In thirteen years my dog has never once listened to me about anything, but that night he did; because of something to do with 345. The air in the hallway was cold and I was tired. I remember thinking to myself'what have I got to lose?' I went over to 345 and Sherman started to growl at the foot of the door. I heard apartment door slam shut round the corner nearly giving me a heart attack. Upon closer inspection of the door I saw scratch marks. Nails? Who knows. The smell of damp coming through the walls was almost overpowering, but Sherman was determined, I grabbed the handle and twisted. It was locked. 'So much for that Sherman! Sorry little man, don't get to find out what's in there today!' I was disappointed but ultimately relieved. I'm a fairly rational guy but I was scared. We walked around to corner back to old trusty 340. My door had locked without the latch unlocked, we were locked out. My nonchalant self thought nothing of it as Mike had another key for my place. I walked back around towards the staircase but as I turned the corner I froze - the door to apartment 345 was open. Sherman stood by my side, growling and barking, the black abyss seemingly covering the doorway staring back at us..... Edit: Its 2:30am here and I'm high and have no idea what I'm doing, tell me if you want more. Glad I finally tried one. Ignore any errors cause I obviously did.

They claim it's a blessing, this cessation of aging. I know better - this is a curse. It is merely the recycling of a single day, over and over again. Every day the body forgets all hurts, all ills, and are returned, remade, renewed exactly as they were the day we were first cursed. Most wouldn't notice it. Most here are too old or incapable or just fortunate in their timing. Not me. You ask me how I can tell? This curse began twelve years ago, and I have had the same miscarriage every morning for those twelve years. Please, can you make it stop?

The rain pelted my body heavily, as I stood over Nassim Hill, peering down at the walled city of Canning. Streaks of lightning flashed across the sky, followed by the loud boom of thunder. Five hundred years ago, standing on top of a hill in a middle of a thunderstorm would have frightened me. But I've been through worse and lived to tell the tale, and a couple of lightning strikes, although painful when they hit, was not going to stop me from accomplishing my task, revenge. I pulled the golden locket out from my shirt, flipping the cover open. Arwen's face smiled at me, like she did for the past five hundred years. Centuries may have passed, but the anger and grief that I felt were like yesterday. When those rich aristocrats denied my Arwen a chance of living through their selfish logic. Just like how they denied seven other billion people. My feet trudged through the mud as I made my way downhill. The wind was picking up, making walking difficult. Several times I had to lie down flat on the ground to avoid being blown away. I cursed at the weather, which for some reason decided to make my final mission difficult. "I'm killing those who did this to you, you forgetful idiot!" I shouted to the sky, my voice drowned out by the howls of the wind. Immediately after I said that, the storm softened down, as if it understood my words. The rain slowed, as the clouds slowly parted. One would expect the sun to shine through from behind the clouds, but it has been close to a thousand years since we last saw the last ray of the sun. All the work of those aristocrats holed up in Canning. Its massive walls towered over me as I approached it, with a collection of sentry towers poking up several meters along it. The walls had been built to keep the middle class out, while the rich enjoyed their blissfully ignorant life inside. Some of the skeletons of people trying to get into Canning laid around the wall, a grim reminder of the atrocities that happened at the peak of the crisis. I gritted my teeth as I slung my grapple unto the ledge, and started pulling myself up. "I will avenge you too," I said, looking at the bones. The walls used to be manned, but without anything to defend themselves from, the guards eventually gave up their job, and retreated back into the comfort of their walled city. Those suckers can never do anything right. I groaned as I pulled myself up the ledge, feeling a sense of excitement that I have not felt in a long time. Glass vials clanked noisily in my backpack, the very serum that they had engineered to give them immortality, while they left the rest of humanity to perish. I had reverse-engineered their magical serum, making it poison to any immortals who drank it. And I made sure to make the entire process as painful as possible. Those idiots will finally atone for their sins. I removed the vials from my bag, carefully examining the swirling purple liquid inside. As I stepped closer to the ledge on the other side, expecting to see a still functioning city with bustling life, only a large crater greeted me, with the remnants of Canning littering the ground. Pillars that had snapped in half, with broken off concrete slabs and charred walls dotted the horizon. The only structure that remained intact was the wall. Far from a functioning city, Canning was a ghost town, a lifeless shell of its past. No sign of those I had swore to kill at all. I fell to my knees, together with the vials. They crashed unto the ground and shattered, spilling their content. I no longer cared, however, as there was only one question in my mind. How long has Canning been dead? rdoritales
