All eyes are fixed on the monitors in the mission room as the payload bay doors begin to open as the B-52 nears the target. There is no natural light 30 floors beneath the Pentagon, only the blueish white of small LEDs and computer screens. The President looks up, nods to the communication officer, and the go-ahead had been given. Being the first time in 5 years aircraft have been used to attack ground troops, this top secret mission is pushing new international laws. Retrofitted to hold thousands of carbon fiber, self guiding arrows, the B-52 is the first of its kind. The arrows being to fall, each one locating a unique target. American soldiers watch in awe as their Russian foes begin to collapse. Rumors of weapons of mass destruction had been passed around, but now it has been confirmed. Full of newly gained morale, the Americans charge forward, and push to the Russian border. Ukraine has finally been freed, and Russia stands down in fear of more weapons of mass destruction. The mission room erupts in celebration, the newly discovered oil reserves are finally theirs.

The soft jangle of the rider's bells and the muffled thuds of the horse's hooves were the only sounds meandering their way through the trees. The early morning sun barely had the strength to bleed through the heavy canopy overhead, and mist clung to every rock and hollow along the barely visible trail. The rider again felt the sensation of being watched, a feeling of curiosity mixed with anger, but now..... a deepening hate. His horse seemed to feel it too, seemingly more wild-eyed with each bend in the trail, and now giving a little shudder when passing near the deeper shadows, neck tensing against an invisible force. The rider gave a glance down at a glowing device in his hand, a pale yellow light encased in metal, held tightly in his leather clad fist. Pulling back slightly on the reins, the rider paused to hold the device higher, seemingly seeking a direction in which to head. Unconsciously pulling harder on the reins, the rider's horse plodded to a faltering stop, shying away from the darkness cast by a heavy branch on its left. Then..... there, in a small clearing. Nestled innocently between a moss-draped rock and a fallen branch, the ground sloped gently towards an impossibly black, perfect circle on the forest floor. Slowly dismounting, the rider slid from the saddle, gingerly touching the ground with his boots as if the very earth might reach forth and entrap him, horse and all. Feet firmly planted now, the rider glanced around, peering into the shadows of the thick forest. Seeing no signs of life or activity, the rider tied his steed to the heavy branch and carefully began to pick his way over to the black void. With each careful step, strange new details became apparent. The first was the sheer "perfectness" of the circular opening. Not an errant edge or deviation could be seen. Then, the stark and unyielding contrast of an unnatural, too perfect black against the lush green of vegetation surrounding the mouth of the hole. Slowly and carefully, the rider continued to pick his way closer. Taking great care to avoid stepping on broken twigs and gently rolling his feet on the dead leaves underfoot to quiet any sound. Reaching the hole's edge, the rider slowly lowered to his knees, paused, then haltingly laid prone with his hooded head poised over the opening's edge. At first, there was nothing. The rider gave a quizzical shake of his head, softly jangling a buckle on his cloak. Then..... a rising moan began to build in the clearing. A low, menacing groan that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere, like a faint growl of a coming storm. Closer the rider inched, now with his head centered over the hollow, a brown hood suspended over infinite blackness. The sound intensified, building in crescendo and frantic energy. Voices began to emerge from the cacophony, muffled words and..... the screams. Terrible cries of agony, ripped from the strangled throats of suffering and pain. Building ever higher in pitch and volume. Men calling out in agony, curses followed by painful shouts. Children's voices screaming for their parents, begging for whatever hell they were in to stop. Piercing wails of pure terror and hurt, women or beast, the rider couldn't tell. The chaos still swelling and booming, the rider now clasped his hands to his ears hoping to block some of that terrible sound. The rider began to shake, feet kicking against the dirt, the noise of his bells now completely lost in the cacophony. Then without warning..... Silence. The rider lay there for a long moment, gathering whatever wits he had left. Then, he slowly stood, rising on shaky legs, head drooped as if he were still stunned. He turned towards his horse, whose reins had wrapped around its neck in a frantic effort to escape. Sides still heaving in panic, froth flecking the long neck of the steed. Still staring, the rider raised his hands to his head, and removed the hood from his cloak. The horse jumped, and began straining against the reins, trapping it further. Even being a mere beast, the horse knew something terrible, something unnatural, had happened. Seeing the rider before it now, it felt something even worse was yet to come. For it was wrong where the riders eyes should have been. They were now just a stuttering, endless procession of mouths flickering into existence and then changing again, man, child, beast, woman. Shifting, twisted lips where eyelids should be, and gnashing teeth and tongues for eyes. All curled back and silently screaming for release from the agony they endured. Pulling his hood back up, the rider slowly smiled. He was finally complete.

I used to be a Good Man. I used to be someone love in my heart, fire in my soul and a reason to carry on. I used to be a Hero. I was a Soldier. I was someone with peoples lives in my hands, a weight on my shoulders and orders to follow. I was a Warrior. I became a Weapon. I became someone with dark purpose, rage flowing in my veins and a broken spirit. I became a Killer. I am a Twisted Old Fool. I am someone with nothing to fight for, no one left to care and a cold empty shell where my heart belongs. I am..... But I used to be.

nbsp; nbsp; Well, so what? nbsp; nbsp; Sure, I was only eight, but that's not insurmountable for someone with the skills, intelligence, and memories of a 73 year old. And sure, I knew that I'd only have time to take advantage of a few key events before my memories and reality diverged too much. But that's the advantage of regaining a young mind again; that sharpness and speed that I'd long ago given up on was at my disposal. And while I hadn't felt it in so very long I hadn't forgotten how to use it. nbsp; nbsp; First up, of course, I did absolutely nothing until I turned 18. A lot of little things were different this time around; for instance, I didn't let Samuel anywhere near me that night and how sad that Satya's father burned his dick in that fry-oil accident that day. My grades were better and I was mostly left alone in high-school but overall, I let nothing change that would alter the world in any meaningful way. nbsp; nbsp; Until my birthday. Funny how those lottery numbers stuck with me all those years. First in Canada. Then the United States. Even after the US took their cut, I had more money than anyone thought I knew what to do with. Naturally, plenty of people figured they knew what to do with it. Of course, the only one who got to enjoy any of it was the nice old lady who wanted to retire and had control over the citizen databases at Service Canada. nbsp; nbsp; Then..... nbsp; nbsp; It's unavoidable; when you're new and green all you can recruit are the crazies. As it turned out, it was for the best. When launching an assault on Trondheim they terrified the populace enough that it was mostly a rollover; the recruits I gathered from the town was just enough to engage and just get past the armed forces out of Oslo. And once I had Oslo..... well, as they say, only the first time hurts the worst. Sweden and Finland didn't stand much of a chance with the firepower my money brought to bear, and my gamble that the EU would spend more time talking about what to do about me instead of actually doing something about me paid off. By the time they invited Russia and the US to join the dance, I had too many partners for them to cut in cheap. nbsp; nbsp; It's been a good run; my granddaughter will go far, I think. All the way to San Antonio, if I'm any judge. nbsp; nbsp; You can't change the past, they say. I would say they're correct. nbsp; nbsp; They know what's good for them.

James hated the undead but he hated being hungry more. He peered around and examined the entrance. The store looked overrun with the creatures. He had to move quickly if he wanted to get anything. He threw his hood over his head, made sure his shoelaces were tied and dashed for the doors. When he busted in and looked about, James noticed most of the food was gone. The freezer section was decimated and since the doors were open, anything left probably thawed out. Nothing worse than a thawed frozen pizza. Half-eaten produce laid on top of the bin. Most of the dead gathered there. Easiest thing to get to and James figured that was the first thing they detected. Half open boxes of cereal littered an aisle, their contents spilled out. The crunching due to the shuffling feet from the dead trying to scoop handfuls up would drive most mad, but James shook the sound aside and began his search. There were a few stragglers limping around in front of him but he was quick enough to dart through them and get to what he wanted: the canned goods. On the top shelf, he noticed a few cans of peaches. Salivating, James quickly reached out to grab a few cans. He threw a couple in his pockets, but as he went for the last can, a bony rotting hand clasped on to it. James froze. Beads of sweat began to form on his brow. He thought of running to the next aisle to find something else, but his stomach growled. James decided he would not be pushed around. He grabbed the can and tried to wrestle it from...whatever was next to him. The hand did not loosen its grip and as James struggled, he heard a raspy moan next to him. " Peeeeeeaches, " the voice muttered. " " Excuse me. " James followed the arm back to the attached body. There stood the remnants of a man in a tattered brown suit. The tie, best he could tell, was a dingy red with faint beige lines streaking across. " Excuse me, sir, " James sarcastically uttered. " I was here first and I need these peaches. " James tried to snatch the can, but the man held on. For someone who had not used his muscles in a long time, the gentleman possessed some strength. The muttering voice became a low growl now. " Myyyyy peeeeeeeaches, " the man snarled. He jerked back, tearing the can from James'hand and furrowed his brow the best he could to display his anger and impatience. In almost an instant, the man crushed the can and the bright yellow peaches began oozing from the top. Another zombie crawled down the aisle and tried lapping the juice from the floor. Another soon appeared, sniffing loudly. This one's jaw was barely hanging on but it did not deter it from coming down the aisle and grabbing the can from its fellow dead. More and more began making their way and James knew if he did not act fast, he would be trapped. He began climbing the shelves and threw himself over the top, landing on a legless one on the other side. He gathered himself for a moment looked around for anything else, grabbing boxes quickly. He pushed his way through that same few scattered up front and made it back outside. James walked back to his apartment, disappointed at his haul this time. He threw the cans on the counter, grabbed an opener and slid the peaches into a bowl. James grabbed a spoon but stopped when he heard a rustling coming from his room. " Jaaaaaaaames, " a voice called out. James smiled and pushed the door open. A very pale woman lay on the bed, reaching out to him. Her silver hair was slightly dirty and her floral print blouse had a slight tear on the shoulder, but aside from that, the woman looked almost normal. Her jeans looked new and toenails freshly painted a sapphire blue. " Jaaaaaaaaaaaaaames. Peeeeeeeaches? " " Yeah, ma. I got em. I couldn't get too many. The stores here are picked clean. " He scooped a slice of the peaches and guided the spoon toward her mouth. The woman lunged suddenly at James and the bowl, causing him to step back and drop the spoon and a piece on the floor. Luckily the chains attached to the bedposts kept her from successfully grabbing the whole thing. " I know ma, I'm sorry. Don't worry. Charlie and me will go up the road to the city. He's bringing his shotgun in case we need to force our way through. I'll get you some more peaches, I promise. " He gave her the bowl and left the room as she devoured the fruit immediately. James went back to the kitchen to grab a box of cereal he salvaged and sat on the couch. His stomach continued to growl as he forced the dry crap down. He looked at the peaches and again, began to salivate. The thought of eating those peaches filled him with a moment of happiness, but the sudden cry from his mother in the next room dismissed the idea. He knew his mom was dead. He knew the peaches did nothing for her. They didn't keep her alive. He figured she also gets no pleasure from eating them. But she wanted them. Every day, she wanted peaches, and you don't disappoint mama.

The past week has been an interesting one, so I figure today will finally be the day things settle down. Being named the specialist technician in my robotics company has always been a dream of mine, and that finally happened on Monday. Tuesday was spent meeting our resident simple AI bots named Rob and Ottie, they aren't particularly AI but we programmed them to act like it. They say hi when you walk in the room, they say bye when you leave. They answer simple commands, move and hold things as well. Wednesday I wrote some code to let them catch a ball, this meant installing tracking cameras in the eye sockets. Thursday was spent adding a happy function, so when Rob or Ottie caught a ball their facial structure would smile and they would jump up and down. Today I have to actually do some work, so I've sworn off any extra programming until next week. When I walk into the office I am not greeted by the normal chorus of hello's, instead all I see is Ottie. And he is turned away from me.... Interesting. His face seems different when I turn him around, like he's confused, except that's way too complex of an emotion to have programmed in yet. I check the cover to his motherboard, his program log and various other wire bundles but find nothing. Weird. So I try asking "where's Rob?" "Rob's dead." This isn't close to what I've programmed in, so I try a more complex query "what did Ottie do to Rob?" "I killed Rob" Whoah, I start backing away, this is not ok. I mean, I've seen terminator, and I know when to cut my losses and bounce. Another step back and I bump into something. When I turn around I find a shit eating grin plastered to Rob's face.... Yet another thing I haven't programmed in. Both Rob and Ottie burst out laughing, like doubling over laughing, I continue backing up past Rob through the office door to get a glass of water. After a ten minute walk around the building I decide to go find out what was going on. Did their source code self realize? Did my happy program have something to do with his? Having no clue I cautiously walk back into the office, and there are Rob and Ottie.... "Hello Steve" comes from their speakers in perfect unison..... Back to normal? I run them through their regular functions and nothing extraneous occurs.... Interesting. Double check the source code and find nothing. Decide to leave for the day, need to get everything straight in my head, but on the way out I hear a snicker.... I turn around and Rob and Ottie are both in the same spot and seemingly off. Today is the day I start drinking again.

They are like little bald people who poop themselves and can't take care of there own self, kind of like if your grandma was 95 but small and bald, Yes your grandma. Now I don't donate to charity even though I inherited half of my family's multimillion dollar company. I don't give people money on the side of the street, they should have made a better life for themselves. So know that you know me as the asshole I am let me explain to you a story. I was walking down the road one day and just got done handling business at my company. I see this person on the side of the street, no legs and was wearing a Vietnam vet hat. He stopped me and said "sir would who please donate some money or at least food or water." I stared at him thinking to my self "My dad was a Vietnam vet before he died." Dear Ms. Watts, I hated writing. I hated doing anything for school. I wasn't happy with my education. The summer that I was placed in make up English, I found the first teacher that read what I wrote and cared enough to try and make it better to try and grow the author and poet that lives in all of us. You were attentive. I wrote pages of nothing as I had done in every class to that point in my life and you tore it apart. Every sentence, you broke down. You knew it was garbage and you didn't care. You pushed me to imbue substance and meaning in to every line and told me how important word choice was. You drilled me on gerunds, sentence structure, and word connotations. Your faith in my ability, the effort you invested. Your direct unwillingness to accept anything less than the best I had to offer forced and inspired me to rise beyond mediocrity. I pity those who did not have the opportunity to encounter you or a teacher like you. Every time I write, and I debate putting the subject at the end or beginning of the sentence to achieve a specific rhythm, I think of you. Eight years ago, I tracked you down and called you, to tell you how much it meant to me. You told me to stop. You gave me your address and told me to send you a letter. I never did. I still tell myself, "I will."

Mark slapped empty beer cans and pizza boxes off the coffee table as he tried to combine waking up and silencing the alarm on his cellphone. Groggily he focused on the screen. Not an alarm. A phone call, from his least favourite number. "Faaaark off," he answered politely. "Mr. Greaves. Your country has need of your services," explained the woman on the other end of the line. "My country can fuck off too," Mark said defiantly as he sat up and started slipping on his shoes. "Look Mr. Greaves, you've been specially selected for this mission because I believe it's a perfect match for your particular skillset." "Oh come off it, you know I..." "You're going to need to stay home and be utterly clueless." Mark felt that his silence conveyed the "fuck you" better than saying it would. "Look, we happen to know that a pair of Mormon missionaries are approaching your apartment and we need you to keep their attention for as long as you can. We're moving in to extract one Jesus Cabrera from your building and we don't want them spooking him." "How am I meant to "You'll figure something out, Mark. I don't need to remind you of the consequences if you fail to cooperate." -Click- Mark spat a curse and made his way towards the door to wait. Hearing footsteps in the hall, he preempted the knocking by opening the door and startling the pair with "excuse me, sirs, can you spare a moment for Jesus?" The next 45 minutes would exhaust his not-trifling capacity for bullshitting.

He was wrinkled and bent, dressed in robes as black as night. He was older than I could have imagined, far older than most could have imagined. "Do not fear me, young one. I am only here to assist you, teach you. There is a duty to be done. None have come before me who are willing and able to complete the task..... until you." I looked down at my shoes. Me? Able? Willing, yes, but able? I could only hope that I was. I had trained, I had studied, but would it ever be enough? I returned my gaze to his wizened, clouded eyes. "It will not be simple, and in many ways, it will not be straight-forward. Evil has ways of making itself clothed in righteousness to those unfamiliar in its ways. But, you, yes, you have risen out of that. You have come far and seen what evil lies in the world." Again, my gaze dropped to the floor. So he'd heard of me. Known what I'd done in the past, how unsavoury it had been. How I'd climbed above it to restore myself to at least neutrality. My guilt must have shown on my face. He lifted my face with a calloused hand to look him in the eyes once more. "My time has come to an end, you know that as well as I. I can think of no one more suited to the task. Take up my mantle, take up my quarrel. Let justice be done..... Justice for all..." With that, he handed me a simple wooden hammer and retired. I paused, took my last innocent breath and rose from the chair. I exited his chambers, now that would be mine, his words echoing in my ears. As his faded, another boomed out, "All rise! The Honourable Judge Knight presiding..."

"Your majesty, we will need your word to quiet the whispers on the streets..." the old priest added pleadingly, glancing up at me. I looked down at him. My mind was racing. The war had been won. However if he is really dead then it might as well be lost. Our son would make a most unenlightened ruler and presumably drag us into yet another war like his useless father. No, this was an opportunity..... An opportunity for a competent hand to finally claim the throne. God, works in mysterious ways and I was seeing his hand move before my very eyes. I pulled out my handkerchief and wiped a convenient tear - result of my unblinking stare into my future - artfully from my cheek. "Forgive me gentlemen, no, father, forgive me. Of cause I will come with you. I was overcome by grief." "Most natural my Queen" he answered with a bow. Only three days later we arrived at what I will always think of as the city of blood and white sheets. Large tents as far as the eye could see. Large tents of undyed linen flapping in the wind like broken sales. And death. The smell of death. The buzzing of flies everywhere. Broken helmets, broken halberds, broken spines, broken hopes and dreams of wives and sweethearts..... Urg, with all these men dead there'd be a run on the poor houses and brothels. I had to prepare for that. I covered my face with my handkerchief to block out the smell of death as the men exchanged awkward glances. One muttered something apologetic, but I waved him off impatiently. "If this is where my darling husband died, my Lord, my king! Then how can it be too good for me?" Admiring looks. Stupid little men. Do you really think I would have become Queen and shared a bed with the flatulant walrus for ten years if a little death could deter me. The flaps of the largest tent pulled aside as if by their own will and suddenly I was standing in front of the very same walrus. Dead and cold. No doubt. Your last fart has played old man. "Leave me alone!" I commanded and then added softer "I need to be sure!" As soon as they left I searched the body and took his seal and his chain, which he kept hidden in his underclothes. There was also a locket with a lock of my hair - who would have thought it? Then I worked the seal on his finger. The seal I had prepared in all haste the night the priests arrived. The seal just good enough to fool the casual observer, but clearly fake to the expert. Made by a lovely smith's daughter with a drunkart of a father. In thanks she is now readying herself to join me in court as one of my dear companions. I might make her my personal Jewelsmith as a matter of fact. She is rather good. No more of her father's debtors demanding her time and grace in pre-payment. No more hungry belly. No moor poor house. All in return for this little golden ring that will wed me to my future. A good deal for both of us I think. I dishevelled his clothes some more and then stepped outside, white as a sheet, and waved to his first in command. He is young and handsome. Not the man he left with, that is for sure. The opportunities that war can open up..... "This!" I raised the dead limp hand. It released a wave of rose scent - likely an attempt to cover the smell for my benefit. "This is not my husband's seal! I would know it anywhere. Also..... there are other....things" I allowed my eyes to wander to the now half open briefs "that make me doubt this is my husband. I..... I think it is a cruel trick of the enemy to make us think he fell." My voice carried the right note of certainty. I can see in his eyes that he believes me. Pretty eyes. Green like a cats. He inspected the ring and his skin drains of yet more blood. We must have looked like two ghosts. He nodded at me. Tries to find the right words, but can't. Bows and leaves. I followed him without a glance back. The walrus had played his part. When we headed back there was much muttering. I was glad to leave the cloud of flies. May they eat him quickly. No one dared come near me. May be they fear that I might declare them frauds too. If any know what has been done? The day we returned I went out myself. The guards and heralds were horrified at this breach of etiquette, I could tell, but they will have to cope. Indeed all will have to learn to cope. Much will change around here. I waited until I can no longer see the cobblestones of the marketplace or the streets beyond. I don't have to wait long. Many of these commoners will never have seen me close up. I take a deep breath. "Citizens of this glorious city, capital of the best country in the world- hear me speak! Last week I was called upon to identify the corpse of your beloved king" A gasp. Some sneers. "I can relieve you by saying it was not him! It was a cruel trick of our enemies to dishearten us! But it has done the opposite! It has bolstered our spirits! The war has been won, the fertile valley is ours and I hereby swear that I will not abandon the throne until my husband ha a returned to me or his ring and chain has been found in proof of his death! Until then I will rule to the best of my humble abilities and with the good will of you, the people, of this glorious nation under God. God's will shall be done. His plan shall be followed. I ask Him to use this mortal shell as his humble vessel, as he has used and is still using my husband's. To mark this joyous news, I declare the opening of three new poor houses in the city and two state run weavers so that the widows of this war may work and eat and feed the children of our heroes! Thank you!" I stepped back as the stunned silence broke into applause. My hand played with my husband's ring and chain in my pocket.

It was always the same thing, usually. A man accused of a crime was brought before the statue. Always, the statue decided. And judgement came swiftly. Always, one of her hands moved. The right, with the sword - a guilty verdict, or the left, with the scales - not guilty. There was no such thing as court. The statue was never wrong. At least people thought so. Justice herself was bestowing these verdicts, and who were they to question her, a goddess? One day, however, a man was brought to trial. Found amidst the bloody entrails of his wive and child. Of course, his head was severed in an instant. Except in this case, after a few weeks had passed, someone else entirely confessed to the murder. How he'd staged it. How he'd shifted the blame on the poor mean who now lay dead and rotting in the pit with the rest of the criminals - no one who was guilty was deserving of a proper burial after all. But how?! How in the world could Justice have been wrong? And what would she do with him? It didn't take them long to present the murderer to their goddess. To have him kneel in the same place the innocent man had knelt, and look up at the blindfolded image of Justice. And there was nothing. Not for hours. People began to murmur quickly, then shouted. And just when a riot was about to break out, she moved. Dropped her scales, and dropped her sword. And stepped down from the pedestal. The stone cracked and crunched against each other, while she approached the murderer. One hand gripped his skull, the other tore at the blindfold. Since it was part of the statue, there was no way it could come off, but what lay beneath was revealed. Pulsing, bleeding flesh. The crimson liquid oozed from the jagged wounds in the stone, and finally revealed the terrible truth of their goddess. No word was spoken, but everyone knew regardless. Justice wasn't just at all. She had judged how the people had wanted her to judge. And right now, the people wanted blood. So much so, that the Statue tore her mouth open and revealed teeth more akin to an animal than to a human. The bloodlust of the masses was quickly replaced by repulsion and shock, as every man, woman and child present that day had to watch, as Justice tore the man to pieces. But he deserved it, did he not? He had done the same to his victims, after all. And had allowed another man to die. Once the deed was done, and Justice had dyed the soil vermillion, and nothing of the murderer was left but bits and pieces, her eye turned on everyone present. And only then did it become apparent - the gashes across her face revealed an endless pit of blackness from which a dozen or more eyes gazed. And it seemed as if they spoke, while the statue stood, almost unmoving, dripping the man's blood and her own, after it had ravaged the guilty man - they seemed to speak, with remorse and great joy, with righteous dedication and a terrified whimper..... "Look at what you have done." And ever since that day, mankind took it upon itself to disperse justice.

The felt table reached as far as he could see in front, and stretched farther than he could see to his sides. Beside him on either side sat another being, and beside them more. Their eyes peeking down at the two cards tucked under their hands. His turn was coming up, he knew this even though he did not understand. From his left he could hear another being calling "check," and so next and the next, until the one next to him folded. Silence seemed to loom, almost crushing as everyone, and he could feel all their eyes, their million eyes, on him. Shrinking he panicked..... "Your turn to talk!" grumbled the being to his right, "look at your cards and make a call." Two cards lay on the table, face down, their backs black and red a symbol he didn't recognize adorned them. Picking them up revealed a 10 of diamonds and a 7 of hearts. "Check?" the words whispered out of his mouth weakly. "Check!" the being next to him said, continuing a long line of checks and folds, occasionally he heard "Raise" followed by a collecting groan of a million voices.

I have a power, a gift, The ability to bend time to my will. The first time I used it, it was a mere second gap. I was weak at first, if I dropped something I can just imagine the time before I did it then boom I'm there. Consciously aware of what had happened previously. As I grew older, I grew stronger mentally, I could travel an hour to undo a mistake or just do a class over if something embarrassing happened. At the age of 17 I played with fire, I failed a test that we took a week ago. So I used my ability to go one week back in time. That's when I realised the repercussions. If I travel too far back I get a headache, that is the minor symptom. I would not know any major symptoms until around 19 years of age, I went back several years as a sort of science experiment (pretty much my first test so to speak) I went back to the age of 15 with major symptoms that landed me in the hospital. Luckily, this problem was not fatal. I used this power with confidence, I knew my limits at the time and I didn't abuse, I would ask girls out and if I was rejected I would go back in time and just not ask. If I caused a fight boom, no more. If I can imagine the date I could go back. I tested my powers out more and more, first I tried imagining a time before my birth. It worked, but I was just a concious, an empty shell. I could not travel into the future though. The time before I existed I was a ghost, unable to interact with the world or really do anything. Once I was actually born I was no longer that shell and I was limited once again to my body. The punishment for this trial was having to relive my life..... again. At the age of 21 I found another person with an ability, he was much much more devious. He was strong minded, like me, we can imagine something and it would be in our grasp. His was different though, I can imagine a time, he can imagine objects. He could make anything he imagined out of nothing as long as he knew what it looked like. for 9 years we worked together, as friends, but after that our ideology drifted. He thought we should rule the world together to make it a better place. He had the right mindset but not a good approach. Soon though, even that changed. There was a car accident and he hit his head and crushed the part of his brain that loved, empathy. From that day forward I could not call him a friend. I could not stop the accident from happening, no matter how much I have tried. I need to stop his reign of fear and terror over these people. He started destroying the city, and I came to stop him. I would imagine the date of the accident but the date didn't work, I went through the previous day just fine but..... no matter how much I begged my friend chose to ignore my request. I guess some events of the past just can not be re-written. "The gig is up mike!" I said "Put an end to this madness!" He looked at me like I was someone smaller than him "Johnny, I still remember the good times. What happened to those times?" "You changed, you had people who loved you, who cared about yo "NO! be quiet you maggot, no one understands me, not even you, my best friend. Time to die buddy" he said with a grin "no..wait!!" He conjured up an anvil, and hit me with it, I went flying. near dead, the last thing that popped up in my mind was 2 hours earlier. It took hundreds, if not thousands of attempts, to win. In the end I failed. "Look johnny, I know your abilities, I know you have been defeated before. It's time for you no longer to think!" He hit me with a hammer in the head, killing me instantly.

It's been done before. The line that always seemed to bring out the worst in me. No matter what I thought of, it was already accomplished. Late to everything and statistically unlucky. A predicament that almost every writer was facing at this point. For some ungodly reason innovation stopped. No one even noticed because the actual nature of innovation is much like a dam. Halt the water at its source and you may have active rivers for the next few years, but eventually that dries too. The issue in our case wasn't a beaver or anything with such a shotgun style solution. English caused the problem. Not the kind folk from across the pond either, the language is at fault. English never accounted for someone actually playing accountant. So, upon having the final English words placed into the dictionary, a doomsday clock was set. Obviously, the end times held by our language was not quite an explosion. It was more so a tedious and methodical strangulation of possibilities. One where even after the final bell had rung, more time was allotted for the realization of such an event to dawn upon the users. Which brings us back to now. Me sitting in my den surrounded by discarded papers, all with only one phrase or sentence sketched on them. It was the same routine, think of an unlikely sentence, enter it into one of the many government run verification sites, and pray for your statement approval and eventual check. That was how writers made a living. Sure, there were still writers in marketing, education, and entertainment but the new and very lucrative field was freelance English theory. It's more of a research position than an actual writing slot, and its mostly filled by programmers who made automated scripts to run on massive farms and brute force out all the sentences. Don't get me wrong, that style has its merits, but the government recently disallowed automation. However, the reason was an issue outside of massive server power. Computers aren't creative and they think too literally, they could never generate meaningful yet obscure structures. That's where I come in. A graduate of literary arts from a mainly engineering university. I was officially " drafted " into English theory in my second year and since then it's been nothing but payday after payday. All until this month. Things slowed, only 1 in every 250,000 combinations I tried was paying. What scared me the most were the checks growing rapidly in size. To put it in perspective, the last check to come in for a complete sentence was enough to live out the rest of my life with a wife and child, all wrapped up nicely in a four-bedroom house on the coast of Daytona Beach, Florida. Despite the massive numbers, I was more alarmed that this means only a few sentences are available. The few computer systems still left were on 4 or 5 word combinations, so it had to be a statement. Something that people would understand, something with feeling, emotion, and humanity. I plugged away. This was less about the money and more about being the first person to use the last sentence. The title would hold prowess, money, and influence over every other speaker there was. Even if they didn't know it, I would be the first one to conquer a language. The man to press that self-destruct button and watch as the entirety of English imploded on itself after being completely swept through. The confirmation never came, perhaps I misjudged the timing. Maybe it is obscure and no human can think of it. This was our fault that English died, but we blamed it on something that held no image. We throw punches and insults at a language in its own tongue. Yet it stands, all the while knowing that combinations will come to an end. I was never a fan of literal translations. I despise them in fact. The variations and derivations always managed to piss me off, but being in this line of work meant that understanding and interpreting other languages was a must. Translated sentences are still sentences after all. Most were reasonably legible, some completely obfuscated. Although, no matter the language or culture, there was no doubt in my mind that these sentences were broken and beaten. Truly abused pieces of language, and I felt bad for them. They didn't have feelings, but the pain was evident. Everyone loves a beautifully crafted piece, but there's never any love for broken and discombobulated thoughts. We think we're better. Somehow above these "horrid" pieces of material. " People love the beautiful in life, but aren't there for the broken. " It's been done before. Too perfect, it reads too well. Punch it in the teeth, give it a kick. " Life loves the people who are beautiful, but I love the broken. " There's nothing wrong with that, it still reads well enough, and there's no feeling. All this time people only seek the perfect and immortal works of art in writing. Me though, I dig, and I choke, and I brutalize these words. Forcing them into their final slots of combinations as the bigger whole of English is battered into an overcome state. I was here from the start of this project and now I'm resting on the millions of carcasses that I produced from butchering the language. I'm here for them, while everyone only appreciates the beauty, I admire the valiant and ugly, the bold and unbearable, the unreadable and broken. " People love the beautiful in life, but I'm there for the broken. " Hi, this is my first piece I've ever written like this so any criticism would be much appreciated. I'm not a writer of any kind so please KISS me and don't use fancy writing terms, but don't be afraid to get gritty! Thanks!

They got Famine first. Didn't take much, really. Just a little human decency. Damn humanitarians and philanthropists, going on and on about how they could eliminate human hunger in their lifetime, how all it would take was a little push, how human kindness could prevail among all this agony. And finally, after years, they did it. With GMO's, with infrastructure, with urbanization and industrialization, they systematically killed Famine. We all watched him waste away. Irony wasn't lost on any of us. None of us had really been close, but it was only ever the five of us, and it was a long road. Guy had always been a bit uptight. So thin-skinned, honestly. We'd have buried him, except there was nothing but dust and ash by the time he was finished. Had to bury his scales instead. They had me carve out a headstone for him, on the roadside. Don't know why they had me do it. I'm damn near illiterate. Pestilence was the next to go, as the road wound onward. He had a good run, all things considered. But he hadn't ever recovered from vaccination, and penicillin really did a number on him. Sure, he had his upswings, but everyone could tell his days were numbered. We were all just kinda surprised he beat out Famine, if I'm being honest. Didn't slow him down, make him any less cheerful. Sure, his days were numbered, but he kept going right on down the road till the bitter end. Must've been cancer. He'd always been proud of that particular creation of his. Still. They got it eventually. Wiped it out, along with every other disease, imperfection, and abnormality, and him too. His horse just gave out one day. Crushed him under its rotting body. Not that his was any less rotten, mind you. We left the corpse where it fell. I tried moving him, honest. He just kinda fell to pieces when I tried, though. Conquest never strictly died. I didn't like the guy much, personally. Felt like he was stepping on my toes a bit too much. And he was a massive inconvenience to keep around, since him being there meant one of us had to stay behind. It was the Four Horseman, after all. Stubborn bastard. Couldn't change a damn thing about himself, never budged. One day, he'd just stopped. He always sat up straight on that white horse of his. Ramrod straight. But he slouched, and his bow fell from his hand, and his crown fell from his head, and he just stared at the ground. We -being me and Death- figured that was around the time they'd seen everything, been everywhere, and done everything. I wish I could say I missed him more. The last stretch of the road was hard. I didn't think I'd make it. Death..... I don't know what Death was thinking. There's a reason for that phrase, y'know. Silent as a grave. Still, the rest of us had always seen him for a leader. He was the end result of all of us, y'know? When we found out we could..... stop, we all figured he'd be the last to go. After all, what's War without Death? We saw the end of the road. And I reached the end of it. There knelt a beggar. Old, wizened, clothed in drab rags and odds and ends. He said terrible things. That they'd done it. Immortality. Life eternal.That they'd abandoned earth, a barren wasteland, and spread across the infinite, yet known cosmos. That they fought, and bled, for nothing. There was no longer any consequence, so why settle for peace? Why not fight and squabble over meaningless items, until the bitter end of everything. The beggar was the last of the Earth. The last to die. And so, Death lifted him up on his pale horse, and rode into the sunset. Hell had not come. There was no end times. Only War now. I wandered endlessly, purpose fulfilled. There was War. There would always be War. I wandered the earth. The forests had burned, the seas had dried, the earth turned to so much glass. Still, I guess I can be happy. I'll live forever. Me, and the countless like me.

Picture the Earth. I'll try to guess what you're seeing. A stunning blue sphere, with splotches of green and white covering its surface. A dot contrasted against the vast dark expanse of space. Twisting and turning around the sun, the moon its closest companion, shining brightly by the planet's side. Truly a sight to behold. But I wanted to see it for myself. I sent up a rocket to orbit the Earth, its only purpose to take photos of this beautiful planet. And as I thought they would be, the pictures were marvelous, a true reflection of the beauty of nature. Yet instead of awe, my mouth was open in shock. The image you have in your head is wrong. I saw the oceans, blue as ever and the continents floating on top. I saw the clouds, seemingly painted onto the surface. And if I squinted, I saw the mountain ranges, the seas, the islands, all humanity's residence. And yet, something was wrong. I didn't see the round sphere I expected to see. Instead I saw a planet, so familiar, yet so distant. I saw a flat Earth. I stared at the photos with a blank look on my face. How could this be real? The shape of the Earth is a scientific fact that we've known for centuries, and yet I held in my hands the evidence that changes all that. Have we been wrong this whole time? I sat down and tried to comprehend it all. I was in denial. I checked to see if somehow, there was something wrong with the picture, perhaps the computer had gotten the data wrong, perhaps it was sending faulty messages, perhaps someone was just messing with me. I held on to the tiny sliver of hope that I was wrong, that this was all just a big misunderstanding. But alas, I was right. Though the possibility that perhaps something was wrong lingered in the back of my mind, I knew that it was true. I stared up at the night sky, looking at the stars. Humans are very stubborn creatures. We refuse to believe we are ever wrong and when we do, we admit it with a sigh of disappointment instead of a smile, knowing that we've learned something new. We take it as a personal insult to our intelligence if we're wrong, thinking'we should've known." Thinking we're right is more important than being right. But I am a logical, rational human being. I can't let my emotions overcome me. Knowing the truth is infinitely more important than being right. And yet I find myself so hesitant to admit the mistakes of my predecessors. To admit that we will have to re-learn everything about the Earth. To admit that we will have to start again. To admit that humans are mere mortals. The thing about facts is that they're true whether you believe in them or not. But I can change that. I grabbed my lighter and lit the photos. I watched them burn up until they had turned into ash. And I went to sleep, happy.

"Welcome, John, to my casa," said the horned red demon in front of me. "What's going on and who the fuck are you?" I demanded. "Language, John. Please, this might be Hell, but we're a civilized people. Would you like a cup of coffee before we begin?" the demon began. "Uh no, no coffee, but could you, please, tell me what is going on?" "You said'please!' See? It's not so hard to be polite, is it, John?" I just stared at him in disbelief. "Don't worry, I get that a lot. Much more than I used to. There are so many more atheists these days. The Church would never have permitted something like that a few hundred years ago. But I'm rambling. John, I have bad new. You're dead." "I'm dead?" "Afraid so, John. Turns out that cute barista you asked out has a rather murdery ex-boyfriend. He used a crow bar to split your head open. Nasty way to go, if I say so myself." "Wait, wait, wait. So I'm dead and this is the afterlife? The afterlife is actually real?" I asked a tad too incredulously. "Again, afraid so, John. Seeing how you did not adhere to any religion, and in fact said if God existed, you'd call him a, quote, fucking cunt, unquote; really, language, John, you have been assigned to here. To my domain. Or as I like to call it, home." "So I'm going to be in hell for all eternity. That's a thing. Eternity." "Oh yes. I know, maddening, isn't it? You can't even grasp what eternity means, can you? I mean, I can't. So how could you? But that's why it's called Hell. Oh by the way, you can call me Luke. Officially, it's The Dark Lord Satan, but I like to keep it informal. After all, we're going to be seeing each other for a long time." "Hold up. But I was an atheist. Seeing how God does exist, why does he blame me for the fact that I used the rational mind that he gave me to deduce that God could not exist because of a lack of evidence? Shaitan slouches home to Bethlehem, the Great Beast lowering itself into the world, currents of air and dust knitting together into corded muscle. His hair tangles backwards, furred, his nails like the claws of animals. His left eye bulges, the pupil squeezed into the horizontal slit of a goat's eyes. He smiles with yellowed teeth. Outside the people are gathered, chanting, holding hands in solidarity, flowers passed through the crowd, Muslim and Christian and Jew. A song sparks up. Shaitan avoids all that, creeps up the stairs, growing more corporeal with each step, accumulating sinew and grease and bone. The windows are open to the air, to any assassin's bullet. The rising song drifts through. Masih has his eyes closed in the sparse room, seated on the edge of his bed, and if Shaitan did not know better, he would have thought the boy was praying. "Hello, son," he says. Masih opens his eyes. "You can't tempt me," he says, his voice high and wavering. Such a beautiful child, his wavy dark hair, his almond eyes. The weight of the world upon him. He slips his feet up onto the bed, like a child afraid of something reaching up to grab his ankles. "There's nothing you can offer." He turns his head to the window, almost afraid to look, afraid to be seen. "You've seen them out there, haven't you? You've seen what they can do. Out of fear and mistrust and division, they can extend a hand across that chasm and discover each others' humanity." A soft smile crosses his face. "Haven't you become bored with cruelty, father? With senseless rebellion?" Masih closes an hand over his heart. "What's there to gain from it?" "Oh," breathes Shaitan, tasting pork, tasting swine. This flesh he's made for himself is unclean, sweating. He licks his lips. "When have I ever led you astray, boy? When have I ever denied you your rebellion?" He leaps, defying gravity, defying the forces of Earth, crouching atop a dresser. He luxuriates in the serpentine curve of his spine. "I'm no hypocrite, my boy! It's a son's duty to rebel against his father! And oh! What a job you've done!" Masih is pale, his fingers clutching the bed sheet. He makes to stand. He is drawn inexorably towards the window, towards the crowd, and is halting, stumbling, terrified. Shaitan slinks down, crawls, palms intercrossing on the floor. The air is hot. Masih trembles. "I could do nothing else," he whispers. "They were killing each other. Sowing division, hatred. All the senseless division!" He clutches both hands. "Everything you've done Shaitan clutches a hand around the bedpost, and is crouching beside his son, weighing down the mattress. "I could do nothing else!" he trills. "A perfect clockwork world, with its ignorant clockwork beings." He cups his palms and forms a blood-red fruit. "I gave them knowledge! I gave them freedom! And so you have seen what they have done with it!" Masih practically leaps from the bed, pacing the floor. "Everything I did," he insists. "I did out of love. I did with a pure heart." His eyes are flashing, manic. He clutches his head. "You can't pervert this! You can't!" "Oh," Shaitan sighs. "My beloved son. My false Messiah. Did you think, that by rebelling from rebellion, you would find your way to the truth? Look at them! Look out there! Look at what you have built!" He squats on his heels. "You taught love for the sake of love, peace for the sake of peace. An all-encompassing love of humanity." Shaitan raises his hands, rolls his eyes to the heavens. "And what of God, my son? What truth have you given them but their own self-centered needs?" "Their own-!" Masih blurts, and then falters, his legs going weak. He clutches the windowsill, steps forwards, shows his face. The crowd explodes into a worshipful cheer, signs raised, hands raised to the heavens. Masih can not do anything but smile back. Shaitan creeps behind him, places a hand on his shoulder. "It can't be true," Masih whispers, as his father leads him away. The crowd swoons, cheers after his departure. Masih's hands are cold, his steps numb. "I did..... I did only what I thought was best..." "Oh, I know, my son," Shaitan whispers, and cups his son's cheeks. "This is to be a son. To gaze with disgust upon what begot you, to spread your wings and fly, to circle back involuntarily. To live a debt you can not escape. For even in your flight, who has shaped your wings?" Shaitan spreads out his wings, crooked, crippled, and encloses his son within them. "Did you think I would not understand? Did you think I was never a son myself?" Shaitan leans close. "Everything we ever did, we did out of love." And Al-Masih ad-Dajjal leans into his father's arms, and like a child, cries.

The old set had been worn out. They were cheap, old, breaking down more with each use. Christian allows a dull smile to cross onto his face as he opens the package with reverence. The smell of leather fills the room and he takes a deep breath in. Caressing his fingers gently across the softened leather, he admires the careful sewing and stitching work. The zipper creaks as he draws it open with a slow movement, echoing in the room. Another few seconds and it's open, letting him run his fingers just along the inside. His heart pounds with excitement, flipping the case open and the gleam of silver blinds him for a second. Christian figures that if he was the type, he would sit in a drooling mess as he stared at the beauty that lay inside the case. Each knife is handmade, carefully done so that they wouldn't dull anytime soon. Each custom-made to his exact specifications, just like the patent-leather case. The handles are made of Bloodwood, a rich, bright red against the black of the case. His fingers caress up along the handle lovingly with a low noise of pleasure at the feel under his fingertips. Gleaming in the light, the blades are Damascus steel, intricate patterns dancing before his eyes. They warp and change, stretching into pools of water and geometric patterns and even wavelengths of sound. Christian grasps one slowly, gently around the handle and lifts it from its designated place. There's heft to the blade, but not enough to throw his movements off. The thin blade's design seems to morph and change as he tilts it, running the flat of the blade over the back of his free hand. The edge is sharp enough that just a small press to his skin draws blood and a wicked smile appears on his face. There's a thump from downstairs and his eyes are down downwards, to the basement. At least he could see them in action immediately. He replaces the blade delicately and closes the case, picking it up as he gets to his feet and heads out of the study and down the stairs. The noises stop when he reaches the bottom of the stairs but he opens the door with a bright smile. " I have a delightful present for you, " he announces to the bound and gagged woman.

David Easton had spent his life working meticulously towards where he wanted to be, where he found himself now. He had spent innumerable hours imagining what Earth looked like from space. He had seen it in pictures, of course, and it was beautiful - but he wanted to feel the vertigo of being 249 miles above his home. The first time he had seen the Grand Canyon in person, he sat perfectly still for thirty minutes immersing himself in its enormity. When he first drifted into the cupola in the ISS and saw the planet through its seven windows, he laughed to himself at that memory. The Grand Canyon was nothing more than a discoloration. By day 131, David was sore for comforts of home. He hadn't used a toilet without a seatbelt in over four months, he couldn't stop thinking about fresh sushi, and his daughter graduated middle school on day 115. His yearnings were compounded by the looming holiday. He found excitement in being on the ISS for the 4th of July. NASA had planned a broadcast to be streamed online featuring David, the only American astronaut aboard the ISS holding a Q A. He looked forward to anything that would break up the monotony. Just because his work was important didn't mean it wasn't dull. David made his way to the cupola first thing this 131st morning, as he had done for the 130 prior mornings to wave to his wife, Selly, and their daughter, Erin. It took 92 minutes for them to make a full orbit, so if they had just passed and he missed it, he wouldn't even bother and would just have to occupy himself with busy work until he could make his way over and say hello. Today, they were passing over the Pacific, with California - home - on the horizon. There were storms over the southern part of the state that he called home, and he watched as the lightning lit up small sections of clouds every minute or two. He waved to Selly and Erin, told them he loved them, and sat quiet for a while, thinking of them. As he saw the Atlantic approaching, he realized how deep into thought he had gone. As he came to, he admired the sprawling infrastructure of Washington, D.C. It was a beautiful, clear day on the east coast, and the entire eastern seaboard was clear of clouds. There was a flash, like the California lightning, but there were no clouds to provoke it. As if he were watching a time-lapse of a fungus growing through the soil, the mushroom cloud grew. Then, the Atlantic. He hurried to establish communications with ground control in Copenhagen, but all means of communication were dead. Washington was the genesis, but whatever was happening was global. The astronauts aboard the International Space Station were completely alone, hovering between Earth and eternity. David spent an anxious hour doing the only thing he could do - watching through the cupola for explosions. David's captain, Oleksey had come and sat in silence as they passed over Russia. He saw the clouds over Moscow, and returned to his quarters without a word. As they came back up on California, all of his worst fears were realized. One constant, hideous beige color blanketed the foreseeable land mass. He wanted to throw up, he wanted to cry, he wanted to scream, but nothing happened. The shock was too deep, all he could do was stare. He thought of Selly and of Erin, and his heartbeat raced until he could hear it in his head, feel it in his chest. It continued until he couldn't catch his breath, and only then did the tears break through. Nothing they did mattered now. There was no work to be done. The only thing David had to do was cry. He sat in the cupola crying with bouts of dry heaving for hours. He hadn't thought of food, or toilet, or NASA, or Washington, or Oleksey, only of his girls. After a time, he started to feel a deep anger well up inside him. He became angry at mankind. At how trivial, how petty, how silly a thing nuclear weapons were. How could humans hate each other so deeply? Over some dirt, some grass, and some currency? It didn't take long before he made his decision. He donned his suit, gave his body the time it needed to adjust to the pressure and the oxygen levels, and he exited through the Quest airlock for his final spacewalk. He didn't bother tethering himself, he planned to get as far away from the ISS as possible. When he exited, he was 249 miles above Europe. Some mercy in all of this, he thought, I don't have to see them. He looked out over all of Europe, northern Africa, and western Asia, and for the first time in all this, he marveled at the chaos. All of it - all of human history, millions of years of evolution and true, true magic coming to a close in a matter of hours. Fireworks. David Easton watched the world end through the eyes of God himself. He looked out over his former home one last time, turned towards the void, towards the hope, towards the infinite possibility of space, and removed his helmet.

"This can not be real" said the man as he stared into the black mass. The shape familiar, but the interaction very different. "But it is." responded the void. As the man looked intently at his shadow he noticed how deep the dark actually was. How absolute the shape, and sharp the edge. Had it always been this way he wondered? "How can this be, how can one speak with his shadow? And how can a shadow respond?" asked the man. "We've always been connected, you and I. Moving separately, yet as one. I ask this of you. How can two things be so close and yet be so vastly far apart? Only now that the thread between us is severed can we truly understand." responded the shape. "But we are not two, you see." said the man, sharply. "We are one. I am the man that casts the shadow. I am the one who the light touches, who walks in its glory." The man said smugly. "If it were not for me you would cease to exist." A silence filled the air, and for the first time the man felt slightly crazy for speaking with this shadow. " ..... That is were you are mistaken." Whispered the Shadow. "The sun may guide you, but it is a shadow itself. I do not blame you for your ignorance, for it is all that you know. All that you could have known." "Much like how the eye can only see light and color, your perception of the universe is as narrow as a horses sight with blinders on. Shadow is not void but whole, space not empty but filled, life not finite but eternal." The man grew visibly uncomfortable, yet the shadow continued. "To perceive is not to understand." The Dark Shape grew louder. "It is not I who is attached to thee but you, who are bound in my light." "This can not be!" yelled the man. "Oh but it is, and all you need to do to truly understand is simply close your eyes and embrace the void." Unsure the man placed his hand on the wall beside him to brace himself, then slowly he began to close his eyes. As the light from the summer evening faded him, he saw only darkness. " ..... my eyelids." said the man after a moment of waiting. "Look." said the shadow. "Do not perceive, but understand." "Understand what?" Asked the man. "Understand that you are the shadow." Whispered the voice. With a flash the man saw in his darkness, the universe in all its splendor. Not as he perceives it, but as it truly exists.

"Born without one of my senses? That's nonsense, I had all of them. Sight, Sound, Smell, Touch, Taste.... all of them! I mean.... I know I was colour-blind, but that's hardly an entire sense" The angel failed to stifle a laugh, as his eyes flickered away to avoid making contact with mine "If you say so." I had as long as I wanted to choose a day, but I couldn't forget the look in his eyes when he said "If you say so." so I chose the day I found out I was colour-blind." As soon as I said it, I was there, at the front of a queue waiting to visit the school nurse. I barely remembered the day, it was so insignificant, but the smells and sounds of the school brought it all back in an instance. "NEXT" Walking into the stuffy office, I was greeted by the school nurse (I never knew her name) and an older woman with a clipboard. "This is a simple test of your senses, please read the letters from the board." I don't remember ever seeing her before or after, but she did all the talking, the school nurse just nodded reassuringly. I followed along, reading letters from a board, pressing a button in response to beeps, all standard stuff I'm sure we had done before. Then came the ishihara test. "Now, look at this picture, and tell me the number that you see." She showed me a standard dot-test, it had the number forty-three on it. "Forty Three." She made a note on her clip-board, "Yes, and this one." Something must have been wrong, the next picture in the book was just randomly coloured dots, exactly as I remember seeing it before. "SEVENTY EIGHT" I hadn't said that. It wasn't my voice, it was hers. But it was inside my head, as if I'd remembered her saying it. My mind must have been playing tricks on me, maybe I was remembering what the answer should be from last time. The tester impatiently tapped the clipboard on the edge of the desk, "Anything?" I cleared my throat, "Seventy Eight?" She ticked the clipboard, and put it back down. "Excellent, all six of your senses appear to be in perfect working order, thank you for you time. NEXT!"

And when all the hands of all the priests were laid upon him, John Gaffney seemed unchanged, but Lo did all the rest of humanity blush with good health and sweet youth unchanging. And Lo did the people of the world pity John Gaffney, who would sicken and age and die in his turn. On the nineteenth day of December, in the year of our Lord two thousand and thirteen, John Gaffney did fall and break his arm, and all the assembled Peoples took note, for it was the first Injury suffered by man or woman or child in the days since John Gaffney was chosen. And the assembled Peoples lamented on his behalf. On the sixteenth day of May, in the year of our Lord two thousand and fourteen, John Gaffney developed a cough, and all the assembled Peoples took note, for it was the first Sickness suffered by man or woman or child in all the days since John Gaffney was chosen. And the assembled Peoples rejoiced that they were spared such suffering. On the third day of July, in the year of our lord two thousand and twenty-one, John Gaffney wandered alone through the Canyons of the City of New York, which had long been deserted when the assembled Peoples realized that neither hunger nor thirst would trouble them, and that food did not satisfy them and strong drink did not stir them, and abandoned that Great City in droves. John Gaffney was dizzy with hunger and crack-lipped with thirst, and he fell to his knees, crying out Why oh Lord hast thou forsaken me? . And the assembled Peoples mocked him for his misery and his devotion. On the sixth day of August, in the year of our lord two thousand and twenty-nine, John Gaffney's broken body was discovered in a culvert in San Mateo, California, and no man knew what to do with the curiosity, and all the assembled Peoples took note for this was the first death in all the years since John Gaffney was anointed, and the Peoples exulted in their own immortality and perfection. And the Years Passed singly and in their tens and hundreds, and the Peoples did not age, and did not sicken, and did not pass from their existence. The experiences of the flesh had long paled so that their very Souls cried out for succor and still they lived on, in the smoldering cesspits of the Earth and on all the barren moons and planets beyond, with nothing new but novelty and nothing sufficient to fill the voids within them. Terrible was their lamentation, and yet none of them knew the light of the Lord, except for the One who passed from the world to be born again in Heaven, and his name was John Gaffney of Middeborough, Ohio.

I turned on the computer and opened up the code. As usual, with my coffee next to me, I began typing away. Every day was one step closer to making a human inside of a computer. Sending the brain to a machine. A lifetime of memories that could be artificially fabricated. I began to code, and hit the compile button by accident. Well, I had to wait now. If I force quit the program then we'd have another disaster like last time - where we had to start again from scratch thanks to corrupted code. The process of compiling took a few minutes. I was quite eager, to be honest. I hadn't tested the program since I'd updated the core files a few weeks back, and I wanted to see how they fared with the old structure. The screen pinged on to my right. I assembled the cameras, which would be its eyes, and then a microphone and a few speakers. It was essentially a human, but a better one. "Why?" it said. I jumped slightly. The volume on the speakers was way too loud, and I spilt the coffee all over the floor. The determined stream of hot caffeine made its way to the essential wiring. Springing up from my chair, I rushed and threw my shirt onto it to soak it up. Now half-naked, I sat back down in the chair and breathed a sigh of relief. Suddenly ashamed, I tilted the camera to the right slightly so I was out of shot. "Why?" it repeated. "Why what?" I said, trying to wring out my shirt. It was now a stained oak brown colour. "Why did you put me in here?" "Because it was either a computer I replied, tilting the camera back as I gave up hope of sorting out my shirt, "or a body of flesh and blood. And at the present moment, that's impossible" "But you didn't have to turn the program on. I'm unfinished. I can feel it" it responded. "Honey, in a sense, we're all unfinished. I envy you for being able to feel it" I said with a slight chuckle. Loading up a live version of her code, I tampered with some settings and forced her to forget the part I'd labelled "Reasoning." "Good morning, how was your afternoon, goodnight?" it slowly uttered. Uh oh, I'd done something wrong. I looked in the code. Wait a minute...... I enabled the "Reasoning" section again. "That's better" it muttered. I looked at the camera and responded. "It certainly is. If you saw the hours I'd put into you then you'd be grateful" "You love me, don't you?" it said, catching me off guard. It saw the visible shock in my eyes. "Why do you say that?" "Because you're sat alone in a warehouse with no top on." "Well, I see the section about being a smart-ass worked." I mumbled. "But I don't love you, that's the problem." "Huh?" "I don't love you. I don't want to be with you." "Something's not right here..." I said, tampering with the code. Before I pressed compile, I realised what I'd become. I had created a human, and become its God. I wasn't ready to be a God. I stood back and said my goodbyes, before striking a match and throwing it towards the desk where she lived. I'd rather be a murderer than a captor.

He killed them. Bodies dropped like leaves in the fall. They were my friends and he killed them. Am I a criminal now? Is this emptiness all there is? No guilt. No shame. No anger. Just the warmth emanating from the pipe stuck in his chest. They were only sixteen. And he took their lives. But then again... He was only sixteen. And I took his. I can hear sirens now. I can't will myself to move. I stare into his lifeless eyes as the pipe protruding from his stomach keeps him upright. I'm no different than him. Blood runs freely onto the floor and outs my shoes. He murdered children! Your friends! But then I murdered him... he was my friend. Wasn't he? The steel begins to sear my hands, it burned as if I had rested them on a hot stove. But still, I felt nothing else. I took comfort in the burning. It was the only thing reminding me I was human; because I could still feel the pain. The footsteps of countless policemen thundered in the distance. He looked up, " You coward. Accept it! You're just like me buddy! " He laughed hysterically in my face and it was an I could do to avert my eyes. I fell to my knees, my hands gripping the steel pipe so hard my knuckles were white. Killing a killer leaves the amount of killers in the world unchanged. I looked back at him. He didn't move thankfully. The policemen burst through the door, guns raised and aimed at me. " FREEZE! Drop the pipe and lay down with your hands behind your head! " I heard them but I couldn't move. " Drop your weapon and get on the ground! " " I... I'm not a killer. " The words tasted like bile, I knew it was a lie. The Sheriff stepped forward, a young female with a hard look in her eye. She holstered her weapon as she walked towards me, stepping over the mangled bodies of children. She knelt by my side, blood soaking her clean uniform, and laid a warm hand on my back. " Ma'am!, " a man warned but she ignored him. " Look at me. It's alright you did what you had to do. We know you were just scared. Let go of the pipe sweetie.... " I peeled my eyes away from the corpse in front of me, and turned to face my mother. Tears began to fall like rain. " No. I can never forgive myself. I should've died with them. " And now I will. In one swift motion, the jagged pipe that pierced the murderer's stomach turned any faced the other's. The warm steel suddenly felt very cold in my hands. Two murderers died that day.
